en: Preface to the *Chanyuan Qinggui* (Pure Rules for the Tiantai Teaching Garden). The *Tiantai Jiaoyuan Qingui* was formerly engraved and placed in the Baiyun Hall on Mount Shang Tianzhu;
it was subsequently destroyed and no longer exists. Now, the Dharma Master Yuanjue Yungwai, fearing that it might long remain neglected and fall into ruin, has retrieved the original [text].

I have re-ordered the Tibetan edition, corrected its errors, and supplemented its omissions, while cross-referencing the differences between Chan and Vinaya for the sake of future students who shall re-carve it.

Formerly, I have heard it said: "The Confucianist establishes benevolence (*ren*) and righteousness (*yi*) through ritual (*li*); one cannot be called a Confucianist if ritual is separated from benevolence and righteousness.

The Buddhist maintains meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) through discipline (*vinaya*); one cannot be called a Buddhist if discipline is separated from meditative concentration and wisdom."

It cannot be said that because one is a Buddha, one need not observe the precepts; for although a Buddha encompasses the three realms through all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*), he must first employ the precepts.
Likewise, a Bodhisattva transforms the four modes of birth (*catur-yoni*) by means of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), yet cannot abandon the Vinaya.

Since the arrival of the Buddha-dharma in the Middle Kingdom, monks have mostly resided in monasteries dedicated to the Vinaya; it was only with Baizhang that separate Zen residences were established. This is the origin of these pure regulations.
The reasons for its creation are as follows: moreover, the times of antiquity and the present differ, and human sentiments likewise vary;

thus, when emperors and kings establish rites, they cannot help but incur some diminution or augmentation. How could it be otherwise for the Dharma established by the Buddha? The *vinaya* rules are like the canonical rites of the sages;
though they may not be convenient or familiar to later generations, they have never ceased to be transmitted to the present day. The pure regulations (*qinggui*) are like those of the ancients...
Although the family rituals (*jiālǐ*) of the Confucians were all established by their respective eras, they have never failed to be rooted in antiquity.
Baizhang innovated the Pure Rules (*qīngguī*) to assist in the implementation of the Vinaya;

the Great Master of Tiantai was likewise proficient in the *vinaya*, and his successors also took the daily practices of the monastic groves (*cónglín*) as a basis for mediation, thereby upholding and sustaining the teaching. Now, in the Garden of the Teachings...
The *Chingui* (Pure Rules) is precisely this. As the years have passed, what is observed by various quarters has diverged from the legacy of Baizhang;

thus, there are aspects of our mountain tradition that cannot fully accord with them. However, if one understands these changes and applies them according to the times, the ultimate goal remains the same.
Master Yunwai was currently devoting himself to the path of practice, yet he was able to turn his attention toward the majestic discipline.
The meticulous details of these ritual protocols are such that the mutual cultivation of the internal and external can be said to have been fully realized;

are they not indeed a model for those who come after? Therefore, without reckoning my own mediocrity, I have accepted this command to compose this preface and append it to the beginning of the work. Thus it is said.
Preface by Huang Min of Jinhua on the third day of the intercalary third month in the summer of the seventh year of the Zhizheng era:

Regarding the practices discussed within the mountain school’s teaching tradition, in the sutras there are the methods for propagating the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* known as the "Three Orbits" (*san gui*) and the precepts of the "Four Practices of Peace and Bliss" (*si anle xing*).
In the biographical records, there are the *Guoqing Bailu*, the *Jiaoxing Lu*, and the *Tianzhu*.

The community codified these writings until they were brilliantly comprehensive and nothing was left unrecorded. As for those who were gradually steeped in the sacred teachings and engaged in formal study for many years, their three modes of action and four postures naturally accorded with the Way;

from the highest to the lowest, all were thoroughly imbued with it, and the multitude lived in harmony. Yet, as the path of instruction grew obscure and declined, scholars for the most part settled into negligence and simplicity, flowing along with vulgar habits;
even in the midst of their daily activities such as eating and drinking, or in their gestures of courtesy and yielding, [the spirit of the Way had faded].
The regulations for prostrations and rising may sometimes deviate from the propriety of ritual correctness; it is for this reason that Master Yunwai’s *Qinggui* (Book of Pure Rules) was established.
Those with discernment can thereby fulfill their sincerity, while those who are ignorant can thereby prevent their errors.
Should we not strive to rectify the prevailing abuses of recent times and establish a grand standard for a thousand years?
In the spring of the seventh year of the Zhizheng era, the bhikṣu Dà'ān, residing at Tiānzhū Língshān Jiàosì, wrote this preface:
"How sublime is the transformative skillful means of the Great Hero (Mahāvīra)! In transforming himself and others, he encompasses all without omission.
Had the various patriarchs who dwelt on Vulture Peak, begged for food within the city, and practiced dhyāna beneath the trees been able to practice the Way as they did themselves..."

The Buddhas abide within the forest of the monastic groves; the three thousand majestic deportments and eight hundred subtle practices—the methods for transforming others—must likewise not be neglected.
Yet, at this late stage of the Semblance Dharma, as the assemblies grow ever more numerous, the Way becomes increasingly obscure;

as the Dharma flourishes ever further, the Māras blaze ever more fiercely. Alas, there must surely be a reason for this! Last year, Master Xiaoyin of Longxiang collated and corrected the *Baizhang Qinggui*.
Master Qing established nine chapters as a comprehensive framework, intended to remedy the corruptions within the Chan monasteries.
Now, Master Yuanjue Yunwai has further revised the *Jiaoyuan Qinggui*, synthesizing ancient and modern practices into ten categories, each marked by a brief preface.
Compared to the version formerly transmitted at Baiyun Monastery, this work is more detailed. Alas, Chan!
The regulations of the forest are already as such, and the regulations of the Garden of Teaching are likewise so. Are these not the compass and the square?
It depends upon those who occupy the great couch and the great mat to issue commands and personally practice; if they do so, others will follow and be transformed.
Then what need is there to worry that demons will not be weakened or that the Way will not flourish? This is what is called "retribution."

The repayment of the Buddha’s grace and the state’s grace does not lie outside of this. Thus we know that those who follow the works of Māra betray the Emperor’s heart, while those who practice these numerical regulations shall continue the seeds of the wisdom-life. Furthermore—

In our dynasty, instruction is preceded by the teaching of the Sūtras and followed by Chan and Vinaya; it is impossible not to cultivate their texts in order to propagate the foundation of the Teaching.
Thus, for this collection, Master Yunwai requested that Huang Gong Jinqing, a Hanlin Academician, compose a preface.
As for what the preface did not cover, I have further commissioned this rustic to gather and supplement it. Since this is a matter of wholesome karma, how could I dare decline? Therefore—
May readers of this historical record not reproach it for its rusticity and impurity.
On the seventh day of the seventh month in the seventh year of the Zhizheng era, Zhang Yu of Densan Hermitage on Mount Inseok recorded and revised this catalog of the *Jiaoyuan Qinggui*.

Requesting a New Abbot.

A special envoy was dispatched; upon his arrival at the mountain, the envoy specifically prepared tea for the newly appointed abbot. The mountain gate provided formal hospitality for both the abbot and the envoy.
When the newly appointed abbot took leave of the assembly and ascended the hall for the tea ceremony, the West Hall officers and the head administrators received their appointments.
The special envoy specifically prepares tea and refreshments for the invitee and presents the Dharma robe for succession;
the monastery provides hospitality for both the invitee and the special envoy.
The invited guests take their leave;
the newly appointed abbot enters the monastery;
the new incumbent is invited to the mountain gate for a vegetarian feast.
Opening the Hall for the Longevity Ceremony; the Mountain Gate specially provides tea and soup for the newly appointed abbot;
that evening, a general discourse is given;
incense is offered at the donors’ hall, the ancestral shrine, and the pagodas; and sutras are recited.
The abbot shall provide hospitality for the special envoy and extend invitations to the two orders of officials;
he shall offer thanks for their visit, attend to their arrivals and departures, hand over the communal utensils,
and oversee the two classes of senior monks as they prepare the tea for the new abbot.
The Abbot regularly ascends the hall on the first and fifteenth days of the month;
on these occasions, tea is served in both the Sangha Hall and the dormitory hall.
The tea service for the assembly of the two orders and the elders;
the tea service for the western order;
and the special preparation of tea specifically for the great monastic leaders.
Various monasteries visit the Abbot’s quarters for tea;
the Abbot receives donors entering the mountains;
various monasteries pay mutual visits (to venerable seniors, elders, dharma relatives, dharma heirs, equals, and neighbors).

The Master of Ceremonies (Dujiang) of renowned virtue and the two ranks of officers shall direct the advancement and withdrawal of the attendants (shizhe) and the head officials (tou-shou). The various quarters shall hand over their utensils and furnishings.
The Abbot shall provide hospitality for the new and old two ranks of officers. Then, the two ranks of officers shall be requested to return to their respective positions.

Compiled and narrated by the Bhikṣu Ziqing, Abbot of the Great Yuanjue Teaching Monastery in India.
Section One: Prayers of Adoration.
"Under heaven, there are no lands that are not the King’s soil; along the borders of all lands, there are no subjects who are not the King’s ministers. From the Three Dukes and the Nine Ministers...
From you, the high officials, down to the common people, all have their regular duties; since punishment follows when these duties are not fulfilled, one cannot help but exhaustively perform them.
How much more so for us, whom the state does not hold accountable in this manner but instead treats with exceptional courtesy—surely because it honors our Way and exalts our character.
This is what you have been taught; as those who belong to my school, you should consider the way to repay this kindness.
In propagating the profound principles of our tradition and providing secret support to the royal transformation, you must fulfill your duties and never be negligent.
On the occasion of the Imperial Birthday,
the Auspicious Festival of Ten Thousand Years, this one-month *Vajra-Amitāyus* ritual arena has been inaugurated; the report is hereby submitted.

The imperial grace is added with solemnity; monks are not permitted to take leave. The *vinaya-dhara* (Vina) shall first instruct the hall attendants (*tangsi*) and the ritual assistants (*xingzhe*) to prepare blank slips and memorial paper for the Office of Records (*kusong*).
He shall further instruct them to proceed to the Secretary’s Quarters (*shuji-liao*) to perform the rites and submit a request, saying:

"For the inauguration of the Imperial Birthday, we request that you compose the text for the memorial. If the Secretary is absent, either a senior elder of the Western Hall or the *vinaya-dhara* himself shall compose it; otherwise, use the standard memorial text provided below. Once completed, write the memorial.
The attendant carrying the tray and cloth approaches the abbot’s quarters to pay respects and request the abbot to sign the draft of the proclamation.

Once the signing is complete, the attendant reports back to the abbot that the ceremony will be inaugurated early the following morning. The *vinaya-dhara* (ritual master) then prepares the notice to be posted on the right side of the mountain gate (both the notice and the draft are written on yellow paper, while names are written separately on red paper).
A register is prepared and a monk is dispatched to ascend the hall; within this register, the names of all former residents are recorded using double characters.
The two classes of monks following [the abbot] shall, according to their order of ordination, calculate the number of the assembly and prepare a roster of assignments.

They shall arrange the daily divisions in a cyclical rotation until the end of the period. On the designated day, each shall adjust their dignified demeanor and wait for the sounding of the great bell to ascend to the hall.

When the great bell sounds at evening, they shall descend from the hall. If officials enter the mountain to offer incense, the bell shall be struck to assemble the assembly for the chanting of sutras and the offering of prayers.
Regarding the offering of praise for the Abbot’s tenure: if the Abbot does not ascend the seat, one performs the ritual of offering praise directly in the Great Hall;

if he does ascend the seat, the attendant shall, on the day prior, instruct the hall-attendant (tangsi xingzhe) to hang the "Ascending the Seat" plaque (shangtang pai) before the meal in the Sangha Hall, and notify the two classes of officials, saying:

"The Venerable Abbot of the Abbot’s Quarter will ascend the seat tomorrow morning. On the following day, after the silence is broken at dawn, the wooden clappers (ban) are struck in all locations three times.
The junior assembly sits in the hall awaiting the entry of the head officials. After the Sangha Hall bell is struck three times and the great bell is sounded, the Dharma drum is beaten.
The Abbot exits his quarters and takes his seat; the attendant and the acolyte follow out, perform a formal greeting (*wenshen*), and stand in a line to one side.
The incense-burning attendant immediately proceeds to stand at the left side of the Dharma seat, waiting for the assembly to enter as the drum rolls through its second cycle. The West Class enters.
The Head Official (Dhūrta) leads the assembly out of the hall into the Dharma Hall to pay respects toward the East Wing;

they proceed to the front of the seats and stand in the West Wing, while the assembly stands in a single file behind them. The Head of the Assembly (Cārya) leads the attendant practitioners (karmadāna) out of the hall;

they first line up facing each other at the lower end of the storehouse hall, also waiting for the second roll of the drum. At this point, the administrative officials (Karmadāna) of the East Wing emerge from the storehouse hall, followed by the attendant practitioners.
Having exchanged greetings, he follows [the Abbot] into the Dharma Hall. He greets those in the West Wing, proceeds to the front of his seat, and stands in the East Wing.
The attendants retreat and line up behind him, leaving the position for the attendant. The two orders face each other and exchange brief greetings;
the attendant then returns to the Tea Hall to invite the Abbot. The Abbot waits until the drum strikes three times, then rises from his sedan chair and walks behind the attendant to the Dharma Hall.
During the winter months before the seat, the abbot removes his cap and the assembly likewise removes theirs; they all bow toward the dust [of the abbot’s feet] and offer greetings.

The abbot performs a *vaṃdana* (homage) and ascends the seat. The attendant follows from the side up to the Dharma seat, carrying a censer with its lid closed containing pieces of incense, which he presents to the abbot.

Once the abbot has finished offering the incense and reciting the prayer for longevity, the attendant receives the incense and inserts it into the burner with both hands, while the abbot takes a pinch of incense with his right hand.

From the incense burner, the attendant briefly offers greetings and descends from the seat. The abbot sits cross-legged; the attendant and his colleagues join their palms together and step out of the ranks.
The junior members lead the way first, passing to the west and standing in a single row before the seats facing the abbot. After the greetings are completed, they burn incense.
The attendant leads the group back to their positions with palms joined, standing behind the eastern section. Next, the head seat (shouzuo) leads his colleagues.

With palms joined, they step out of the ranks and stand before the abbot within the incense chairs; having finished exchanging greetings with the abbot, they likewise exchange greetings with the assembly.
Once the greetings are concluded, the Head Seat leads the group back to their positions with palms joined; after a brief greeting, the East Order members receive the greeting in turn.

Next, all the administrative officers (zhishi) join with palms joined and step out of the ranks; the Vice Abbot (fusi) first leads them to the western side within the incense chairs to face the abbot and exchange greetings with the assembly.

When the practitioner has finished the inquiries, the head monk (Du-si) leads the assembly to join their palms and return to their positions; after brief inquiries, those from the western order follow with inquiries.
Next, the eminent monks from the eastern hall and those from the western hall emerge in a procession, approach the front of the seat, and perform inquiries facing the Abbot.
Once this is concluded, the attendant ascends the seat, holding the incense censer in his right hand and offering incense with his left hand; he then turns to face the Abbot for further inquiry.

The inquiry (known as "requesting the Dharma on behalf of the assembly"): Stepping back to stand by the side of the seat, the Abbot takes up the whisk, bows to the assembly, and delivers his discourse (as follows).
Upon completion, he turns the merit from his seat, saying: "On the [day] of this month, we reverently encounter the Imperial Birthday, the Sacred Festival.

This monastery has prepared in advance for the [day] of this month to inaugurate a one-month-long Vajra-Amitāyus Maṇḍala. Daily, monks shall take turns ascending to the hall to recite and study the scriptures. On this day, the inauguration is held; the presiding monk, a subject, [proceeds]."

"May the profound causes accumulated by this person ascending this seat to expound the wondrous meaning be dedicated solely to the prayer for the Ten-Thousand-Year Peace and Security of His Majesty’s Longevity. Having concluded the closing of the session, he says aloud:

"The assembly, maintaining their dignified deportment, proceeds to the Great Buddha Hall to inaugurate the observance of the Imperial Birthday; this is respectfully announced. Thereupon, the temple bell is struck.

The Abbot leads the assembly to the hall, where they stand in their respective order. The Abbot first burns incense and offers tea; the Head Administrative Officer (Upādhyāya) hands it up to the Attendant, who serves the tea, followed by the Novice (Śrāmaṇera).
The Mingba (Ming-ba) Venerable turns to stand before the incense burner outside the hall and bows. The attendant for incense (*xiang shizhe*) holds the incense censer, and the Abbot offers incense.
Next, the two orders of monks join their palms and emerge in pairs in succession to pay homage to the Buddha, inquire after his well-being, and offer incense.

Having completed this, they bow to one another, turn to face the hall, and inquire after his well-being before returning to their positions. Subsequently, the Elder of the East Hall and the Elder of the West Hall step out of the ranks to burn incense and then return.
The ritual positions being completed, the *vina* (chant leader) makes a final circumambulation and inquiry, burns incense, and returns to his position to stand.

The Head Seat (*shouzuo*) leads the assembly in chanting "Namo Amitābha Buddha," and they perform three prostrations in unison (this is done to offer congratulations on the Buddha’s birthday). When this is finished, the assembly withdraws their implements.

The Abbot does not withdraw his implements; he kneels, and the *zhikě* (guest master) kneels to present the incense burner, while the attendant (*shizhe*) kneels to present the incense box. The Abbot then burns the incense.

The *vinaya-dhara* (Venerable Leader) proclaims the memorial (*śāstra*) to the Buddha, saying: "O King of Kings, whose rank stands above the hundred kings; O Sage among Sages, whose Way surpasses the thousand sages. We look up, hoping for Your vast compassion, and pray that You will graciously deign to behold us.

On this day, we inaugurate the ceremony for the Sacred Festival of Longevity. The memorial reads as follows... [The format of the memorial is shown below]. Once the *vinaya-dhara* has finished proclaiming the memorial, the *karmadāna* (Guest Master) kneels to receive it, while the ritual attendants collect the implements.
The *śrāmaṇera* (Head Seat) intones the *Śūraṅgama-mantra*; when the recitation of the mantra is completed, the *śrāmaṇera* raises [the next liturgical text].

The Venerable *Karmadāna* of Amitāyus Buddha’s [Assembly] recites the Dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), saying: "I humbly look up to Your Great Compassion to once again grant Your illuminating discernment. For the inauguration of the Sacred Festival of Longevity, we have chanted secret chapters and extolled the Holy Name.

May the vast merit thus accumulated be dedicated solely to the prolongation of the life of His Present Majesty the Emperor, with all beings in harmony chanting: 'Long live! Long live! Ten thousand times ten thousand years! May He be blessed with a celestial lifespan as immeasurable as that of Amitāyus Buddha. To all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time, to all... [and so forth]. [The ritual concludes with] the dispersal of offerings.

On the anniversary of the Sage’s birthday, the procedures are the same as before. When the current abbot arrives at the official residence, he shall offer congratulations and praise alongside the officials.

The head seat (shouzuo) kneels at his designated side position; the hall attendant (tangsi xingzhe) kneels to present the incense censer; and the tea master (zuosi chadou) kneels to present the incense box.

After the incense is burned and the memorial text (shu) is proclaimed, the hall attendant again kneels to receive back the incense censer. (The procedures for offering tea on the days of the Buddha’s descent from heaven and his attainment of enlightenment, including the procession out of the ranks to burn incense, are identical.)
Preface to the Commentary on the Teachings (The opening is as in the previous notice).
Herein, I humbly observe that the Greatness of Heaven is vast and boundless, beyond the reach of naming; it shines alongside the sun.

The brilliance is so pure and radiant that it can no longer be surpassed; wearing His virtue, we know not its height or distance, and receiving His light, we cannot fathom the extent of His illumination.
Desiring to exhaust my loyalty and sincerity as a subject, I venture to offer these devout prayers like those of the people of Hua-feng:

may the fifty thousand scrolls of the Sanskrit scriptures, which unfold the twenty layers of the Flower Store (Avataṃsaka) universe, all be contained within Your domain; and may the sixty thousand words of the sublime meaning, which encompass ten billion lands, likewise be gathered therein.
All the minor kings have returned to your transformative influence; we humbly extend this small, drop-like offering to repay your vast grace.

We respectfully pray that you may live as long as Heaven does not age and traverse the earth without limit. May your longevity be celebrated with the jade cup, and may your emerald carriage forever attend at Changle Palace.

May your achievements be realized in the cinnabar cauldron, and may the Yellow River repeatedly manifest its clear currents. This memorial is respectfully submitted on the [day] of the [month] of the [year].

Preface for the Distribution of Offerings: I humbly submit that Heaven gave birth to the Sage to serve as the lord of the people under Heaven. When the state faces its great destiny, it must return to the Way of the state.
From the harmonious prosperity of the reigns of Tang and Yu to the complementary governance of Wen and Wu, more than ten thousand years have passed.
May you attain longevity; may the span of your life be extended without limit. For one month, I shall observe a period of solemn fasting and prayer, earnestly entreating that you remain present.

With the utmost reverence, I pray that under the protection of Heaven and the support of Earth, your virtues may be equally shared. The Shang dynasty valued simplicity, while the Zhou valued refinement;

I now double the merit of their achievements in offering my most profound prayers for wealth, longevity, and many sons. May the blessings of universal unification extend even to the barbarian tribes. That I did not anticipate this is what I respectfully record.
Commentary. On the [day] of the [month] and [year], this commentary was written.
Every day, during the morning service, after the assembly has taken their places and stood still, first recite the *Mahākaruṇā-dhāraṇī* once and invoke the name of the Buddha.

The Venerable of the Amitāyus Assembly’s Dedication of Merit: “I humbly entreat Your Great Compassion to graciously look down and clearly discern the vast causes accumulated through the aforementioned chanting of secret chapters and the invocation of the Holy Name.

These merits are solely for the purpose of praying for the Ten Thousand Years of Peaceful Sovereignty of His Present Majesty the Emperor, and for increasing the Heavenly Count [of his years], and so forth.”
On the four fasting days of the auspicious mandate, on the evening of the day prior to the ritual,
the attendant of the Hall (堂司行者) reports to the Abbot (方丈) and the two classes of officials (兩班), and thereafter hangs the notice boards for the single-celled quarters (單寮).

At dawn, when the temple bell ceases its tolling, the assembly gathers to recite the *Amitābha-dhāraṇī* (or alternatively, the *Mahākaruṇā-dhāraṇī* or the *Āpad-vinodana-dhāraṇī*), while chanting "Namo Amitāyus."

The Buddha, the Sangha, and the *huiguan* (Venerable Leader) perform the Dedication of Merit (*huixiang*). "May Your Great Compassion look down and clearly perceive this. On this auspicious occasion of the four fasts, we, the monastics, have gathered reverently to hasten to the precious hall to chant secret scriptures and extol the holy names.

the Tripitaka Hall bell and drums are then sounded, and those assigned to the Tripitaka Hall are ordered to turn the scriptures. When the assembly gathers, the Head Seat recites the Śūraṅgama Dhāraṇī while circumambulating the Tripitaka.
When the recitation of the dharanis is finished, stand firm and chant: "Namo Śākyamuni Buddha; Namo Amitāyus Buddha; Namo Buddhōṣṇīṣa-Śūraṅgama;

Hong first offered prayers for the longevity and well-being of the present Emperor, followed by aspirations that the Buddha-sun may increase in brilliance and the Wheel of Dharma may turn perpetually, including invocations of Amitāyus Buddha and the Benevolent Kings Bodhisattvas, and so forth.

On the evening of the day before the arrival of the Qianqiu Festival (the Emperor’s birthday), the attendant of the late hall reports to the Abbot, the two classes of officials, and the monks in private quarters, and the notice board is posted.

May the great merit thus accumulated be offered in prayer for the Imperial Prince’s sagely life-span to endure for a thousand autumns, and that His Highness, with reverence and obedience, may receive these flourishing rites. May his station be worthy of the rank of the Blue Palace, his mild and refined character illuminating the fame of the Three Virtues, and his continuing radiance harmonizing with the celebration of the Double Li (the sun).
To all beings of the ten directions and three periods of time... [and so forth].

The third, fifth, and ninth months are known as the "Three Months of Good Fortune" (*samyuk*), during which people observe the three-month fast. To pray for blessings, a Dharma hall is established each month;

one day prior, the attendants of the Hall Office notify the Abbot and the two ranks of officials, and a plaque for the "Month of Good Fortune" is hung before the main hall. Upon completion of these preparations:

The scriptures and single volumes are placed together in a register, and monks are assigned to ring the great bell daily, ascend to the hall to read the scriptures and offer prayers of praise until the bell is struck and they descend from the hall.
At the end of the month, the titles of the scriptures are listed, and a formal report is prepared for the concluding ceremony. (The *Tilijing* states:

"The various heavenly deities, Śakra, princes, messengers, Yama, ghosts, and spirits all use the first days of the first, fifth, and ninth months to inspect the kings, ministers, and people regarding their good and evil deeds. As the four seasons change, they conduct three reviews at the end of the year to cross-examine [the records]. They report to the Four Heavenly Kings once every month, six times a year, so that there may be no injustice or error in examining and verifying the sentient beings.")

"Sin and merit follow one like a shadow: performing good brings down blessings, while doing evil brings down calamity. By imperial decree in the third year of the Kaihuang era, it was prohibited throughout the realm to kill living beings during the first, fifth, and ninth months, as well as on the six days of the *zhāi* (fasting) observances.

In the second year of the Wude era of the Tang dynasty, a decree was issued that during the ten days of the *zhāi* in the first, fifth, and ninth months, no executions, slaughtering, or fishing were to be carried out—a practice that continues to this day under our Sacred Dynasty with even greater devotion. May all monasteries, upon reaching these periods, not be remiss. (The reason people of the world regard these three months as taboo for those in office is simply because they avoid carrying out executions during them.)
Section One: The Gate of Prayer and Praise; Section Two: The Gate of Averting Calamity and Seeking Blessings.

While the Buddha takes compassion as his means of transformation and Heaven takes the love of life as its virtue, the common people bring calamity upon themselves through their own transgressions, thereby invoking these consequences.

To lose the scriptures and turn our backs on the eternal is contrary to the intent of our school to ordain monks based on the national dynasty for the sake of praying for the people; you should therefore apply yourselves with even greater diligence to manifest the compassionate grace of the Buddhas and devas.
If calamities may thus be averted before they sprout and disasters transformed into blessings, what need will there be for the leisure of dwelling in ease?

A period of three days of solemn observance was established; at the two meal times of rice gruel and congee, the bell was struck to assemble the community, who ascended the hall to chant and offer prayers.
At the outset, the Head Seat (Śrāmaṇera) raised his voice to recite: "Namo to the Tathāgata Righteousness-Illumination of the Past" (and so forth).

The monks of the temple, numbering several dozen, shall divide themselves into several groups; each group shall recite the dhāraṇīs a certain number of times while invoking the names [of the Buddhas] with earnest prayer.
In this manner, they shall proceed in succession and rotation without interruption from morning until evening, taking spiritual response as their goal.

Furthermore, they shall separately cultivate meritorious deeds and fruits, ensuring that the ultimate efficacy is achieved before concluding the rite and performing the final repentance and thanksgiving. (In the event of calamities or anomalies where there is an urgent need for prayer...)

When officials enter the mountain to offer prayers, or upon their prior arrival, immediately order the attendants of the Hall Office to inform the Abbot.

the abbot (zhuchi) takes up the incense burner and leads the assembly to welcome him at the gate. Upon entering the hall, they offer incense and perform prostrations.

The administrative officers (zhishi) should have previously inquired about the official’s demeanor and intentions, conveying this to the abbot and the heads of the various departments (toushou), ensuring that no negligence occurs. Then, the mantra is recited, the titles are invoked, and the merit is dedicated (huixiang)—whether by the abbot or [another].

The head monk shall not be restricted; once the ceremony is concluded, he is invited back to the Abbot’s quarters or the Dharma Hall, where a seat is prepared and tea is offered according to the ritual.

While accompanying him on excursions, one should engage in conversation without discussing worldly affairs. However, regarding urgent matters concerning the Dharma or the monastery, one should assess the situation and report them;

one must not act impulsively, as this would damage the dignity of the institution. When departing, the bell is struck and the assembly sees him off at the gate (if welcoming or seeing off high-ranking officials, the bell is likewise struck).
Next, the tower bell is struck, followed by the bell before the Sangha Hall.
For praying for clear weather: "The sun of stainless, pure, and luminous wisdom destroys all darkness; it can subdue calamitous winds and fires, shining universally upon the world."

The rains have not ceased, and all things are unable to fulfill their natures; the embankments and ponds are on the verge of bursting, causing the four classes of people to share in universal anxiety.

It is not that the Great Sun fails to shine upon us, but rather that hidden karmic entanglements within the myriad species have invoked this calamity. We hereby extend our earnest prayers, hoping for a manifestation of divine clarity.
Accordingly, on the [day] of the [month], we have solemnly inaugurated a ritual site for praying for clear skies, assembling the multitude every day.

Reciting the secret chapters and extolling the holy names, we pray for merit and offer supplications to the eternally abiding Triple Gem, the Greatly Compassionate Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, the deities who receive blessings and protect the Dharma, the various celestial lords, Śakra Devendra, the Four Heavenly Kings of the four gates, and the Sun Palace Mahā-sūrya-devaputra (and so forth).
We pray with equal sincerity for a manifestation of their response; may it be our humble wish that all darkness be swept away.

May the mists be cleared from the earth so that the bright sun may shine forth, and may the boundaries of heaven be opened and purified. May the benefits of the land be abundant and the conditions of heaven be harmonious.
I pray for rain: with the body of compassion as the thunderclap and the mind of mercy as the wondrous great cloud, may the nectar-like Dharma rain pour down to extinguish the flames of affliction.
Water is the lifeblood of all things; how could it withstand the power that scorches stones? Food is the heavenly provision for the people, evoking deep sighs of longing for the rain-clouds.

These conditions are moved by the shared karma of those below; it is not that the High Heaven is partial in its observation of things. To achieve universal relief, one must rely upon prayer and invocation.
Therefore, on the [day] of the [month], we respectfully inaugurate a rain-praying ritual site (*dharmapūjā-maṇḍala*), gathering the assembly daily.

Reciting and expounding the secret chapters, extolling the holy names, and offering prayers for merit (as detailed above): may blessings be bestowed upon the deities attending to protect the Teachings;
the Dragon Kings who bring rain from the five directions; the Thunder Lords, Lightning Mothers, Wind Masters, and Rain Teachers of the six realms; the sacred assemblies of the Rain Department;
and the hidden and manifest Dragon Kings of all streams, sources, pools, and caves, as well as the numinous altars and shrines of mountains, rivers, and valleys.

(As stated above) We pray with equal sincerity for a manifestation of response. We humbly beseech that lightning may flash and thunder roll to stir the dragons and serpents from the streams and marshes;

that clouds may move and rain fall to revive the grain crops in the fields and meadows. Thus may the five grains yield a bountiful harvest, and may the four classes of people find joy in their vocations.

Praying for snow during the winter season so that it may be like spring, lest the common people suffer from pestilence; if no snow falls before the end of the year, how can we hope for a bountiful harvest in the coming year?

We reverently express the sincere devotion of the entire assembly, wishing to behold the auspicious omen of the six-petaled snowflake. Looking up to Your vast creation, we humbly beseech You to grant [our prayers].

In detail, we have assembled the multitude to chant secret mantras and extol the holy names; through these merits, we pray for the eternal abiding of the Two Treasures and the Greatly Compassionate Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
We respectfully offer blessings to the various celestial lords, including Śakra Devendra, and all honored deities who protect the Dharma (and so forth).
We pray with equal sincerity for a manifestation of response. We humbly beseech that flowers may fly from a thousand li away, and that auspicious signs may appear upon the level earth.

When the harvest fills the span of a foot, the nine autumns yield abundant crops; the people rejoice in a year of plenty, concealing and subduing baleful vapors while guiding and proclaiming harmonious qi.
To rescue the sun—

The accumulated virtue and redoubled radiance illuminate all four continents, which look up in reverence; even the celestial bodies lose their courses, and throughout the eight directions, all are struck with awe and trembling.
Although we rely on the auspicious calculations of the calendar, we fear the calamities of hidden baleful influences.

Desiring to restore the Golden Wheel and return to the ancient vision, we must rely upon the Azure Marks to graciously manifest their guidance; thus, we promptly offer prayers to seek your protection and deliverance.
Therefore, we have assembled the multitude to chant secret mantras, extol the holy names, and pray that the Three Jewels remain eternally present;

that Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, Sūryaprabha Bodhisattva, the deities who receive blessings and protect the Dharma, and the myriad spirits of the three realms and the assembly of sages filling the void, may all join in this equal supplication to manifest their responsive grace.
We humbly beseech that light be returned to the universe, that the Yin and Yang may harmonize, and that Heaven...
Below all is tranquil; how could there be need for the art of brandishing a spear to dazzle? The signs of Great Peace are manifest; what necessity is there for the reproach of the overturned basin?
All quarters sing the praises of Yao’s fame, and the eight directions share in the radiance of Shun’s virtue.

Savior of the Moon (O World-Honored One, Buddha of Great Wisdom and Diligence, I now take refuge in you and prostrate before you; O Rāhula, who torments our kind, may the Buddha look upon us with compassion and grant us protection).
As the moon reaches its zenith tonight, its orb is perfectly full; yet as the comet unleashes its malevolence, the perfect disk is now eclipsed this very evening.
Thus, as the lunar mansion enters the stellar cycle, it is a divine warning to the hearts of men.
Desiring that all under heaven may once again look up in reverence to its pure radiance, we have assembled here to offer praise to the Great Creator and to chant the secret mantras. We extol...
Through the merit of these sacred names and this prayer, we entreat that the Three Jewels remain ever-present, and that the Greatly Compassionate Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva,
Candraprabha Bodhisattva, the deities who protect the Dharma by bestowing blessings, the sovereigns of both provisional and ultimate truth, the myriad spirits of the three realms,
and the assembly of holy beings filling the void, may all equally grant their response. We humbly pray that the jade axe shall not begrudge its work to restore the full orb of the moon.

The rabbit revives once more and returns to its ancient golden pitcher; the great earth, mountains, and rivers are universally illuminated, the palaces of the Vast Cold Palace are all opened, the myriad phenomena shine with brilliance, and the colors of the nine heavens are pure.

We dispatch this memorial regarding the locusts: startled to see these flying locusts entering our borders, arriving in such numbers as to obscure the heavens and cover the fields, we observe that such exotic creatures portend disaster. How can we avoid the tragedy of their destruction of the crops and the damage to the grain?
We rely upon the officials to capture them; yet what benefit would mere pursuit bring to the farmers who have already been trampled by them? We venture to place our trust in Your Majesty’s grace.

Through the efficacy of these sublime applications, the blessings of averting calamities and inviting prosperity are formally bestowed. Accordingly, on the [day] of the [month], we have assembled the multitude to chant secret scriptures and recite the sacred names;

through these merits, we pray for [the fulfillment of our wishes]. (As stated above. We respectfully offer these blessings to the Dharma-protecting deities seated in the assembly, the various heavens, the two polarities of the Three Realms, the sovereign lords filling the void, and the sages of Yin and Yang who govern creation and transformation and administer reward and punishment. (As stated above.)

We pray with equal sincerity for a manifestation of your compassionate response. We humbly beseech you that the wind of your mercy may blow fiercely, dispatching the multitudes of beings to the realm of non-being;
and that the ocean of your vows may flow everywhere, sweeping away all crawling and flying creatures into the principle of eternal quiescence.
Not only shall the calamities and anomalies of a single object be dispelled, but the entire universe shall share in a heart of joy.

Thanking the brilliant and radiant glory that proclaims its light across a thousand li, the clear splendor opens the eyes of those who gaze afar; the common people look up to its virtue as the bright colors of the eight directions stir their hearts with joy.
Were it not for the clarity of the Great Way’s downward reflection, how could one behold the illumination of the Great Sun as it opens the gates? I present this once more.
I, Jian Shan, venture to respond to this great bounty (as detailed above). I humbly pray that my petitions may be granted at once, already portending the auspicious signs of a bountiful year;
and that through such resonance, the harvests of the autumn fields may soon be foretold, while the Yin and Yang follow their proper order, and all people and things flourish in peace and prosperity.

Some petitioners for rain may have acted contrary to principle, yet for over ten days we were startled by the power of the drought-demon; Heaven did not abandon its people, and with this single rainfall, it comforted us with the bounty of the *sang-lin* grove.
Relying upon this abundant moisture, our hearts’ desire for the burgeoning of life is suddenly fulfilled. Having been bathed in these waves of grace, how could we dare forget?

Lung-de (and so forth). We humbly pray that the eight directions offer their congratulations and every person cherish the song of the *jirang*; that the four seas rejoice together and in every place there shall be the chanting of the hymn of the drumming belly;
that all beings may universally benefit from this singular flavor, and that its glory may increase.

Section Three: On Repaying the Fundamental Source.
The Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs arises from this very principle that the Dharma is the ultimate foundation. Thus, for all who are resolved to...
Can those who seek the Way not know its source? The entire Great Canon of the Teachings has the nature of sentient beings as its root;
the Buddhas have revealed it and shown it, and the Patriarchs have confronted it and proclaimed it.

Through written words, they have widely disseminated the primary meaning throughout the world, so that those who recite these books and cultivate this Way may all have a means to restore the root of their nature and ascend the stages of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.

It is likewise so with the substance of birth and death, which is illusory existence; if one knows how to repay the debt owed to the source of its generation and growth, how much more so for those who gave birth to the unsurpassed *dharmakāya* of both the mundane and supramundane realms!

If one can truly use the wondrous Way of transcendence to guide and assist all beings so that they fully restore their original nature, what could surpass this as the ultimate repayment of the source?
Furthermore, the present dynasty has established its foundation and bequeathed its legacy.

The former emperors were all of the fruition stage (*phala-bhūmi*) and thus fit to govern the world; the Great Dharma King likewise assisted in the transformation of beings through great skillful means (*mahopāya*).
Now that their transformative tasks have concluded, they have all returned to the realization of the ground (*bhūmi-sākṣātkriyā*).

May the grace bestowed upon us cause both the teachings and our prosperity to flourish together, so that we disciples may investigate and restore our original nature—would this not allow us to trace back to our own source? On the anniversary of their posthumous names, I pray with earnest and sincere devotion.
Reflecting with earnestness, one should revere [the Buddha].
As the day of the Tathāgata’s birth (the eighth day of the fourth month) approaches,
the Abbot shall single-mindedly command the storehouse office to prepare offerings and direct the attendants to [serve] the Buddha.
In the Hall, a basin for fragrant bath-water is prepared in the Vimalāvana Garden, wherein an image of the Prince is placed and two small ladles are set within the basin.
On the appointed day, after the offerings and the fragrant bath-water have been fully arranged, the attendants of the Hall Office strike the gong to summon the assembly.

Each member, assuming a dignified demeanor and bringing the funds for the fragrant bath-water, awaits the sound of the bell and proceeds together to the Great Hall, where they stand in their respective positions. The Abbot then offers incense.
After three prostrations, one does not fold the sitting mat but steps forward to offer hot water and food. The attendant hands it up, and the server receives it and places it upon the table.

Once the inquiries have been completed, one returns to their position and performs three prostrations. Again, incense is offered and a monetary gift (*dakṣiṇā*) is presented; tea is served, followed by another three prostrations.

One folds the sitting mat, and the two orders of monks step out of the ranks. The *vinaya-dhara* (Venerable) bows for the incense according to the previous ritual. The assembly performs three prostrations, folds their mats, and the Abbot kneels.

namely, wandering through the world with a compassionate heart. Having received a human lifespan of a hundred years, he then filled the station of the fourth Buddha of the Bhadrakalpa;
taking the central land of twelve thousand kingdoms, he manifested the thirty-two marks of excellence.
The Responding Body (the Nirmāṇakāya), which dares to take the lead for the world and calls itself the most excellent among men, does not envy the nobility of those who succeed Heaven;

it manifests the supremacy of the Buddha alone. Though his responsive traces have passed away, he remains as bright as the morning star; though his transformative仪 (rites/manifestations) have departed, his influence still rises like a white rainbow.
Having fortunately encountered this occasion of the bestowal of his shadow, I humbly offer this slight tribute of fragrance. I respectfully present [this offering].

We humbly pray that his supreme transformation may flourish ever more, that the patriarchal tradition may be propagated, and that the imperial wind may be revived once again.

The Great Zen Master Zhizhe, Treasure-Awakened Dharma-Emptiness, the Founder of Tiantai, possessed a vision as vast as Mount Ling;

His teachings pierced the ultimate proclamation of the One Vehicle and penetrated the profound mysteries of the three periods of time. As the midday sun shone forth, he revealed the pearl while exposing the imitation fish-eye; the Great Way was thus made vast and clear.
Like the empty sky, the licentious music of Zheng disrupted the refined *yue*; like the moonlight through the curtains and the fragrance of cypress, he made offerings of the True Dharma.

At Jinge Temple in Jiangling, he followed the ways of the world with effortless grace and attained the *ekavīcika-dhāraṇī*. To briefly show the traces within traces, he contemplated three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* as the ultimate among heavens;
fragrant winds blew upon the *udumbara* flowers, and the iron drum pierced through the *nāga* realm.
Rāyaṇa’s arrow drew from the source of the Jade Spring, raining down a vast deluge within a dream; gazing up at Mount Huading, he brought down the multitudes of Māras within a mirror.

may the six flavors reach their ultimate fulfillment, and the spring be breathed forth across the nine earths. Have pity on this autumn of swirling dust and confusion; lament the extreme state of withered seeds and scattered branches.

Together with Zhiyi, you have silently mastered the teachings through mental penetration. I respectfully venerate you.

Tiantai Baoshou compiled the Dharma-treasury, and Chan Master Zhang'an, the Venerable Total-Holding (Zongchi), returned in fulfillment of his past vows to receive instruction from the present master and excellently continue his legacy.

because they took it upon themselves to overcome the world's most difficult challenges, they surpassed all other disciples, subsisting on vegetable food, water, and fasting while sitting upon ice-cold benches.
Braving the snow, he did not decline the toil of composition; transcending the clouds, he surpassed the seals of realization, and leaping beyond the foundations, he outstripped the luminous canopies.
How could one have anticipated such excellence in his exegesis? Alas, that this literature might seem to fall into ruin! Yet, the nectar of the Dharma is shown to be present here and now.

As the Dharma-banner of the Eastern Palace was just returning, the precious terrace of the Inner Court was already awaiting him. I pray that you will once again descend to bring tranquility to this white day, so that the various heroes may not need to exert even a finger-snap to turn back the surging waves.

Deeply concealing yet upholding the grand principles alone, you were sustained by Heaven; as the sun was drawn from the Yu-yuan abyss, the teachings and contemplations of the Tai and Heng masters were thus re-illuminated.

It is fitting that the legacy of Lingyue be far-reaching, like the hereditary succession of the Ji family. We, [Name] and others, have unworthily shared in unrolling this scroll and truly feel our gratitude.

His emergence of clarity is like the bright sun revolving in the sky; it is not merely the extinguishing of a mere torch-flame, but rather the manifestation of the *tāmarasa* flower.

We respectfully venerate the Great Master Fazhi of Zhongxing Jiaoguan, the Venerable of Siming. Born in his youth at the waters of Ningbo, he possessed the spiritual essence of a Buddha’s son left behind by a divine monk;
from his very first month, he received the essential teachings of the *Heart Sūtra* from Baoyun. Thus, he composed [this work].
He became a true vessel for the ocean of Dharma, a gathering place for a vast multitude of disciples. He proclaimed the One Vehicle and encompassed all the scriptures.

For over forty years, he practiced the difficult austerities of Tiantai, his side never touching the mat. He recorded texts previously unrecorded in Piling, his hand never ceasing from writing nearly ten million characters.
Disciples in blue gowns gathered like ants; the red banners spread like clouds. Thus, he restored the teachings and contemplations.
Having abandoned his teacher, who else could so distantly carry on the legacy of the *ji* and *qiu* (the loom and the hammer)? You alone were such a person.

That the color of the crane-forest changed and the grief of the "beam of Liang" was entangled—now, with only the empty remains of the manuscripts in hand, it is difficult to turn back toward the state of tranquil concentration. Now, as for our Benevolent One (Maitreya), he established a system of moving residences every three months to avoid the eight impurities; the keeping of livestock, trees, stones, fields, and villages was all permitted and regulated.

The four types of offerings were supplied by those who looked up to him from the ten directions. Although there were monasteries (*vihāras*), they did not involve permanent residence or productive land;

thus, there was no mention of "residing and maintaining" property. When the teaching spread to China, the government established nine offices, and their official residences were referred to as having the "dharma-regulations."
The place was named a *si* (temple), and the monastic dwellings were subsequently designated as such to provide a secure residence for the assembly.

It was necessary to select those who were honored both for their seniority and virtue to serve as models for the community and to preside over them; thus, the title of *zhuchi* (abbot) first came into being.

To this day, the present dynasty carefully scrutinizes the selection of candidates, ensuring that only those whose virtuous conduct can command the respect of the assembly and whose discourse can admonish the world are appointed.
When they are elevated and appointed, if their talent and virtue do not match the office, they shall not be granted it even if they are advanced in years.

Therefore, all those who enter this selection grasp the handles of the Great Dharma, extensively disseminate the sacred words, and enlighten future students; they cause the Dharma-vehicle to flourish during the Age of Semblance and bestow blessings upon living beings across all lands.
This is precisely how they supplement the King’s transformation of the world and glorify the teachings of the age—how could they possibly harbor [selfish] greed?

If one’s station merely suffices for the enjoyment of emolument, what is there to hold in high esteem? Discussion on the Appointment of the Abbot.

The position of Abbot should not remain vacant for long; the retired elders of the two orders shall first convene at the Kusi (Storehouse Office) to discuss and determine a candidate, submitting a formal petition to the presiding master.

They shall then notify the three patriarchal lineages and the various mountain monasteries to arrange for the assembly of the temple’s clergy and renowned guests from all quarters to jointly evaluate and select one who is upright in conduct, eminent in learning, in accord with public opinion, and whose rank corresponds to his station.
Those deemed worthy to serve the public expectation shall follow the established precedent of the Office of Commissioners (*shikanshin-in*): ten names shall be drawn by lot and three selected.

Subsequently, the *kanke* (verification slips) shall be filled out and submitted to the Office. Regarding all *chiji* (administrative officers) and veteran monks of the various mountains, one must not select them based on regional ties, family relations, private favoritism, or bribery, regardless of their merits or demerits, lest they bring disgrace upon the Buddhist teachings.
In recent times, factions have been formed and private interests pursued such that virtue does not match [the office].
The decline of monasteries and the failure of the religious tradition to flourish stem from this very cause; therefore, one must be most diligent and cautious in observing the precepts.
(Gongbo, having already settled the matter with the elders of the two classes [the nobility and the clergy], the various mountain abbots subsequently drafted the initial agreement.)
Requesting the new abbot (ten items in total):
dispatch a special messenger;

draw lots for the positions of the head of the administrative office (*yuan-dang*) and the hall master (*yuan-tang*); once these are determined, await the official notice; on the following day, the Chief Administrator (*du-si*) shall go to the Head Seat’s quarters (*shou-zuo-liao*) to deliberate upon the appointment.

On the following day, the administrative office convenes the two classes of senior monks (*kinko*). After the tea ceremony and incense offering, the Chief Administrator (*dōji*) returns to his seat and announces:

"We have selected [Name] as the new abbot; he will enter the monastery on such-and-such a day. We now request [Name] to serve as the special envoy. Having finished speaking, he turns his chair, offers incense, and presents hot tea.
In the evening, the envoy is entertained, and a capable attendant monk (*gyōja*) and a senior official (*rōrō*) are appointed to deliver the formal letter in advance.

Next, select individuals to draft the monastery’s formal petitions (*shūsō*), the tea and soup notices (*chāsō-hyō*), and the banners (*hyō*). These banners shall be made of silk or fine cloth, with dimensions according to the prescribed rules.

A dedicated messenger from the West Hall—either the head seat (*shusō*), the rector (*uinā*), a West Hall monk (*sitō*), or a veteran monk (*kinjū*)—must go accompanied by at least one administrative official (*jishi*) to oversee the finances and deliberate on affairs. They must record in detail all the monastery’s assets, properties, and utensils.
Knowing that all ceremonial attendants must be assembled for the day of departure, the special envoy shall visit the various quarters to bid farewell.
The bell before the Sangha Hall is struck to gather the assembly for a formal send-off. Canopies are hung at the main gate, and a special seat is prepared inside.

The two orders of monks and the retired officials (qinjiu) serve as escorts. The protocol for the tea and soup offerings follows that of the head official; if the head official departs, the junior official takes his place.

The head administrator performs the rites as for a senior official; when [the guest] departs, the head administrator performs the rites, bows to the seat, burns incense, and returns to his position to accompany [the guest] in drinking tea.
Rising again, he burns incense, bows to the special envoy, offers incense, and returns to his position to accompany [the envoy] in drinking soup.
The special envoy rises, expresses thanks, and departs.

Once the special envoy has arrived at that mountain, he first visits the guest prefect (*kōshaku*) and, together with him, goes to the administrative office (*kusishi*) for an audience. After this is concluded, he escorts the guest to his quarters to settle his luggage.
He then visits the attendant (*jidai*) to announce his arrival to the abbot (*jūji*). If the abbot grants his request, he is instructed to set out a table and mats.

The Abbot’s Attendant delivers the letter of notification to the two orders [of monks]. Upon arrival, the Abbot goes out to receive the special messenger, inquires after his well-being, and invites him to sit cross-legged.

The Abbot stands in the center while the messenger offers incense. **First Fold:** "I, [Name], having been sent by the Mountain Gate, have had the honor of approaching your venerable presence. My humble feelings are overcome with the utmost awe and gratitude.

**Second Fold:** "On this day, I wish for the newly appointed Hall Head Abbot to enjoy constant health and prosperity in all your movements and activities. **Third Fold:** Three prostrations; the Abbot responds with one.

[The Abbot] bows: "I, [Name], examine myself and find myself incompetent and mistaken; it is difficult for me to accept this request. Your great ceremony has been bestowed with excessive courtesy, which I cannot bear as such a profound intrusion. The special envoy presents the memorial and invitation slip. The abbot receives them;

attendants on both sides advance and place them upon the table. The abbot looks over them. The attendant bows to the special envoy and invites him to sit. The two classes of monks and the head seat (shouzuo) take their respective seats.
Facing the abbot, the special envoy sits. The attendant burns incense and offers tea. The servants who came together perform a prostration.

Once the two ranks of officials have escorted the special envoy back to his residence and the ceremony is concluded, the abbot immediately performs a prostration from afar and returns to the abbot’s quarters.
The hall attendants strike the bell in front of the Sangha Hall; the two ranks of officials, together with the assembly, proceed to the abbot’s quarters to offer congratulations.

When the assembly has dispersed, the guest prefect leads the special envoy on a tour of the monastic quarters. Upon completion, they return once more to the abbot’s quarters to present the temple’s *Xuzhi* (Regulations) and ritual implements.

On the evening of the day the objects [of the offering] are presented, the special envoy shall specifically prepare medicinal decoctions; at night, the soup and fruits are all offered with an invitation for the great elders and the two orders to attend as honored companions, while the administrative office (kusi) arranges the provisions.
The special envoy specifically prepares the tea and refreshments for the newly appointed official.
The special envoy first consults with the newly appointed abbot regarding the weight of the offerings for the *zhāi* (fast-day) meal.

For the two orders of monks, the veteran elders, local laypeople, Dharma relatives, and those who have handled administrative affairs, he prepares supplementary offerings and materials for the meal. The envoy personally delivers the currency to the Treasury Office (*kūsī*) to procure the necessary items.

On the day of the ceremony, the envoy proceeds to the Abbot’s Quarters (*fāngwǎng*) to offer incense and extend an invitation. The first formal presentation is made as follows: "This coming noon, we shall specially prepare tea and refreshments in the Cloud Hall; we humbly beseech your compassionate presence."

[Again] expressing my deepest feelings, I am overcome with extreme trepidation and perspiration. [Second time: As before. [Third time: After performing the three prostrations, the Abbot bows his body slightly in response.
He then instructs the attendant who receives guests and the attendant on special missions to announce the invitation to the two classes of officials and the senior elders (*dajiu*).

A signboard for the tea service is hung, and the assembly is notified. Within the Sangha Hall, the seat of the presiding master is prepared; at the head of the *zhike* (guest prefect) board, the special mission attendant is stationed.

When the time for the midday meal arrives, the messenger shall go before the Sangha Hall to await the abbot’s entry. Upon his arrival, the messenger bows to inquire after his well-being and returns to his position to bow for him to be seated.
He then goes to the center to bow and bows for the assembly to be seated. He burns incense before the Sacred Monk (Śāstṛ), followed by the upper and lower sections, and then outside the hall.
Returning inside the hall, he burns incense before the abbot at the upper and lower sections, and finally outside the hall. He then bows once more and returns to the center.

Inquire after his well-being, step back to one side, and stand for a short while awaiting the distribution of food. Once the food has been served to all, burn incense again and descend to offer the *kṣaṇa* (alms-offering) to the Abbot, followed by the *kṣaṇa* for the two orders of officials, the retired elders, and the assembly of the great multitude.
Having completed this, return to your seat to partake of the meal. Wait for the water for rinsing the mouth (*zhéshuǐ*) to be brought out;

then, when the drum is struck, the special messenger rises again to burn incense and perform the rites as before. When the tea service is complete, inquire after his well-being as previously done, collect the Abbot’s cup, and the special messenger proceeds.

At the first prostration, he says: "I have humbly prepared this simple meal; I am deeply grateful for your compassionate acceptance of my invitation. At the second prostration, he exchanges greetings regarding the weather. At the third prostration, he escorts the abbot out.
Returning to the hall, he burns incense, performs three full prostrations (*dazhan*), and circumambulates the hall once.

He then proceeds to the outer hall and returns to the inner hall, where he bows in greeting at the center and collects his bowl. The bell is struck three times, the assembly withdraws, and the special envoy follows.

First, he goes to the Abbot’s quarters to express his gratitude; next, he goes to the administrative office (Kusi) to thank them for providing the meal; then, he returns to the Abbot’s quarters to invite the Abbot to take his evening meal.
At night, he invites the two orders of monks and the retired elders to accompany him for the soup and fruit offerings.
The Monastery Gate shall provide hospitality for the Abbot and the Special Envoy;

the administrative offices (Kusi) shall hold a council meeting to arrange this hospitality one day prior. The Head Administrative Officer shall go before the Abbot to offer incense and pay respects, requesting him to attend;
he shall then proceed to the Guest Quarters to inform the Special Envoy and request that the Kusi’s Guest Master invite the members of the Two Orders and the Venerable Elders to grace the occasion.

The attendants shall prepare the ritual offerings and gifts according to the prescribed rites; they must not treat the words or the performance of the ceremony with contempt, treating them as identical to the special rites.
Within the main hall, the abbot’s high seat is spread out, and seats for the special envoy and the two orders of officials are arranged according to the following format.

Servants who come from afar to receive the guest shall be provided with hospitality, while those from outside shall be separately rewarded. (Regarding the reception of the newly appointed official at the Mountain Gate: the central seat is prepared, facing the special envoy.)
If the appointee is the incumbent acting as a special messenger (*chuan-shi*), he shall part ways with the Head Seat (*shouzuo*) and not occupy the central position.

When the newly appointed official takes leave of the assembly and ascends the hall for tea and soup, the special messenger visits the various quarters to bid farewell; the newly appointed official then ascends the hall to express his gratitude to the two orders of officials. Upon the day of departure, the special messenger visits the various quarters once more to take his leave. The newly appointed official ascends the hall to offer thanks to the two orders of officials and the diligent practitioners.

According to the ancient *Dàzhòng Fǎyǔ* (Dharma Words for the Great Assembly): The *xiàzuò* (junior monk) personally goes to strike the drum three times, stands before the Dharma seat, and bows in greeting to the entire assembly.
He then exits through the western corridor and strikes the great bell and various ritual instruments. The assembly escorts him to the gate; the attendants stand in formation outside the gate.
At the mountain gate (*shānmén*), a canopy is hung and a high seat is prepared in the center, facing inward. The *shǒuzuò* (senior monk) faces outward.

The abbot takes his seat in the western hall; the retired elders (*qinjiu*) divide into groups to serve as companions on the eastern and western sides of the courtyard. The head of the assembly and the administrative officers (*zhishi*) perform their rites:

they bow to invite the abbot to sit, bow to offer incense, and return to their positions. Tea is served, the cups are collected, and the assembly rises again to burn incense. They bow to offer incense once more and return to their positions. Soup is served;

when it is finished, the assembly rises to express thanks, and the abbot departs in a sedan chair. The two orders of officials and the retired elders prepare the sedan chair and escort the abbot a long distance.
One should strive to avoid such occurrences by ringing the great bell and having the abbot’s sedan chair halted from afar.
For many abbots, upon moving to another mountain, find that monks harbor old grievances and immediately spread malicious rumors.
Because of the ignorance of a single individual, an entire temple suffers an ill reputation; thus, the senior elders and lay patrons of neighboring regions ought to intervene.
While it is right to exercise restraint and caution, as an abbot, it is appropriate to leave behind a legacy of kindness in all matters.

When a special messenger arrives at the temple on behalf of the West Hall Head or a senior official (Doushou) seeking an invitation, they should first visit the Guest Master (Zhike) to inquire after him and briefly reveal the purpose of their mission. The Guest Master shall then first dispatch someone to...

The person who has been invited shall prepare to receive the special envoy. After a short while, the attendant (zhuke) shall take the letter and documents, wrapped in a cloth covering (banfu), and go together with the envoy to the quarters of the invited person.

They shall burn incense and perform the rites (the same as the rites for inviting a contemporary). Once this is finished, the person who accepted the invitation shall entrust the attendant to accompany the envoy to the Abbot’s quarters (fangzhang) to perform the rites and announce:
"Now, [Name] Temple invites [Name] to serve as the abbot. When the rites are completed, they shall proceed immediately.
The various quarters, the treasury office, and the personnel office shall invite the person who has returned from his mission to the quarters where he is staying to rest.

In the evening, they shall invite him for tea and fruit, with the two classes of officers serving as companions. On the following day, the Abbot shall inform the two orders of officials and the elders to go together to the quarters of the invited person to offer congratulations.
Once the sequence of receiving congratulations is complete, the personnel office shall conduct a tour of the quarters. That same evening, the Abbot shall host a reception.
The newly appointed official and the special envoy shall be accompanied by two attendants each for the serving of fruit and medicinal decoctions.
The special envoy, having specifically received the invitation, shall prepare the tea and refreshments;
he shall first send money to the treasury office to have the preparations made, and only after visiting the newly appointed official to finalize the arrangements shall they proceed.

The master’s donation, along with supplementary donations from the two orders of monks, the retired elders, renowned figures from various regions, local laypeople, and Dharma relatives, shall be presented.

On the appointed day, after the morning gruel, a special messenger, carrying incense, shall go to the Abbot’s quarters (*fangzhang*) to prostrate and make the formal request: "This morning at noon, we shall gather in the Cloud Hall (*yuntang*) to prepare a simple vegetarian meal specifically for the newly appointed Abbot;

we humbly pray that you will graciously deign to honor us with your presence. Thereupon, the messenger proceeds before the newly appointed Abbot to prostrate and make the same request (following the same ritual protocol). The Abbot and the guest master (*ketou*) shall act together.

The special messenger-in-charge shall request the various attendants to hang the "Tea and Refreshments" sign inside the Sangha Hall, opposite the Abbot’s seat, and establish a seat for the newly appointed official;
at the head of the guest-master’s board in the outer hall, a seat for the special messenger-in-charge shall be set up.

The attendant in charge shall be instructed in advance to invite the newly appointed official to the Abbot’s quarters prior to the mealtime to sit briefly, awaiting the striking of the board for the assembly of monks.
The special messenger enters the hall and proceeds to the Abbot’s quarters to invite the incumbent Abbot (and the newly appointed one) to attend the hall together.

The messenger follows them into the hall, first bowing to the incumbent Abbot and returning to his position; then bowing to the newly appointed Abbot and returning to his position. He returns to the center of the hall, bows to inquire after their well-being, and bows to the assembly as they take their seats.

Advancing before the incense burner, he burns incense (holding the incense case in his right hand and placing the sticks on the burner with his left hand). Turning to the left, he first bows to inquire after the incumbent Abbot’s well-being.

Again, burn incense before the newly appointed abbot and inquire after his well-being (the remaining rites are the same as before). After the food has been served, the distribution of *dakṣiṇā* (monetary gifts), and the tea ceremony are concluded, first collect the abbot’s cup.

The special envoy approaches the abbot; for the first formal prostration, he says: "I have prepared these humble vegetarian offerings, and I am deeply moved by the Honored Master’s gracious acceptance.
For the second prostration, he says the same. He then performs three full prostrations (*chu lǐ*). The abbot briefly replies. The special envoy escorts the abbot out to the outer hall.

Returning to the hall once more, he again collects the cup for the newly appointed official (*xinming*). When the special envoy arrives before the newly appointed official, [the latter] performs two prostrations with opened sitting cloths (the wording is as before).
Thirdly, he performs a prostration by touching the ground; the newly appointed official briefly replies. He escorts the newly appointed official out.

The special envoy returns to the hall once more, burns incense, performs three prostrations with fully opened sitting cloths, circumambulates the hall once, and together with those in the outer hall, returns to the center to bow in greeting, thanking the assembly. He then collects the cups.
After the bell is struck three times, the special messenger shall leave the hall and go to the Abbot’s quarters to thank the incumbent Abbot; next, he shall thank the newly appointed Abbot;

and next, he shall thank the administrative office for providing the vegetarian feast. He shall then invite both the incumbent and the newly appointed Abbots to attend the evening meal, followed by the medicinal congee at night and the fruit soup.

On all these occasions, the two classes of officials and the retired elders should be invited to serve as companions (this is an ancient custom that ought to be diligently observed; nowadays, it is often treated with excessive brevity, consisting merely of the distribution of monetary offerings).
Regarding the entrustment of the Dharma robes to a successor:
the Buddhas and Patriarchs transmitted them so that mind may illuminate mind; masters and disciples received and bestowed them such that the "cracking" and the "pecking" occur simultaneously.

Those who attained their records at Vulture Peak all transmitted the Tathāgata’s teachings and contemplations; however, because the conditions for their flourishing rested with Kāśyapa, he entrusted them specifically to one individual.

The oral lineage of the Golden Mouth was transmitted through twenty-three generations until it reached Siṃha (Shizi). Our Second Patriarch, under the Northern Qi dynasty, realized that the three wisdoms of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* are attained within a single moment of mind;
he distantly inherited the tradition from Nāgārjuna and bestowed it upon Nan-yueh and Tiantai.

When [Tiantai] first met Nan-yueh, the latter taught him the four practices of peaceful dwelling (*catur-āśvāsa-caryā*) so that he might cultivate his mind through study. He attained a wondrous realization of samādhi, and thus the succession has been maintained down to the present.

Its radiant glow still shines upon us today; thus we know that what has been transmitted are the teachings and the contemplations. That which was transmitted by Yì (Huineng) was merely a token of faith. Alas!
The corruption of prevailing customs causes people to forget the root and pursue the branches, remaining in a state of ignorant confusion as to what it is they inherit.
To say "master" and "disciple"—is this not truly shameful? If one receives a new mandate to succeed to the Dharma...
The Master first confided his intention to his closest confidant and requested that he receive the Dharma robe.

On the day of the transmission, the new appointee respectfully visited the Master’s private quarters; the Master then sat cross-legged in the center and delivered a brief word of exhortation before bestowing the robe.

Immediately, the newly appointed one removed his old garments, donned the Dharma robe, performed nine prostrations before the Master, and withdrew. That same day, the new appointee was formally invited to take office.

At the conclusion of the midday meal, the distribution of alms (*dakṣiṇā*) shall take place; that evening, the medicinal food (*bhaiṣajya*) will be served, and all dharma-relatives are invited to attend as companions.
The monastery shall provide hospitality for the invitees and the special envoys.

One day prior, the guest-inviting attendant (*pūrvavastu-vaiyāvṛtyakara*) is first dispatched to the quarters of the newly appointed official to invite him and his special envoy. On the following day, they proceed to...
