In the center of the inner side facing the main hall, the seat for the newly appointed official is established; to the left and right, the seats for the special envoys are established.
In both rows, the veteran officials and honored companions burn incense and offer monetary gifts (*dakṣiṇā*), while the incense-bearer performs the ritual according to the usual procedure.

On the day the person invited to officiate departs, after the morning gruel has been consumed, they shall go together with the special envoy to the Abbot’s quarters (*upadhivāra*) to offer incense and pay their respects.

Next, they shall proceed to the storehouse office (*kośa-sthāna*) and bid farewell to all the various administrative offices. The storehouse office shall have someone in advance hang a curtain at the entrance of the mountain gate and arrange seats for the occasion.

The great bell is struck to assemble the community for a formal send-off, during which the tea and soup rituals (*kaddan-rai*) are performed; the head administrator (*shuso-chishitsu*) burns incense (the performance of the ritual is the same as in contemporary practice).
If the person being sent off is a renowned elder, a Great West Hall Abbot, or a Head Seat (*shuso*), the incumbent abbot must ascend the seat (*jōza*).

Furthermore, the newly appointed official must, on the night before, have his attendant and colleagues carry incense to the Abbot’s Quarters (*hōjō*), where he performs a prostration with unopened sitting cloth (*sokurei*) and requests the loan of the Dharma seat (*hōza*).
The following day, after the morning gruel has been consumed, a seat for the newly appointed official is set up facing the Dharma throne; to its left, a seat for the incumbent abbot is also prepared.

The drum is struck to assemble the assembly, and the incumbent ascends the throne. He instructs an attendant to invite the newly appointed official to take his seat (although invited, he must not sit upon it, as doing so would obstruct the assembly).

The incumbent praises the virtues of the new appointee, explaining that he has come forth for the sake of the Dharma; he then exhorts the community to offer praise and soothes the thirst of the assembly’s longing.

After the Dharma talk, the abbot descends from his seat (this refers to what the ancients called the "method of leading the assembly"). The abbot returns to his seat and stands to the left, facing outward.

The special envoy, together with the attendant, approaches the newly appointed official; after the salutation is completed, the newly appointed official steps forward to salute the abbot, followed by saluting the two orders of the assembly.
He then ascends the seat to proclaim the Dharma, expresses his gratitude, and concludes the session. Upon descending from the seat, he proceeds to the abbot.
First, perform three prostrations with contact; next, stand facing the Dharma seat and take leave of the assembly by performing three prostrations with contact in unison.
Exit through the western corridor while the assembly sees you off at the gate, where the ceremony for serving tea and soup is conducted as before.
The New Abbot’s Entry into Office (Total of Ten Items):

Regarding entry according to the ancient method, the abbot carries his waist-bag and wears a bamboo hat to the head of the mountain gate; there he removes the hat and offers incense, for which there is a formal discourse (*fayu*).

Before the Sangha Hall, at the designated place for unpacking and washing one's feet, one takes up the robes and puts them on. Entering the Sangha Hall, one burns incense before the Holy Monk (Śāstṛ) and performs three prostrations with the sitting cloth fully spread;

the accompanying attendants prostrate along with him. Having completed the formal registration (*guādá*), he proceeds to the Buddha Hall to offer incense according to the ritual manual, performing three prostrations with the sitting cloth fully spread, followed by a formal address.
He then offers incense in the Earth Deity Hall and the Patriarchs' Hall, each accompanied by its respective formal address. Finally, he enters the Abbot’s Quarters.

The Abbot occupies the quarters and delivers a formal discourse; subsequently, he performs prostrations in the hall to offer prayers for the Sage. This was the ancient custom, though nowadays it is rarely practiced.

When a newly appointed official arrives, one must consider where they will be stationed. If they are arriving from nearby, the assembly goes out to welcome them; if from afar, only the two orders and the retired elders do so.
The Abbot shall instruct a special messenger to announce the arrival in advance, thereby exempting the assembly from traveling far to receive them. If [the guest] is stationed...
At the lower quarters, preparations for the hot water and fruit offerings shall be completed; the elders of the two orders shall serve as attendants.

On the appointed day and hour, the Abbot’s quarters shall order the officials of the various bureaus to prepare everything in advance. The hanging of the Abbot’s plaque shall be announced to the assembly.

At the designated time, the great bell and all ritual instruments shall be sounded. The assembly shall welcome him at the gate, standing in two rows; the junior servants shall stand outside the assembly, while the new arrivals stand within.

When the new appointee arrives at the gate, he burns incense, turns his body, and stands still; he recites the formal liturgy and proceeds directly into the Great Hall to burn incense and recite the liturgy.

He performs three full prostrations with opened sitting cloths (*kṣauma*). The bell before the Sangha Hall is struck, and the assembly first returns to their bowl-positions. The new appointee stands in his position;

the new incumbent enters the hall, burns incense before the Holy Monk (*Seng-seng*), and performs three full prostrations with opened sitting cloths. The attendants prostrate together. The Rector (*Vina*) then approaches the Abbot.

First, the new appointee performs a greeting and leads a circuit around the hall once; the two orders escort the new appointee back to the bowl position (*bō-wèi*), where he performs a prostration with the head touching the ground (*chù-lǐ*).

(Alternatively, if the new appointee has previously served administrative duties at the mountain monastery, he does not lead the circuit. Next, he proceeds to the Hall of the Local Deity (*tǔdì-táng*) and the Patriarchs’ Hall (*zǔ-táng*) to burn incense, for which there are specific ritual instructions (*fǎyǔ*).

Upon reaching the Abbot’s quarters (*fāngwǎng*), he takes his place in the room; the attendant (*shì-zhě*) steps forward, offers incense, and bows in greeting, then stands to one side awaiting the delivery of the ritual instructions, after which he departs.

The new appointee advances to the table, where the administrative official (jishi) has prepared the formal document (as seen below). A tray and cloth cover are brought forward, and the temple seal is presented for the new appointee to inspect the seal-closure.

The administrative official opens the seal; once the new appointee has inspected the seal-impression, he first applies his flower-signature (kakyō) upon the document, followed by the date, and then affixes his seal.
The administrative official collects the document, the attendant (shisho) collects the seal, and they withdraw from the table. The abbot then rises.

The entire assembly of administrative officers (zhishi) stands in formation before the incense chair; the head officer inserts incense and performs three prostrations with two full bows (*liangzhan sanli*). The first bow says:

"On this occasion, we humbly receive the grace of the Venerable Master (Heshang) in presiding over the Dharma assembly and the mountain gate; we are overcome with honor and fortune. The second bow says: "At this time of year, we respectfully wish that the newly appointed Hall Head Great Monk (Daheshang) may enjoy much well-being in his daily life.

Third, they perform prostrations touching the ground (*chuli*). Next, the head officers (*doutou*) and veteran monks (*qinjiu*) step forward to insert incense (the incense is not accepted). [This applies to] the various mountain monasteries (*zhushan*).

When the *caohé* (congratulatory ceremony) is finished, the guest master and attendant monks announce: "We request the various mountain abbots, the Head Preceptor, the two classes of officials, and the elders to take their seats for the offering of hot water.
When the hot water offering is concluded, the official guests and the various mountains are invited for refreshments (*diǎndìn*).

If the former abbot has been reassigned and has not yet arrived, or if he is retired and has not yet occupied his quarters in the East Hall, the ritual of succession is performed; once the newly appointed abbot has completed the *caohé*, the bell in front of the Sangha Hall is struck.
The Abbot shall personally escort the predecessor to his quarters and perform a single prostration with the head touching the ground (*tai-chuk-ri*).
Next, the two classes of officials and the assembly shall offer congratulations, after which the Abbot returns to his quarters; finally, the attendants shall all pay their respects.

Upon receiving the new appointment, the head administrators of the Monastery shall wait for the formalities in the quarters to be completed; once the necessary items—such as the ceremonial cloth (*pān-fu*), incense burner, and candles—are prepared, they shall carry incense in their sleeves and proceed to the Abbot’s Quarters (*fangzhang*) to request the midday meal.

They perform two prostrations with hands opened and three prostrations with hands folded. At the first prostration, they say: "At the hour of noon, we have prepared a vegetarian meal in the Cloud Hall (*yuntang*) and await your gracious presence."

I humbly pray that you will graciously deign to grant me your presence; your servant is overcome with trepidation and perspiration. (Secondly, unfold the letter and exchange greetings regarding the weather. Thirdly, perform three prostrations. The abbot briefly replies.

When the administrative officials present their petition, the guest master receives it at the abbot’s quarters. The storehouse guest master prepares the seating within the Sangha Hall for the abbot’s position.
The officials perform their rites in the same manner as when they are specially entertained.

Regarding the ancient custom of opening the hall for a long-life ceremony (*zhùshòu*) at monasteries within the imperial capital: the court would dispatch an official on a fast courier to respectfully invite the master;

alternatively, a provincial commissioner or local officials from the prefecture or county would send ceremonial gifts to request that he attend a certain monastery, or that the monastery itself provide funds and provisions to establish a vegetarian feast and open the hall.

The individual petitions of the officials, as well as the notices for tea and soup services, can be found in various collections of official documents. Recently, when opening the hall at various temples, the officials provide their own provisions.
Upon arrival, the attendant (śrāmaṇera) assigns the novices (karmadāna) to arrange the Dharma seat (dharmāsana), cover the various quarters, and hang the "Upward Hall" (shàngtáng) plaque.
A written list of the names of the officials and the various mountain abbots (zhūshān) is prepared in advance and presented to the abbot (vihārasvāmin) while he is on the seat.

On the left, the seats are prepared, with tables, cloths, and cloaks laid out, and incense burners, candles, and the written petitions (sū tiē) arranged in order. The *Weina* (Venerable Leader) first proclaims the official document;

the *Shouzuo* (Head Seat) proclaims the petition for the Main Gate (*shānmén*). Subsequently, the various *Toushou* (Senior Officers) or renowned masters from various mountains and rivers proclaim the remaining petitions.
The administrative officers (*zhīshì*) have previously invited a senior master from among the various mountain abbots to preside before the seat and strike the gavel.

The officials are seated facing [the abbot], and the attendant covers the abbot’s quarters while the drum is struck and the assembly gathers. The attendant enters together with the special envoy to invite the abbot to come forth.

With the ringing of bells and gongs and the carrying of banners, flowers, peach-wood staffs, and lamps, they welcome him to the Dharma Hall. He stands at the principal seat where the cushions have been laid out, as was done during the formal invitation.
Once the robe has not yet been picked up, the robe is drawn out, the dharma words are recited, and the dharma robe is donned; when this is finished, the special envoy steps forward.

Inserting incense and performing the ritual prostrations: First, unfolding the mat, one says: "Humbly receiving the Master’s grace in presiding over this Dharma assembly, our innermost feelings are overcome with the utmost awe and gratitude. Second, unfolding the mat again, one exchanges greetings regarding the weather. Third, touching the ground in prostration, the Abbot returns one bow.
The special messenger presents the official document; the Abbot receives it and recites the Dharma words.

The special messenger takes it and hands it to the Rector (Vina), who reads it aloud. The attendant carries the memorial scroll (su). Next follow the scrolls from the Mountain Gate, the various monasteries, and the various masters of the rivers and lakes.

Each successive section contains dharma words for distribution and recitation. When requesting an incumbent official to open the hall, there is a formal petition which the official personally receives;
upon its completion, there are dharma words. The abbot turns toward the seat within the incense burner and bows in greeting, then points to the seat with dharma words.
Ascending the seat, he picks up the incense to offer prayers for the Emperor, followed by prayers for the Imperial Preceptor (Di-shi) and the various provincial, court, and regional authorities.
The civil and military officials of the district and county, along with the incense-bearing attendants, each offer incense once, followed by the burning of *congxiang* (incense from the rear).

Only the *chenglingxiang* (incense for receiving instructions) is taken out by the Abbot from his breast pocket and personally inserted into the burner. He then folds his robes, sits in the lotus posture, and the attendant descends from the seat to perform a formal greeting (*wensun*) toward the Abbot.

The two orders of officers then step forward from their ranks to perform a greeting (the ritual is identical to that performed during the morning and evening formal sermons). The abbots of various monasteries escort him back inside.
The head monk (yuanzhuang) shall also come forward to inquire after the abbot’s well-being; once the abbot has risen and the greetings are concluded, he shall return to his seat.

The attendant (shizhe) ascends the platform to burn incense and inquire after the abbot’s health. The abbot shall then direct the attendant to invite the officials and the heads of various monasteries to be seated.

The head of the assembly (shangshou) from among the visiting monks shall step forward and strike the mallet once, saying: "In this Dharma assembly of dragons and elephants, one should contemplate the primary meaning. Once the abbot has finished presenting the main outline (tigan), he shall first express his gratitude to the officials.

[The assembly] includes the various mountains, rivers, lakes, famous sites, and veteran practitioners (and so forth). On this day, the opening of the hall is specifically for the purpose of offering prayers for the Emperor; I dare not elaborate further in my introductory remarks.

The special envoy, the administrative officers, the heads of departments, the veteran practitioners, and the great assembly have been briefly mentioned as they passed before our ears; the details will be presented during the evening *can* and the general discourse (*pushe*).

Having concluded the session, the striker of the gavel strikes once again and says: "Observe closely the Dharma-King’s Dharma—the Dharma-King’s Dharma is thus! [Then] he descends from his seat. First.

Once the officials have finished their congratulations, the *jishi* (administrative officer) escorts the guests to their seats, while the *guanban*, *ketou*, and *xingzhe* (attendant monks) immediately advance with incense burners and candles, arranging them in a single file before the seats.
The special envoy offers incense, performs two prostrations with hands opened (*liangzhan*) and three full bows (*sanli*), and concludes.

The hall attendant then calls out: "Greeting from the various mountain monasteries. Next, he calls out: "Greeting from the West Hall. After the prostrations are performed, he again calls out: "Greeting from the administrative officers," followed by two prostrations with hands opened and three full bows.

The Ritual Master again calls out, "The Head Seat and the Assembly attend to their duties. All the veteran monks (*qínjiù*) simultaneously insert incense and, together with the assembly, perform two prostrations with opened sitting cloths and three full prostrations (*liǎnzhǎn sānlǐ*).

Next, the renowned masters from various regions, former associates, Dharma relatives, and fellow countrymen complete their greetings and proceed to the seat of the Abbot. The Abbot takes his place upon the chair.

The Attendant (*shìzhě*) inserts incense and performs three full prostrations with opened sitting cloths. The junior disciples (*xiǎoshī*), grand-disciples (*shísūn*), and others insert incense and perform three prostrations. Next, the Ritual Master...
The hall attendants (*jūgyōsha*) insert incense and perform prostrations; next, the head of the assembly (*santō*) leads the group of attendants to insert incense and perform prostrations;

next, the hall stewards (*chikishitsu*), palanquin carriers (*kyōban*), stable keepers (*shōkō*), head laborers (*sakutō*), senior servants (*rōrōjin*), and male servants (*hikoku*) complete their prostrations.

Thereupon, the abbot proceeds to the guest quarters to express his gratitude to the officials and the various mountain abbots. After the midday meal, they visit the administrative offices (*shurō*) in successive order, and all the various monastic halls gather at one location.
Outside the gate, incense stands, censers, candles, and seating are arranged, each with its proper decorum. They await the arrival of the Abbot;

when he reaches the lowest-ranking seat, they welcome him inside and invite him to sit cross-legged. The Abbot offers incense, and the head official replies with incense, briefly exchanging pleasantries regarding the weather and expressing thanks before escorting him out.
Alternatively, if the long corridors are divided into several sections, seats are set up in each, and the various head officials' quarters also arrange seats within their doors.
The lower-ranking officials shall welcome and escort [the new abbot]; when the former abbot proceeds through the hall, they shall also go to offer a single stick of incense.
Upon his return, he shall pay respects to the assembly of practitioners, who stand in two rows to inquire after his well-being.
The monastery shall specially provide tea and soup for the newly installed abbot.

The tea service announcement board shall be posted in advance in front of the Sangha Hall, both upper and lower sections; the Kusi (Storehouse Office) shall also prepare a formal invitation document (the format is shown below).

Accompanied by a carrying cloth (*bun-fuku*), an incense burner, and candles, they shall proceed to the Abbot’s quarters (*hōjō*) to offer incense and pay respects to extend the invitation. If the Abbot declines, they shall perform a prostration with unopened sitting cloth (*sokusai*).

Having made the request, they say: "We have come to serve tea specifically for you; we humbly pray that you will graciously condescend to attend. Once this has been stated, they present the document and immediately instruct the *Kakutō* (Guest Master) to invite the two orders of officials, the retired elders (*kinjū*), and the assembly.

The attendant carrying the "Tea and Soup" sign hangs it up and notifies the assembly. Within the Sangha Hall, the seat for the Abbot is prepared. When the meal is finished (the board is struck three times and the drum rolls once), the assembly is gathered.
The administrative officers bow to the Abbot as he enters the hall and returns to his place; they bow as he sits. One incense stick is burned;
the Abbot bows before the incense burner, circumambulates behind the Holy Monk, and returns to the center to perform a formal greeting while standing, awaiting the special tea service.
Having bowed before the Abbot, one withdraws to the rear of the Sacred Monk (Śāstṛ) and exits to the right. Holding the incense, one performs three prostrations with the *zhǎn* (cloth) spread;

rising, one leads the entire assembly before the Abbot for two *zhǎn* and three prostrations, escorts him out, and returns to the hall to burn incense. One bows to the upper and lower sections and withdraws after collecting the bowls.
The rites for the serving of hot water (*tāng*) are identical to those for tea.
That evening, after the general sermon (pūsē) and the meal, the attendant informed the abbot, saying, "This evening there is a general sermon.

He ordered the hall administrators' attendants to hang the sign for the general sermon to notify the assembly, and instructed the tea-heads to set up seats in the abbot’s hall. [The text continues: "I, the humble and small Dharma-robe wearer..."
The incense burner, flower vase, candle stand, ceremonial cloth, and attendant shall be prepared;

the names of the special envoys, the elders of the two orders, renowned figures from various regions, and those temporarily visiting the abbot’s quarters, the library, or the storehouse must be recorded.

The attendants entering the hall for the first time, as well as any government officials or monastics from other mountains who have been invited to stay overnight, shall each have their names listed in order and submitted in advance for formal notification. Once the evening bell tolls, the hall office acolyte shall inform the attendant.
The abbot covers [the bowl] and, next, the two classes of officials cover theirs; the boards of the various quarters are struck three times, and the Dharma drum is struck once.

The assembly gathers, and the two classes of officials return to their positions and stand still. The abbot emerges and ascends the seat; the attendant and the two classes of officials come forward to perform the ritual salutation (wensun).

Once this is finished, the abbot delivers his formal discourse (fayu) and concludes with an expression of gratitude. The ritual assistant (xingzhe) holds a candle, and the attendant presents the list of names. I first express my thanks to the one who knows [the proceedings].
The administrative heads (shishoutou), those of the East and West Halls, special envoys, veteran monks, and the assembly shall ensure that all matters are thoroughly detailed.

At the conclusion of the session, the guest-head attendant (kezitou) and the junior practitioners (xingzhe) shall call out: "The Abbot invites the venerable masters from various mountains, the two classes of officials, the single-cottage residents, and the veteran monks; please proceed to the Abbot’s quarters for the offering of hot water.
The administrative staff shall escort the visiting guests back to their seats. The Abbot shall serve hot water and fruit to the venerable masters from various mountains and his attendants.
The following day, the donor’s memorial altar is used for the chanting of scriptures (as well as at the pagodas of successive abbots).

Incense is offered at the treasury office, where a person is dispatched to solemnly prepare offerings; the donor’s memorial altar for the temple’s land-granting benefactor is also prepared with offerings. Once the morning gruel is finished, the assembly is gathered.

The abbot arrives, offers incense, and serves tea and soup; having completed these, he returns to his seat. The Head Seat begins the scripture recitation, while the Rector faces toward [the assembly].
If there are pagodas from previous generations that one should visit, one must go to each personally to offer incense, present food, and perform prostrations;
the administrative office (kusi) shall prepare the sacrificial offerings and entertain the special envoy.

The administrative officer shall first report to the Abbot regarding the special envoy and those who will proclaim the memorial and the official notice, as well as the weight of the offerings, the full set of robes and bowls, and the supplementary offerings;

these must all be prepared in accordance with proper ritual propriety. On the appointed day, the items shall be hung and displayed in the dormitory hall, and seats shall be arranged for the two orders of monks and the retired elders to serve as companions.
A special seat shall be prepared specifically for the envoy, and the Guest Master shall personally invite the envoy. The rest...
When a layperson requests an invitation for the guest master of the abbot’s quarters, the ritual procedure is the same as for a special invitation to ordinary guests.

If they request that the two orders of officers be invited, the two orders shall wait until the reception of the special envoy is concluded; they should then be invited to visit the abbot’s quarters to consult and inform him, after which they may withdraw. The abbot must not grant permission immediately.

Suddenly, out of consideration for the guest, the abbot graciously saw him off, instructing the attendant and the guest-head acolyte to prepare a tray, cloth, incense burner, candles, and hot water utensils.
The abbot, accompanied by his attendant, proceeded to the administrative office (*kusi*) and various quarters to urge the guest-head to remain;

the guest-head first announced that he was withdrawing, and as the guest departed outside, the abbot went to the right side of the gate to welcome him back in, leading him to the seat of honor. They sat facing each other, and the attendant burned incense.

When the abbot serves hot water and takes back the bowl, he should treat the visitor with full courtesy and urge them to remain. Even if their term of office has expired, they must remain patient and wait until the abbot has a moment of leisure before formally requesting leave to depart.
Upon returning from a visit, one should report the matter and express gratitude.
This applies to all arrivals and departures.

After entering the monastery, one must first have an audience with the local magistrates and their subordinates, followed by visits to the patrons (*dānapati*) and high-ranking officials residing nearby.

When visiting these officials and nobles, it is customary to present a ceremonial silk scarf (*paozi*) as a token of respect; this must always be prepared in advance and kept ready for use as the occasion arises.

Regarding the various monasteries, formal letters of introduction (*menshuang*) must be used to announce visits, express thanks, or inquire after others. All matters concerning these visits must be reported and submitted one by one to the administrative officers (*zhishi*), who shall then inform the Abbot (*zhuchi*).

When departing for a distant journey, instruct the attendant to convey the message to the head monks and administrative officers, and notify the storehouse office to keep watch for the date of his return.

Instruct the hall office attendant to hang up the Abbot’s plaque to inform the assembly, and have them wait for his arrival at the mountain by ringing the great bell to assemble the community for a gate reception.

First, have the attendant deliver a message to waive the formalities; upon exiting the sedan chair, he should inquire after their well-being (saying, "Do not trouble the assembly") and proceed directly to the Buddha Hall.
At the ground altar, the Head Seat leads the assembly to burn incense before the Abbot’s quarters. Once the Abbot has received them, he bows in greeting; the assembly then withdraws.

The Guest Master bows and invites the two classes of officials and the elders to offer hot water; after a brief exchange of conversation, they retire. The Abbot’s attendant then inserts incense and performs prostrations.
Next, the Head of the Assembly leads the assembly of attendants to perform prostrations. Upon completion, the Abbot must visit the various quarters to acknowledge his courtesy. If...

When entering or leaving the city walls at dawn or dusk, there was no fixed time; it was not necessary to announce one's movements. However, whenever one returned secretly to the abbot’s quarters, the two orders of officers and the veteran monks would all go to the abbot’s quarters to pay their respects.

After the handover of the miscellaneous items and entry into the monastery, the senior members of the two orders shall discuss in detail the affairs of the mountain gate. All imperial calligraphies, precious vessels, land deeds,
and miscellaneous items shall first be presented to the abbot, and subsequently presented to the senior members of the two orders for inspection and verification in their presence.
Item by item, verify and settle the accounts with full clarity; calculate the ledgers of wealth and grain to determine exactly how much is currently held, and present this to the Abbot.

Furthermore, prepare a public notice to inform all the monasteries: "Be aware that in many places, when an abbot is about to retire or be replaced, those in charge often engage in fraudulent practices and exact extortionate levies, leading to grave consequences. This must not be overlooked."

On the day prior to the inauguration ceremony, the retired officials (*gynju*) of the two classes of nobility, along with the head seat (*shuse*), the administrative officers (*chiji*), and the retired officials, each leading one person, shall go to the abbot’s quarters (*bajang*) to offer incense and formally invite the abbot.
Next, they shall invite the attendant (*sidae*) and junior disciples. On the actual day, a special seat for the abbot shall be established within the meditation hall (*immnang*).

The seating order for the two ranks of officials (*liǎng xù*) and the retired elders (*qín jiù*) is as usual. After the attendant novices (*xiǎo shī*) have finished their inquiries with the abbot, they take their seats at the end of the row of the two ranks and retired elders.
When the time comes, the Head Seat (*shǒu zuò*) requests the abbot to emerge from his quarters; he bows to the abbot’s seat and performs the formal salutations.

If the abbot declines the invitation, he burns incense, steps forward to perform a prostration with open hands (*wèn xùn*), and distributes alms (*xià qīn*). The three leaders—the Head Seat, the Administrative Officers (*zhī shì*), and the Retired Elders—then perform their salutations.
Upon returning to their seats and finishing the meal, the Head Seat (shouzuo) rises to burn incense, returns to his seat, and partakes of tea.

If elders from various mountains, those who have served in office, Dharma relatives, or junior disciples invite [the assembly] to the Quarters Hall for tea service, the ritual procedure is the same; however, the relative height of the seating arrangements for the host of the tea service should be determined according to the circumstances of the moment.
The Ten Regular Duties of the Abbot:

On the evening of the day before the assembly for the New or Full Moon, the attendant reports to the Abbot, saying, "Tomorrow morning there will be an assembly for the blessing of the Emperor. The Abbot then orders the hall steward's acolyte to hang the notice board for the assembly.
The hall plaque is covered for the two shifts; the early attendant again reports to the Abbot.

The guest-head acolyte spreads the Dharma seat, the tea-head acolyte burns incense and lights the candles, and the hall-office acolyte strikes the *kuòbǎn* three times each to notify the assembly to enter the hall.
Upon the striking of the drum, the two orders of officers lead the monks to the front of the Dharma seat, where they perform a bow and divide into their respective ranks.

Regarding the formal procedure (if among the assembly there are those who do not wait for the leader to arrive but instead take their seats first, this is contrary to the Dharma): Once the Abbot has ascended the seat, offered incense, and completed the prayer for longevity, he sits in the lotus posture.

The two classes of officers perform the *wenshun* (inquiry) bow. After the attendant has ascended the seat and requested the Dharma, [the Abbot] expresses his thanks—either the administrative head (*zhishi*) or a senior officer (*shoutou*) first follows the custom of the mountain gate, followed by the West Hall monks and the retired elders (*qijiu seng*). (Note: In winter, when the Abbot addresses the assembly, he says: "The weather is cold; please each cover your heads.")

If there are various mountain abbots or those of great renown present among the assembly, seats are arranged on the left side and seats for the officials and guests on the right side (if one recognizes the etiquette of honoring the Dharma, one does not sit).
Regarding the expression of thanks: those of the two ranks [of monks] first proceed to the foot of the Dharma seat to perform their bows of gratitude;

those of the subsequent two ranks express their thanks after the first group has done so, then proceed to the abbot’s quarters (*fangzhang*) to pay their respects. This has been the tradition of the mountain schools (*shanjia*) since ancient times.
One should not be bound by the regularity of the new and full moon services; since these have recently been neglected, they must be performed.
When offering prayers for the Emperor’s longevity, one should instead propagate the Dharma lineage and guide future generations by expounding upon the essential meanings of the teachings.

Regarding the affairs of the monastery, discuss them directly with the Abbot during tea meetings; do not speak of worldly matters that cause the assembly to grow weary of listening. As for the eminent monks of the West Hall:
When the Head Seat (Shouzuo) of the front hall accepts an invitation from another mountain, the Abbot leads him to the seat to deliver a formal discourse; he does not offer incense.

This applies equally when a donor invites him to ascend the seat, as these occasions are not restricted by time. (Other protocols are as previously described in the "Section on Benedictions and Praises").

Regarding the diagram for the Dharma Seat on the first and fifteenth days: when the粥鼓 (congee drum) sounds during the first and fifteenth days of the month, the tea-head of the Abbot’s quarters shall prepare the hot water, tea, bowls, and cups, and place them upon the platform in the Sangha Hall (as well as the dormitory hall). For the serving of tea, the congee drum is struck at the time of the first and fifteenth-day congee meal.

First, invite the visiting guests. Wait for the person who distributes the bowl-water to exit, then take your seat. Invite the two orders of monks and request the elders to come forward for greetings, saying:

"The Abbot invites you to the Small Hall for tea. The attendant waits for the person distributing the bowl-water to exit, returns to the center to greet the Holy Monk, burns incense before him, and then proceeds to greet those in the upper and lower sections as well as the outer hall’s upper and lower sections, finally returning to the center.
Standing at the side to inquire after [the abbot’s] health, strike the bell once; as the cups are passed, strike the bell once;

as the tea is being served, when half the cups have been distributed, the attendant, as before, inquires after the health of those in the inner and outer halls, returns to the center to inquire, and withdraws. Strike the bell once to collect the cups, then strike the bell three times.

Upon leaving the hall, the Abbot’s quarters strikes one round of the small board (*banban*). When the assembly arrives, they inquire after his health; once the sounding of the board ceases, they depart.

When the assembly is seated, the attendant burns incense (standing with his head toward the east and facing inward). He returns to the center to inquire after the master’s well-being, then steps forward three and a half paces before the incense burner for a minor inquiry.

He opens both hands; leaving the lid on his left forearm, he holds the base of the burner with his right hand and places it back upon the lid. With his right hand, he burns the incense, holding the base of the burner on the side-table. He then takes the lid with both hands, closes it firmly, and performs a minor inquiry. Turning to the left, he takes three and a half steps and performs another inquiry. When the tea arrives, he inquires after the master’s well-being, bows for the tea, and withdraws.

The Seating Order for Tea and Soup for the Senior Monks of Both Quarters (Senior Monks of the East Quarter from the Prior to the Assistant Prior; Senior Monks of the West Quarter from the Rector to the Scribe).
Generally, when the Abbot convenes tea or soup, the Head Seat divides the ranks. If the Head Seat’s position is vacant, the rank is divided down to the Guest Master.

It is improper for administrative officers (*zhishi*) to intermingle with the ranks; the positions of the heads of practice (*doutou*) in the western division must likewise not be mixed with those of the eastern division.
Regarding the seating order: if high-ranking monasteries arrive, the various mountain abbots divide the seats, with the Head Seat (Shouzuo) taking the first position followed by the others in rank.
If it is a seasonal gathering at the monastery or if smaller monasteries arrive, only the Head Seat divides the seats while the other abbots face the Abbot and sit in their designated positions.
If the Abbot does not rise for the tea or soup served in the Monks' Hall (Mengtang), the senior retired elders (Dajiujiu) occupy the host’s seat in the Monks' Hall.
When the Head Seat (Shouzuo) departs to attend to the Abbot’s duties, the position of the Head Seat is likewise vacant; the Senior Monks (Qijiu) then face the Abbot.

The seating arrangement for the Abbot is established according to the rites used in the Great Hall or the Dharma Hall. Whenever the Abbot’s seat is vacant, it remains empty; the seating order for the two classes of monks follows the standard protocol.
Regarding the tea service for the assembly at the West Hall:

the head seat (shouzuo) of the West Hall shall divide the participants. Those who have served their home mountain and those from various other monasteries shall sit according to the rank of their respective offices;

those of equal office shall sit next to one another (the format is shown below). Lately, many disputes over seniority have arisen due to the seating order, thereby causing discord within the monastic community.

If the ritual propriety (*li*) of the assembly is neglected, the abbot (*zhuchi*) must act according to public consensus; this is what is meant by the guest observing propriety while the host selects [the participants].
The same applies when the administrative office (*kusu*) convenes the West Hall (*xi xu*). If the abbot does not attend, the Chief Administrator (*dusi*) acts as presiding head;

if the head of the quarters (*toushou*) or the Head Seat (*shouzuo*) acts as presiding head, the Head Seat does not attend, and the next-ranking head takes his place. This is the protocol for the primary seat on the mountain.
When a high-ranking monk departs from one mountain to join another, or when a monk of the "Jianghu" (wandering) rank departs,
it is specifically for the sake of the Great Mountains that the abbot is provided with tea and refreshments.
One day prior to his departure, the abbot orders an attendant to carry a tray and cloth, upon which are placed the letter of invitation, an incense burner, a candle stand, and an incense case.

The attendant goes to burn incense and offer a formal invitation, or may omit the bow; on the following day, he prepares name-identification tablets according to the guest list, sets them out on a table covered with a ceremonial cloth and a colored shroud in front of the Abbot’s Hall.
When guests arrive, they first identify themselves by their tablets. The attendant reports their arrival to the Abbot, who receives them.

Once the guests have entered, performed the ritual salutation (*wenshen*), and briefly exchanged greetings regarding the weather and well-being, the attendant performs a salutation and requests the Abbot to "return to his seat for the sake of the guests."

Bowing from one's position, turn to the left and stand at the southeast corner. Wait until everyone is seated; the attendant then performs a *wenshen* (inquiry/greeting) and proceeds before the incense burner.
Turning the body slightly to the side to avoid the designated seat, perform a minor *wenshen* and burn incense (as previously described). Turn to the left and depart;

perform a *wenshen* before the person for whom the service was intended, then turn back to the original spot at the southeast corner and perform a major *wenshen*. Finally, burn the "light-accompanying" incense (*guangban xiang*).

The *xingzhe* (attendant) enters the hall and distributes the food in order, waiting for the time when the rice arrives. The robe-bowl attendant instructs the *xingzhe* to carry out the *qin* (offering).
The attendant burns incense and performs the inquiry for the specific person [as before]. After the *qin* offering is completed, the drum for tea is struck once in sequence;
when the drum ceases, the attendant again burns incense [as per the previous example]. The *xingzhe* advances with the tea, and the attendant advances with the offering for the specific person.
After the initial inquiry and the ritual bow for tea, he turns back to his original position and stands there to inquire after the assembly.

Once the incense has burned out, the attendant collects the bowls, the drum is struck three times, and they exit. Then, acting as a special representative for others, he proceeds to the incense table to bow in thanks.

When abbots from various monasteries come to offer ceremonial tea to the abbot of this monastery, they must first visit the attendant one day prior to briefly explain the purpose of their visit. Together they proceed to the abbot’s quarters;

the attendant announces their arrival, and upon the abbot’s emergence, they present incense and formally invite him. It is not necessary to send a written invitation, as such formality would be considered overly burdensome.
When receiving an invitation from an equal-ranking person, as soon as the invitation has been accepted, one shall have the robe-and-bowl attendant lead the way to visit the storehouse attendant.

The storehouse attendant shall transmit the Abbot’s instructions to prepare the meal. That evening, he shall have the Abbot’s guest-master, together with the attendant who brought the invitation, invite the two classes of officials, the West Hall masters, and the eminent elders to serve as companions. The attendant shall then assign the seating arrangements and oversee their setup.
When the time arrives, the guest is summoned; once the guest has arrived, the person serving tea and refreshments bows and invites him to enter his place and stand.
Only then does the server invite the Abbot to come forward, exchange greetings, and return to his seat. The server bows for him to sit, then steps forward to the incense table to bow.

Proceeding to the side of the incense burner, he performs a minor bow, burns incense with his left hand, turns to the left, and bows before the Abbot. He then turns back toward the west of the incense chair.

Inquire after the health [of the abbot], burn incense, and return to one’s place to wait for the arrival of the meal. When it is time for the meal, burn incense again and go before the abbot to inquire after his health, standing there and waiting.

When the *kṣaṇa* (offering) is presented, stand in line before the abbot to inquire after his health and return to one’s place. Once the meal is finished, rise immediately, burn incense, and go before the abbot to inquire after his health.
When the tea arrives, inquire after his health once more and bow for the tea; then turn around and burn incense at the west side of the incense burner.
The attendant incense returns to its place; the practitioner collects the bowls and withdraws from the table to offer thanks.

Alternatively, if the assembly is served tea or snacks, the "Tea/Snack Service" sign is hung, and on that day, the abbot’s seat is formally prepared in the Sangha Hall. The seat for the person serving tea or snacks is set opposite the abbot.
If the successor to the Dharma arrives at the temple to serve tea or snacks, the seat for the successor is set upon the *zhike* (guest prefect) board.
When the head fire-board sounds, the assembly proceeds to the hall. The person serving tea and cakes invites the Abbot; the Abbot enters the hall and bows to take his seat.

Turning toward the Sacred Monk (Shōsō), he burns incense, then performs a formal inquiry before the Abbot. Turning behind the Sacred Monk, he exits. The Abbot extends his hand to bow the server of tea and cakes to his seat.
When the distribution of food is complete, the server rises, burns incense, and distributes the monetary offerings (*shōchin*). He then asks for permission to depart.

The abbot and the assembly exchange greetings; after the distribution of rice is completed, the bowls are collected and the abbot withdraws from his table. The person serving tea and refreshments burns incense and approaches the abbot to exchange greetings.

Following behind the Sacred Monk (Śāstṛ), they exit and exchange greetings before the brazier. The bell is struck to signal the serving of tea, which is distributed until it reaches the abbot, who bows in greeting.
Once again following behind the Sacred Monk, they proceed to the abbot’s presence and perform two formal prostrations with open palms (*prāñjali*).

At the first unfolding of the three prostrations, he says: "A humble ritual performed in secret for the Exalted One; you have especially condescended to honor us with your presence. Our innermost feelings cannot bear the height of this profound awe. At the second unfolding, [he says] as before. At the third, he performs the prostration of touching the ground to escort the Abbot out.
The person serving tea and refreshments returns to the hall to burn incense, bows to those in the upper and lower sections to thank them for their companionship, and returns to bow to the center.
The bell is struck to collect the bowls, and he proceeds to the Abbot’s quarters to thank him for his gracious visit. The Abbot follows him to the guest quarters.
The Abbot offers thanks.
The patron enters the mountain;
upon arriving at the temple, he first goes to the Guest Prefect’s quarters or the Treasury Office, and is then escorted to the Abbot’s quarters for the offering of tea.
When escorting [the guest] to his lodging, if he is a high-ranking official or a great patron (*dānapati*), one should strike the bell to assemble the community to receive him;

together they proceed to the Abbot’s quarters (*upādhyāya-śālā*) to offer tea. If the patron requests that the Abbot ascend the seat (*āsana*), one first requests the administrative officers (*karmadāna*) to deliberate, then proceeds together to the Abbot’s quarters to offer incense and formally invite him.
On the appointed day, the Dharma seat is prepared, a seat for the patron is arranged before it, the "Ascending the Seat" plaque (*shàngtáng-pái*) is hung, and the bell is struck.
The drum is struck to assemble the community; the Guest Master (zhíguǐ), together with the donor, proceeds to the Abbot’s quarters (shàngfāng) to invite the Abbot.

The Abbot emerges and ascends the seat, sitting cross-legged. The donor sets up a prostration before the seat; the Guest Master bows and leads him to his place to listen to the Dharma (*however, if one accepts the prostrations and remains standing, this constitutes a slighting of the Dharma*). Upon descending from the seat, the donor bows in thanks.
If the meal is for the Sangha, the ingredients and expenses must first be discussed and settled with the administrative officers (zhīshì); the Rector (wéinà) shall verify them.

The number of monks participating in the assembly and the amount of the distribution of offerings (*dakṣiṇā*) should follow the intention of the donor and must not be arbitrarily determined by the monastic community.

Within the Sangha hall, a seat for the donor shall be prepared; after the meal is finished, the administrative officers (*karmadāna*) shall accompany the donor to stand briefly in the Sangha hall to await the departure of the assembly, at which time they shall offer thanks.
Subsequently, the abbot and the administrative officers shall go to the guest quarters to express their gratitude. If there are any items left behind, they shall be returned.

Regarding the funds for the monastic feast (*qiánzāi*) and the abbot’s provisions, the administrative officers (*zhīshì*) must be held accountable to ensure that all offerings and distributions of alms (*pāochǔn*) are prepared in full.

These funds must never be diverted or misappropriated, lest one incur karmic causes and their subsequent effects. As stated in the *Réntiānbǎojiàn*: "One night while Zen Master Zhì of Yúngài Mountain in Húnán sat in his quarters, he suddenly smelled the scent of burning and heard the sound of shackles and manacles.

Upon looking, he saw someone carrying a flaming cangue; the fire flickered incessantly, and the tail of the cangue rested against the door threshold. Startled, the Master asked, 'Who are you? Why have you suffered to such an extreme? The bearer of the cangue replied, 'I am Shǒushùn, who previously resided at this very mountain.'"

"It is not permissible to use the offerings of a donor intended for the Sangha to construct a monastic hall; therefore, one undergoes this suffering. Zhì asked, "By what means might one avoid this? I pray you, tell me. Yuàn said, "I hope that you will provide an appraisal of the value of the monastic hall and provide the funds to fulfill the provisions for the Sangha;

thus you may be spared. Zhì used his own wealth to repay the costs according to those words. One night, he dreamed of Yuàn, who thanked him, saying: "Relying on you, Master, I have escaped the sufferings of hell and been reborn among gods and humans. After three more lifetimes, I shall again become a monk. Even now, the scars from the burns on my face remain.

"If even Master Yuàn—who used the property of the Sangha to build a monastic hall—still suffers such retribution for misappropriating communal goods, how much more so for those in the monasteries today who deny cause and effect? Not only do they misappropriate shared resources, they even go so far as to steal the permanent assets of the monastery and claim them as their own. What should be done about this?"
When visiting various mountains (to see venerable elders, seniors, dharma relatives, dharma heirs, peers, or neighboring monasteries), whenever a venerable elder arrives at the temple,
one must first present a formal notice at the gate; once they reach the Abbot’s quarters, a plaque shall be hung to formally receive the venerable guest.

The bell is struck to assemble the community, who welcome him at the gate. If he prefers a more informal reception, he enters the temple incognito. The abbot prepares incense and candles in the dormitory hall to receive him;

the *sēngtáng* (monks' hall) bell is then struck to notify the two ranks of officials and the general assembly. After they have offered incense and performed the ritual salutation (*wènxùn*), the assembly withdraws.

The two ranks of officials and the senior elders then join him for a seated session, burning incense and drinking tea. When this is finished, the attendant offers incense and performs a prostration, leading [the guest] away.
The attendants, novices, servants, palanquin-bearers, and the officials of the administrative bureaus follow to pay their respects to the Abbot;

the head of the attendants and the various groups of novices, servants, palanquin-bearers, and guards then pay their respects in succession. The attendant burns incense and offers hot water once more, then escorts the guests to their seats.

The Master sits on the right and leads them in; they enter, insert incense, and the guests decline further formalities, briefly exchanging greetings of seasonal well-being before departing. The two classes of officials then pay their respects.

The guest master (kètóu) shall separately escort the guests to their lodgings and prepare sedan chairs; the abbot (zhǔchí) shall accompany them on a tour of the quarters (xúnláo) to pay formal respects, with the attendant (shìzhě) following in attendance (if visiting other monasteries, the attendant shall lead the tour).
The guest master shall notify all the quarters in advance. Once the tour is complete, the abbot shall enter the abbot’s quarters (fāngwǎng) together with the guests to converse.
If there are fellow countrymen or old acquaintances present, they shall return to the lodgings to receive them, and the guest master shall then proceed to invite the guests for a meal.

The attendant goes to the guest seat and bows to invite him, saying: "The Abbot invites the Venerable Master to take his evening meal in the dormitory hall; we humbly hope for your compassionate presence.

In the dormitory hall, curtains are hung and a seat is prepared (the rites are performed according to the usual form). When the meal is finished, he is again invited for tea and fruit, with both orders of monks requested to accompany him as honored guests.

The attendant reports this to the morning assembly, where the Master thanks them upon ascending the hall. The following morning, he is invited for tea; the attendant burns incense and inquires after his well-being.
The attendant bows and greets the cook, inquires after the servants, and expresses concern for their well-being; once they have eaten their gruel, he requests tea.

The attendant reports again that the Master is about to ascend the hall for the midday meal. If the Master is a great elder, the Head Seat and the various heads of the community report to the Abbot, requesting him to provide an instruction on the essential points of the Dharma for the assembly.
The Abbot first goes to the Guest Quarters to state his intention; if it is granted, the Head Seat [proceeds].
The two orders of the assembly, bearing the formal petition, proceed together to the Guest Seat (*kèwèi*) to offer incense and pay obeisance to request [the guest master] to take his seat.

Next, they request the Abbot to lead the way to the hanging of the plaque and to notify the assembly. Seating is arranged to the left and right before the Dharma Seat. When the time arrives, the drum is struck;

the Abbot descends with the others into the Dharma Hall and stands before their respective positions. The Abbot first leads the way to the seat (as in the regular *shàngtáng* ceremony). Upon descending from the seat, the two classes of officials proceed to the presence of the Venerable Elders (*zūnsù*).
Inquire after the health of the venerable elder; proceed before the abbot to inquire after his health, then return to the center to inquire after the health of the assembly at large.

Ascend the seat; the attendants and the two orders of officers come forward from their ranks to inquire after his health. Upon the conclusion of the sermon, the abbot descends from the seat and inquires after his health before him.

He then inquires after the health of the assembly at large. The abbot, the two orders of officers, and the assembly then proceed together to the guest quarters to offer incense and bow in thanks, requesting [the guest] to remain.

The guest attendant shall prepare a formal document requesting that a special service be held specifically for the administrative head (guan-shi) of the mountain gate, providing food and preparing offerings (kěn).
The Abbot shall provide supplementary offerings (tie-kěn), and the two classes of officials shall serve as attendants to perform the rites, which are identical to those of a regular special service.

If a venerable Dharma relative arrives first, the various mountain protocols for meeting shall be performed; once concluded, the guest shall take the central seat, while the Abbot offers incense and prostrates, performing the rites appropriate for a Dharma relative.

When sitting within the abbot’s quarters, one should yield the central seat; when personally burning incense, the guest should decline with all due courtesy, and the attendant shall perform the rites of reception and escort as previously described.

If a dharma-grandson who has inherited the lineage or is attending to administrative affairs visits, the abbot should go in person to the abbot’s quarters and immediately order the monastery bell to be struck to assemble the community.
Prior to this, he should invite the abbot to sit in the center and perform the rites of a disciple toward his dharma relatives.

Regarding the sequence of ceremonies for visiting various monasteries, the protocol for receiving and escorting guests is the same as previously described; however, for special hospitality, the guest-inviting attendant (qingke shizhe) shall light incense and submit a formal request without submitting a written petition.
In all cases of visits between monasteries, distinctions are made based on the relative size and distance of the institutions.

If visiting a major monastery, one should receive them with the same honors as for the aforementioned venerable seniors (zunsu). If visiting a monastery of intermediate rank where the status is equal, one should exercise discretion regarding the appropriate level of courtesy.
This is permissible. If neighboring monasteries follow a simplified procedure, they may proceed directly to the abbot’s quarters, exempting the assembly from the labor of receiving them;
the ritual shall follow the standard form.
(Form for the Request to Ascend the Seat and the Request for Hospitality)

[Seal of] the Head Seat Bhikṣu [Name] of this monastery. The undersigned, [Name], ventures to request that on the coming day you will exalt the fundamental tenets and provide instruction for the benefit of later students. We humbly entreat your venerable compassion to graciously grant your consent. This memorial is respectfully submitted on the [day] of the [month] of the [year]. [Seal of] the Abbot Bhikṣu [Name] of this monastery.

The undersigned, [Name], ventures to inform you that today at noon we shall gather in the Meditation Hall to prepare a simple vegetarian meal. We humbly entreat your venerable compassion to deign to honor us with your presence.
This memorial is respectfully submitted on the [day] of the [month] of the [year]. [Seal of] the Abbot Bhikṣu [Name] of this monastery.
(Seal of the Disciple; Respectfully Requesting the Abbot Dharma Master of [Place Name]; Seal of the One Holding the Proper Rank; Respectfully Sealed.
If the retired abbot is elderly or ill and unable to fulfill the duty of guiding others, he should gracefully yield and seek out a worthy successor to take his place.

If, during this period, one’s physical strength or mental power becomes exhausted, or if circumstances regarding the Dharma do not accord with one’s wishes, it is appropriate to know when to withdraw.

Funds for the permanent endowment must have clear and distinct ledgers; the personal effects of the Abbot’s quarters must be inventoried and handed over with a detailed list prepared in two identical copies.
Both copies must be signed by the members of the two orders and the retired elders, and stamped with the temple seal. The Abbot and the administrative office shall each retain one copy.
At the request of Master Zhao, one person was appointed to guard the abbot’s quarters until the day of his retirement.

On the day he ascended the hall to express his gratitude and take leave of the assembly, he descended from the seat and personally went to strike the drum three times before departing. If he remains at this temple to reside in the East Hall and succeeds the current abbot, he must treat him with the utmost courtesy and kindness.
Chapter Four: The Abbot’s Office;
Chapter Five: The Two Orders.

The offices of the two orders are established for the sake of the assembly to maintain the discipline of the monastic grove, to implement ritual protocols, and to circulate the teachings and contemplative practices.
Those who serve as models for future generations and are tied to the West Wing (Xixù) are responsible for managing the affairs of the temple and overseeing its income and expenditures;

they devote their hearts and exhaust their strength, ensuring that even the most minute details are clearly accounted for. Those who attend to these duties at the East Wing (Dōngxù) are charged with revitalizing the Dharma community.
These two roles are like the two arms of a single body; how could one be neglected? In ancient times, those who held office rotated between them, experiencing both fully.

When one is burdened with heavy responsibilities and returns to the station of a master, both mundane and supramundane dharmas are applied spontaneously and appropriately; there is nothing that is not suitable.

Yet, why is it that they have now split into two factions, looking at each other from east and west like travelers passing through an inn, even going so far as to revile one another instead of treating each other as guests?
This is likely because those who first entered the path were not well-versed in the teachings, and furthermore, those who took charge [of the tradition]...
It is simply because they do not distinguish between the worthy and the unworthy; let those who hold this office be cautious, be cautious.
[The seven positions of] the Head Officials of the Western Wing: the First Seat of the Front Hall (Chángtáng Shòuzuò).

A model for the monastic community and an exemplar for humans and devas, he devoted himself exclusively to expounding and interpreting the teachings to inspire future generations. When leading the assembly, his movements conformed to the rules and standards;
when entering the hall, he looked both ahead and behind with circumspection. Whether the food and gruel were fine or coarse, he exhorted the administrative monks to diligence.

Should their conduct fall short of propriety, he disciplined them according to the Dharma. He constantly kept the three modes of training in mind as he fashioned others, and he relied upon the flavor of the teachings and contemplation as if they were a personal support.

Carrying the staff and matting to show compassion for the aged and infirm, escorting the deceased, and attending to all matters concerning the monastic community (aranya)—these practices are all fully observed.
Even toward those of venerable standing and great virtue, the abbot should treat them with courtesy for the sake of others, rather than competing over titles or status.
Just as the various Great Beings (Mahāsattvas) extolled the Buddha’s transformation, Mañjuśrī assisted Śākyamuni, and Avalokiteśvara [assisted Amitābha].
Those who assist Amitābha are all ancient Buddhas manifesting through skillful means as leaders of the assembly; considering it in this light, how could their responsibility be deemed insignificant?
—The Rear Hall Head Seat.
Occupying the position on the rear board, you shall assist in upholding the tradition of the school and preside over the protocols for lectures and discourse.

As a junior member, you must maintain the same standard of conduct and ritual propriety as those in the front hall; this division of two offices is established because of the large number of participants. Having accepted this responsibility, do not treat it with negligence.

Regarding the *Sānshǒu Sānmèi Chàn Fǎ* (The Repentance Method of the Samādhi of the Repentant Head), those within our school who hold this office must ensure that both their understanding and practice are fully perfected.

If one is already muddled and ignorant oneself, how can one cause others to be clear and bright? The essential task lies in leading by example and providing exhortation and guidance to practitioners morning and evening.
Chen Qibai: When sitting, reciting, or circumambulating before the sages and worthies, always maintain the contemplation of the Way;

then both the subject that obstructs and the object that is obstructed will vanish, and both the act of repentance and the object repented of will be forgotten. Throughout the day apply effort, yet throughout the day there is no action.

First take the repentance of principle through non-arising as the primary focus, and then employ the rituals and practices. Once the ritual practice is diligent, the contemplation of principle will advance even further. One should emulate Ciyun...
Those who merely seek outward style or claim that the Perfect and Sudden Teaching lacks such practices are truly pitiable.

The abbot shall preside over all matters pertaining to literary composition, including the recording of monastic regulations, drafting official notices and petitions, and composing prayers and correspondence.
When one is exclusively entrusted with the Great Dharma, what leisure is there for literary texts? Yet this office is certainly indispensable;
that those who preside over it possess a profound understanding of the Chan vehicle and a comprehensive mastery of external classics is not the result of a single day’s effort.

Furthermore, as to why the Zen school is so numerous while this school is so few—it is not that there are no capable individuals, but rather because its rank is inferior to that of the Weiwei (Vimalakīrti) position, and thus they have receded.

To conceal it and not act upon it—just as the position of the *shuji* (secretary) in the Chan school ranks below that of the *shouzuo* (head seat), yet when applying that precedent here, it should properly rank above the *chan-shou* (confession leader).
This is because the role of *chan-shou* in the Shanjia (Tiantai) tradition is no light matter;

since one must be proficient in both doctrine and practice, and possess excellence in both understanding and cultivation, they are equal to the *shouzuo*. That the rank of *shuji* cannot be placed to the right [of the *chan-shou*] is because...

For this reason, the Vinaya Master (Weina) of our own school has previously served in positions such as Incense Burner and Guest Attendant, and furthermore has presided over the reading of the *Shuowen*, performed prayers, and dedicated merit;
his experience in these duties is as extensive as that of those at the Five Mountains and Ten Monasteries.

Since he is already included among those recommended for office, how could he possibly be willing to yield it? Now, the argument is established: if one requests a Secretary (Shuji), it is also because he has previously held such positions.
The positions of *shizhe* (attendant), *zhike* (guest master), and others shall first be established, and thereafter individuals shall be promoted according to their capabilities.

The assistant teacher (*jiuzhu*), who must be as vast as the waves of the sea in repelling external insults, must also concurrently perform the duties of lecturing; his rank shall be above that of the outer *weina*.

When his term of office is complete, he shall be granted the title of *baoyuan* (preserved master); this shall be the fixed rule. Formerly, during the assembly at Upper Zhufo Guanghua Monastery, there was this mountain, which was named "Shuji" (Record Keeper) by imperial decree.

When the *shuji* (secretary) leaves his seat, how could it be that the *vina* (disciplinarian) does not show him deference? If the *vina* were to bypass the proper order and ascend directly to inquire about the "Qi-zhao" poem, this would not be considered within the scope of our discussion—provided, of course, that he is not ignorant of it.
The *vina*.
The head administrators shall provide detailed care and regulation for the assembly of monks; when disputes arise among them, they must investigate and reconcile the matters.

When receiving new arrivals into the hall, they must verify the authenticity of their ordination certificates (*du-jiè*) and examine the order of seniority based on their years since ordination (*là*). They must carefully scrutinize the assembly of monks and manage the funeral rites and transport for those who have fallen ill or passed away.

Regarding leave of absence, attendance, and the observation of seasonal rituals, they must ensure that the performance of dedications (*huíxiàng*) and prayers is conducted with the utmost sincerity. Should there be other matters...

If, due to circumstances, one must temporarily leave or enter [the monastery], one should entrust the guest office with authority to manage the duties, such as the inspection of texts and the recitation of the *Śabdavidyā* (phonology), with the aim of promoting new learning.
Or, during the *Poṣadha*, one should revere the *Vinaya*; on the anniversary of Tiantai’s passing, one should perform full rites of veneration.

Among all duties, none are more arduous than these. (The *Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan* states that "Vina" is a combination of both Chinese and Sanskrit terms: "Wei" [綱維] is the Chinese term meaning "to maintain the framework," while "Na" is the Sanskrit term for "Karmadāna," though the characters for "Karma-dā" have been omitted.)

The *Sengshi lüe* states: "In Sanskrit, *karmadāna* is translated as 'knowledge of affairs' (*shizhi*), and is also called 'pleasing the assembly' (*yuezhong*), meaning one who knows the affairs and pleases the assembly. Furthermore, according to the *Shenglun*, it is rendered as 'succession' (*cidi*), meaning one who knows the succession of monastic affairs.
The *Yinyi zhigui* states: "The Sangha is like a net; it requires a person of virtue to serve as the main cord of that net."

The duties of the Guest Master (zhikè) consist of attending to guests. Whenever venerable elders from various regions, officials, benefactors, or renowned and eminent figures arrive, he must receive them with courtesy and engage in conversation with dignified elegance.
He shall first instruct an attendant to notify the Abbot, and thereafter accompany the visitors to the Hall for an audience, assessing the situation as appropriate.

The Abbot shall weigh matters carefully and act accordingly. In the *Dangguo* (Guest Quarters), firewood, charcoal, lamps, and oil must be kept in constant supply to provide comfort for those who arrive temporarily.
He shall oversee the recitation of texts in the Dharma Hall and the serving of hot water and tea. In the Sangha Hall, he shall supervise the serving of morning gruel and meals for visiting monks.

He shall take charge of the funeral arrangements for visiting monks who pass away. In the event that the Hall Monks (*Tang-seng*) pass away, he shall jointly manage the accounts with the *Weina*. Should the *Weina* be on leave, he shall assume his duties.
The deeds of the Master extend far, yet they are rooted in the near; may you take care not to disparage yourself. The fine reputation of Faxi remains undiminished to this day.
Attendant, incense-bearer, secretary, and guest-inviter—these duties are appended.

The true successor who enters the room with robe and bowl attends the teachings morning and evening, awaiting the moment to realize the heart-seal of the school. One should observe the transmission within the interstices of coming and going, speaking and remaining silent.

The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* is the foremost of the teachings for contemplating the flavor of the various sections; it was the attendant of Ānanda, the joyous one, and the attendant of Guo-tan [Zhiyi] at Zhang’an.

Since the Buddhas and Patriarchs entrusted it with such gravity, how can it be treated with negligence? Whenever a master resides in office and opens a lecture, he must correlate the text according to its sections and pre-arrange the topical outlines (*mukō*).

Regarding the lectures, compositions, and inquiries, one must record them so as not to forget; furthermore, one should practice reading, engage in question-and-answer sessions, and undergo formal examinations.

In selecting personnel, one must act with supreme impartiality. For matters such as providing auxiliary support to the Dharma-society, observing seasonal festivals, and specifically overseeing general administrative coverages—including the reception of visiting monks, the burning of incense, and the performance of rites—these are the duties of the Incense-Burning Attendant (Xiangxiang Shizhe).

Whenever the Abbot engages in correspondence, whether sending or receiving letters, petitions, or formal documents, he must first prepare a draft and present it [for review]. If the position of Secretary (Shuji) is vacant, the Abbot shall handle all such literary affairs for the Mountain Gate (Sanyuan).
The attendant’s duty is to write the formal letter on behalf of the Abbot.
Generally, it is the duty of the attendant to receive guests, manage their reception, and prepare special written invitations for ceremonies such as the New Year and the winter solstice.
If the Rector (Weina) or the Guest Master (Zhike) are both unable to attend the assembly or are on leave, the three attendants shall collectively assume these duties.
When the abbot remains for a long duration, he departs and returns to the assembly; when the various officers stand for a short time, they do not leave their positions.
The roles of robe-bearer, bowl-bearer, and attendant do not stand in the ranks, as they are able to offer loyal counsel, rectify errors, and recruit talent.

Thus, all internal and external affairs are handled with comprehensive adaptability and perfect harmony, ensuring that those above and below are harmonious and that east and west are in accord. This would not be possible were it not for a monastic community.
The elders of the monastic community must not be entrusted with this task; do not allow juniors and latecomers to disrupt conduct, ruin virtue, or cause grave harm through error.
(The Administrative Officers of the Eastern Wing, totaling four positions.)

The *duguan-si* (General Supervisor Temple) was established during the Buddha’s lifetime for the *kārmadāna* bhikṣu to manage communal affairs; this was the ancient precursor to today’s *duwei* (General Supervisor).
He oversees all the secular and religious duties of the temple, attends to the incense and lamps morning and evening, and reverently receives officials and their ceremonial carriages.
As the director of income and expenditure for money and grain, purify yourself with a public mind and examine the ledgers frequently. Ensure that the annual accounts show a surplus in all respects.

Instructing the junior monks and employing the servants, if they commit any transgressions, reprimand or punish them according to the circumstances; do not rely on intimidation or violence to provoke trouble.

In managing the duties of the storehouse, ensure appointments are made with impartiality. Constantly apply your efforts toward the excellence of providing for the assembly and the repair of monastic buildings.
In receiving others and treating them, one must not be disrespectful; one should relieve their burdens and revitalize what is neglected.

One must regulate the use of utensils and attend the two periods of the *zhāi* and *zhōu* meals with a mind that must proceed to the hall. Servants should perform their duties naturally and with solemnity.

For all matters, great and small, one should consult the Abbot before acting; thus, conduct will not fail its duty and the assembly will have no cause for reproach. If one is as vigilant and fearful as at evening twilight, then—

To be good from beginning to end is not a matter of mere expediency if one seeks to make oneself prosperous; how could one wish to escape [the consequences] when holding such an office? The responsibilities of the abbot are no light matter.
One must select as abbot those who are upright and capable, impartial and prudent, of advanced seniority, and who have served with a record that earns the respect and admiration of the community.

Having invited such a person with due ceremony beforehand, the community should then request his service. Upon the completion of his term, he should be escorted back to his private quarters. Furthermore, this was the practice of antiquity...

Although the number of retired attendants (*qinjiu*) in single quarters at even large monasteries rarely exceeds ten, this is primarily because it is difficult to find those who are both virtuous and capable, as well as upright and diligent.
Once such individuals are found, they may remain for several years without change, or even be requested to serve again;
how could it be that there is no one worthy of public service? Shenzhao’s assistance to Siming and Shichuang’s support of Hongzhi serve as exemplary models.

The *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* states: The Buddha told Kāśyapa, "I permit two kinds of bhikṣus to manage communal affairs: first, those who can maintain pure precepts; second, those who fear the future world. Furthermore, there are another two kinds: first, those who understand the retribution of karma;

second, those who possess a sense of shame, modesty, and remorse. Again, there are another two kinds: first, arhats; second, those capable of practicing the eight liberations (*aṣṭau vimokṣāḥ*). These two kinds, I permit to manage communal affairs."

The Chief Administrator (Jansha) oversees all affairs of the mountain gate and the entire monastery; since these matters are numerous, the Jansha is established to ensure that all income and expenditure of the monastery’s gold,
grain, money, and silk are recorded in a ledger at all times, and that the storekeeper manages their collection and disbursement accordingly.
The daily record of income and expenditures, signed by all and presented to the Abbot, is called the *jirudan* (daily register).

Alternatively, a settlement made once every ten days is called the *junudan* (ten-day register); there are also those settled monthly or settled annually, which record the presence or absence of items currently under management.
In addition to the general ledger (*nitō*), there are separate ledgers for rice, flour, and the five flavors, all of which must be audited and calculated according to routine practice.
Regarding the management of assets, even the smallest fraction belongs to the Sangha of the ten directions;
