thus, it is improper to falsely record expenditures or engage in embezzlement for matters such as those outside the temple gates—such as officials, donors, or guests arriving for formal greetings, celebrations, or condolences—and the attendant duties thereof.
Furthermore, the upper and lower storekeepers must be selected for their diligence, their ability in writing and arithmetic, and their personal integrity and prudence.
If there are sick monks who require supplies for their care, these must be provided immediately.
Should the storehouses be leaky, resulting in damage from birds or rats, or if rice, wheat, or any other items become damp or moldy, they must all be promptly inspected and protected;
one must not allow them to go to waste.
The duties of the Vice-Abbot (Fusi) are to serve as the deputy to the Chief Administrator (Jiansi), sharing in the labor of the monastery.

He must personally oversee the receipt and disbursement of the permanent endowment’s funds and grain, acting with a public mind and refraining from private bias or concealment. He shall ensure that all necessary provisions are always kept in sufficient supply, planning in advance for any potential shortages.

The Head of the Kitchen (Upādhyāya) must always be cautious regarding drainage; every day he must prepare firewood, and at night he must patrol for fire and theft—the responsibility is no small matter, so he should exert his utmost effort. The Chief Cook (Mahānasa-adhikṛta).
Pure food within the Sangha serves as a necessary provision to benefit the physical body; when the body is at ease, the Way flourishes, and when the Way flourishes, the foundation is established.

Therefore, those who preside over these duties should always maintain a sincere heart and provide offerings accordingly. At both meal times—morning gruel and midday rice—as well as for all ritual feasts, the provisions must be refined and pure, with a focus on abundance.
The ingredients should be harmoniously blended, and the management of affairs must be strictly regulated down to the very grain.
One must not discard even a single inch of rice or a piece of firewood; when the gruel or rice is being ladled out, one should first go before the Sangha Hall to burn incense and prostrate.
Next, proceed to the hall for the two daily meals, taking the gruel and rice from the kitchen and eating no differently than the assembly.

One should instruct the novices to study the scriptures, perform communal labor (pǔqǐng) with diligence, and never be indolent. Adhere strictly to the rules and regulations, distribute benefits equally, and provide care and support to all.
When gardeners plant vegetables, they must weed and irrigate them in a timely manner so that they do not become overgrown; they must ensure that the supply for the temple kitchen is always abundant.
When performing public works for the sake of merit, one should apply this same mindset.
Appointments (totaling seven offices): ensuring the hall is always clean;
replenishing oil for lamps at regular intervals; frequently dusting the sacred images; and performing daily offerings and rituals.
If wind should arise, one must extinguish the fire within the incense burner and tie up the ends of the banners; do not allow them to come near the *vaidūrya* (crystal) [statues].
Whenever seasonal festivals or the four days of the *poṣadha* (fasting) occur, open the gates of the hall to facilitate the coming and going of those who wish to pay their respects.

Funds for incense and funds for oil offered by donors must not be used interchangeably; let the donor give according to their own inclination and joy, and by no means press them to give so as to cause them distress.
Feeling weary [of worldly affairs],
he realized that the *Zanglun* was composed by the Great Being (Mahāsattva) of the Liang dynasty out of compassion for those in the world who did not recite the scriptures and were illiterate.
At the Śāla Grove Monastery (Śālavana-vihāra), a revolving scripture repository (dharmacakra-kośa) was first established to enshrine the Buddhist sūtras. Its vow stated:

"If anyone with faith can turn it a single revolution, its merit shall be exactly equal to that of reciting the scriptures. Nowadays, various regions imitate this practice, for they hold the Dharma in high esteem.
Those who preside over this office should constantly add punctuation and collate the contents, arranging the volumes and catalogs in their proper order, and completing whatever is missing therein.

Those that are damaged shall be repaired; those that are damp shall be dried over a fire; those that are broken shall be glued back together. Whenever anyone requests a scripture for study or recitation, each case shall be marked and issued;
once the reading is finished, each item must be returned and stored away, so as to prevent loss or dispersal.

Regarding the knowledge of bathing: whenever a bath is opened, a notice board shall be hung before the midday meal. In the cold months, one bath is held every five days; in the hot season, one bath is held daily to wash away sweat.

The bathhouse shall be prepared by hanging hand towels, setting out face basins, arranging the shoes, and laying down foot cloths. The head of the assembly (sanchu) shall assign the attendants to these tasks.
After the meal for the bath, once the head has been washed, the *vinaya-dhara*, the *śayanāsana-grāhaka*, and the *venerable abbot* finish their ablutions. Then, the drum is struck three times.
Within the sacred bathing tubs, a small amount of hot water is placed, incense is burned, and prostrations are made while visualizing the invitation for the sacred bath.

Following this sequence, the board is struck three times as one circulates around the corridors. When the drum is struck for the first round, the assembly of monks bathes; for the second round, the junior and senior officers bathe.
Regarding the three stages of bathing: the first stage is the bathing with powdered incense; the second stage is the bathing by the ritual attendants (*jishi*);

the third stage is the bathing by the laborers (*ninriki*). The supervisor and the practitioners bathe last. They enter to perform the ritual of *tansen* (the rite of expulsion). According to the precedent for the Abbot, they enter the bath at the third watch to undress in the small chamber and bathe, using a folding screen to partition the space.

If there are practitioners, they enter the bath at the second watch; they do not use a screen, nor do they enter the small chamber, but simply undress at the head of the row where the leaders stand. A notice shall be posted outside the bathhouse announcing the entry.

Regarding the sequence for the bathing funds: inside the bathhouse, hang small tablets with white characters. (Strike the wooden board once to add broth, twice to add water, and thrice to stop. During the bath, one must refrain from clamor and noise.
After the bath, carefully attend to the fire and candles. If a donor has provided the means for the bath, one should recite sutras and perform the dedication of merit;
for when "wondrous touch proclaims clarity" and one attains the station of a Buddha’s son, then no ritual action will be in vain.

The janitor must sweep the floor, prepare incense, change the tally-sticks, clean the latrines, boil water, and replenish the supply at the proper times; should there be even the slightest disorder, it must be immediately cleaned.
Hand towels must be kept constantly clean. The crystal lamp must remain brightly lit throughout the night. Clean buckets and shoes must be maintained.
In inspecting and replenishing all that is provided for this office, one must do so solely out of a self-aroused aspiration for the Way.
The water-head monk should pre-accumulate firewood to boil water at midnight for the assembly’s ablutions; he must arrange the basins early and light the lamps.

Prepare the candles, ivory combs, medicine, and hand towels; keep them clean. In the winter months, warm them over the fire so that they do not become cold and cause an incident by making the assembly lose their concentration.
—The Head of the Monastery.
The monastic estate (*zhuang*) is the vital artery of the sangha and the fundamental basis for all affairs of the mountain gate.

In recent times, the decline of the monasteries has begun with the neglect of these estates; when even the skin no longer exists, where can the hair remain? I shall briefly cite one or two instances here to serve as both a warning and an encouragement.

First, regarding the management of the estate: disputes frequently arise over its administration. Since there are few administrators but many residents, how could everyone be reached? This inevitably leads to the harboring of resentment by the *zhuchi* (abbot/resident).

First, those in charge of the upper and lower precincts do not fulfill their duties; being far removed from the temple’s administration, they engage in every kind of misconduct, inciting strife and litigation.

Consequently, all funds for the community’s provisions and grain are squandered, and heavy arrears accumulate to burden future generations, thereby causing the monastic discipline to decline and the tenant farmers to become insolent, refusing to pay their rents and taxes. Second, even if one were to employ experienced and capable elders... [text ends]

As affairs increase, the officials and clerks who manage the responses of the prefectures and counties, as well as the functionaries of the districts and villages, the wealthy neighbors, and others must all be entertained.
Once this precedent is established, even a slight lapse gives rise to conflict and resentment. Although no expenses are openly disbursed, they are skillfully deducted through various accounts;
thus, the expenditures at the monastery gate are twice those at the manor gate. Third, I request that the incumbent abbot and the veteran monks...
Do not follow personal biases; consult with one mind and appoint those who are honest, capable, and pure in their conduct. Be cautious not to act rashly.
When the head of the estate arrives at the estate, he shall repair the buildings, mend the embankments and ponds, supervise agricultural affairs, and provide comfort to the householders and tenants.
Minor incidents should be settled as they arise. Matters concerning major principles shall be submitted to the temple for final decision; do not engage in extortion or oppression.

Only when one exerts every effort in devising strategies so that the fire-keepers feel a sense of retrospective responsibility and the permanent residents derive the benefit of surplus can one be said to have fulfilled their duty. —
Supervisor of Collection.
The various administrators who oversee the collection of provisions for the Sangha have invited unsuitable persons to serve, causing no small amount of harm.
This is due to several causes: there are those where long-standing incumbents privately appoint unsuitable individuals; there are those who yield to private interests for the sake of profit;

there are those where incumbents and office-holders monopolize positions for years on end; there are those who rely on their influence to seek appointment; and there are those who establish factions to divide up the appointments.

Among them, there are those who vie for power through physical force, and there are those who divide the resources for their own private gain; such harms are too numerous to list, and though one wishes to rectify them, it is of little avail.

If only we could obtain upright and diligent veterans to assist the abbot, selected with public fairness and invited with due ceremony to the monastery, so that they may daily inspect the accounts and apportion the duties among the tenants and laborers to protect the gates of the estate.

Diligently apply yourself to ritual recitations and do not permit licentious sacrifices that recklessly harm living beings. Select an auspicious day to open the granary and establish a fixed limit for the collection of rice;

take advantage of fine weather to supervise its loading into the storehouse, inspecting the quality of the grain and ensuring no private concealment occurs. The weighing and measurement of both receipts and disbursements must be conducted with impartiality.
Set aside provisions for the monastic meals and dispatch them to the temple; once the three collection periods have yielded sufficient amounts, the accounts shall be settled with complete clarity.

Make self-restraint your constant thought and serving the community your primary concern; do not exact harsh levies from the tenant farmers, and do not allow the permanent endowments (*changzhu*) to suffer depletion.

If you act thus, spiritual merit and worldly blessings will naturally become extraordinary and supreme. (On the day of the collection, invite the elders of the two orders for tea; provide them with full hospitality. On the day of departing for the branch temple, perform the ritual of tea and soup at the main gate, strike the bell to assemble the assembly, and see them off at the gate.)

Please [invite] the Virtuous Head Lecturer (Dujiang), the Great Dharma Head Lecturer (Dafang Dujiang), and those of long-standing virtue in the monastic community who serve as teachers and models for devas and humans, and who lead the propagation of the Dharma-way through the vehicle of the lineage (Zongcheng).
It is appropriate that you treat this with gravity and earnestly present your request, repeatedly entreating them. If they grant their consent, the Abbot shall invite two [of them].

The Preface for Requesting the Abbot to Offer Tea and Make a Formal Announcement: "Since there is a large assembly here, it would be fitting to have a wise person deliver a lecture on the interpretation of the scriptures.
Fortunately, there is a certain person among us whose learning and insight are profound; he is one upon whom the guidance of the community depends.

We request that the two orders of officials go together to his quarters to formally invite him to serve as the *Dujiang* (Chief Lecturer) for this mountain monastery. Having finished the announcement, the assembly proceeds together to the abbot’s quarters. The abbot offers incense and performs a full prostration (*chuli*) along with everyone present.

Upon rising from the single prostration, he says: "The assembly has long turned their hearts toward you, hoping for your instruction; we humbly entreat your compassion to grant us your permission. He replies: "I am fortunate to have found refuge here, seeking only to conceal my incompetence. Since I have been invited by you, I dare not refuse.
On the following day, he specifically ascends the hall to extol the donor's great virtue and formally expresses his thanks for the invitation.

After descending from the seat, he joins the assembly in bowing before the incense burner. Once the prostrations are complete, he is then invited to the Abbot’s quarters (shang fangcang) to burn incense and offer tea.

The senior and veteran monks serve as honored attendants. When the tea ceremony concludes, the hall attendant strikes the *sēngtáng* bell, and the assembly accompanies [the guest] back to his quarters.

The abbot performs a single prostration with full prostration (*duìchù lǐ yī bài*) and escorts him out. Next, after the two ranks of officials and the assembly have finished their inquiries (*wènxùn*), they proceed to the abbot’s quarters (*fāngwàng*) to offer thanks, performing two formal bows (*liǎnzhǎn*).
After three prostrations with full prostration, they go to the administrative office (*kūsī*) and inquire after all the various quarters, finally returning to the abbot’s quarters.
When preparing grass-rice meals, evening medicinal decoctions, and fruit offerings, these shall be served separately on other days, with both classes of officials invited as companions.

If this office is dedicated solely to lecturing, its position in the ritual procession shall be after the Head Official (Tou-shou) and before the assembly. If it also includes duties in the Front Hall, it shall occupy the rank of the Head of the Class;

thus, the advancement and withdrawal of the two orders will not be confused, and there will be no overlapping of their respective jurisdictions. (For instance, when the Chief Lecturer declines the invitation for the Abbot’s formal address [shang-tang],...)
The protocols for the invitation of the two classes [of officers] to the dormitory are the same as those for the formal invitation.

Regarding the advancement and retirement of the head officials (*doushou*), these individuals serve as the models for the monastic community; therefore, one must select those whose talent and virtue are appropriate for the role. Lately, there has been a tendency toward excessive luxury.

When administrative affairs consist merely of food, drink, and wealth, those who maintain their poverty and embrace the Way will find it ever more sweet to withdraw and hide away; how then can the Dharma community be revitalized?
Administrative officials (*zhishi*) are a grave responsibility for the mountain gate; they must be selected with care from among those who are upright, capable, and worthy.

According to ancient regulations, even at great monasteries there were no more than five such officials. Even today, the established quota set by the Imperial Court remains fixed, yet in recent times many have yielded to private favoritism.

Reverend Lei requests that [the items] be returned to the treasury so that he alone may enjoy abundance; yet he has never considered that the communal property of the monastery is gradually becoming depleted and the Dharma-gate is daily declining.

If one investigates the origin of this, to whom does the blame belong? When the term of office for the two classes of administrators expires, they shall wait for the evening bell to toll, proceed together to the Abbot’s quarters, burn incense and perform a prostration with the head touching the ground, and then request leave. The administrators shall then hand over the inventory records and keys to the treasury.
If there are those among them who wish to remain for a second term, the abbot should take the opportunity to conciliate and harmonize with them so as not to permit their departure.

On the following morning, he should personally visit their quarters; the attendant should burn incense and serve hot broth to earnestly entreat them to stay. Regarding the two classes of officials newly appointed, one must not act rashly or grant them positions haphazardly.
If the right person cannot be found, it is better not to seek perfection; if they truly prove worthy, do not refuse them merely because they do not meet every requirement.
Please entrust this matter to those you trust most closely to facilitate the mediation. Only the Head Seat (*shouzuo*) and the Chief Administrator (*dusi*) may have the Abbot go in person to mediate.

When the time comes for the invitation, the Abbot must provide a list of those being invited, including the former two classes of officials and the venerable elders, and instruct the guest master and attendants to invite them;
after the morning gruel, they shall assemble for tea. The former administrators shall wait in front of the inner Sangha Hall.
Distribute the gruel throughout the day; when the person on duty goes out, enter before the Holy Monk (Śāstṛ), inquire after his well-being, burn incense, and perform three prostrations.

Proceed from behind the Holy Monk’s kitchen to the side of the *chui* (wooden mallet), strike it once, and say: "We, [Name] and others, having been commanded by the Abbot to serve as administrators (*karmadāna*) in the storehouse for one full year, our minds and strength are exhausted with toil.

We respectfully request to retire and return to our quarters. This is to inform you. Strike the *chui* once more, go before the Abbot, perform a prostration with the forehead touching the ground (*chuli*), and proceed through the assembly.

Having circumambulated the hall once and exchanged greetings in the center, they withdraw. After the gruel has been finished, the attendants urge the new and old officials (*liangban*) as well as the elders (*qijiu*) (the new officials may be invited by the guest-attendant) to the dormitory hall.
The Abbot receives them and they take their seats. The attendant burns incense, and after tea is served, the Abbot rises personally to burn incense.
The assembly stands while waiting for the Abbot to return to his place, at which point they all sit down. The Abbot addresses the assembly.

[Note: The two preceding officers have resigned; as this duty must not be left without personnel, we now appoint [Name] to serve as Head Official and [Name] to serve as Administrative Official, with their names clearly recorded one by one. The invited persons step forward and decline the honor.
The Abbot and the assembly move to the left side, while the invited persons move to the right side and perform a prostration with touching foreheads.
After exchanging greetings regarding the weather, the Attendant bows to the two newly appointed officials, who then return to their special positions and stand in two rows facing inward.
Once seated at the side, the attendant burns special incense and proceeds to the front of the special seat to inquire after [the guest's] well-being, then withdraws to stand in the center.
Waiting for the server to bring down the hot water, the attendant returns to the front of the special seat to bow for the water; the Dharma drum is struck once.

Returning again to the center, he inquires after [the guest's] well-being and burns a stick of "light-accompanying" incense. When the serving of hot water is finished, the bell before the Sangha Hall is struck to assemble the community.
To escort the new *liangban* back to their quarters: first, the current abbot escorts them; next, the former *liangban* offer congratulations; finally, the assembly offers congratulations.

Once these are concluded, the abbot and the assembly escort the former *liangban* back to their quarters. When this is finished, the new *liangban*, carrying incense, go to the Abbot’s Quarters (*fangzhang*) to pay their respects and express their gratitude.

The Hall Attendant (*lingtangsi*) and his attendants then lead them to the quarters of the reporting official (*baochu liaozhu*). The abbot invites them for a meal of coarse rice, soup, fruit, and refreshments to provide them with hospitality.
As is the usual custom (when a *vinaya-dhara* or monastic officer retires, they also perform the ritual in the Sangha Hall in the same manner as other officers).

Once the attendants (*shizhe*) have completed their formal salutations with the two classes of officials, the former attendant approaches the Abbot and reports, saying: "We, [Name] and others, have long served the Venerable Master; we now wish to request our retirement. We humbly hope that..."
Having offered incense with compassion and performed three full prostrations, he withdraws. The abbot orders his attendants to convene the new attendants;

once they have been finalized, he issues a formal notice to the Hall Administration and the *vinaya-dhara* (Vina). First, the *shouzuo* (head seat) is invited, followed by those appointed as attendants.

They proceed to the *vinaya-dhara*'s quarters, where they bow in greeting. Once seated, incense is burned and tea is served. After this is concluded, incense is burned again, and [the new attendants] face the *shouzuo* with palms joined.
The White Announcement (Presented at the Compassionate Command of the Abbot to Request the Venerable Master to Serve as Attendant, etc.):

Having completed the announcement item by item, the Head Seat turns around and, together with the Rector, performs a full prostration facing the Attendant (without the formal tea ceremony). They then exit together to see off the Head Seat.
Once the Head Seat has departed, the Rector leads the Attendant to the Abbot’s quarters. As the Abbot comes out, the Rector steps forward and reports: "Just now, [we received]..."

The Abbot’s gracious command is to invite such-and-such a person to serve as the attendant for such-and-such a master; now, lead the way for the incense offering and prostrations. The Abbot sits in the center, while the Rector (Vina) sits at the side.

The new attendant offers incense and performs three full prostrations with open sitting cloths (*daizhan*). The robe-and-bowl attendant immediately comes out to receive him into the inner chamber for tea.
Thereupon, the Attendant-in-Charge is requested to join the Rector and the robe-and-bowl attendant in escorting the new attendant back to his quarters.
The remaining head officers and others shall successively offer congratulations. The Guest Prefect (Kōchaku) acts as the escort during the inspection of the quarters (shurikō).
At the Hall of the Abbot’s Direct Office (Hōjō Chitsū), the lamp is lit. The attendants of the Hall Administration (Dōshi Gyōja) notify the various quarters, and the Abbot listens for the call.

He then requests the new and former attendants (shijō) to partake of the evening medicinal gruel and fruit offerings together within the inner chamber of the Abbot’s quarters. The robe-and-bowl attendant (ibatsu shijō) shall accompany them to the ceremony of thanks, which they must attend.
When making inquiries before the Abbot, if the Abbot invites the two classes of head officers and others, the attendant must sit separately— either in the quarters of the head officers,
the administrative office (*kusō*), or having come from another mountain to attend the tea service at the Abbot’s quarters; the attendant may never sit in the same row as the Abbot.

Regarding the handover of furniture and utensils for the head monk’s quarters and other lodgings, the monastery administration has long established regulations so that these items remain intact; yet, the incumbent officers often treat these quarters as mere temporary shelters.
Upon their departure, their servants pack up and carry everything away until the place is left utterly empty, leaving those who enter the new quarters at a complete loss as to what they should do.
The administrative office (kūsī) shall prepare one ledger in which all items of property being transferred between the various quarters are recorded in detail.
The abbot and the administrative officials (zhìshì) shall jointly certify this. Furthermore, smaller ledgers shall be distributed to each quarter for mutual cross-referencing.

Whenever heads of quarters (tóutiǒu) undergo rotation, the administrative office shall instruct the storehouse keeper and the attendants of the Hall Office to verify the inventory against the ledgers. Even if there are items that have been damaged, they must...
When items in the communal quarters are lost and require repair, the resident monk of that specific hall must compensate for the missing ritual objects.

The storehouse official (kūshi) shall provide replacements, increase their inventory numbers, and record them in the ledgers so as to prevent further loss. The head administrators and the abbot should attend to these matters with due propriety;

to treat them as if they were ordinary affairs is utterly contrary to the principle of honoring the worthy and employing the capable. As a head administrator, once you have settled your own affairs, you should likewise [attend to the community].
It is fitting that you all embody this understanding, for it is the very foundation upon which one’s career begins.
One day prior to the Abbot’s reception of both the new and old officers,
the guest-master is instructed to invite the new and old officers, as well as the venerable elders, to serve as honored companions.

At noon on the following day, the guest is urged to stay, and the abbot comes out to receive him; once they are seated (the seating order is the same as during the invitation), the attendant burns incense.

First, he goes before the newly appointed head official for a special offering and bows in general greeting; next, he goes before the newly appointed administrative official for a special offering and bows in general greeting.
He then turns around to burn the accompanying light incense, enters to the table, serves the soup, and serves the food. When it is time to serve the rice, he burns [incense].
After the incense has been offered and the meal concluded, the incense is burned and tea is served; the *hōko* (dharma drum) is struck once.

The attendant, as before, proceeds to the front of the two classes of officials (*ryōhan*), performs a bow (*monjun*), burns the *kōban* incense, and after the tea is finished, strikes the drum three times.
They then withdraw from their seats, the two classes of officials offer thanks, and the abbot sees them off.
Please invite the two ranks [of officials] to their seats.
After inviting the two ranks, on the third day before the morning assembly, the Abbot shall order an attendant to go to the new officials and invite them, saying:
"The Venerable Abbot invites you to come early for the morning hall tea service; please return to your seats. At the following morning's assembly, the *jang* (long) bell is struck.
When the time for the *ban* (board) is signaled, the assembly is summoned to the Abbot’s quarters (*fangzhang*). The Abbot receives them and seats them; the Attendant burns incense and offers tea.

Waiting for the temple bell to sound, the Abbot proceeds together with the assembly to the entrance of the Great Hall (*dadian*). One attendant bows in greeting to the Head Officials (*tou-shou*) and invites them to the West Section;

another attendant bows in greeting to the Administrative Officers (*zhishi*) and invites them to the East Section. After the recitation of mantras, the circumambulation, and the dedication of merit (*huixiang*) are completed.

The Attendant for Entering the Hall waits for the two orders of officials to enter the gate of the Sangha Hall; they each bow according to protocol as requested and take their respective seats at the *bō* (alms-bowl) positions.
The *Gòngtóu* (Vessel Head) then delivers the bowls.
Section Five: The Gate of the Two Orders.
The Sixth Section: Gathering the Assembly.
The Way is not transmitted except through an assembly, nor does an assembly reside except in a proper place; this is why monastic groves were established.
Our Patriarch Zhiyi attained wondrous realization of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and spread the teachings of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* throughout more than sixty provinces wherever he went.
His followers numbered several thousand, yet he never took offense at such a multitude. On the eve of his passing, he said to his disciples: "I led you as disciples too early;
this was a sacrifice of myself for the benefit of others. It was my profound warning against those who, fearing the future, might fail to cultivate inner practice while seeking outward fame.
Nevertheless, even in worldly affairs, the teachings of the world still censure those who study alone and remain ignorant; how much more so in the case of one who has transcended the world?"

If one does not seek the wondrous Way from teachers or friends, how could one ever hear its truth? Recently, I have observed that scholars carrying their bundles and books do not shrink from the toil of traveling great distances;
yet once they enter among the masses, they are only anxious to pursue fame and profit, and few are not led astray by the blind crowd.
If one can direct one's intent toward the ancient Way, then one need not worry that one’s reputation will not be established.
The Ritual for Tonsure (in ten sections):
The ordination of monks is a great matter of vital importance for the continuity of life and the transmission of the lamp of the Buddha-Dharma;

therefore, one must select those who have repeatedly passed the hall examinations and are capable of fulfilling the duties. Accordingly, the Imperial Court has repeatedly issued decrees for the examination of scriptures to ordain monks.
The enlightened edict was not without its gravity; it was never intended to establish the name of "parties" for the sake of securing one’s position.

Should the malady of forming factions once take root in the heart, its resulting calamities will accumulate to a hundredfold before the cruelty of its lingering poison can be exhausted—even were a Buddha to appear in this world again, he could not remedy it.
Be most earnest and cautious in your warnings! As for the practitioner who has first received a *duodie* (ordination certificate):
Carrying a tray and cloth, present them to the Master and the members of the two orders; each person offers incense and performs three prostrations.

Then, request the Head Seat (Śrāmaṇera) to provide guidance and the Rector (Karmadāna) to lead the invitation, while the Chanting Master (Brahmasvara) selects the date for the offering and the ritual site for the tonsure.

According to the Vinaya regulations, the area should be exposed ground sprinkled with scented water in a circle seven feet in diameter, with banners suspended from each of the four corners. This is the practice of the present day.
Whether it be in the Dharma Hall or at the Dharma seat, one must arrange an image and provide offerings of incense and flowers.

Beneath the seat, to the left and right, establish two seats for the Masters, each with a small table; upon these tables, place incense burners, candles, flower vases, and a ritual ruler (*śikṣāpada-yaṣṭi*).

Arrange the seating positions for the assembly and also designate a position for the *brahman* master. If this is done in the Great Hall, the same applies; however, the seats of the two Masters should be positioned directly facing the Buddha.

In the Sangha Hall, the Abbot shall arrange the positions as follows: the position of the *ce-dao-shi* (ordination preceptor) is set to the right of the seat of the Holy Monk (*sheng-seng*), while the position of the *fan-shi* (preceptor for shaving the head) is set opposite the *ce-dao-shi*.
On the eve of the ordination, the candidate changes his clothes and bathes. He proceeds to the Xing-hang (practice hall) where tea is served, and he takes leave of the assembly.

His hair is shaved, leaving four locks around the sides and eight locks at the back, along with the *cūḍā* (Sanskrit for *cūḍā*, here translated as "small topknot") on the crown of the head. Thereafter, he is further instructed...

The hall attendant (tangsi xingzhe) reports to the quarters that the hanging of the plaque has been arranged; on the appointed day, after the morning gruel is finished, the bell is struck to assemble the assembly.

The Abbot invites the Preceptor (ce daoshi) to return to the Qianfeng Hall (Fangzhang), where they sit side by side. When the bell ceases, they rise together and proceed to the place of the ritual, where they take their seats.

Once everyone is settled, tea is served in the Hall of Practice (xing tang), using two tables upon which a tray and cloth are placed with the *kāṣāya* robe and the ordination certificate (*du lüe*) atop them. The bell is then struck.

Having struck the *ghaṇṭā* and led the person being initiated out to the local shrine (*tiandi tang*), the ancestral hall (*zutang*), the Buddha hall (*fodian*), and other locations, they burn incense and perform three prostrations.
Once this is complete, the officiant takes his position nearby to await the guidance of the ritual master.

During this interval, the instructions and citations of causal conditions (*nidāna*) should be revealed according to the individual's capacity; they need not be fixed in one way. For now, I shall present a single method, listing ten points in detail.

The Ritual Procedures (1. White Seat; 2. Invitation of the Master; 3. Expression of Gratitude; 4. Exhortation; 5. Prostration to the Buddha; 6. Tonsure; 7. Bestowal of Robes; 8. Taking Refuge; 9. Opening the Mind; 10. Benediction).
Once the assembly has gathered for the white-robed ceremony, the *karmadāna* rises and strikes the wooden mallet once to signal the *brahmadatta*.

To manifest the Buddha’s knowledge and vision to sentient beings is the aspiration of the Saṃgha; to cause all sentient beings to awaken to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision is the aspiration of the Saṃgha;
to cause all sentient beings to enter into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision is the aspiration of the Saṃgha.
If one can truly act as a member of the Saṃgha in this way, and if one can truly apply the mind in this manner, then one may transform the great earth at will.

After prostrating to the Buddha, the invoker leads [the candidate] to the presence of the preceptor (*ācārya*). Approaching him, [the candidate] kneels with his right knee on the ground and wraps a clean cloth around his shoulders. The preceptor says:

"Good son (*kulaputra*), since beginningless time, there has been nothing that has not increased your pride (*māna*) and the ocean of greed (*lobha-samudra*), which receives the flowing streams and causes them to flow..."
Transmigrating through birth and death, I could find no rest; now, for your sake, I have shaved off my beard and hair to eliminate arrogance, and I wear robes of dyed color to eliminate craving.
In a mere moment, I am no different from the venerable ones of the Three Vehicles—this may truly be called a source of great joy.
Indeed, the shaving of beard and hair symbolizes the severing of the four encircling afflictions of the nine stages within the three realms.
The hair on the crown of the head represents the afflictions of the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) and below; shaving it off signifies the abandonment of these.

The hair-curls upon the top of the head represent the afflictions of the ninth stage, the Sphere of Neither Perception Nor Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). These delusions are difficult to sever once they have been grasped;

therefore, you should go to the Preceptor and request that he shave them for you. You must maintain sincere resolve and not give rise to attachment. (Chanting: The assembly contemplates renunciation; the verse says: "To destroy one's physical form..."
Maintaining one’s vows and integrity, severing attachments, and having no worldly kin, one leaves the household life to propagate the holy Way, vowing to deliver all people (from the *Duren jing*).

Seventh: The Circular Topknot and Receiving the Robe (*ce dao* guides the candidate; having shaved the hair around the four sides while leaving the topknot, he proceeds before the Upādhyāya and kneels with palms joined).
The Upādhyāya asks: "Now that you have removed the hair from your crown, is this acceptable? He replies: "Yes. The Upādhyāya says: "O son of good family, you have shaved your hair..."
By removing greed and severing delusion, the tearing of this robe signifies the abandonment of finery and the settling into tranquility.
Just as the former Ācārya shaved the hair around your four sides to symbolize the destruction of the afflictions of the lower eight stages (*bhūmi*),

so now does he shave the topknot upon your crown to symbolize the destruction of the afflictions of the single stage above, the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

Delusion is difficult to sever; only when these afflictions (*kleśa*) are severed can one truly be called a renunciant (*pravrajita*). This is because one has departed from the home of the triple world (*tridhātu*).
Thus, one may rise from the depths of ten thousand kalpas and establish the path to Buddhahood. This is something to be cherished and honored; do not treat it with levity.

Good son, now that you have completed the shaving of your hair, I shall now bestow this robe upon you.

Since you have now first left the household life, you should receive the Three Refuges and Precepts; there is no fixed rule regarding the borrowing [of robes].
The sitting mat is also called the "following-sitting cloth"; in Sanskrit it is called *niṣīdana*, used for protecting the body and protecting [the seat].

The Eight Refuges (Kneeling before the Preceptor with palms joined, listen):

"Good son, you have now fulfilled the external requirements; it is essential that your internal understanding be further clarified. Only when the internal and external correspond will it be perfectly complete.
According to the *Vinayamātṛkā-śāstra*, once one has shaved the hair and donned the *kāsāya*, one is then granted the Three [Refuges]."

One returns to the five precepts, the ten precepts, and so forth; however, regarding these five and ten precepts, you should personally receive and uphold them at the time of ascending the altar, so as to avoid breaking the precepts and creating obstacles.
Furthermore, I now cause you to turn away from heterodoxy and return to the correct path by conferring the Three Refuges.
This means turning away from the heterodox mind of beginningless time and returning to the Three Jewels and Perfect Enlightenment. From this day forward, for the remainder of this life, you vow—

Relying on the vow to take the Buddha as teacher, the vow to study the treasury of the Dharma, and the vow to be one with the ocean of the Saṅgha, you should sincerely follow the voice and chant along (the Inviter leads the chanting):

"O son of good family, you have now successfully entered the homeless life; you have already shaved off your hair and beard; you have already donned the kāṣāya; you are now [a member of the Saṃgha]."
The Buddhas and the ranks of sages are of one accord regarding this outward manifestation. An ancient worthy said: "Leaving the household life is the business of a great man;

it is not something that generals or ministers can accomplish. This is because it enables one to widely uphold the Buddha-vehicle of the three periods and to deliver those within the nine streams of existence;
truly, this is no minor matter. From this day forward, be careful not to be indolent or lax, lest you waste your time in vain. As it is said: [the following verse]...

When our Buddha, the World-Honored One, was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he left behind these instructions: "You should diligently cultivate wholesome dharmas by day so as not to let the time pass in vain;
during the first and last watches of the night, you must not neglect your practice; and in the middle watch, recite the sūtras to examine yourself.
Do not, on account of sleep, allow this one life to pass empty-handed without attainment. This is based upon [that teaching].
In the Buddha-Dharma-Saṅgha, one who cultivates the conduct of renunciation must arouse a mind of diligence and distance themselves from all evils;
they should first consult their preceptor to prepare the three robes and one alms bowl for the purpose of receiving the precepts.
These robes and bowl are the orthodox ritual of the Buddhas of the three periods and the hallmark of the noble Śramaṇas; even the ninety-five kinds of external paths do not know their names.

These characters reveal this unprecedented Dharma only when a Buddha appears in the world. If one does not discern this for oneself, or if one relies on temporary borrowing at the critical moment, one must determine according to the Vinaya that the precepts have not been obtained.
Because one lacks the precepts, one has in vain received the offerings of the faithful throughout one’s life;
in the future, one will follow the evil paths and transmigrate through long kalpas, with no means of liberation. This is no small matter; it is essential to apply [this teaching] with earnest care.

The mind must first select and follow a wise master to receive the full precepts (*upasampadā*), thereafter diligently studying the Mahāyāna to propagate its teachings and contemplations, aspiring to ascend through the stages of realization and continue the ancestral lamp; this is truly my highest hope. Exert yourselves, students!

Do not be indolent, do not be negligent! You should now proceed before the Buddha, pay homage to the Triple Gem, and recite this verse of self-congratulation (the *śrāmaṇera* proceeds before the Buddha...).
While kneeling with the right knee on the ground, the verse says: (The inviter chants; the śrāmaṇera repeats after him. "How wonderful it is to encounter a Buddha! Who would not rejoice?
May blessings and vows meet with their time; may I now obtain the benefit of the Dharma."

Ten Verses of Praise (Whether for the Upādhyāya, the Ācārya, the Inviter, or the Ritual Proclaimer, any may hold the incense burner and ascend to offer incense; when the Rector strikes the wooden mallet once, they dedicate the merit as follows):

The accumulated merit from the aforementioned monastic tonsure ceremony and the performance of Buddhist rites are respectfully offered as a blessing for the Devas and Nāgas of the upper realms. Eight.

May the various devas, Brahmā, Śakra, the Four Heavenly Kings, the local deities of this land, and the true lords of the monasteries each manifest their majestic spiritual power to settle the Sangha, protect the Dharma,

and ensure that the current Emperor’s holy life lasts ten thousand years in peace; may the civil and military officials always abide in their positions of emolument, and may the teachers, monks, and parents likewise enjoy long life and prosperity.

May all those who know and deliberate upon good and evil, the donors and faithful of the ten directions, and all sentient beings of the Dharma-realm, by virtue of these roots of goodness, together ascend to the other shore.
Contemplate the pure Dharma-body of Vairocana Buddha (recite the ten titles, etc.). Perform a *bai* (chant): "Abiding in the world like empty space... (etc.).

After the distribution of offerings (*mansan*), the *śrāmaṇera* proceeds before his preceptor and performs three prostrations; he then prostrates three times to the ordination master (*śikṣādātrī*) and three times to the assembly. Having finished, he goes outside and stands with hands lowered. When the assembly has completed their inquiries, he approaches the preceptor and offers incense.

Perform nine prostrations with wide-open mats (da-zhan) to pay respects and offer thanks at each of the various quarters. Every morning and evening, go before one’s own teacher to inquire after his well-being and report on one’s practice; the procedure for entering the hall (can-tang) is as follows.
Receiving and guarding the precepts:
for the precepts are the fundamental basis for correctly following liberation, the essential gateway to the Three Trainings, and the opening chapter of all wholesome deeds.
Śīla (morality) being impure, the Buddha-dharma does not manifest; throughout the three periods of time, there have never been Buddhas or successive ancestral masters who did not [uphold them].
One enters the Path by means of the precepts; if one does not receive the precepts, one is not counted among the ranks of the Great Sangha. Therefore, one must receive the precepts.

After receiving them, one must further protect and uphold the five precepts, the ten precepts, the two hundred and fifty precepts, and the Mahāyāna ten grave and forty-eight light precepts, ensuring that no transgressions occur.
The retribution for the offense of violating the precepts is as clear as an image reflected in a mirror.
However, reflect upon and examine this:
regarding the requisites for practice (totaling seventeen items),

which one should prepare before entering a monastic community (*saṅghārāma*), the *Madhyama Āgama* states that those items accumulated which may serve as resources for sustaining the body are as follows:
This is the means for increasing wholesome dharmas; it is the Bodhisattva Precepts Sūtra, the provision that accords with the Path.

Regarding the three robes (*tricīvara*—the *saṃghāṭī*, the seven-strip robe, and the five-strip robe): to refer to the seven-strip robe, the side-garment (*pratisaṃkhyāniḥsargika*), and the lower skirt as the "three robes" is incorrect.

The first is the *saṃghāṭī* (translated as "variegated fragments" because of its many strips; it is also called the "robe for the assembly" because it is worn when entering royal palaces, villages, or when begging for food and preaching the Dharma). Furthermore, the *saṃghāṭī* is divided into...

Each of the three grades consists of three sets: The Lower Grade comprises nine, eleven, and thirteen strips, with two long and one short strip. The Middle Grade comprises fifteen, seventeen, and nineteen strips, with three long and one short strip.

The Upper Grade comprises twenty-one, twenty-three, and twenty-five strips, with four long and one short strip. 2. *Uttarāsaṅga* (this is called the upper garment; it is the seven-strip robe). With two long and one short strip, it is known as the robe of middle value.

Regarding its use, it is said to be the robe worn when entering the assembly, during liturgical recitation, and during ritual feasts or lectures. 3. *Antarvāsaka* (this is called the inner garment, meaning that which stays close to the body). With five strips, one long and one short, it is known as the lower garment.

Regarding the robes used for walking within the monastery and miscellaneous work: [The robe] is named "Field of Merit" (*puṇyakṣetra*). The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "When the Buddha was staying before the Indra Cave, he saw the furrows and ridges of a rice paddy clearly defined. He said to Ānanda: 'The appearance of the robes of past Buddhas was like this;

from now on, fashion them according to this. *Zēnghuī jì* (Record of Increasing Radiance) says: 'Just as a field’s ridges hold water to grow fine seedlings that nourish one's physical life, so too the field of the Dharma-robes is moistened by the waters of the four benefits and increased by the seedlings of the three virtues to nourish the Dharma-body and the life of wisdom. The appearance of the Field-robe is as shown in the diagram."
*Kāṣāya* is translated here as "improper color" (*fēngzhèngsè*); it is named after its color. According to the *Huìzhèng*, this refers to a type of grass that can be used to dye clothing;

thus, the name of that grass is applied to the designation of this robe. It is also called "ruined color" (*huài sè*). As stated in the *Jièmù* (The Tree of Precepts): "There are three types of ruined colors;
within each color, one may ruin it according to one's preference—whether blue, black, or madder-brown. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* identifies "blue" as verdigris.
"Blue" refers to black; "black" refers to *tzu-ni* (a dark dye); "mud-colored" (*nie*) refers to *mu-lan* (madder), a tree bark that can be dyed a reddish-black.
However, these three colors share names but differ in substance; they must be distinguished from the five primary colors and five secondary colors used in secular life.

In general, when manufacturing the three robes (*tricīvara*), one must use plain cloth (*pāṭa*). Silk is not permitted. How could one use wealth obtained through the killing of living beings to practice compassion?

Regarding the robes, the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* states that the Tathāgata wore a coarse *saṃghāṭī*; however, the substance of such a robe must be sought for its thickness and density, remaining free from all flowery ornamentation.
The Vinaya states that if it is fine, thin, or coarse—such as *kṣauma*, hemp, *jāta*, or wild flax—it is not permitted;

likewise, silk, brocade, embroidery, gauze, fine *gu* silk, and fine *xiao* silk are all non-Dharmic items. Nowadays, many do not believe the Buddha’s words and greedily wear these various [forbidden] garments.

Regarding the robes: these three robes must all have the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) performed for them. The ritual for the five-strip lower robe (*antarvāsa*) is as follows: "Venerable sir, please attend to me with a single mind.
I, the bhikṣu [Name], am holding this five-strip *antarvāsa* robe, which consists of one long and one short piece of cut cloth. This is recited three times.
The rituals for the other two robes should be understood by analogy with this example.

The term for the sitting mat in Sanskrit is *niṣīdana*; this is translated here as "cloth for sitting upon" (*suizuo yi*) or "sitting mat. It is like the types of stools or cushions used in this land [of China].

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that according to the Vinaya, it should be made to measure: two *vitasti* (spans) of the Buddha’s length (according to the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, one *vitasti* of the Buddha is equivalent to two *zhou* [Chinese feet], which would make its current length...).
It is four *chi* in length and one *zhai-shou* and a half (i.e., three *chi*) in width. The method of its construction and its color are the same as those of the *kāṣāya*.

Regarding the bowl: *pātra* is the Sanskrit term, which in this language means "appropriate vessel" (*yingqi*). It is so named because it is used by one who is worthy of receiving offerings. As for the robes and insignia, it is said that they are called such because they are fit to receive alms.

The *pātra* (now colloquially called *bō*, or alternatively *bōyú*; this is a name combining the Chinese and Sanskrit terms). The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states that the noble ones of the Three Vehicles all carry earthenware bowls to beg for food as their livelihood;

because they take the four seas as their home, they are called *bhikṣus*. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that the bowl is the vessel of those who have left the household life and is not suitable for laypeople.

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that the bowl is the insignia of the Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and must not be used improperly. The Buddha established the rule permitting the use of earthenware and iron bowls. The Vinaya states that, in brief, there are two types: those made of clay and...
[Regarding] "Iron": The *Udānavarga* (Chuyao jing) states that seven days after the Tathāgata attained enlightenment, three merchants offered him food, but the Buddha did not wish to accept it.
He reflected, "I should observe what food the Buddhas of the past used. Then the devas in the sky [informed him that] the Buddhas of the past all used alms bowls (*pātra*).
The Heavenly King immediately presented a bowl, which was not crafted by a skilled artisan but was spontaneously accomplished. He then further reflected...
If the Four Heavenly Kings take four bowls and set aside three while taking only one, it would not be appropriate;

therefore, they should take them all and press them together into a single bowl (as also stated in the *Buddhacarita-saṃyukta-sūtra*). The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "The bowl, the half-bowl, the large *kañcika*, and the small *kañcika*" (*kañcika* is pronounced *qián*;

*kañci* is pronounced *zī*; the *Jīngyīnshù* says that the small bowl within the bowl is used as an auxiliary vessel). The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states: "The *kañcika* enters the small bowl; the small bowl enters the next bowl; the next [bowl]..."

The *pātra* (alms bowl), the *mahā-pātra* (large bowl—this Vinaya states that the "small bowl" is equivalent to the *mahākacchapa* [large tortoise-shell] bowl of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*; the "intermediate bowl" is equivalent to the half-bowl); and the *pātrādhiṣṭhāna* (bowl-rest—the Vinaya states that if the bowl is not level, one is permitted to make a bowl-rest).

Regarding the regulations for the *pāṃśukūla-kaṭhina* (herein called *bōzhǒu yī*, "arm-covering garment," or *yǎnyè yī*, "armpit-concealing garment"), this is a long robe that covers the left shoulder and conceals the right armpit to serve as an undergarment for the *kāṣāya*.

Furthermore, there is the regulation for the *fùjiān* (Chinese: "shoulder-covering"; the Sanskrit term is unknown), which conceals the right shoulder; however, this was practiced only in the Western Regions.
Many people bare their shoulders out of fear of giving rise to public censure; therefore, they must cover them.

These two garments are also similar to the *kāṣāya* in being square-cut, differing only in that they lack the vertical and horizontal stripes. In ancient times in this region, people wore the *saṃkakṣikā*;

however, during the Wei dynasty, palace ladies saw monks exposing one elbow and did not consider it proper, so they added right sleeves and sewed both sides together, calling it the "partial" [sleeve].

The *shān* (shirt) has a cut collar and an open front that still preserves its original form; thus we know that the left shoulder of the *piānshān* (partial shirt) corresponds to the original *zhīzhī*, while the right side corresponds to the *fùjiān*.
(That the current version joins the collar and opens along the spine is likely a vestige of the Wei dynasty.)
The term for "skirt" (*nivasana*) in Sanskrit is translated into Chinese as *qun* (skirt).

In older translations of the various Vinayas, it is sometimes called *niepanmeng* (nirvāṇa-saṃgha), sometimes *niyuanseng* (nirvāṇa-saṃgha), sometimes translated as "inner garment," or as "chuiyi" (the character *chui* is pronounced *huang*; it refers to a round vessel for storing rice; resembling such a vessel but without a lid, this [term] is derived from its shape).
(Regarding the meaning of "yuan" [complete/perfect]).

As for the *zhidu* (straight robe), it was traditionally handed down by predecessors that when they saw monks who had a *pianshan* (side-garment) but no skirt, or who had a skirt but no *pianshan*, they would consequently combine the two.
Two robes are used as a *zhidu* (straight-cut robe).
Regarding the water filter (*chushui nang*), the *Zenghui ji* states: "Although the vessel is small, its function is very great; it serves to protect living beings and is thus an act of compassion."
I suspect it lies herein; the *Nanshan Chao* contains a formal model (the text is extensive and not recorded here).

If one makes a water-strainer (*chalu-shuidai*) in the shape of a ladle, once the water has been strained, it should be returned to the water. The *Chao* states: "Today there are unworthy men who, upon seeing someone holding a strainer, say that studying the Vinaya consists solely in the use of a strainer-bag.

Yet they do not know the proper way to act; this deeply harms living beings and obstructs the Path. Some do not even keep a strainer; others keep one but do not use it; some use it but do not pour out the insects; others pour them out but kill them. If one does not even observe the single precept against taking life, how can one expect to follow the other majestic [precepts]?"
[The Ritual Code] states that life is constantly submerged therein. The *Mūla-ekottara-karman* says there are five kinds of water filters (*parisrāvaṇa*):

first, the square filter (made of three or two feet of silk according to the size required at the time; the silk must be fine and dense so that insects cannot pass through). The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that if the insects are too small, one should make it with three layers, or use fine, tightly woven silk. If one uses coarse silk, thin gauze, ramie cloth, or hemp cloth, it lacks the original intent of protecting living beings.
Second, the dharma-flask (the yin-yang flask). Third, the *jun-chi* (tied with silk at the mouth and suspended by a rope to sink in the water; once full, it is drawn out). Fourth, the ladle.

The water filter and the five types of robe-corners (the term "robe-corner" here does not refer to the corner of a *kāṣāya*, but rather to a square piece of fine silk about one span in size, used either to tie around the mouth of a flask or placed inside a bowl to filter water).

Furthermore, according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, one must not travel even half a *yojana* without a water strainer; if none is available, one may use a robe-corner as a strainer. Regarding these robe-corners, there are two differing explanations. However, these five types are for private use;

if they are to be kept in a communal area, one should follow the model prescribed in the *Nanhai jigui neifa zhuan* (Record of Buddhist Practices Sent Home from the Southern Seas), using five feet of silk with [strainers] at both ends.
A vertical post is fitted with a hook to which a strap is attached; this is spread open by a horizontal bar in the middle and supported below by a basin.

(In Master Jikaku’s *I-gong ji*, there are thirty-one verses concerning the sutras and vinaya, though many are not recorded here. It is said that the world finds it difficult to install a water filter for large assemblies. In the first year of the Chongning era, [Master] Yi installed a large water trough at the edge of the well in front of the kitchen of Hongji Monastery.

A smaller trough was placed near the rim of the large one, with an outlet pierced through its corner. When the water filter was placed beneath it, no water splashed or overflowed at all, and the five groups of monks were fully provided for. Behind the bathhouse was a monk’s latrine. This monk went to the toilet.

Furthermore, filtering water is the fundamental path of those who have left the household life. Later, while residing at Changlu, [the Master] explained that there are over twenty locations where well-water must be filtered; if one does not filter the water, the transgression falls upon the person in charge of the monastery. May everyone hope to strive to practice this accordingly.

The *khakkhara* (staff) is called *khaṭvāṅga* in Sanskrit; here it is translated as "tin staff" (*xizhang*), because when shaken, it produces a "tin" (*xi*) sound. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "It is a 'sound staff'.
The *Trisahasra-vidhi-sūtra* states: "One must not enter the assembly while holding the staff, nor may one hold it after midday."

(One should know the time at midday. One must not carry [the staff] upon the shoulder. The *Śikṣāpada-sūtra* states that the Buddha told the bhikṣus: "You should receive and uphold the khakkhara-staff. Why is this? Because all Buddhas of the past, future, and present have held it.

It is also called the "Staff of Wisdom" (*jñāna-daṇḍa*) and the "Staff of Virtue" (*guṇa-daṇḍa*), because it manifests the root of wisdom, conduct, and merit. It is the emblem of the sages, the clear record of the worthy ones, and the banner of the Dharma. Kāśyapa asked the Buddha, "What is the name of the khakkhara-staff? The Buddha said, "'Khakkhara' means lightness.

By relying on this staff, one eliminates afflictions and exits the triple world; thus, 'khakkhara' signifies clarity. Because one attains the clarity of wisdom, 'khakkhara' signifies awakening. Because one awakens to the suffering, emptiness, and fetters of the triple world, 'khakkhara' signifies lucidity. (From the *Xisu*).

It is also said that holding the staff distances one from the five desires and severs them; if it has two prongs and six rings, it was fashioned by Kāśyapa Buddha, and if it has four prongs and twelve rings, it was fashioned by Śākyamuni Buddha. The *Wǔbǎiwèn* (Five Hundred Questions) on the Vinaya states:
"Holding the khakkhara staff serves many purposes, as it can alert evil insects and venomous beasts."
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that the Buddha permitted the keeping of a staff because its tip should be made of iron for the sake of durability; it is truly a beneficial aid for travel.
The *Vinaya* states that there are two reasons why the Buddha permitted the use of a staff: first, for those who are aged and infirm.

The two instances of being without strength are due to being afflicted by the suffering of illness. (Whenever one uses a staff, if one encounters a venerable elder or a teacher, one must set the staff on the ground and perform a greeting.

If it is a teacher, one must certainly lean the staff against something while performing the greeting. When acting as a teacher’s attendant with a staff, if the teacher has a question, one must hold the staff to respond.)
"Yongyi" (如意) is, in Sanskrit, *anilodhu*, which means "according to one's wish. Its shape resembles a cloud-leaf, like the character for "heart" (*xin*) in the seal script of this region.

Because it is held by those who teach the Dharma according to the inclinations of humans and devas, and because its external appearance and form are such, it is called "Yongyi" (According to One's Wish).
I recall that in the past, Emperor Yang of the Sui dynasty invited the Great Master of Tiantai to lecture on the sutras.

The Master unleashed his unimpeded discourse and deployed his eloquence like a flowing river, so delighting the Emperor’s heart that he was specially granted a rhinoceros-horn *ruyi* (ceremonial scepter).

If one consults the *Shishi yaolan* (Essentials for Buddhist Practitioners), which this Master compiled, it states that the *ruyi* is currently held by lecturing monks; however, these are mostly private records of textual sections and benedictory phrases.

The handle is provided to prevent forgetfulness; when the time comes, one holds it in hand and looks at it with the eyes. Because it accords with one's intention, it is called "Yìrúì" (Wish-Fulfilling).
According to what others have said, even if Mañjuśrī were to hold it, would it not also serve to prevent forgetfulness? Nowadays, many who preach the Dharma hold a whisk (*kaṭaka*).
If they privately record the essential passages but later forget them, where else could they write them down? This is merely the talk of the vulgar.
This is indeed the speech of a rustic from the east.

Regarding the *bīḍāla* (whisk), the *Vinaya* states that because bhikṣus were troubled by grasshoppers, the Buddha permitted the making of the *bīḍāla*. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that the Buddha permitted the making of the cord-whisk (*sūtra-bīḍāla*).

One must not hold a broom made of woven cloth, one made of grass stalks, one made of tree bark, or one made of yak-tail hair, cow-tail hair, or horse-tail hair— even if they are fitted with handles adorned with gold or silver.
[This applies to] the water flask as well.
In Sanskrit it is called *kuṇḍikā*; formerly abbreviated as *junzhi*, this is translated here as "flask. It is used to constantly store water for the purpose of purifying the hands while traveling.

(The *Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan* states: "Regarding water, there are two types of flasks: the pure (*śuci*) and the touched (*spṛṣṭa*). The pure flask is made of clay or porcelain; the touched flask may be made of copper or iron. When taking water from the touched flask, one washes it with touched water; when putting water into the pure flask, one uses pure water.")

"Perfume burner and casket" (*xiānglú lián*) refers to a vessel for holding incense; some say that the burner and the casket are two separate items (in certain versions of the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra*,
the character "casket" [*lián*] is absent from "perfume burner").
The *Dāśaśloka-laṅkā-sūtra* states: "In order to cut one's *kāṣāya*, it is permitted to keep a knife four inches long, with a blade shaped like a crescent moon.
Today, these are traditionally called "precept-protecting knives" (*hujièdāo*). The *Sēngshìlüè* states: "Precept-knives are all ritual implements (*dōujù*) for the purpose of cutting robes."
Regarding the "knife named precept," this refers to the Buddha’s prohibition against cutting or severing any grasses or trees and destroying the villages of spirits;
since he forbade it even for grass and trees, how much more so for other things. [This concludes the section on] the rosary.
The *Mūlamandaradharāṇī-sūtra* states that in Sanskrit it is called *akṣamālā*, which in the Liang language means "rosary";
it is an implement for binding the mind and cultivating practice. The *Bodhi-akṣa-sūtra* says: "Formerly, there was a king named Pāriyātra who said to the Buddha: 'My country is small and remote;
for many years there have been epidemics, grain has been expensive, and the people are in distress. I have always not falsely [neglected] the profound treasury of the Dharma.'"
"May it be widely disseminated so that it may not fail to reach all; I only pray that you will deign to reveal the essentials of the Dharma.
The Buddha said, "Great King, if you wish to extinguish the afflictions, you should string together one hundred and eight *ambhoja* seeds and always carry them with you.

With a sincere mind, recite 'Namo Buddhāya,' 'Namo Dharmāya,' and 'Namo Saṃghāya. If you can pass even a single syllable [of these names], you shall gradually progress in this manner until you have reached a thousand."
If one recites [this mantra] twenty thousand times with body and mind undistracted, eliminating flattery and crookedness, at the end of life one will be reborn in the Yāma Heaven.

If one completes one hundred thousand recitations, one shall eliminate the one hundred and eight fetters of karma (*karmāṣṭottaraśata-saṃyojana*) and attain the fruit of eternal bliss. The King said: "I shall respectfully practice this. [Regarding the] "one hundred and eight fetters":

these are the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *vitarka-kleśa*). The afflictions of views are expanded into eighty-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*). As the verse says: "In the Desire Realm, there are thirty-two; in the Form and Formless Realms, there are twenty-eight each; together across the three realms, they constitute [the total]."

The *Abhidharmakośa* explains this meaning in detail across eighty-eight verses; summarizing the afflictions of thought (*cetanā-kleśa*), they are combined into ten verses, which state: "In the desire realm, there are four types of thought-afflictions—namely, greed, anger, delusion, and pride. In each of the two upper realms, anger is excluded, resulting in a total of ten.

Having reflected upon this, when the views and thoughts are combined, they constitute ninety-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*). To these, the ten entanglements (*paryavasthāna*) are added. The verse on the entanglements states: "There are eight entanglements: lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), envy (*īrṣyā*), stinginess (*mātsarya*), regret (*kaukṛtya*), sleep (*middha*), restlessness (*auddhatya*), and dullness (*styāna*). Alternatively, there are ten, adding anger (*krodha*) and concealment (*mrakṣa*). When combined with the preceding [proclivities], they form a total of one hundred and eight fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Regarding traveling to seek instruction:
a novice who wishes to go on pilgrimage must select a place where there is a Dharma to be studied and request to "hang the banner" (register as a resident).

According to the Vinaya, a bhikṣu should reside in a place where there is both Dharma and food; he should also reside in a place where there is Dharma but no food; however, he should not reside in a place where there is no Dharma, even if there is food.
One should not remain in one’s quarters; rather, upon first arrival, one should proceed directly [to the guest office] with full decorum.

Having selected a person well-versed in monastic affairs as the leader (*sanchou*), they go together to the Guest Office (*kesi*) and say: "We have come for a brief visit. The Guest Master comes out to receive them and says:

"On this day, we wish you, the Dharma Master who presides over both host and guest, every blessing and long life. Having long heard of your reputation for the Way, it is our great honor to behold you in person. Our humble hearts are filled with boundless gratitude. He replies: "It is the good fortune of this mountain gate that we have received your visit from afar. He then bows and invites them to be seated.

Incense is burned and tea is offered; the guest briefly inquires about his origins, rises to thank for the tea, and departs (or is escorted to the Guest Office, the hearth-side area, or elsewhere to rest).

The Chief Guest Officer (Zhiké) immediately returns. The Guest Receptionist (Líkè) leads him in, and they exchange greetings. The Chief Guest Officer says: "I hope all you venerable Dharma masters are enjoying good health and prosperity.

We have received your esteemed visit today and offer our sincere thanks; we are deeply moved by your kindness. He replies: "It is our duty to receive you; why do you urge us to honor you? The Head of the Assembly (Cántóu) personally escorts the Chief Guest Officer out.
If one wishes to pay respects to the Abbot (Zhuchi), one first goes to the Attendants' Office (Shisi) to meet him and perform the rites as previously described.

Rising, one reports: "We, [Name] and others, have come specifically to pay our respects to the Master; we venture to trouble the Attendant to announce this. The Attendant bows and invites them to sit again, inquiring about their purpose for coming.

If it is after the morning gruel has been finished, the Attendant immediately goes to announce: "[Guest Name] has announced his arrival. He then reports back to the Abbot; if permission is granted, he proceeds at once to the Abbot's quarters.
If the formal visit (*kànxiàng*) occurs after the midday meal, the attendant says: "Please return to your quarters; Guest So-and-so reports for leave. The attendant then reports this to the Abbot;

if permission is granted, on the following morning at the tolling of the bell, the attendant directs the guest master to announce the visit. (If the Abbot is otherwise occupied, the attendant goes to the guest's quarters to announce the courtesy and offers words of comfort.
After the morning gruel, the head of the assembly leads the group to the dormitory hall; the attendant enters to inform the Abbot, who then comes out to meet the head of the assembly.

Stepping forward, he says, "Please, Venerable Abbot, sit cross-legged. If the Abbot declines, the attendant offers incense and spreads the ritual implements; if he declines again, the attendant performs a single prostration with unopened sitting cloth (*chuli*) and makes an inquiry, saying:

[The Dharma Master’s] spiritual body has been established in this dwelling, which is a place of great merit; it is fitting that I visit your quarters to pay my respects. To receive such an honor is beyond what I could have hoped for, and my inner feelings are overcome with the utmost profound gratitude. The Attendant says: "The monastery is most fortunate to receive your distinguished visit from afar. Our apologies for the delay in repaying your courtesy; our inner feelings are filled with no small measure of shame.
In ancient rites, the Abbot would respectfully go out to meet the guest and return the greeting, as a mark of respect for the guest's long journey.

Nowadays, this is no longer heard of; rather, when visiting a person of renown, one proceeds directly to the guest seat to return the greeting. When visiting a student (a junior monk), one likewise proceeds to the guest seat to return the greeting.

At the lower level of the Dharma Hall, one should go out to meet and receive the abbot’s return greeting; there is no need for the trouble of descending from one's seat to show honor. However, at the great monasteries of the Five Mountains (*wǔshān dàchà*), the abbot does not return the greeting.

At the halfway point of the meal, the abbot’s quarters (*fāngzhàng*) invites [the guest] for refreshments (*diǎndīn*); that evening, the medicinal food (*yàoshí*) is served (furthermore, that evening a special soup is provided, and the next day, after the morning congee, the custom of inviting [the guest] for tea is performed by the abbot).

If one seeks to reside or seek lodging, one should again go to the Attendant’s Office (Shi-si) to pay respects, sit for a short while, and then rise to report, saying: "We, [Name], having admired the Master’s spiritual influence, have come specifically to take refuge at your feet;
we beg the favor of the High Attendant to announce this. The Attendant shall nod in acknowledgment and record the names of those seeking residence in writing to present to the Abbot.

After the tea reception, incense is burned and tea is offered. When this is finished, the head of the assembly (*candou*) rises and reports, saying: "We, [Name] and others, have just received the compassionate decree from the Abbot’s quarters, ordering us to rely upon his presence.

We humbly pray that you will graciously accept us. The response is: "The mountain gate is fortunate to share in this quiet seclusion with you all. Then the head of the assembly and the rest each take their ordination certificates (*dujie*) and pass them one after another.

Together with the *vina*, he shall take the register of seniority (*kaṣāya-lakṣa*) and immediately return it to its place. He shall then deliver the formal letters (*mángzhuàng*) to the Abbot’s quarters, the two orders of officials, and the various dormitories;
each person shall have one letter for their respective dormitory, and names must not be shared.

This is not the path of the Buddhas and Patriarchs nor the intent of their transmission; all those in positions of authority should strive to avoid it. The next morning, the *weina* shall instruct the hall-attendant to observe when the Abbot has leisure and report it immediately.

Next, he is led to the administrative office (*kusī*) and the quarters of the various heads of the community to present his credentials and perform inquiries. This is done briefly.

After offering incense, one does not receive formal greetings; this is the sequence for observing ritual propriety. Next is the matter of visiting the various quarters and the various refectories (the Hall Attendant’s acolyte announces: "The new arrivals are visiting the quarters";

nowadays, people often merely pass on word and do not meet in person, which is contrary to ritual. If they are old acquaintances from the same hometown, one should visit them one by one again the following day).
Immediately upon returning to one's own quarters, one awaits the head officers to return the courtesy (it is improper if they do not return the greeting).
During the morning session of entering the hall (*santáng*), when the wooden fish (*múyú*) sounds, the head of the assembly (*cāntóu*) leads the members of the hall back to the hall.

The virtuous and honorable one shall repair the single quarters (*dānliao*), personally inspecting and arranging them so that tables, beds, and all necessary utensils are fully prepared.
On another day, the abbot shall assemble the two orders and the retired elders for tea. The abbot rises personally to burn incense, then returns to his position and stands, saying:

The administrative office (*kusi*), the heads of quarters (*tou-shou*), the monastic quarters (*liao*), and the retired elders (*qin-jiu*) shall return their bows on a separate day; the Abbot (*fang-zhang*) will specially provide them with hospitality.

On the first and fifteenth days of the month, they shall be invited for tea along with the retired elders (this applies according to the protocol for those of high standing; for others, it shall be determined by circumstance).

When those renowned throughout the rivers and lakes seek lodging—as if seeking to hang their banners—or when they arrive the following day after the tea ceremony, they should report their request immediately; or on another day, after the morning gruel, they should go specifically to the abbot’s quarters and report, saying:

"We, [Name] and others, having long admired the Master’s spiritual influence, have come to seek refuge under you; we humbly hope you will grant us your acceptance. If the abbot grants permission, he shall issue a notice.

The Head Seat (Shouzuo) is requested to escort [the guest].
