"The Abbot has issued an order that because such-and-one from such-and-such a place has come from afar to join us in maintaining this quietude, we request the two orders of officers to escort him to the refectory. Having finished the inquiries of well-being, the person who escorted [the guest] returns to the host’s seat. The Head Seat (Shouzuo) moves to the guest’s seat and leads the administrators (zhishi) and the Rector (Weina) in performing mutual inquiries of well-being.

In the case of a small monastery, those who have passed through their terms of office are not included in the protocol for seeing off the guest; furthermore, one must consider the individual's character and talent.

Move the bedding and personal effects from the quarters to the Hall Office (*dangsi*) to present the "Bedding Relocation Form" (*zhuanzhai zhuang*) for detailed inspection by the *weina* (chant master).

Present it again to the *weina* for formal submission. Then proceed to the Attendants' Office (*shisi*), where the attendants shall join you in the same manner.

He must cross-reference the inventory against the ledger and hand over the miscellaneous items, tables, benches, beds, and furnishings.

once it has been determined that one will reside there, one immediately performs the ritual of hanging the plaque. If the abbot treats subsequent applicants with excessive formality, they should wait until later to seek residence.

Those who have returned to the hall prior to the summer retreat shall offer their thanks at the same time as the hanging of the portrait in the tower; those who have returned to the hall on the eighth day of the fourth month shall offer their thanks as for an ancestral memorial feast;

and those who have returned to the hall on the twentieth day of the eleventh month shall offer their thanks. Among them, those with the highest number of years since ordination shall serve as the head of the group (*santō*).
The head of the group must prepare a small diagram and practice the ritual procedures; three people shall form one procession, and one person from each procession shall serve as the leader.

The head of the assembly (sanchou) shall carefully record the liturgical phrases and instruct the hall-attendant (tang-si) and the acolytes (hang-hsing) to collect five hundred cash from each person for incense offerings.

He must then trouble the attendant (shi-tse) to go to the Abbot’s quarters (fang-wang) to inquire about the amount of incense returned—approximately how many bundles and how many pieces—and report back so that the date for the "Thanksgiving for Hanging the Portrait" (hsieh-kua-ta) may be determined.
On the appointed day, the attendant shall set up an incense table with a burner, candles, and lamps in the Meditation Hall (shen-t'ang), while the head of the assembly leads the proceedings.
The assembly stands in formation according to the diagram; the *candana* (senior participant) and the attendant enter together to invite the Abbot to come out.
Once he has returned to his position, the *candana* and the assembly perform a formal greeting (*wensun*). The *candana* steps forward and reports: "Please, Venerable Master, sit cross-legged.

He then withdraws, places his right foot to the side, turns his body to the right toward the empty space beside the incense table, walks past it, and returns to his position. After the assembly has finished the greeting, the *candana* [proceeds] together with them...
The three individuals first perform a greeting. The *sanchō* (head of the assembly) proceeds to the incense burner and performs a small greeting.

Taking the incense from his breast, he inserts it into both hands and passes them over the empty space on the right side, then returns to his position. The three individuals together perform a formal greeting (*monshin*) and unfold their ritual implements (*kutsu*).

The *jūji* (abbot) extends his hands to signal that they should be excused. The *sanchō* steps forward and says: "We, [Name] and others, have been fortunate throughout our past lives to have attained this opportunity to dwell here; our hearts are filled with the utmost joy. He then withdraws and returns to his place. This concludes the inquiry.

The attendant bows again, unfolds the *ju* (offering cloth), and the Abbot again agrees to waive its receipt. The attendant steps forward once more and says: "On this day and at this auspicious hour, I respectfully wish the Venerable Abbot a long life and much merit.
He then withdraws to his position and performs three prostrations with the head touching the ground (*chuli*). The Abbot briefly replies.

First, the attendant performs an inquiry bow, passes to the left side, and joins the end of the line of attendants. They proceed up the hall in groups of three (*sansan*). (The words for offering incense and the ritual procedures are the same as before. When the ceremony is concluded, everyone performs a general inquiry bow.
After withdrawing, on the following day, the Abbot invited him for refreshments (*diǎndìan*).

Regarding the seeking of instruction: whenever one wishes to seek instruction from the Abbot, one must first go to the Office of Attendants (*shìsī*) to report the matter in detail to the Attendant (*shìzhě*), who will then consult with and report back to the Abbot.

Please have the attendant inform the master, and have the acolytes (*xingzhe*) prepare the incense and light the candles.

Having prostrated and received the formal document, one steps forward to inquire after [the Master’s] well-being, saying: "We, [Name] and others, humbly submit that we are dull-witted and have no gate for entering the Way; we beseech Your Compassion not to weary in instructing and admonishing us.

One then withdraws, bows the head, stands respectfully to one side, and listens attentively to the Dharma instruction (if one is a novice, the instructions should also include the rules for joining the assembly). If asked about one's background, one answers truthfully from beginning to end.

Having stepped forward to inquire after his well-being and withdrawn, one next proceeds to the Attendant’s Office to pay respects and thank him, or to request further instruction from the West Hall Master.
The Head Lecturer (Dujiang) shall then request one member of the same lineage to report in advance; if the request is granted, the ritual is the same as before.

The Master should establish a daily curriculum and assign texts for them to read until they are thoroughly mastered. (After the morning gruel, during the robe-vesting ceremony, after the midday meal, and even at night while holding their robes, they shall all proceed to the Dharma Hall to chant aloud.

Do not allow them to study superficially or rely on mere rote memorization—though their knowledge may grow day by day, their understanding may remain impoverished month by month; one must cherish every moment of time. To the right, oil lamps are lit.

If one has spent as many days as there are hours in study at a monastic school, yet specializes only in intellectual understanding without being familiar with the practice of cultivation, the teacher should suspend [other texts] and show them the sublime principles of works such as the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* (Stopping and Seeing), enabling them to suddenly cultivate the Buddha-vehicle. If one establishes practice based on understanding alone without contemplating the mind, it is like a poor person counting treasures.
As the Venerable Jingxi said: "Contemplating the mind is the pivot and hinge of the teachings and practices; one must contemplate it."
The capacity and measure of the mind-consciousness in a single thought-moment are boundless; its essential nature is eternally abiding.

Buddhas and sentient beings mutually encompass one another without exclusion, like a single jewel in Indra’s net: the reflection of one jewel pervades all other jewels, and the reflections of all other jewels converge within that one jewel.
The present single thought-moment is likewise so. A beginner practitioner should immediately take this supreme *sāmbhogakāya* (peaceful light) as the substance of their contemplation.
When the eyes and feet assist one another, the cool pond may be reached.

Compiled by the Bhikṣu Ziqing, Abbot of the Great Yuanjiao Teaching Monastery in India. Chapter Seven:
The Gate of Summer Retreat (*Anju*).

The regulations for the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat) have no other purpose than to prohibit wandering, protect the lives of sentient beings, and establish a fixed period for cultivation and realization.
According to the Vinaya, this applies generally to all three seasons; however, here it refers specifically to dividing the year into three periods.

The reason for exclusively observing the summer retreat is that during the summer months, even a square inch of ground contains insects; if one wanders about without necessity, one will inevitably tread upon and injure them.
The transgression of failing to observe the precepts during the summer retreat invites slander; therefore, one should regard the other two periods as even more critical.
Otherwise, how could it be that the practice of cultivation exists only during the summer and not during the other two periods?

That those who heard the wondrous teachings from my ancestor Jiangling for ninety days and received the compassionate rain at Yquan for one summer were able to enter [the Way] upon hearing them provides sufficient proof. Those who now inherit his lineage...

Dwelling wherever one may be, one should carefully choose one's teachers and friends; upon hearing the teaching, one should immediately put it into practice, so as to perfectly shatter delusion and perfectly manifest enlightenment, thereby verifying the reality of cultivation and realization, rather than merely being preoccupied with the trivial concerns of ignorant beings.
Regarding the date for the issuance of the *caosuan* (grass list) and the *dansuan* (individual list): if it were on the first day of the third month, it would be too early;
if it were on the tenth day of the fourth month, the *vinaya-dhara* (ritual master) would be pressed by too much urgency. Therefore, it is now fixed for the first day of the fourth month.
This may be changed. The *vinaya-dhara* (Venerable Leader) shall follow the Master to ascend the hall;

he shall first issue the instructions for the seating order (the form is shown below) and have the attendant of the Hall Office present it first. Only after the two classes of monks have passed it on shall it be presented to the Abbot for his critique (*yún yún*). (Note:

Recently, there have been those who, having newly received the precepts at this mountain and being assisted in their tonsure, immediately rank themselves above the senior monks. Should such transgressions occur, the Master must instruct them according to the Vinaya laws: those who received the precepts earlier sit in front, and those who received the precepts later sit behind.)

Do not ask whether one is old or young; do not sit like the ignorant followers of external paths who have no order, following the manner of soldiers or slaves. In our Buddha-Dharma, if one sits in a manner that does not accord with the proper sequence, one commits a minor offense (light defilement).
For three days prior to hanging [the roster] in front of the Sangha Hall, all must remain after the midday meal and prepare a table upon which pens and inkstones are arranged.

Should there be any errors or omissions, please correct them yourselves. This is done to prevent confusion when the names are first entered onto the register. After three days, proceed according to...
Next, the name tablets shall be displayed, and each person must identify their own name according to the seniority of their precepts; the order must not be transgressed, lest the Dharma be disturbed.

Recently, there have been those who engage in quarrels and disturbances, often relying on their strength or harboring private grudges to smear one another, dragging each other onto the hall, shouting and clamoring to annoy the assembly—this is most improper.
Those who violate this shall be expelled. If there should indeed be an error, it must be reported to the *Venerable* (the presiding officer).
The head seat (shouzuo) reports this to the abbot (zhuchi).

Incense, candles, tables, and stands are arranged before each. The Hall Attendant and his assistants notify the assembly, who then don their robes, examine the diagrams, and identify their respective seats.

As the commencement of the *varṣā* retreat approaches, one should go back and forth to perform the formal rites several days beforehand; this is called "paying respects for the commencement of the *varṣā*.

Lately, many have made it a practice to rush about in competition, which greatly violates the rule of *pāda-bandha* (confinement of the feet). On the morning of the fourteenth day, the Hall Master shall conduct the ceremony.
Hang up the talismanic water plaque. On this day, after the morning gruel is finished, strike the bell to assemble the community and enter the hall to stand in their respective positions.

Lead the Great Compassion Mantra; while walking the path, stand still and recite the mantra until it is finished, then immediately chant "Namo."
