I, the bhikṣu [Name], now rely upon the saṃghārāma of such-and-such monastery..."
This is for the purpose of repairing dilapidated dwellings during the first three months of the summer retreat within the boundary.
(The *Guangju ji* states: "Based on one year of the Buddha-dharma...")
Regarding the three seasons, if one month of four months constitutes a single season, then the autumn season is omitted;
within the Vinaya, there are three types of *vassa* (rainy-season retreat), namely the early, middle, and late. [The retreat lasts] four months and ten days.
The sixth day is the seventeenth day of the preceding *pūrvavārṣika* (early rains retreat);
from that point until the fifteenth day of the fifth month is called the *madhyamavārṣika* (middle rains retreat); the sixteenth day of the fifth month is...
Regarding the later retreat (paścimā vārṣikī), if it is entered on the sixteenth day of the fourth month,
then until the end of the night of the fifteenth day of the seventh month,
it is called the completion of the summer retreat; this refers to the preceding three months.
If one does not enter the rains retreat during the middle of autumn,
it is not called "sitting through the summer" (because the latter part of the rains retreat lasts until the fifteenth day of the eighth month, when it is then concluded).

Dedication Ritual for the Grounds of the Various Halls (The Earth Deity is called the "Spirit" and the Celestial Deity is called the "Sage"). As the light of the celestial deities is already manifest and not obscure, their responsive resonance is unfailing in every thought-moment. We look up with hope for your sagely compassion to look down upon us and clearly oversee our affairs.

At this temple, [Name], as the blazing heat of midsummer arrives and the August Emperor presides over the realm, it coincides with the occasion when the Compassionate Honored One (the Buddha) rested his feet, and the day when the sons of Śākya protect living beings. For ninety days we shall distinguish the Way and, setting a fixed term, break through obstacles to achieve success. During this summer retreat (*varṣā*), we pray for your reliance and protection.

The deities shall preside over and protect [this assembly]; thus, we reverently gather the great multitude... We pray that the ancestral tradition may flourish further, restoring the profound path of our successive patriarchs; that the sun of wisdom may shine forever, ensuring the lineage of Buddhas remains unbroken in future generations; that the mountain gate be solemn and the ocean-like assembly be at peace;

that donors and believers turn toward us, and the Wheel of Dharma turn eternally throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time—all beings of the ten directions and three periods of time... (and so forth).

Wei Tian (the Heavenly General Wei), who serves as a bulwark for the Buddha’s transformation, has fundamentally realized this through deep realization to provide a secure protection for the Mountain Gate, manifesting great power to bring benefit. We look up to you with these hopes... At this time, at the beginning of summer, we are about to undertake the *an-gu* (rainy-season retreat).

To manage internal and external affairs without hindrance, one must rely on progressive cultivation in an orderly manner... We humbly pray that the Dharma-center shall remain as firm as the mountains and peaks, and that the ocean of the Teaching shall flow as long as the Milky Way. May the Three Studies flourish and the Four Offerings be gathered; may both public and private matters be harmonized, and may fire and thieves be doubly extinguished... (as above).

The Supervisor of the Kitchen (the "Austere One"): He governs the boundaries of the entire monastery; as the master of the hearth, he presides over the sustenance of the multitude. His spiritual power is upright and impartial, free from private bias. Now, as the warm breeze gently blows, it is precisely the time for the commencement of the retreat;

as the brilliant sun blazes, it is truly the season for *an-gua* (summer seclusion). While the Wheel of Dharma must be turned, the Wheel of Food comes first. To ensure that the offerings at the Fragrant Accumulation Hall are abundant, one must rely upon the protection and assistance of the deities.

We humbly pray that morning cooking and evening fires shall never suffer the distress of wasting firewood or igniting a fire within a curved roof; and that the temple drums and gruel-bowl fish shall forever possess the flavor of *dharmaprīti* and divine joy.
The Protocol for Three Days of Tea and Soup in the Sangha Hall (The procedures for both the commencement and the conclusion of the retreat are identical).

Following the ceremony for the inauguration of the retreat, where the Chief Administrator specially offers soup for the Abbot, the Head Seat, and the assembly, the Chief Administrator carries incense and proceeds to the Abbot’s quarters to perform a prostration with the head touching the ground (*chuli*), making the following request: "Tonight, at the Cloud..."

The Abbot personally prepares the hot tonic for the Head Seat, the assembly, and the rest; we humbly entreat your compassionate presence to descend and grace this occasion. (A notice for the tonic is attached below.

The guest master attendant shall prepare a tray, cloth, incense burner, and candles, proceed to the quarters of the Head Seat in the front hall, offer incense, perform a prostration with touching of the forehead, and make the request (as stated above).
The notice shall then be presented to the Head Seat, who will immediately instruct the lead tea server to deliver it to the ritual assistant, who shall affix it to the Sangha Hall.
In the lower section of the front hall, the administrative office (Kusi) shall further instruct the guest master to invite the successive head officers and various elders;

meanwhile, a sign for the serving of medicinal soup (tang-pai) shall be hung inside the Sangha Hall. Incense tables, censers, and cloths shall be arranged in both the upper and lower sections, and in the outer hall, large incense burners and flower vases must also be aligned directly in front of the Sacred Monk (Sheng-seng).
Beside the Sacred Monk’s shrine, a special seat for the Head Seat (Shouzuo) shall be established.
The Abbot faces him and dispatches an attendant to prepare the special seat and the various bowls and utensils for the soup.
At evening, the hall-attendant strikes the corridor board three times; the assembly returns to their respective bowl-seats, followed by the head monks, with the Chief Seat (Shouzuo) entering last.
Each returns to his own position. The bell is struck three times and the board is struck three rounds. The Chief Administrator (Dusi) enters and bows to the Chief Seat before returning.

The person in the special position bows to the Head Seat of the Rear Hall and takes over the position of the Fore Hall (if the Rear Hall seat is vacant, he bows to the next-ranking head official and proceeds to the head of the board).
He exits from behind the right side of the Holy Monk’s kitchen and stands by the door of the inner hall. Upon hearing one strike of the bell, he goes out to welcome the Abbot;
as the Abbot enters the hall, the assembly rises and stands.
Holding the incense censer, he briefly bows to inquire after their well-being, returns to his position, and the Chief Administrator steps forward to bow and invite him to be seated.

He turns to return to the center, bows to the assembly as they take their seats, proceeds before the Holy Monk (*seng-seng*) to burn incense, and then burns incense at each of the upper and lower sections.
He exits to the outer hall to burn incense, returns to the kitchen area to place the incense censer down, proceeds to the special seat (*te-wei*) to bow, and finally turns behind the kitchen.
Having bowed before the Abbot, he makes one circuit of the hall and the outer hall, then returns to the center of the hall to bow and stand to one side.
Again, the bell is struck once; he first enters before the Abbot and the Head Seat for the special tea service (*tokubetsu-tō*).
He bows before the Abbot and the Head Seat, then turns behind the image of the Holy Monk (*shōsō*) in the kitchen. Again, the bell is struck once, and he proceeds with the bowls for the assembly.

When the bell is struck once, the assembly awaits the serving of hot water. As the distribution of the water is about to conclude, the Head Monastic Officer (Dusi) proceeds as before, starting from the head of the front hall and circumambulating the hall once;

having exited the outer hall, the Attendant first collects the abbot’s cup. The Head Monastic Officer steps forward before the abbot, bows in greeting, and performs two formal prostrations (*chandan*).

For the first prostration, he says: "On this occasion, we have prepared this humble hot water; we humbly receive the Venerable Master’s gracious presence, and our inner feelings are moved beyond measure. For the second prostration, he remains silent.
[The abbot] says [the seasonal greeting]. He performs three prostrations with touching of the ground (*sanchu*). The abbot does not respond. The head steward (*dutse*) escorts the abbot out.

[The assembly] returns to stand before the kitchen, turning left to take their positions. The head seat (*shouzuo*) emerges from behind the kitchen to the right, bows in greeting, and thanks [the assembly] for the hot water.

The head steward escorts him out. [The assembly] returns to the center and burns incense, bowing in greeting between the upper and lower sections. They withdraw. One strike of the bell signals the collection of the bowls; the hall bell strikes three times as they leave the hall.

The Rules of Purity Notice (The *Weina* prepares the notice in advance and presents it to the Abbot for his signature; it is read either on the sixteenth or seventeenth day. Once the reading is finished, it is hung before the Sangha Hall.
Three days prior, the attendant of the Hall Office carries it there on a pole).
On the sixteenth day, at the time of the midday meal, the *Zhibo-shui* (Bowl-Washing Water) is served. The *Zhike* (Guest Master) rises to burn incense, stands in the center, and reads the notice.

Regarding the communal rules for the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat): the south-seeking chariot is fundamentally intended for those who are lost, and the mirror for clear observation is originally meant to reflect those who are deviant.

If there were no deviance, where would the mirror have application? If there were no delusion, what use would the chariot have? Thus, those who travel the Way should seek excellence in both virtue and learning.
How could one wait for a minor punishment before being able to apply the whip? However, the younger generation lacks self-awareness, and their conduct is no different from that of public laborers;

since there is now no other choice, strict discipline must be enforced. On this day of communal regulation, I shall briefly set forth these conditions based on the *Guoqing Bailu* and the *Tianzhu Zhongzhi*.

During the ninety-day period of *kaṭhina* (the summer retreat), one must plan to cultivate the Way; whether through lecturing, repentance, meditation, or recitation, there should be no leisure for eating or resting.

How could one afford to be negligent or wander in and out at will during these three months? As a general rule, leave of absence shall not be granted within this period, except in the event of the misfortune of one's parents or preceptor, for which the Hall Office must provide a formal certification specifying the dates before permission is issued. Failure to comply with these regulations shall not be tolerated.
Furthermore, those who rely on false pretexts to enter or leave at will shall not be permitted to dwell here.
Morning repentance, daytime lectures, recitation of sutras, study, and the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa* are the constant regulations of the monastic garden and the universal custom of all quarters;
this is especially fitting for the summer retreat, when one ought to practice with even greater earnestness. Now, those who manage affairs for the mountain gate or are ill are exempted.
Regarding those granted leave for water-related duties, whether they be novices or elders, all must rise from the assembly, eat their fill, and sleep soundly;
thus they evade the communal rules and waste the faithful’s offerings, which is deeply improper. Therefore, when the assembly gathers, the *karmadāna* (Vina) shall arrange them in order;
for any who fail to attend, their names shall be recorded and they shall be fined five *liang* of incense. Upon the striking of the mallet, they must offer a formal confession and apology.

For a first offense, the penalty is double; for a second offense, one is not permitted to dwell together with the community. If one arrives late to the assembly, the penalty is three *liang* of incense;
if one absents oneself secretly during the proceedings, the penalty is three *liang* of incense.

During the two periods for the morning and evening meals, one must arrive early; once the wooden fish gong has sounded, it is not permitted to enter the hall, nor to make noise while unfolding the alms bowl, nor to let spoons or chopsticks fall to the ground, nor to laugh or speak while eating with food in the mouth.
Upon finishing the meal, one must be among the first to rise. Those who violate these rules shall be penalized with five *liang* of incense.
The decorum within the assembly values solemnity above all; it is not merely for one's own sake, but also gives rise to the goodness of others.

In all places where the community gathers, it is forbidden to engage in conversation or laughter. When exiting the corridors, one must not drape a hand-towel over the arm or walk with hands clasped or in a hurried manner, as such conduct violates dignified demeanor. Any who contravene this shall be fined five *liang* of incense.
Except for those with reasons for illness, no one is permitted to strike the gong at the two meal times for rice gruel or vegetarian meals;
furthermore, it is not allowed to privately store food in front of the Sangha Hall. Those who violate this shall be severely punished.
All those residing in the quarters, regardless of seniority or experience, shall take meditative stillness and the recitation of scriptures as their primary tasks.
They must not privately allow monastics or laypeople to stay overnight, eat, consume meat, or drink alcohol; those who violate this shall not dwell with the community.

As for clothing, adornment, and etiquette, one must naturally conform to the Dharma. When walking along the corridors, one must wear the *kaṣāya* robe, and during the midday meal, one must likewise do so.
One must not expose one's shortcomings; those who violate this shall be fined five *liang* of incense.

New students must maintain a resolute will and reverent demeanor, staying close to their superiors to receive instruction, recite the texts thoroughly, and inquire about the principles of the teachings.
Those in superior positions should demonstrate proper regulations and constrain them with daily assignments, awaiting the arrival of midsummer.
Examinations shall be conducted with rewards for those who pass and penalties for those who fail.
The name of the Sangha signifies harmony, patience, forbearance, and yielding; it does not permit contentious calculations, raised voices, or harsh expressions.

Those who compete with one another shall each be penalized by thirty-seven prostrations before the assembly to offer public repentance and apology. One who is reviled but remains unmoved shall be exempted from physical punishment.
When interacting with others, one should not inquire after their trivialities or engage in mutual lodging; those who do not retaliate when struck shall be exempt from punishment.
One must not allow mutual overnight stays in the *śālā* (monastic quarters); violators shall not dwell together.

Playing the lute, playing chess, singing, chanting, and various other vulgar activities truly obstruct the path of practice and must not be performed; those who contravene this shall be penalized seven times.
Prostrations.
One who composes anonymous writings shall not live with the community once their identity is established.
Regarding those who violate the precepts through such acts as theft or failing to maintain the *vinaya*, they shall be dealt with according to the Pure Rules (*qinggui*).
The conditions listed above should each be duly observed. For those soaring high in flight, what need is there to fear the net? For those hidden deep in the abyss, how could they dread the trap?
By relying on conditions one advances on the Path and gains manifold benefit; by depending on the assembly one establishes oneself, and thus it is necessary to protect it.
We request that the Hall Administration comply with this and not allow any violation, lest you incur regret later. Shown on the [day] of this month.
The Abbot’s Seal; the Abbot’s personal signature.
The Abbot specially prepares tea for the Head Seat and the assembly.
On the second day, the Guest-inviting Attendant prepares the tea notice (see below), arranges trays, cloths, incense burners, and candles, and takes the Abbot’s tea [to the guest quarters].

Holding the notice with both hands, he proceeds to the Head Seat’s quarters, burns incense, performs a prostration touching the ground, and makes this request: "The Abbot has retired from his morning meal and will now serve tea in the Cloud Hall specifically for you;
we humbly hope that you will deign to honor us with your presence. He presents the notice and posts it on the upper section of the wall in front of the Sangha Hall.

The guest attendant (kètóu xíngzhě) then requests the various head officers, administrators, and elders to hang the tea-serving plaque. At the time of the midday meal, when the long board gong sounds, the guest attendant enters the hall.
Request the monks to come forward and burn one stick of incense; turn to the left, perform three full prostrations with the robes fully spread, and circumambulate the hall once.

Request tea, then exit to the outer hall to exchange greetings with those in both the upper and lower sections. Turn back to enter before the Holy Monk (Śākyamuni) and exchange greetings there, then withdraw.

Wait for the attendant to descend from the hall; meanwhile, within the hall, the special seat for the Head Seat (Shouzuo) shall be established opposite the Abbot’s seat, and the boards for the various quarters shall then be struck.

The three [officers] descend to the assembly, enter the hall, strike the tea drum, and burn incense; the attendant performs the rites (all of which is identical to the special tea ceremony for the Abbot, except that they do not bow to the Abbot).
The Head Seat proceeds before the Abbot to express thanks for the tea. The first unfolding of the mat says: "I, [Name], having now received this prepared tea, hereby offer my thanks;

my humble feelings are overcome with gratitude. The second unfolding says: "On this day of early summer... and so forth. He performs three prostrations with unopened sitting cloths (*sanchu-ri*), and the Abbot returns one bow. The Head Seat turns...
The Master emerges from behind the Sangha of Sages on the right and stands; the Abbot briefly escorts him back to his position. The attendant holding the cup burns the "light-accompanying" incense.
The attendants of the upper and lower sections exchange greetings. The bell is struck once to collect the cups of the assembly; it is struck three times, and the assembly descends from the hall.
On the third day, a special tea service is held for the abbot in the front hall and for the assembly in the rear hall.
First, the Head Seat (Shouzuo) goes to the Abbot’s quarters (Fangzhang) to request tea, presenting a formal tea invitation (as seen below).

He then proceeds to the rear hall to request tea from the Head Seat there (if the position of Head Seat in the rear hall is vacant, he requests it from the Repentance Leader [Chanshou]). The sequence of ritual observances is roughly the same as before, with the exception that the "light-accompanying incense" (guangban xiang) is not burned.
Seal of the Rear Hall Head Seat and the Assembly. Respectfully requested by the Fore Hall Head Seat, Bhikṣu [Name].
Sealed with care.
The Abbot and the two classes of officials serve tea in the Hall (the procedures for opening and closing the retreat are identical).
Upon concluding the retreat, after the Abbot has finished serving tea in the Sangha Hall, the Attendant, together with the Guest Master, proceeds to the Hall to serve tea.

The Guest Master notifies the Head of the Assembly in advance to hang the "Tea Service" plaque and informs the community; he then invites the Chief Cook to accompany them in heating the water and distributing the cups.

The Abbot sends the Tea Attendant (Chashijue) ahead to the Kitchen Office (Kusi), where the Head Cook (Dianzuo) receives him. The Head of the Hall (Tangzhu) leads the assembly to welcome him at the gate.

The Attendant takes the seat of honor on behalf of the Abbot; the Head Cook stands by his side. The Attendant steps forward from the center to burn incense, then returns to his position and bows with his hand to the assembly as they sit to drink tea.
Once the tea ceremony is concluded, the Head Cook escorts the Attendant out, and the Head of the Hall sees him through the gate.

They immediately proceed to the Abbot’s quarters to express thanks. The Tea Steward (Cha-k'u-si) awaits the Abbot’s serving of tea; once the Abbot has finished, the Administrative Officers (Chih-shih) go to the Hall to serve tea.

The Administrative Officers take their seats at the head position, while the Chief Cook (Dian-zo) distributes himself among the ranks to perform the rites. They escort the Abbot’s attendants out the door together and call out:

"The Head of the Assembly and the Great Congregation go to the Tea Steward's Office to express thanks for the tea. The Tea Steward reports back, saying: "The Administrative Officers have conveyed a message that the expression of thanks for the tea is waived. [The Head] Officials...

When the serving of tea in the Sangha Hall has concluded, the attendants of the Hall Administration (Tangsi) shall notify the Head of the Assembly (Cantou) to post a notice and inform the community that the Chief Cook (Diansuo) is invited as a guest to perform the ritual together with the administrators of the Treasury Office (Kusi). (The chanting of thanks upon exiting the door and the chanting for dispensation from formalities are the same.)
The duty officer on call must ensure that the *karmadāna* prepares a register in advance prior to the commencement of the retreat (*sīmā-bandha*).

He shall verify the number of *ācāryas* and, according to their ordination seniority from junior to senior, rotate them every three days, beginning again from the bottom once the cycle is complete. This shall be recorded daily according to the established rules.
The names of those on duty for the preceding days shall be listed individually at the end; the *vinaya-dhara* (ritual master) shall carry them to the Abbot’s quarters for formal inspection.
First, the hall attendant shall deliver them to the meal hall of the person currently on duty.

On the evening of the third day, after the recitations are completed, the *vinaya-dhara* shall take the *xuzhi* (regulations manual), the *ta* (stupa), and the vestments and deliver them to the meal hall of the next person on duty. When the three-day period is complete, they shall be displayed.
All regulations are forwarded and appear below. The person on duty shall stand at the end of the attendants' row. One must know the proper forms:

though a craftsman’s skill may be exquisite, he does not abandon the compass and square for producing squares and circles; likewise, those newly studying the monastic life must learn the protocols of the *conglin* (monastic community).
This is the great progression for one emerging from the multitude and the initial gateway for entering the Way; it is direct and applies throughout the three periods of the day.
One must not, from beginning to end, make excuses or defer on account of various conditions. Hereafter, the rules for daily life are set forth in detail.

At dawn, in the Great Hall, chant the scriptures while awaiting the striking of the hall bell; then, together with the attendants, return to the ranks and stand. When the bell ceases, strike two introductory strikes.
Once the two Head Seat monks have finished reciting the incantations—approximately four or five lines—strike two introductory strikes.

When the practitioners have finished their recitation and are standing still, strike two introductory strikes. When the Head Officers raise the titles, strike one introductory strike; when the assembly has completed the three chants, strike the concluding bell.
Give one strike (as in previous examples). The *vinaya-dhara* performs the dedication to "All Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time" and strikes once;
"All Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas" and strikes once; "Mahāprajñāpāramitā" and strikes twice. Then lead the assembly to the hall.

When performing the repentance ritual, wait for the bell in the Repentance Hall to ring; return to your position as the attendant of the day and stand. When the bell stops ringing, strike it twice to lead [the assembly].

Continue until the repentance and the making of vows are completed, then bow and rise. Strike the bell twice to lead [the assembly] again. The presiding practitioner raises his hand and leads the chanting of the Buddha’s name, striking the bell once for each syllable.
This continues until the recitation of "Namo to the Sangha of the Ten Directions" is finished. Immediately turn your body to face the presiding practitioner and perform a formal inquiry (wenshen).
Proceed slowly [in a clockwise circumambulation], chanting the names of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas while striking the gong once for each name.

When the recitation of the Buddha’s name has nearly finished, stand still and strike the gong twice. Raise the *triśaraṇa* (Three Refuges) and, upon concluding with "Homage to the Holy Assembly," bow and rise, striking the gong twice.
Recite "Amitābha Buddha of True Gold Color" and finish by striking the gong once. Then, raise the [name of] each Buddha.
Chant the ten sounds with one strike to lead them, continuing up to one hundred sounds; chant the invocation with two strikes.
For each instance of raising the name of the Bodhisattva, chant ten sounds with one strike to lead them, ending with the final "Buddha" at two strikes.

For each instance of raising the verses for repentance, making vows, and dedication of merit, chant with one strike to lead them (for the "All Tathāgatas of the Ten Directions and Three Times," chant as previously described). Then return to the Sangha Hall.

At dawn, proceed to the hall for the morning gruel and complete the repentance ritual. Upon the striking of the second signal for the *yin* (leading bell), exit the main hall door, turn to the side, perform a brief *wenxun* (bowing with hands raised), and slowly ring the *yin* as you proceed to stand on the right side outside the inner hall door, waiting for the assembly to enter.

Once the Abbot has entered, follow him into the inner hall and stand on the right side, awaiting the Abbot’s completion of the incense offering and his return to his seat; then, strike the *yin* two times.

When the assembly has finished their inquiries and is seated upon the platform, strike the bell three times for entering meditative concentration (*samādhi*); the first stroke is heavy and the subsequent ones are light (after approximately several dozen breaths, recite one scroll of the *Hṛdaya-sūtra*).

Strike the bell three times for emerging from concentration; the first stroke is light and the subsequent ones are heavy. Upon inquiry, exit to the outer hall and sit in the position of the day’s duty officer.
Upon hearing the bell, immediately descend from the meditation platform, maintain a solemn and dignified demeanor, and proceed slowly to the right side outside the inner hall.
Standing to the side, when the drum rolls and the signal is given, he enters the inner hall and bows before the Sacred Monk.

He performs a minor bow before the incense burner, burns two sticks of incense with his left hand, and performs another minor bow. Stepping back three and a half paces, he bows again and joins his palms.

Circumambulating the Sacred Monk to the right, he passes behind the kitchen and proceeds to the hall where the drum is struck; as the drum ceases, the mallet strikes once, and the head monk raises and displays the alms bowl.
At the conclusion of each verse, strike the wooden gavel once and say: "I inform the assembly:

on the morning of the first day of the bright fortnight (*śukla-pakṣa*), each person shall individually maintain the six recollections. (If it is from the first to the fifteenth day, say: "From the sixteenth day onwards, this month is of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇa-pakṣa*"); on such-and-such a morning, each person shall individually maintain the six recollections.

Having finished, strike the wooden gavel once and dedicate the merit, saying: "May the morning gruel bring special benefit" (first look at the daily deity manifestation, etc.). For this purpose and recollection, the assembly shall chant "Pure."
The Buddha Vairocana of the Pure Dharma-body strikes the mallet once (using the left hand to form a covering gesture and press down on the mallet base while striking the mallet with the right hand;

the height should not exceed five inches, and one should lower the mallet only after the sound has ceased, ensuring the rhythm of urgency and relaxation is appropriate). For each invocation, strike the mallet once; when finished, wait for a long duration before striking the mallet again to signal that the food distribution is complete.
Strike the mallet once more. The Head of the Assembly then recites the verse for bestowing food; when the verse is finished, strike the mallet once.

Silently perform the five contemplations and strike the wooden mallet once. The head monk raises the verse for receiving food, then exits from behind the kitchen and proceeds to the front of the Holy Sangha to pay respects.
Returning to his position as the duty-day officer, he receives his food. Waiting for the water for rinsing to be brought out, he enters the hall and pays respects before the Holy Sangha.
Continuing until the mallet station, he briefly pays respects and observes the assembly wrapping their bowls. Finally, he strikes the wooden mallet once.
First, after reciting the verse for the conclusion of the meal and striking the wooden mallet once, the Hall Attendant strikes it again to lead the assembly to the main hall;
there they chant together, and the person on duty is the last to leave the hall.
When the board for the midday meal sounds, enter the hall with the assembly and take your seat at the position for the day’s duty attendant.

Wait for the drum to sound, then descend from the meditation seat and stand to the right outside the inner hall. Wait for the drum to turn, and when the bell in front of the Sangha Hall tolls, enter the hall and burn incense (the rest is as before).
When the lecture is about to begin, the bell before the Sangha Hall is struck; the assembly follows to the Dharma Hall and takes their seats in the positions assigned for that day.

When the drum strikes the second round, they rise and go before the incense burner to perform a bow. They then proceed to the quarters of the Abbot to perform a bow, turn back, and stand beneath the shoulder of the attendant.
Waiting until the drum strikes the third round, they perform another bow and request the Abbot to rise from his sedan chair.
Upon arriving at the front of the Dharma Hall, the Abbot dismounts from his sedan chair; the two *mingyin* strike twice, and the assembly stands up.
The Abbot proceeds directly to the western side and stands there. The Abbot burns incense, turns to perform a greeting (*wenshen*), and the two *mingyin* strike twice. The Abbot ascends the hall;

the Head Seat and the attendant on duty enter from the second row on the western side to the place where the gavel is struck, waiting for the Abbot to burn incense and perform the greeting before the *mingyin* strike.

After the second [officiant] has finished sitting in the half-lotus position (*paryaṅka*), he strikes the wooden mallet once. The Abbot takes up the hand-incense burner and recites the verse beginning with "The fragrance of precepts, the fragrance of concentration...

and so forth. The Abbot performs the dedication of merit until reaching the phrase "for this purpose," at which point the assembly chants the sacred name ten times, striking the mallet once for each repetition.

When this is finished, the Abbot again recites the "Dispelling Obstacles" invocation, calls upon the names [of the Buddhas], and spreads open the scriptures. Having done so, he strikes the mallet once more and returns to his seat.

Regarding the Merit of Preaching and Listening (extending to all Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time): strike the mallet once; [all Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas]—strike the mallet once; *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*—strike the mallet once.

The Abbot descends from his seat and proceeds before the great incense burner to inquire after the assembly’s welfare, striking the mallet twice as a lead. The assembly disperses. The Head Monks (*śreṣṭhin*) shall deliver the lecture;
this applies to all cases, but on the first day they shall invite the Abbot to the quarters, and from the second day onward, they shall go to the monks’ cells to invite him.

After the meal, chant the *Anrakugyō* (Practice of Peace and Bliss) while waiting for the assembly to descend from the hall. When the temple bell is struck to signal the return to their positions, stand in place once the bell has ceased.
Strike the bell twice as an introduction; when the Head Monks raise the scripture to the character "品" (*bun*), strike it once.

Recite until reaching the phrase "First, dwelling securely in the bodhisattva’s sphere of practice," then strike the bell twice. When reaching the line "Practicing the Way," stand still at the end of the subsequent verse and strike the bell once as an introduction.

Upon reaching the verse "Beholding the Buddhas of the Ten Directions," strike once for the *yin* (lead-in) signal; when the assembly joins their palms at the conclusion of the sutra, strike twice for the *yin* signal. Raise the title [of the scripture] with the *yin* signal as before.

Recite the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* while waiting for the palace bell to be struck; then return to the position of the day’s duty attendant. When the bell ceases, strike twice for the *yin* signal, followed by the *tou* (head) signal.

The leader first recites one invocation of the mantra with a single strike of the bell; the assembly joins in recitation until reaching "Indrāya," at which point there is a second strike and the bell is rung rapidly for several strikes as they proceed through the recitation until reaching "Tviṣīmān," at which point there is one final strike and the bell is rung rapidly for several strikes until the end of each section.
The leader then raises the next section again, concluding it as before with rapid strikes for several counts until reaching the fifth section, where he rings the bell with a single strike.
Strike twice to establish the ritual boundary; when the incantation is finished, strike once to lead [the assembly] and raise the title for the dedication of merit, striking as before.
When performing the *śrāddha* (offering of food), wait until the recitation of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* and the dedication are complete, then strike once to lead [the assembly].

The congregation turns around and recites from "Namo to the Buddhas of the Ten Directions" up to "Namo to the Greatly Compassionate Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva," striking once to lead [the assembly] up to the third [verse].
When the recitation is complete, strike the bell twice and lower it; then recite the verse: "By the empowerment of divine mantras, the food and drink are purified" (recite the eight-line verse).
At its conclusion, strike the bell once and raise it; then recite the mantra, striking the bell once at the end of each repetition until seven repetitions are completed.

Strike the bell twice and call upon the names of the four Tathāgatas, striking the bell once at the end of each name until three repetitions are completed. Strike the bell twice and recite: "You ghosts..."
[The assembly of deities] (conclude with the four-line verse). Sound the signal once. Recite: "May this merit... (conclude with the four-line verse). Sound the signal once.
[Recite "In the ten directions," etc., sounding the signal as before]. ○ (The sequence now follows the method of the Repentance Master, as fully detailed in the *Shishi Tonglan*).

After the morning recitation session, continue chanting until the "Bestowing upon Beings" (Shisheng) section is finished. On the day of duty (*zhirì*), the bell in front of the Sangha Hall is struck intermittently;

for each strike, chant the Great Compassion Mantra (*Dabei Zhou*) approximately once. Anticipating that the Abbot will light the lamps, go to the Dharma Hall and strike the bell three times in succession, then pause.
Upon reaching the Dharma Hall, perform a formal greeting (*wenxun*) before the Abbot, strike the bell twice as an introduction, and then return to your position on the day-duty row.
Sitting and waiting for the abbot, when the ruler is struck twelve more times, he rises to await the abbot’s distribution of the lots (*jiū*).
He speaks aloud, saying, "So-and-so will lecture on So-and-so," or if the second name is drawn, it is done in the same manner. Once the proclamation is finished, he returns to his seat.

Next, the selection of the *kāi-kē* (the opening of the curriculum) and the recitation of the text proceed as before, until the recitation is complete. Two strikes of the *yǐn* (conductor's gong) signal the assembly to disperse. The details are as follows in the subsequent section on the formal procedure.
Ritual. The names of those on duty in rotation follow one after another, beginning again from the start: [Name], [Name], [Name], [Name], [Name].
On this day of this month, the Hall Attendant,
bearing the seal of the Abbot, has performed the *Dabei Chanhua* (Great Compassion Repentance) ritual. [Seal] performed.

On the morning of the twentieth day of the fourth month, prior to the commencement of the Great Compassion Repentance Rite (*Mahākaruṇā-pūjā*), the attendant of the Hall Office (*táng-sī xíng-zhě*) shall notify the Abbot, the two classes of officials, and all the monastic quarters.
Furthermore, he shall hang a signboard announcing the performance of the repentance rite to inform the assembly, and instruct the shrine-attendants to spread out *pútán* mats.
The attendant of the Hall Office shall prepare incense burners, candle stands, and flower scattering trays, placing them upon a small table and arranging them there.
Before the main practice, at dawn on the day of the ritual, the temple bell is struck; the assembly returns to their positions according to the diagram and stands as prescribed.

The sequence for the methods of practice is fully detailed in the *Buzhuyi* (Supplementary Ritual). One must master both the ritual procedures and the contemplative visualization (*li-guan*) with complete proficiency.

Regarding this *dhāraṇī*, one should give rise to resolute faith and cultivate it with a mind of diligence, exerting all effort in both the aspect of form and the aspect of formlessness, thereby eliminating obstacles in the present life.
All afflictions are cleared away, and rebirth in the Pure Land is unfailing; the extensive benefits are fully recorded in the scriptures.
On the day the abbot inaugurates the lectures and the ritual of repentance, the abbot initiates the discourse. Indeed, it is the proper duty of the abbot to preach and instruct his disciples.

To investigate the subtle and seek out the hidden, scholars must apply their minds with diligence. One day prior to the commencement of the lecture, the attendant shall inform the Abbot, who shall issue a written notice stating:
"Tomorrow, the Abbot will deliver a lecture on a specific text, from a certain volume and section.
The temple administrator’s acolyte shall then post the "Lecture Notice" board in front of the Sangha Hall. On the morning of the appointed day, the Abbot is invited once again for the morning gruel.

The Hall Administrator (Tangsi) and the Attendant (Xingzhe) inform the Abbot that the lecture is to begin; they wait until the bell signaling the end of the session has ceased for a short while, then strike the "Silence Bell" (Jingzhong) three times.
The Attendant instructs the attendants and the head of the table-setters to arrange the lecture seat.

Once the Hall Administrator and the Attendant have informed the Abbot and the two classes of officials have struck the corridor boards and the bell before the Sangha Hall, the tower bell is sounded once.

At the eighteenth strike, the drum sounds; the Abbot emerges from his quarters and takes his seat in the hall. When the drum strikes for the second time, the assembly recites the "Entrustment" chapter (*Parīndanā-parivarta*) of the *Lotus Sūtra*.

When the drum strikes for the third time, the Abbot mounts a palanquin. If the Dharma Hall is distant from the Abbot’s quarters, he may order the person on duty (*zhiriri*) to go ahead to the Dharma Hall and stand in wait.
Upon reaching the front of the Dharma Hall, the Abbot dismounts from the palanquin, and the introductory music (*yin*) is played.
The two lower assemblies fold their sitting cloths (*kaṭhina*), rise, and receive the Abbot. The Abbot returns to the center to burn incense.

If this is the first time he is giving a lecture, he should perform three prostrations, withdraw his sitting cloth, and inquire after the assembly's well-being. Entering from the east, he inquires after the well-being [of the assembly] again, ascends the seat, burns incense, and inquires after the well-being once more before sitting cross-legged.
The two classes of attendants advance together to offer incense and perform a prostration; next, the elders (*vṛddha*); next, those from various regions (*jiahu*); and finally, the hall residents.

Each person follows this procedure (the head of the assembly shall pre-emptively provide funds to purchase incense and candles; in subsequent years, one need only carry an incense case and burn incense, and formal prostrations are not required—though those newly returned to the community must still observe them).

If there are visiting abbots from other mountains, West Halls, Head Seats, or long-standing associates who have come for discussion, the attendant must step forward in advance to prevent them from bowing.
Once the consultation is concluded, the attendant shall invite them to seats to the left or right of the Dharma seat to engage in discourse.

Having concluded the discourse with a formal expression of thanks, the assembly descends from their seats. If the visiting scholar is a person of renowned virtue, the abbot shall prostrate before the incense burner and return the greeting;
however, if the visitor is a subordinate or a junior, it is not necessary to return the salutation.
In all cases, those who have come from other regions to lecture are immediately instructed by the attendant in charge of guests to proceed to the Abbot’s Quarters for refreshments.

While performing *caṅkrama* (walking meditation) and reciting scriptures, when the time for the morning meal arrives on the day of the *qichan* (confession and repentance), the hall attendant (*tangsi xingzhe*) waits until the signal bell for descending from the hall has finished sounding;

he then strikes the temple bell to assemble the assembly. Once they are standing in order, the head monk (*toushou*) intones the "Peaceful Conduct" (*anle xing*), which refers to the practice of walking while eating. They perform the circumambulation (*xingdao*) until they reach the standing position.

The *Dingjing* (Concentration Sutra) concludes with the invocation: *Namo Śākyamuni Buddha; Namo the Lotus Sutra; Namo Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva*. Dedication (*huixiang*): "May the three obstacles be extinguished. On this day, following the formal assembly, the *Lengyan* (Śūraṅgama) Assembly is inaugurated.

It was also announced on the preceding day by the attendants of the Hall Office (*tangsi*) during the confession service (*chan*), stating that the *Lengyan* Assembly would be established in conjunction with the confession.
A notice board was hung to inform the community. At evening, the bell for the Sangha Hall was struck.

The preceding bell gathers the assembly; they stand in formation. The Head [Monk] recites the incantation for walking the path (*caṅkrama*). When the recitation is finished, there is a universal dedication of merit (*pariṇāmanā*) (as detailed).

Once this is concluded, the assembly turns their bodies toward the outside and stands. To perform the *śrāddha* offering, one should press the vessel with the right hand and recite the incantation seven times.

Then, snap the fingers seven times and extend the arms to perform the fearless gift (*abhaya-dāna*). Thereafter, pour the food onto clean ground and visualize that all ghosts and spirits partake of it.
(The methods for offering food and the visualizations are fully detailed in Venerable Ciyun’s *Jinyuan ji*). Regarding the *Poṣadha* ritual:
the *Buddha-vinaya* stipulates that the *saṃgha* as a whole should observe the *poṣadha*; how could it be merely a matter for the *karmadāna* alone? Now, those who perform these rites...
The virtuous *karmadāna* (Venerable Vinaya Master) shall convene [the assembly] in accordance with the precepts and maintain himself with dignity according to the Dharma.

After the *karmadāna* has performed the formal closing of the retreat (*jie*), he must first discreetly carry incense and visit each of the quarters to convene them for the recitation of the precepts and the formal announcement of the proceedings.

In the interim, he must also ensure that representatives are prepared; furthermore, he shall record the names of each individual and report this to the Abbot for his awareness, requesting that the Abbot issue an invitation.

Guest practitioners are requested to each take their seats in the Abbot’s quarters for the serving of tea. When the guests arrive, they burn incense and perform the rites (according to the usual custom).

After the tea is finished, the Abbot makes the following announcement: "This is a great occasion for the monastic community; the recitation of the precepts is of primary importance and shall be performed shortly. We request the First Seat to respond to the Dharma; [Name] to recite the precepts; [Name] to provide the Sanskrit chanting;

[Name] to preside over the formal announcement; and [Name] to conduct the ritual of purification, and so forth. Having made this announcement, he immediately rises, bows universally to all present, and escorts the guests out. One must prepare for this one day in advance at the Dharma Hall.
When preparing for the ritual procedures of the invitation ceremony, one must select those who are thoroughly practiced and instruct them repeatedly until they are proficient;

do not wait until the last moment, lest there be lapses in the proper decorum. Once proficiency is achieved, [the training] ceases (during the sequence of the harmonious assembly and at the time of the recitation of the precepts, the protocols for hospitality shall be conducted according to the traditions of the mountain gate).
1. On the fifteenth day of the dark fortnight of the fourth month, forty [rules] were expanded; (the rest is abbreviated). 2.

On the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight of the fifth month, thirteen [rules] were expanded, including the two *aniyata* rules; (the rest is abbreviated). 3. On the fifteenth day of the dark fortnight of the fifth month, thirty [rules] were expanded;
(the rest is abbreviated). 4. On the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight of the sixth month, ninety *tiśa* rules were expanded; (the rest is abbreviated).
5 (June): On the fifteenth day of the dark fortnight, the extensive *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra* is recited (the remainder is abbreviated). 6 (July):
On the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight, the *Poṣadha* is not recited (alternatively, the *Śrīmālā-siṃhanāda-sūtra* is recited).
On the morning of the day [of the Uposatha], hang the plaque (when pasting the notice, go to the Dharma Hall for the recitation of the precepts; each person prepares a piece of incense).

At the time of the early morning gruel in the Sangha Hall, the attendant on duty waits until the bowls have been spread out, then strikes the mallet once and says: "Virtuous Sangha, listen! Today is the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight" (if it is the dark fortnight, say:

"the tenth [or fourteenth] day of the dark fortnight of this month [specifying whether it is a large or small month]"). The assembly of monks is in harmony; at this hour, we shall proceed to the Lecture Hall for the recitation of the precepts. Strike the mallet once."

Announce to the assembly as follows: "In the early morning, each person shall individually observe the six recollections (as usual). If the *Poṣadha* is held at the hour of the Dragon (7–9 a.m.), the bath shall be opened after the gruel meal;
if the *Poṣadha* is held at the hour of the Monkey (3–5 p.m.), the bath shall be opened after the midday meal.

Furthermore, order the Dharma Hall to be swept and cleaned, arrange the chairs and benches, and set out the two seats for the Sacred Monk and the Abbot at the eastern end of the hall facing west. Place the wooden mallet (*kaiti*) at the western side of the hall.
Inside the front section, arrange chairs facing west (this is the position for those performing the formal announcement; some may arrange them facing the abbot, but this is not correct).

The hall attendants (táng-sī xíng-zhě) shall line up hand-incense burners, flower trays, tally boxes, water basins, soup basins, and hand towels in front of the main incense burner, and place a meditation cushion on a stand before it.
Furthermore, they shall arrange an incense burner, a flower vase, and candles upon the seats.

Regarding the incense burner stand and other items, one must cherish the *śīla* (precepts) and not treat them with casualness. (The current method is presented here as a single path, with the ten categories listed in full.

1. Gathering the Assembly: On the day of the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), the storehouse officer (*kū-si*) awaits the arrival of the time and prepares the refreshments (*dian-xin*) to be sent to the hall.

The office official (*tang-si*) requests those who will recite the precepts and perform the ritual duties. Once the refreshments have been served, the *vinaya-dhara* (*wei-na*) instructs the hall office acolytes (*xing-zhe*) to inform the abbot.
The *Chishi* (Holder of the Staff) and the two attendants strike the corridor boards and ring the bell before the Sangha Hall.

When the assembly has gathered before the hall, they take their places according to the order of their bowls, standing one by one with palms joined in the *añjali* mudrā; their deportment must be solemn and disciplined, and laughter or speech is forbidden.

When the Abbot arrives, the striking of the bell ceases, and the Head Seat stands beneath the Abbot’s shoulder (to facilitate his answering the Dharma), while the *Fanyin Shi* (Master of Chanting) stands opposite him.
The Abbot and the Preceptor of the Recitation of the Precepts stand facing the Head Seat (Zhǒuzuò) and the two classes of the assembly, all arranged according to seniority in the order of ordination;

those presiding over the formal announcements and ritual duties stand in the lower hall behind the assembly, while those performing the purification of offerings (shuōjìng rén) stand in the upper hall behind the assembly.
Only the two individuals on duty stand opposite each other directly above the Abbot and the Chant Master (Fànsī).
Stepping back to a short distance, the assembly gathers; the great bell is struck three times. The official on duty strikes the *yin* (introductory) bell twice and says:

"The Great Assembly, each should recite the 'Exquisite Verse upon Hearing the Bell'. He strikes the *yin* bell once more, and the assembly joins their palms and says: "Subduing the power of Māra’s enemies, Exhausting all fetters without remainder, Striking the *gandi* in the open air— Monks who hear it shall assemble.
All you who wish to hear the Dharma, To cross the flood of birth and death, Upon hearing this exquisite sound, All shall gather like clouds here."
Second, entering the hall: After the verse for hearing the bell has been recited, the attendant on duty strikes the *yin* (lead) twice.

After performing a brief inquiry (*wèn xùn*) before [the master], the *yin* is struck intermittently to lead the assembly into the hall. The assembly proceeds in two rows according to seniority to the incense burner in front of the lecture hall;
a large tray is prepared and placed upon a stand, and the entire assembly takes turns placing small pieces of incense into the tray one after another and then stands still.

The holder of the Dharma-seat (dharmāsana) bows in greeting and returns to his position, standing firmly. Next, each member of the assembly bows in greeting to the Dharma-seat and proceeds to their respective seats, standing in order in the upper and lower halls.

The person presiding over the ritual stands at the head of the west-side cross-legged chair, while the person who performs the *śuddhi-vacana* (declaration of purity) stands behind the head seat (the *śraddhā-deśaka*).
[Note: In this tradition, one seat is suspended for the sake of the one performing the *śuddhi-vacana*. Once the assembly has stood together, the signal is struck twice to lead them forward.

The junior assembly inquires after one another’s health and the ritual leader announces: "May the great assembly each recite the sublime verse for entering the hall: 'When the precepts are pure like the full moon, and body and speech are bright and free from blemish;

when the great assembly is harmonious and free from contention, only then can the *poṣadha* be performed together. Each person spreads their sitting cloth and performs three prostrations (with one strike of the gong at each prostration).

The assembly then kneels with their right knees on the ground, and the ritual leader announces: 'At this time, as the assembly has gathered and the Elder is joyful, the Abbot says: "Great assembly, take heed! I, Bhikṣu [Name], from the previous *poṣadha* until the present..."'"

[The officiant] says: "In the meantime, [I] have been troubled by many unwholesome thoughts regarding the three karmas and four modes of conduct, thereby disturbing the great assembly. I pray that the assembly will, out of compassion, grant their joy through the gift of their approval. Holding the *bai* (white-staff), he speaks again: "May the great assembly each simultaneously request their joy.

The assembly says: "The assembly remembers... [and so forth, as before]. Holding the *bai*, he says: "Joy has been granted. He strikes the bell once as a lead; the assembly gathers up their requisites and rises. He strikes the bell twice as a lead;
the assembly performs the greeting (*wensun*), adjusts their robes, sets aside their requisites, and sits cross-legged.
Third, take up the pure basin and the tally-sticks. Four persons who hold the formal announcement (*śukla-vācanā*) and oversee the ritual rise from their seats and perform a salutation;

those holding the announcement proceed first, followed by the other four. Upon reaching the incense burner, the one holding the announcement stands in the center, while the first person overseeing the ritual stands to his right, the second to his left, the third again to the right, and the fourth [to the left].
The person on the left likewise performs a greeting, holds the white cloth, and burns incense; then they withdraw and perform a greeting together.

They all unfold their ritual implements and perform three prostrations without folding the implements; rising, they perform a greeting, join their palms while holding the white cloth, and perform a self-greeting.

Turning their bodies toward the east, they proceed to stand before the water basin, perform a brief greeting, and kneel with lowered knees (*hukuì*) to recite the verse for the water: "The water of the eight merits purifies all dust; Washing the hands removes the impurities of the mind."

Maintain the precepts without defilement or attachment, without deficiency or transgression; all sentient beings are likewise so. (The following sections for washing hands and wiping with a towel are all to be treated according to this example. When the verse is finished, rise and perform a greeting (*praṇāma*), then proceed westward to the vessel for hot water.

The first attendant shall likewise perform a greeting. Turning back toward the vessel for water, the two attendants must look at one another to coordinate their pace—whether quick or slow—and wait for each other.
They shall briefly exchange greetings, then kneel on their right knees (*hu-kuei*) and, holding the ladle, recite the formula for the hot water.

The verse says: "Perfumed with fragrant water, one bathes away all defilements; The Dharma-body is fully endowed with the five parts, Prajñā is perfectly illuminating, and liberation is complete; All sentient beings gather together, merging into the Dharma-realm. [The following verses for washing with water and wiping with a towel are all treated according to this example.
When the verse is finished, the first person recites the Water Verse (as above). When the verse is finished, they rise together.
The second person likewise performs a greeting and holds the white cloth to return to the place of origin. The first person follows them to the front of the basin for the fragrant water. Second.
The other persons also circumambulate to the water basin, briefly exchange greetings, and kneel on their right knees to recite the verse (as previously stated). When finished, they all rise together.

The third person likewise exchanges greetings until the fourth person finishes reciting the verse; they then return to their positions, perform a simultaneous greeting, and advance three steps forward.
They briefly exchange greetings once more, kneel on their right knees, take the tally-stick (*śalākā*), and hold the water basin, hand towel, and incense censer.

Recite the verse for raising the bathing tally (*yùchóu*) to the left and right while bathing the tally with hot water, saying: "The Arhats and Holy Sangha assemble; the assembly of ordinary beings is in harmony.

With fragrant water, we bathe the pure tally, performing the *poṣadha* to deliver sentient beings. This ritual procedure is the same as that in the *Lüyuan* (Garden of Vinaya); where there are differences, they are recorded here together for selection according to local custom.
From the time the five persons first arrive before the incense burner, they perform three prostrations and do not put away their ritual implements. Rising, they perform the mutual inquiry (*wensun*).
The first person and the second person step forward and perform a minor inquiry; both kneel with their right knees on the ground (*hukui*).
The second person first recites the verse for water (*yunyun*), and the first person subsequently recites the verse for hot water (*yunyun*). When the verses are finished, the two persons [rise].

Together they rise and perform a brief inquiry (*praṇāma*). After the one holding the vessel has announced the matter, they pass each other's positions and stand facing one another to perform an inquiry.
They then proceed forward together to perform another brief inquiry. Kneeling on their right knees, the first person first recites the verse for water (*yathāpi tad...*) on the left side;

the second person subsequently recites the verse for hot water (*yathāpi tad...*) on the right side. Together they rise and perform a brief inquiry, then step back and perform another inquiry before the one holding the vessel.
After the formal announcement (*jñapti*), the third and fourth persons pass by each other in turn to enter and take the positions of the upper hands;

the first and second persons withdraw to stand at the positions of the lower hands and perform a simultaneous salutation (*praṇāma*). The third and fourth persons step forward, kneel with their right knees on the ground, and recite the verses (*gāthā*) (as follows).
Upon completion, after the one who held the announcement passes by, they each return to their original positions and perform a simultaneous salutation as before.
Two people step forward to take the water ladle; next, two people step forward to take the hand towels (the attendants passing them one after another).

The four turn around to face each other, holding the white cloth with its inner side toward themselves, and together kneel in the *hukuei* posture. Holding the white cloth, they recite the two verses for the water and the ladle.

Having finished, they take the tally (the attendant passing it to them). They slightly moisten the left and right sides with the water and ladle, and then raise the bathing tally while reciting the verse for the bathing tally (*yuchu chou-ge*, etc.).
The Four Procedures for Water, Soup, Basins, and Hand-Washing. The five persons rise and stand upright to perform the inquiry (*wenshen*).

The person holding the announcement (*bingbai*) goes first to the place where the mallet (*chui*) is kept and stands facing inward. The four others follow; the person with the water arrives at the mallet station, and the person holding the announcement announces that the cloth covering the mallet shall be lifted.
The person with the water uses their hand to moisten the mallet with water, while the person with the towel follows closely behind to wipe the mallet with the towel, reciting the following:

Next, the one holding the hot water follows the same procedure as the previous four people. They proceed in order before the Sangha, kneeling slightly before the *zhuchi* (abbot) and the assembly, and moving along the line.
Each person washes their hands in turn, dries them with a towel, and recites the verse. When the four have finished, they return to the center and stand in a row, bowing to one another.
Two people step forward to place the water and the basin for hot water; two others step forward to hang up the towels.
Stepping back, they inquire after one another with a single prostration and withdraw their ritual implements, returning each to their original position to sit while inquiring after one another.

[The procedure for] the five-fold distribution of counting sticks (*śalākā*) is as follows: the *bai* (announcement) is made by striking the wooden mallet once, and it is proclaimed: "Virtuous Sangha, listen! Who among you is the youngest to receive and guard the [counting sticks]?

[This is asked] three times in the assembly. Upon first hearing the proclamation, "Who among you is the youngest to receive and guard [the sticks]," the fourth person in the order of seniority immediately stands up and inquires.

After the formal announcement (*bhāṣaṇīya*) has been made, the inquiry is conducted briefly; one stands with hands joined in *añjali* and makes the announcement three times. Upon its completion, strike the gavel once and say: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
There is a pure great śramaṇa from outside entering [the boundary]. (The phrase "There is... from outside" is repeated three times).

If there are visiting bhikṣus, they must all assemble at this place. After the announcement has been made three times, strike the gavel once again and proclaim: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen! The junior members of this assembly have already been gathered and protected; the pure great śramaṇa from outside has already entered within."

The exterior is tranquil and free from all difficulties; it is fit to cast the voting sticks (*śalākā*) and perform the *poṣadha* extensively. I, the bhikṣu [Name], shall cast the voting sticks for the Saṃgha to perform the *poṣadha*. May the Saṃgha be single-minded in mindfulness and perform the *poṣadha*.

May the senior, middle, and junior monks each receive their voting stick in due order according to the Dharma. (Recite "May [it be so]" three times. Strike the wooden gong once. (Receive the voting sticks according to the Dharma, as well as the voting sticks of those who have received delegations.

If the assembly of monks is small, simply announce the matter and distribute the voting sticks; the junior members collect the sticks. If the assembly of monks is large, divide the voting sticks into two parts and conduct the ceremony in the upper and lower halls respectively.
The Ritual Official (*xingzhi*) holds the white tally and approaches the Abbot (*zhuchi*). He kneels slightly before him, and each person receives one tally.

The Abbot receives them with both hands (or, alternatively, he may kneel with his ritual implements spread out along with the assembly to receive them, or remain seated to receive them). He recites the verse for receiving the tally: "Kingly and unimpeded are these tally-sticks of liberation, Difficult to obtain, difficult to encounter.

Now that they have come to me, I receive them with joy upon my head; May all sentient beings likewise do so. The person in charge of collecting and guarding [the tallies] also approaches the assembly before the Abbot and kneels slightly with both hands.

The Abbot receives the tally and recites the verse for returning the tally, saying: "Endowed with purity, I receive this tally; Endowed with purity, I return this tally. Firm in joy and equanimity, without transgression, May all sentient beings be likewise.
The Proclaimer (Baizhang) distributes the tallies in order as he circumambulates the hall. The assembly each receives a tally and recites the verse for receiving the tally (*etc.*).
If there are those with business affairs or who are ill and cannot come to hear the precepts, their names should be written down in pairs in advance.

One explains the *śuddhi* (purification) to those who have received the [distribution of] desires; those who have received the desires then record that those who did not come have received a certain number of counting sticks (*śalākā*).

The Sanskrit term *poṣadha* is translated here as "Pure Abiding" (*jìngzhù*). Nanshan [Daoxuan] says it means "purifying body, speech, and mind by abiding in accordance with the precepts. The *Vinaya* states that its purpose is to cause one to recall transgressions every half-month and to confess them before a person who has not committed such offenses, so as to hope for the reforming of past errors.

First, it prevents further commission of offenses in the present; second, it serves as a deterrent against future negligence regarding the Dharma. Thus, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states that if on the day of the *poṣadha* there is no one capable of reciting the precepts, one should proceed according to the *poṣadha* ritual by distributing voting sticks (*śalākā*) and making a formal announcement (*jìbái*).

One person is then appointed to preach the Dharma and recite the scriptures. As for "distributing voting sticks," it refers to knowing the number of monks in the assembly. Furthermore, the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* relates that when a donor arose to inquire about the number of monks but they did not know the count, the Buddha ordered the distribution of voting sticks. When the number of *śrāmaṇeras* was also unknown, he instructed that they be counted by means of the voting sticks.

If a person donates items for the *poṣadha*, a *śrāmaṇera* also receives them; although he does not go to the place where the *poṣadha* ritual is performed, he receives his share because of the distribution of voting sticks (*śalākā*). Thus, the fourfold division of receiving offerings through the distribution of voting sticks includes *śrāmaṇeras*.
Even one who has not yet received the ten precepts may receive a voting stick, as they likewise partake in the offerings.

They shall draw it as before and hand it to the duty officer. The verse says: "For the [Name] Upādhyāya of [Name] Hall, the Recitation Text.

Whether there be two or three people, the one reciting the text shall hold the volume with both hands, perform a prostration with joined palms (*wènxùn*), and follow those already present into the presence of the Abbot.

After the initial greeting, one places the text-bound volume before the Abbot and greets him once more. Proceeding to the seat assigned for the day’s duty, one sits and recites the text one has studied;

the wording must be polished and fluent, delivered with measured and appropriate pacing so that it may be heard clearly from beginning to end. If the performance is meritorious, one may be rewarded with paper, brushes, and other supplies.

If the recitation is somewhat lengthy, the Abbot may select a passage to test the student by joining in the recitation; provided the student continues without interruption, [the text] remains upon the desk.
A snap of the fingers stops the recitation; the reciter halts his voice, rises, and proceeds before the Abbot to inquire after his well-being.
He takes the text he has recited, returns to his original seat, and sits. The subsequent proceedings are the same for all. When the recitation is finished, the signal bell is struck twice.

The Abbot exits first, and the two classes of officials and the assembly follow him to the three sections of the hall, where each offers a congratulatory toast. On the following day, the members of the three sections visit the Abbot’s quarters.

The Ritual for the Various Administrative Offices and Head Monks to Present Their Thanks for the Feast (At ten monasteries, the *weina* must not participate in the preliminary review; this must be recited by a newly ordained monk).
The Format for the Subjects of the Locked Examination.
After the lectures have been concluded since ancient times, the "locked examination" (*suoshi*) method is employed to evaluate the candidates' talents and test those who have not yet advanced.
This is like a furnace for smelting gold where the lead dross does not remain, or like a chisel for carving jade where the *wuqu* stones are entirely removed.

The abbot shall instruct the attendant to prepare paper four or five days prior to copy the list of those who have lectured and passed the examination (including names of those who have achieved excellence and are outstanding scholars wishing to participate in this selection). [The applicant must submit a formal petition together with these documents.]

The administrators shall collectively sign a waiver of all advancement or retreat; then, having selected a quiet location, they shall set up a crimson curtain within it. Inside, they shall install an image of the Great Master and arrange offerings and ritual implements.
Furthermore, they shall set out chairs and tables to extensively display the Four Books and the various major and minor texts for the purpose of consultation.

On the day prior, the attendants shall post a diagram of the seating order outside the curtain and instruct the hall stewards and attendants to arrange the locks and test-boards, and to invite those holding official positions to appear.

The Head Official (Dushou) and the entire assembly of officials, along with one Director of the Monastery (Duwei), shall invite two eminent monks from the West Hall (Xidang) and the Head Seat (Shouzuo), as well as two venerable elders from the East Order (Dongxu), to come on the following day to witness the locked examination at a designated location.

On the day of the examination, after the morning gruel has been served, the attendants of the Hall Office (Tangsi) shall notify the candidates in advance; each candidate must take their assigned seat according to the seating chart and is not permitted to carry anything in their bosom or pockets.
The private secretary shall dismiss the attendants; one supervisor shall patrol and ensure that no outsiders enter to cause clamor or confusion. Hang up the sign for seclusion.
Once the assembly has gathered, each person shall burn incense and wait for the abbot to arrive. Leading the assembly, they shall stand in formation before the image.
The abbot steps forward to burn incense and performs nine prostrations together with the assembly, chanting: "Namo Xuan Tuoluoni Pusa. Having completed the prostrations, they conclude.
Each person shall sit according to their rank. The attendant stands in the center to inquire after their well-being and burn incense.

Once the tea server has finished distributing the tea, the attendant presents paper and a brush and requests the Abbot to produce a topic for discussion—either a difficult passage from the current lecture text or a point of doubt within the commentaries of the various patriarchs—to be used as a trial question.
These two types of questions must be composed with words that are concise and meanings that are clear.
The attendant shall transcribe those passages within the two chapters whose phrasing and meaning are difficult and profound, and send them to the lecturer for review.
Next, the person who has prepared the topical outline (kē) and the person who has pre-arranged the sections (yùkē) must each prepare their own brush, ink, paper, and inkstone.

They should reflect upon the various texts cited regarding the divisions, flavors, teachings, and contemplations, responding to each point in full detail. The responses must be logically sound rather than merely verbose; the format for these scrolls is as follows.
As stated below: if one wishes to wash one's hands while both parties are nearby at the same location, it is not permitted to make excuses to return to the hall;
one must inquire of the teacher as prescribed in the text. Others should be measured and penalized accordingly.

The Abbot shall assign the Kitchen Office to prepare half-noon refreshments (*dianxin*) along with the midday meal, all served at the dining table. The Guest Office shall provide tea before the bath; each of these items must be sealed separately.
The name of the ritual hall and the names of the two [monks] are inscribed on the scrolls. After bowing before the image of the Great Master and bowing before the Abbot, one withdraws.
The attendant writes down the number of scrolls and carries them to the Abbot’s quarters to hand over to the *yibō* (robe-and-bowl) attendant, who receives them.
On the following day, the Abbot examines the scrolls, critiques them, and selects those that are superior; if the explanations of the meaning are pure and correct, they are retained.
Those whose understanding of the principles is profound should be commended and promoted to official positions;

however, those whose speech is careless or erroneous, or whose answers do not correspond to the questions asked, should be admonished. As for other matters reported, they shall be subjected to censure and critique.

Following such evaluation, the robes and alms bowl of the deceased shall be handed over to the incense-bearer attendant according to their original inventory, and a register shall be prepared and issued.
Once the master has finished reviewing the critical annotations of the transcribed texts, he invites the person responsible for the grading to go together to the attendant’s office (*shisō*).

There, they shall open the scrolls in each other’s presence to ensure that names containing taboo characters are clearly distinguished. They shall then mark the respective scrolls with their signatures in the register.

Furthermore, the scrolls must be presented to the abbot for his inspection; only at this point will the abbot be able to verify whether each person has been reading and studying them on a daily basis.
There are varying depths in one's cultivation. The method of the "Curtain-Test" (*suǒshì*) has long been abandoned and is no longer practiced;
I shall preserve it here provisionally, awaiting someone who might revive it. Formerly, the Venerable of Siming had thirty chapters of questions and answers behind his crimson curtain.
If we inquire into these forty-two chapters, their summary in the *Jiaoxinglu* states: "He drew back the crimson curtain and questioned his disciples; the wording was solely essential."

The purport is extremely subtle, so that no one might arise to usurp the merit of disseminating the teachings and cause those who are not quick-witted to seize the ambition of those who study with vigor (and so forth).
As for those who recite texts, their essays may be presented every five days, or they may answer minor difficulties on a separate day;
these two categories must not be conflated.
