Format of the Lock Examination Scroll;
Ullambana Assembly.
The world merely claims that nourishing one's parents constitutes filial piety, yet fails to realize that bringing disgrace upon oneself or one’s name is unfilial;
the world merely claims that severing affection is unfilial, yet fails to realize that clarifying the supramundane path to repay their kindness is true filial piety.
Thus, our World-Honored One abandoned his station and left his kin to realize the fruit of enlightenment, repaying the debt of gratitude to his father in Kapilavastu and repaying his mother.
The grace bestowed upon the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven by further initiating the Lanpen (Ullambana) festival and leaving this teaching for future generations may truly be called the height of filial piety.

If one who has left the household life can act in such a manner, what cause for shame could there be? Otherwise, being unable to proceed or retreat, what filiality could be greater than this lack thereof?

On the first day of the seventh month, the Lanpen Assembly is inaugurated. The night before, the hall attendants report to the Abbot and the various offices of the two orders, hang up the notification boards, and inform the assembly to maintain solemnity.
The Hall of Repentance is prepared and offerings are arranged. On the morning of the appointed day, the bell of the Hall of Repentance is struck;
the assembly gathers, and the Repentance Leader leads the recitation of the name of Amitābha Buddha and performs the Shorter Amitābha Repentance, including the verses of praise for the Buddha.
The verses having been composed, the announcement was made (as detailed). On the following day, the assembly gathered and spoke in unison:

"We, sharing the same intent of filial devotion, shall practice the causes for rebirth in the Pure Land to repay the kindness of our parents, repent for and eliminate the sins of the three obstructions, so that those who remain may obtain blessings and longevity, and those who have passed away may attain transcendence; may all enemies and kin throughout the entire Dharma-realm be born together in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing.

When the Three Refuges were completed, they chanted the name of Amitābha Buddha, "Golden-Colored One" (as detailed), and focused their mindfulness on Amitābha Buddha one hundred times, followed by Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and the assembly of the Pure Sea.

If there is one person [chanting] ten times), at the conclusion of the recitation, perform the dedication as follows: "By virtue of these roots of goodness cultivated through this practice, may we repay the labor and kindness of our parents: for those who remain, may their blessings, joy, and longevity be inexhaustible; for those who have passed away, may they be freed from suffering and reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*Sukhāvatī*).

May all sentient beings within the four debts of gratitude and the three realms of existence, and all beings suffering in the three miserable paths and eight difficulties, together receive this repentance to wash away all stains, so that they may all leave the cycle of *saṃsāra* and be born in the Pure Land. [Recite] "The Ten Directions and Three Periods of Time... and so forth.

After the gruel meal has ended, wait a short while, then the hall attendant (*táng-sī*) and the ritual assistant (*xíng-zhě*) shall strike the signal to rise again, and proceed to the Hall of Repentance (*chàn-diàn*) to perform the Great Amitābha Repentance.
The bell of the Confession Hall is struck, and the assembly stands in their respective positions. The leader of the confession recites the *Amitābha Sūtra* (or the *Ullambana Sūtra*).

When the ritual of offering incense and circumambulation is completed, [the name] "Amitābha Buddha" is invoked three times. They unfold their ritual implements and perform prostrations; having finished the verses of praise for the Buddhas, they continue with the words: "We, of one mind in filial devotion... and so forth.

Upon the conclusion of the ten minds of compliance and resistance, [the name] "Amitābha Buddha" is invoked three times. The text for repentance is then recited. (The fivefold repentance texts are all according to the *Buzhuyi*, with the exception that for "I, the bhikṣu [Name]... [the appropriate title is used].)

If one wishes to offer repentance for the sake of one’s living or deceased parents, one should enter into sincere repentance and so forth (as detailed in the *Smaller Amitābha Sūtra Repentance Ritual*, where the procedure for repentance is likewise).

Upon concluding the sections on sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) and dedication of merit (*pariṇāmanā*), chant the name of Amitābha Buddha forty-eight times. Then, recite the text of the Vow (as detailed), and at its conclusion, continue with these words:

"Whether my parents who gave me birth are currently living or have already passed away, wherever they may reside or wherever they have been reborn—may Amitābha Buddha, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, and Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva shine their light upon them and sustain them through their power of vows. May their three obstacles be eliminated and their five faculties be perfected, and may they awaken the mind of Bodhi."

I vow that those who cultivate the causes for the Pure Land while living shall fulfill their allotted lifespan and ultimately return to the Jewel Realm; those who have passed away shall immediately leave behind all realms of existence and take birth within a lotus womb. May they behold the wondrous marks [of the Buddha], clarify their minds, and enter the stages by listening to the profound discourse.

May they receive the prediction of enlightenment in person, manifesting emanations throughout the dust-motes of lands to extensively deliver sentient beings, so that we may ascend together to the wondrous land. I further pray that our filial and obedient hearts may penetrate deeply into the Dharma of the Ultimate Path, leaving nothing behind. May we become members of the retinue destined to be born together in the assemblies of all future Buddhas, fully equipping ourselves with the two adornments and perfecting the three enlightenments.

May the limits of the Dharma-nature be reached and our vows be infinite, until we finally enter the ocean of the Tathāgata’s vow-nature. Having made these vows, one should take refuge and pay homage, etc., until the three refuges are completed, at which point the recitation is raised.
Upon completing the circumambulation (or recitation) of the *Ullambana Sūtra* (or the *Amitābha Sūtra*), do not again chant the praises beginning with "The True Golden Color of Amitābha Buddha.
Instead, recite the name of the Buddha one hundred times and the names of the Bodhisattvas ten times. Then perform the dedication, saying: "By these cultivated roots of goodness...

and so forth, as previously stated. After the meal, strike the bell of the Repentance Hall once more to assemble the assembly for the chanting of the *Amitābha Sūtra* (or the *Ullambana Sūtra*) and the offering of praises.
The Buddha (as before), reciting the name of the Buddha one hundred times and that of the Bodhisattvas ten times; dedicate the merit (as before).

After the session, strike the bell to assemble the congregation, chant the *Amitābha Sūtra*, and when the circumambulation is finished, offer praise, saying: "The Buddha Amitābha is of true golden color... (and so forth).

Recite the name of the Buddha one thousand times and the names of the Bodhisattvas one hundred times (or ten times). Make the vow, saying: "May my parents who gave me birth... (as before). Transfer the merit for rebirth (as usual).
The Kusi (Storehouse Office) shall, every evening, instruct the head attendant to take turns assigning practitioners to distribute fans and serve hot water.

Two attendants from the Tangsi (Hall Office)—the Head Attendant and the Assistant—shall manage the tally-slips: for every ten chimes of the chime-bell, one slip is struck; for every hundred, one lead-chime is struck;
and for every thousand, two lead-chimes are struck. One person shall oversee the large numbers and another the small numbers, following this procedure daily.

On the fifteenth day, when performing the Great Amitābha Repentance, after the section on praising the Buddha has been completed, the presiding officiant composes the liturgical text for the distribution of offerings.

The Hall Attendant (Sànchàngsī) and the ritual assistants (Xíngzhě) first lead the assembly’s funds back to the Treasury Office (Kùsī) to prepare the hundred-flavored offerings for the *Lánpén* (Ullambana) ceremony.

They then notify the Record Keeper (Shūjì) to compose the memorial (shūsū); if the Record Keeper is absent, the Rector (Weíná) shall compose it himself or use a previous draft—there is no fixed requirement. The format of the memorial is as follows; it is to be displayed before the midday meal.

For the offering of the hundred-flavored *bowl* (Lanpen) ceremony, the priority is that it be abundant and pure. After the ritual master has prepared the hall, the attendants strike the gong to assemble the community.

Facing the Buddha, they stand in formation. The Head Seat (Shouzuo) intones the name of Śākyamuni Buddha, and the assembly chants in unison. They perform three prostrations with their sitting cloths (*kōju*) spread out; they do not withdraw the cloths.

The Abbot offers hot water and presents food, and the assembly likewise performs three prostrations. He offers tea, and again the assembly performs three prostrations. Finally, they withdraw the sitting cloths.

When the Venerable Karmadāna has finished reciting the memorial text, he shall chant the *Ullambana Sūtra* and call out the names [of Śākyamuni, Amitābha, Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and the oceanic assembly] three times each.

The assembly shall then recite the vow, beginning with "May our parents who gave us birth... and so forth. In the evening, the *hu* (offering bowls) shall be distributed and fully dispersed, either before the hall of repentance, in the Water and Land Hall, or at the entrance of the mountain gate, according to the custom of each respective monastery.
On the fifteenth day of the seventh month, the bhikṣu so-and-so, abbot of such-and-such temple on such-and-such road, together with the assembly of bhikṣus,
humbly coincides with the anniversary of the Great Being Maudgalyāyana’s salvation of his kin; we have already engaged in preparatory cultivation for half a month.
Through the practice of repentance, the chanting of sutras,

and the mindful recitation of the sacred names of the Land of Bliss, we now perform this *bowl-offering* (*ulambana*) ceremony upon its conclusion to honor the Three Jewels of the permanent residence and the assembly of monks throughout the ten directions; by these extraordinary merits, may our karmic debts be repaid.
One’s biological parents have been enemies or kin throughout kalpas; all sentient beings within the Dharma-realm are born together in the Pure Land.

I humbly submit that Heaven is called Father and Earth is called Mother, truly providing impartial shelter and protection; the Buddha is worthy of veneration and the Dharma is worthy of being a teacher, providing a refuge upon which to rely.
While the children of the world are trapped in the misery of fire and brimstone, the Supreme Being brings benefit and joy to the dust of this mundane realm.

In contemplating the Emperor’s heart of universal enlightenment and salvation, which reaches all things and occasions to rescue the green sprouts from their precarious state and uproot those hanging in distress, the conditions for such grace have been manifested;

thus the teaching has been transmitted for the sake of posterity. Now that the time approaches the full moon of the seventh month, as the autumn wind suddenly rises, one feels sorrow for the traveler longing for his native land;
seeing the solitary white clouds drifting, one thinks of one’s parents dwelling beneath them, especially when drenched by the dew and frost.

When the dampness has already descended, there arises a withered desolation and a profound sense of grief that is difficult to bear. Having lived for three years, one is released from the mother’s breast;

how can such things be fully described? When a single day’s labor is employed, who can ever repay it? We offer this meal as a *pūjā* on the *Ullambana* vessel and perform the essential rites of repentance according to the Lotus Society (*Lotus Saṃgha*).
Our aspirations were formed in the past, and we now fulfill our resolve today. We humbly pray that we may generate much merit.
Throughout kalpas of existence, parents have been both enemies and kin; now, like the wild surges of a thousand-fathom river dried up, not a single drop remains.

As the pure nature returns to the single orb of the empty sky, its brilliance shines again with lofty clarity. Whether appearing to vanish or remaining present, may they always abide in peace and joy. This brief memorial is respectfully inscribed.
Explanatory Commentary on the Ritual for the *Pravāraṇā* (in two parts), composed on the [blank] day of the seventh month in the [blank] year.
The Extensive Ritual for the *Pravāraṇā*.
At the conclusion of summer and the end of the year, one should observe the ritual of *pravāraṇā* (self-reproval).

Three or five days prior, the abbot shall convene the head seat of the front hall and two senior monks who are learned in the Dharma to serve as the five virtuous witnesses (*pañca-guṇa*). Preparations for their reception and hospitality shall be made.
On the evening of the fifteenth day, the *karmadāna* (ritual director) shall invite the six officials to offer hot water; by dusk, they shall practice the procedures for the ceremony.
On the morning of the sixteenth day, the duty-holder shall wait in the Sangha Hall until after the bowls have been displayed, then strike the mallet once and announce:

"Venerable Sangha, listen! Today, the first day of the dark fortnight, the community of monks is in harmony; at the hour of the dragon (辰), we shall proceed to [place name] for the *pravāraṇā*. After the morning gruel is finished, the bath is opened.

The *karmadāna* shall order the hall attendants and servants to sweep and clean the place of *pravāraṇā*. He shall arrange *bōtuán* (cushions) according to the number of monks (as with the seating arrangement for the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*; chairs need not be arranged). Furthermore—
Prepare two *pūtā* mats and place them in the center before the assembly of monks, intended as the seats for the two groups of five virtuous ones (*pañcavarga*) who will perform the ritual.
Furthermore, provide incense, flowers, counting sticks (*śalākā*), scented water, an incense burner, candles, and vases (as prescribed in the *Poṣadha* ritual).

Prepare several bundles of green and white grass according to the number of monks; each bundle should consist of approximately twenty to thirty stalks, about two feet in length, and be placed in two boxes.

Place the cloth bundle upon the central table between the two pillars; in front of it, set a small desk beside the abbot’s meditation cushion, and place the hand-incense burner, whisk, and still-measure (shijing) upon it. One meditation cushion must be placed at the abbot’s upper shoulder.

Once the position for the Sacred Monk has been established, the *vinaya-dhara* (ritual master) must inspect all these matters to ensure they are entirely solemn and orderly. When the time arrives, proceed to the various halls.
Then, the hall attendant (tangsi xingzhe) strikes the signal board (daq) and rings the bell in front of the Sangha Hall;
the assembly gathers before the hall and stands in two rows, the upper and lower sections. The great bell is struck, and the verse for hearing the bell is recited (*etc.*).
Entering the hall, the verse for entering the hall is recited (*etc.*); they perform three prostrations and sit in the lotus posture. Five people rise to perform the ritual duties...

The formal announcement (*jñapti*) and the verses are to be recited according to the ritual for the *poṣadha* (with the modification that when reciting the announcement, the phrase "two words" is changed to "self-discipline" [*pravāraṇā*]).

From the formal announcement until the counting of the voting sticks is finished, when the sound of the assembled beings has ceased, one immediately says: (Each recites the pure and wondrous verses from the Vinaya).

The assembly says: (Pure as the full moon, pure, we obtain self-discipline; with body and speech karma pure, we then perform the self-discipline together). The formal announcement is then concluded, the gong is struck, and those performing the rite—the four persons—also rise.

Scatter flowers and sprinkle water (following the ritual for the recitation of the precepts). Holding up the *bai* (announcement), strike the wooden mallet once and recite the verse for scattering flowers; the assembly says: "Adorned with scattered flowers... and so forth.

When finished, everyone joins their palms, and the *Fan-shi* (Brahmin Master) performs the *Fan* (Brahmanic) rite: "I bow my head... and so forth. When finished, there is no further need to recite the verse for transmitting incense;

instead, the Abbot alone holds the hand-incense burner, pinches the incense three times, and recites: "The fragrance of the precepts... and so forth. When the verse is finished, he holds up the *bai*.
The abbot strikes the mallet once and returns to his seat. He strikes the sounding-block twice; the whisk-bearer joins his palms and bows to the assembly, who respond with a bow.

The abbot addresses the presiding officer (as detailed below). He then proceeds to announce the appointment of personnel, saying: "The Dharma Master [Name], West Hall, shall serve as the first Five Virtues; the Dharma Master [Name], Seat-Head, shall serve as the second Five Virtues;
the Dharma Master [Name], First Seat, shall respond to the duties of the Dharma Abode. He strikes the sounding-block twice. The abbot and the Head Seat briefly [conclude].

[The Abbot, holding the Dharma, asks the Head Seat (the respondent for the Dharma): Question: "Is the Sangha assembled? Answer: "The Sangha is already assembled. Question: "Are you in harmony? Answer: "We are in harmony. Question: "Have those monks who did not come declared their *chanda* (consent) and *pārisuddhi* (purity)?

The person conveying the *chanda* kneels facing each other and says: "Venerable Sangha, listen! That monk named [Name], etc., has entrusted his *chanda* to me for the *pravāraṇā*. He grants his *chanda* for the *pravāraṇā* regarding the legal matters of the Sangha as they arise.

[If there is no one, say: 'In this assembly, there is no one to declare *chanda* or *pravāraṇā*. Answer: "[The *chanda* and *pravāraṇā* have been declared. [If there is no one, the one who previously conveyed the *chanda* says the same: "There is none. Question: "..."

[Question: "The Saṃgha is now in harmony; what shall it do? [Answer: "A formal motion (*jñapti*) for the *pravāraṇā* ceremony to harmonize the Saṃgha. The Abbot says: "Appointing a person to receive the *pravāraṇā* is performed through a single formal act (*ekakarma*), with the entire assembly in accord as witnesses.

The wording is as stated in the *Karmavācanā-sūtra*: 'Venerable Saṃgha, listen! If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha permits, let the Saṃgha appoint the bhikṣu so-and-so and so-and-so as the persons to receive the *pravāraṇā*.

Thus it is. [Question: "Is the formal motion (*jñapti*) established? [Answer: "It is established. The Abbot says: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen! The Saṃgha appoints the bhikṣus so-and-so and so-and-so as the persons to receive the *pravāraṇā*. Which Elder approves of the Saṃgha appointing the bhikṣus so-and-so and so-and-so as the persons to receive the *pravāraṇā*?"

"If those who permit [the *pravāraṇā*] remain silent, who would not consent? Since the Saṃgha has consented to appoint the bhikṣu [Name] as the one to receive the *pravāraṇā*, and because the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter shall be held thus. Question: "Is the formal motion (*karmavācanā*) established?
Answer: "It is established. The Abbot says: "Since the ritual procedure is completed, two sets of five virtuous ones (*pañcavarga*) shall emerge from the assembly to perform the duties.

The two sets of five virtuous ones then collect their requisites, take the incense box, inquire after the health of the assembly, leave their seats with dignified composure, proceed to the location of the two middle mats, stand firmly there, and perform a single round of inquiry.

The two groups proceed to the front of the incense burner, each performing three pinches of incense. They place the incense casket upon the table, step back to their respective sides, and emerge from their *pútuán* seats.
After performing a formal greeting (*wènxùn*) and unfolding their ritual implements for three prostrations, they rise and sit facing one another for a brief moment.

The two individuals join their palms and bow to each other in turn. The first *wǔdé* (virtuous official) says: "The *zìzī* (self-examination) is performed through a *duānbái* (single-announcement) *jiémó* (formal act); may the great assembly with one mind bear witness to this ritual procedure. (The wording is as found in the *Jiémó jīng*)."

"Venerable Sangha, please listen. Today the Sangha performs the *pravāraṇā*. If the time has come for the Sangha, may the Sangha, being patient and attentive, grant permission for this harmonious *pravāraṇā*. (Having thus asked, does the ritual procedure succeed? Answer: "The ritual procedure succeeds.
After a short interval, four officiants emerge from the assembly and stand in a row at the front. They simultaneously pay their respects;

two on each side proceed separately toward the east and west, each reaching the place where the grass is located. One person lifts a chest, another distributes the grass, while the Holy Sangha stands before the Abbot.
The person in front should kneel and offer the grass; the next person should offer it by lowering their body, but must not offer it by tossing it while standing upright.

Each person receives the grass in turn and recites this verse: "The Auspicious Youth offers soft grass; The Tathāgata, having accepted it, attained Perfect Enlightenment. We bhikṣus, following the Buddha’s example, Sit upon the grass for the *pravāraṇā*, purifying our three karmas.
Having finished the recitation, they shall unfold the grass and place it on the ground before the sitting mat, spreading it to a width corresponding to the space occupied by one person when kneeling.
Second, five virtuous monks (wude) should first spread their grass mats (*kuśa*) in their respective positions to avoid any haste or confusion at the time of the rite.
Second, when the ritual proceedings are conducted, they move back and forth from both ends; once the spreading of the grass is finished, the boxes are returned to their original places.

Stepping forward before the incense burner, they all perform a simultaneous greeting (*praṇāma*) and return to their positions (ensuring that the movements of entering and exiting the ritual area are dignified). The two groups of virtuous monks then turn their bodies to face the Buddha and kneel with their right knees touching the ground.

With palms joined, the second person chants: "All the Sangha approach the grass seats, baring the right shoulder, kneeling with the right knee on the ground, and joining the palms. Upon the completion of the chant, the two *pañca-vṛddhāḥ* (five-virtuous elders) collect their implements, rise, and exit from both sides.
The first *pañca-vṛddhaḥ* proceeds before the Abbot, spreads his implements, kneels with the right knee on the ground, and joins his palms.

The Abbot steps forward, kneels upon the grass seat (*tṛṇāsana*). (Regarding those who sit upon the grass seat: this is for the sake of repentance; the assembly does not dare to occupy a high seat, yet it is not the grass seat used for the sitting of one who has attained the Way. Join palms.

With these reflections, [we recite] the Pure Dharma Body... [and so forth], adding the ten Buddha names and the title of the Great Master of Tiantai (up to) the *Pāramitās*. This is the place where the Brahmans dwell in this world.

Hereafter, I shall briefly present ten articles of instruction for all students. [End of Section] Following this, the ten articles of instruction are set forth. 1. Regarding the matter of robes and bowls: if you have not yet received the full precepts, you must not wear the *kaṣāya* (robe) nor carry the *pātra* (bowl). You may only wear a simple cloth garment and carry a small bowl. If you do not observe these rules, you commit an offense. 2. Regarding the matter of entering the meditation hall: you must first wash your hands and rinse your mouth before entering. You must not enter with unwashed hands or an unclean mouth. If you do not observe these rules, you commit an offense. 3. Regarding the matter of sitting in meditation: you must sit upright and maintain a dignified posture. You must not lean forward, lean backward, or slouch. If you do not observe these rules, you commit an offense. 4. Regarding the matter of reciting the Buddha’s name: you must recite with a focused mind and clear voice. You must not recite with a distracted mind or a muddled voice. If you do not observe these rules, you commit an offense. 5. Regarding the matter of circumambulating: you must walk with a steady pace and a reverent demeanor. You must not walk too fast or too slow, nor look about idly. If you do not observe these rules, you commit an offense. 6. Regarding the matter of receiving offerings: you must receive them with both hands and place them on the ground. You must not receive them with one hand or hold them loosely. If you do not observe these rules, you commit an offense. 7. Regarding the matter of eating: you must eat with mindfulness and moderation. You must not eat greedily or speak while eating. If you do not observe these rules, you commit an offense. 8. Regarding the matter of sleeping: you must lie down on your right side in the "lion's posture. You must not sleep on your back or your stomach. If you do not observe these rules, you commit an offense. 9. Regarding the matter of attending the assembly: you must rise promptly and join the ranks in order. You must not arrive late or leave early. If you do not observe these rules, you commit an offense. 10. Regarding the matter of maintaining decorum: you must always maintain a humble and respectful attitude toward seniors and elders. You must not act with arrogance or negligence. If you do not observe these rules, you commit an offense. [End of Section] Following this, the ten articles of instruction are concluded. These ten articles are established to guide those who have newly entered the path, so that they may gradually attain stability and not fall into error. If these hinder the arising [of virtue], they must be increased or diminished, and the community shall collectively determine them.
First, as for the differing root-natures of individuals: some attain the Way by practicing alone, while others achieve liberation by relying on the community.

Those who rely on the community should cultivate three practices: first, sitting in meditation according to the hall; second, performing repentance in a separate area; and third, attending to monastic affairs. This...
The three types of practitioners must be fully equipped with the three robes and six articles of requisites; if they possess even one of these practices, they may be accommodated.
However, if there is a deficiency in their clothing or requisites such that none of these practices are present, they shall not reside together.
Second, regarding the monks residing in the hall: their fundamental duty is to practice seated meditation during the four periods and perform prostrations to the Buddha during the six periods;

these constitute their constant tasks. Meditation and prostrations must not be omitted for even one of the ten periods. Once the specific rules for the conduct of the monks have been completed, after three days they must immediately conform to the community’s schedule for the ten periods.

If one fails to perform even one period of prostrations to the Buddha, one shall be penalized by performing three additional prostrations before the assembly as a confession. If the omission is total, [the penalty shall be more severe].

If one fails to perform the ten prostrations during a single session, one shall undergo public repentance before the assembly; if one completely neglects all six sessions, one shall be penalized once. The same applies to the rector’s failure to sit in meditation during the four sessions.
However, those who are exempted due to illness or other obstacles must first inform the administrative officers, in which case they shall not be penalized.

Third, regarding the practice of prostrating to the Buddha at the six times of the day: the great *saṃgha* should wear the *pravrajita-vastra* (robe for entering the assembly). If the robe lacks pleats or ridges, or if it is a plain seamless garment (*sāṇḍasaṅghāṭī*), one must not perform the three prostrations.

One should assemble early, arrange the seats, and hold the incense burner while kneeling with the right knee on the ground. Until the chanting begins, one must not recite [scriptures] oneself; until the *svādhyāya* (recitation) is concluded, one must not engage in idle conversation.
Prostrating with the head, snapping the fingers, dragging the feet, or moving up and down in a disjointed or uneven manner—all such actions are strictly prohibited.

The intent of the fourth category, "Individual Practice" (*betsugyō*), is that because one is among the assembly, the practice is considered lax; therefore, one should diligently cultivate the four kinds of samādhi.

If one merely makes a pretext of being in a ritual site (*dōjō*) without conforming to the intent of individual practice, and this is verified through investigation, the punishment is one term of service as a *vinaya-dhara* (ritual master).
Fifth, as for those monks serving as administrators (*karmadāna*), their original purpose was to establish and promote the welfare [of the community],

yet they instead cause depletion and harm by seizing the community’s resources for their own enrichment and acting out of personal favoritism. Even if it is but a single hair’s breadth of unreasonable encroachment upon communal property that has not been openly declared,
once an inspection confirms the facts, such conduct shall not be tolerated.
Sixth, regarding those who eat at the two designated times: if one is not ill, or if one’s illness does not require lying down, or once the illness has been cured, one must all emerge from the hall.
One must not request food or enter the assembly for meals. As for eating utensils, it is permitted to use vessels made of iron, ceramic, or lacquered wood;
however, bowls, cups, spoons, and chopsticks may not be made of bone, horn, bamboo, wood, gourds, dyed leather, or shell. Furthermore, none of these may be brought into the hall.

One must not make sounds while sucking or slurping from one’s own bowl, nor speak with food in the mouth, nor seek for oneself, nor privately take sauce or vegetables to eat alone in the midst of the assembly;
whoever violates this shall be punished with three prostrations and must perform repentance before the assembly.

Seventh: Whether they be members of the Great Sangha or those observing minor precepts, whether traveling near or far, inside or outside the monastery, they must not steal or consume fish, meat, pungent vegetables, or alcohol, nor eat at improper times.

Upon investigation, if it is found that they are not living together [in violation of these rules], except in cases of grave illness where one attends to the patient according to a physician’s instructions and goes outside the monastery for treatment, then there shall be no punishment.
The eighth name for the Saṃgha is "Harmony" (Sāmagrī), because it is characterized by gentleness and forbearance. "Harmony" means yielding; "Concord" (Saṃgha) means that there is no contention.

If those who engage in disputes, harbor pride, use foul language, or compete through both voice and facial expression, each shall be punished with thirty prostrations before the assembly. Those who do not respond [to the admonition] shall not be punished.

As for those who physically assault one another, regardless of whether the offense is light or heavy, they must not dwell together. However, those who refrain from using their hands [in assault] shall not be excluded.
Punishment:

Ninth, if one commits a grave offense, they shall be dealt with according to the Vinaya. If one is falsely accused, the accuser shall not be punished; however, the accuser shall not share the same dwelling.
This is because when a student has not yet entered the assembly, they have not received training from the master of the assembly, as they have not yet been incorporated into the community.
If that person, claiming to be a bhikṣu, enters the assembly and commits a grave offense or falsely accuses another, they shall be punished as previously described.

Tenth, establishing the administration of medicine based on the sūtras: if one administers medicine without first diagnosing the location of the illness, what benefit is there in vomiting the medicine?

As for the nine preceding rules regarding prohibitions, permissions, and repentance, these pertain to repentance; however, one who lacks a sense of shame and remorse cannot reform themselves. This is...
Those who have vomited up [the medicine] should be made to leave the assembly; if they can reform themselves, they may later be permitted to return.

However, those who violate various precepts and obstinately refuse to repent are people of this heterodox region; since they do not follow the communal regulations, they shall not dwell together with us.
On the fifteenth day of the fourth month in the seventeenth year of the Kaihuang era of the Great Sui Dynasty,
the temple monk (Guanding), having received the imperial decree, wrote this edict;
the Hall Superior (Hui Chen) held the decree and carried out its execution.

The Ritual for Bestowing the Bodhisattva Precepts (*Jiaoxinglu Jinyuanji*) Originally, the Mahāyāna Bodhisattva precepts are the root of the bodhisattva path and the foundational cause for the fruit of perfect enlightenment. Therefore, the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states:
"The precepts are like the sun and the moon, and also like a jeweled necklace; they are the foundation for the multitude of bodhisattvas as numerous as motes of dust."
By this, one attains perfect enlightenment. The method for requesting and receiving [the precepts] has been briefly explained as above;

however, if one wishes to know the ritual procedures in detail, they should be sought in the *Jiaoxinglu* (Record of Teaching and Practice) and the *Jinyuanji* (Collection from the Golden Garden) composed by the two venerable masters Faji and Ciyun.

As these texts are extensive, they are not recorded here; those who require them should consult them directly. Although there are differences in the number of sections established, their essential meaning is largely the same.
Establishing Separate Regulations (A Separate Collection from India):
Regarding the two sciences of liberation and practice, how could the aspirations of scholars lie elsewhere? Only after this can they apply themselves with diligence.

Those of later generations, being ignorant, treat their own virtue and learning as if it were public labor; since they cannot help themselves, strict governance must be exercised. Herein, the essential conditions are briefly set forth.

Thereafter, there were further additions and deletions (totaling nineteen articles; their essentials are briefly indicated within the "Methods for the Community during the Rains Retreat," while the remainder are as found in that text and must be followed one by one; they are not listed here again).
Admonitions for the Administrators (*Guoqing bai lu*):

In my youth, I was beset by toil and hardship and experienced every kind of difficulty. I traveled to study in the regions of Jing, Yang, Yong, and Yu, wearing only a single set of robes for over thirty years, never removing them from my body whether in winter or summer.
From the Son of Heaven above down to the scholar-officials and commoners below, although there were those who offered me gifts, [I would not accept them].

One receives [offerings] but does not treat them as private property; once a single fruit or a single thread has been entered into the community, there is no longer even a thought of longing for them, let alone intentionally encroaching upon them.

The reason for this is that the treasures of the Sangha are most venerable: if they can be increased, it is called a garden of nectar (*amṛta*); if they are diminished or destroyed, it is a garden of thorns (*kaṇṭaka*).
To satisfy oneself is to harm oneself; whether one falls or rises depends on this. This can be understood through reflection—what need is there for many words?

When a person resolves their mind and engages in any activity—whether reciting, studying, listening to the teachings, lecturing, walking in meditation, repenting, making offerings, or practicing generosity—they must not allow it to remain incomplete from beginning to end;
one must be careful not to stop midway. To stop midway is to violate one’s original resolve.

If one attempts to act again but encounters obstacles at the point where one previously stopped, then the cultivation of practice will not be accomplished; there will be manifest hindrances in this life, and they will become even more severe in the future.
This practice which obstructs the Way is a great taboo for practitioners; one must exert every effort to ensure a good beginning and a successful conclusion.

Once one's karma is made tranquil, the retribution will likewise be fulfilled, and this may be attained as one desires. Formerly, there was a monastery with several hundred masters and disciples who spent their days and nights in meditation and lecture, never wasting a moment.
A lay attendant (*karmadāna*) eavesdropped on their sermons, and having heard them, he applied his mind to them whenever he winnowed grain or washed it in a sieve.
He maintained his mindfulness and cultivated his practice, using a pure mind to winnow away what was unwholesome and cleansing impurities with the pure water of dhyāna.
Whatever he did, he applied his mind at every thought-moment. At one time, while tending the hearth, he observed that as the fire burned the wood, each moment of fuel was consumed until it was gone;
impermanence and transience were so swift. Thereupon, crouching before the drain, he entered meditative absorption in stillness; the fire was extinguished and the water grew cold.
The *karmadāna*, fearing that the communal meal would be interrupted, informed the *sthavira*. The *sthavira* said, "This is a superior matter; the assembly should endure it.

Be careful not to disturb or provoke him; let him arise on his own. After several days, he finally realized what had happened and went to the *sthavira* to recount the realization he had attained, describing how the Dharma had become increasingly profound.
The *sthavira* stopped him, saying, "Everything you previously spoke of was within my own realm; as for what you have now..."
He said, "Do not speak further of that which is beyond my knowledge. He then asked in turn, "Do you perhaps know of your past lives?
He replied, "I know it but slightly. Again he asked, "By what karma did you become low-born, and by what merit do you so easily awaken?

He replied, "This lowly body was, in a previous life, the teacher of the elder disciples of today, and likewise the ancestral teacher of the juniors; thus, teacher and disciples were one and the same."

"Whatever the assembly has learned was all previously taught by me. At that time, there were many private guests whom I constantly restrained so that they would not dare encroach upon the community's provisions.

Yet, when an urgent guest suddenly arrived, I would take a small amount of vegetables for them and forget to provide a double portion. Because of this, I was censured and have now become a slave to the community. My former habits have not been long forgotten;
with little cultivation, I easily awakened to my past lives, their merits and faults. Such is the matter. When the assembly heard this, [they were moved].

How can one not be cautious when even a mirror cannot withstand such sorrow? Master Zhao, my fellow student, was foremost among the assembly at Mount Nanyue in his ascetic practices and meditative concentration.
He once used a single pinch of salt from the communal store to prepare a drink for a meal; though what he consumed was but a small amount, he did not consider it a transgression.
Later, while practicing the Vaipulya (fangdeng) teachings, he suddenly saw signs arise, and by calculation, [the retribution] would reach its full extent after three years.
I have urgently ordered that several dozen *hu* of salt be prepared; furthermore, sell your clothing and assets to purchase more salt to repay the community.

This matter will not last long, nor is it merely hearsay—it should be taken as a rule so that you do not regret it later. Although my virtuous conduct is meager, I am sought after by people from near and far;
however, being separated by the Shan Ling mountains, it is difficult to travel on foot. As I am old and infirm, I mostly rely on a group of donkeys to escort me when coming and going.
"This was my guest's private calculation for the reward of his labor; let there be no fault on either side. I am the master of the assembly, and as for the donkey, it is mine as well.
Since it has been relinquished to the assembly, it is no longer mine; I ought not to use it. If it is not mine, what can be said?
This one point being thus, all other matters are the same."

I caution future monastics that they must prioritize maintaining their proper station and take the observance of the precepts as their foundation. If one acts contrary to principle and follows unwholesome paths,
it will not only leave oneself without a place to stand, but will also bring disgrace upon the monastic community and the Buddha’s precepts.

Each of you must maintain these precepts with the utmost diligence. As the Tathāgata has established these prohibitions, one must not commit killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, frivolous talk, harsh words, double-tongued speech, greed, anger, or delusion. Should anyone violate them, the offense incurred shall not be slight; please take this to heart.
In our dynasty, we rely on the monastic community to uphold and follow the Buddha’s precepts;

with the exception of cases involving criminal offenses or grave crimes, which by custom fall under the jurisdiction of secular authorities, any internal transgressions among monks shall be regulated according to the pure monastic rules.

Should they act unlawfully and recklessly, defile their conduct through dissipation, exploit the monastery’s permanent property, privately misappropriate funds, or engage in strife, breach the social order, or incite discord with their speech—[these matters shall be dealt with accordingly].

For those who agitate and disturb the assembly by flapping their tongues, the light punishment shall be prostrations, fines in money, fines in incense, or fines in oil, with a public notice displayed.
If the matter involves money or goods, they shall be held accountable for a formal statement and required to reimburse the loss. For serious offenses, they shall be subjected to flogging;

their robes and alms bowls shall be burned before a gathered assembly, and they shall be expelled through a side gate to demonstrate their disgrace, thereby compelling them to reform and start anew. Examine this provision of the regulations in detail.

There are four benefits: first, to avoid defiling the pure assembly of sentient beings through our respectful demeanor; second, to avoid disparaging the monastic form by following the Buddha’s regulations;
third, to avoid disturbing the public offices by reducing litigation and disputes; fourth, to avoid broadcasting external scandals by protecting the fundamental principles of our school.
Be careful, be careful as you dwell together in harmony.
Regarding the principles of the sun and moon,
for one newly entering a monastic community, it is first necessary to thoroughly understand the rules and rituals and to practice them with proper decorum and reverence,
binding the mind as the *Āgama* Sūtras state: "There is no one who, lacking reverence and failing to bind the mind, can claim their deportment (*īryāpatha*) is complete."
It is impossible for one who does not maintain proper deportment to fulfill the training in the Dharma;

it is impossible for one whose training in the Dharma is not fulfilled to attain even *nirvāṇa* without remainder. Therefore, you should diligently study, be reverent, focus the mind, and act with cautious heedfulness.
In daily life, every action performed is none other than the Path; within the four modes of deportment, do not fail to take yourself as your own teacher.
Suddenly!
Rising early to enter the assembly and study the Way, you must be diligent and energetic. Do not fall asleep before others, nor rise later than anyone.
Before the five-watch bell has even sounded, rise light of body; do not startle your fellow practitioners, but shake off lethargy and collect your spirit.
Sitting upright with a focused mind, one should reflect upon the texts recited each day, whether they are compositions yet unfinished or contain difficult passages that remain unresolved.
As the Patriarchs have said, this is the correct path for contemplating the subtle in a quiet place. When rising from the seat, one should contemplate the following verse:

"From the dawn of morning until the evening dusk, may all sentient beings protect themselves. If by my feet I have inadvertently harmed their bodies, may you be reborn immediately in the Pure Land. Oṃ yid-te rgyal-mtshan svāhā. [Then] take [the seat].

With the hand-towel, one should lightly open the door with the left hand. When leaving, one must not pull back the curtains or hangings. One must not carry shoes on one's arm. If one coughs, one must make no sound.

Turning the hand to take the basin for washing the face, one should not use too much hot water. When rinsing the mouth, one must lower the head to spit out the water, guiding it downward with the hand.
One must straighten the waist when spitting water, fearing it might splash into a neighbor’s basin. One must not wash one’s hair; there are four reasons for this.
One must not harm oneself or others (such as by using a dirty bucket, a soiled towel, or dried hair to wipe the eyes). One must not make sounds within the nose, nor spray water onto one's face.
One must not vomit loudly, nor defile the bucket with mucus or saliva.
Regarding ritual recitation: when performing ritual recitation, first recite the mantra for purifying verbal karma.

Next, when donning the *kāṣāya*, join the palms at the crown of the head and recite: "Excellent is this robe of liberation, the signless field of merit; I now receive it upon my head, that in every life I may always wear it. Oṃ siddhaye svāhā.
When folding the *kāṣāya*, it must be done neatly and placed upon a rack. After paying respects, one should depart. One must not hang the sitting mat on the same rack as the *kāṣāya*. If...
When ascending the hall to burn incense, one must not stand in the center; rather, one should stand about three and a half steps to the left side and perform a *wenxun* (greeting/prostration).
After offering the incense, turn to the left and perform another *wenxun* at three and a half steps. When burning incense before seniors, one must stand slightly back to yield precedence.
When prostrating, do not occupy the central position (as this is reserved for the Abbot). One must not chant or recite scriptures aloud.

As those performing prostrations pass by the head of the hall at the striking of the fifth watch bell, they should recite this verse of contemplation: "May the sound of this bell transcend the Dharma-realm, Reaching all the way to the dark confines of the Iron Encircling Mountains;

May those in the three miserable realms be freed from suffering, And may all sentient beings attain perfect enlightenment. When the long wooden board is struck, the assembly shall proceed together to the hall to await the chanting or the performance of repentance rites.
Each must approach with utmost sincerity to pay homage to the Buddha, deeply realizing that the essence of the Buddha is not separate from one's own mind, being of one and the same substance.
The Source of Awakening responds wondrously to this invocation; with a single body, one reaches before all Buddhas. A single prostration universally eliminates boundless transgressions.
Kneeling alternately, the right knee touches the ground (this is called "alternating kneeling" because three parts of the body are raised and prominent; it is the ritual custom of India).

Joining the palms with both hands at the heart (in this land, clasping the hands is considered respectful, whereas in the Western lands, joining the palms is the mark of reverence; the hands are originally separate on both sides, now joined as one to signify non-dissipation and single-minded devotion. The *Fayuan* states that there are cases where the fingers are joined while the palms remain apart).

Or, with palms joined and fingers spread, it is surely because the mind is arrogant and the spirit is lax and scattered. When prostrating, one should straighten the body and maintain dignified deportment, casting the five limbs to the ground (the *Fuxing* commentary states: first the two knees advance, then the two hands follow, and finally the forehead touches the ground;

one should imagine the liver and gallbladder reaching the earth, visualizing the Buddha’s feet before one's eyes and placing the hands beneath them to support them. Whether the middle and thumbs are pressed together, the palms are placed against the face, or the hands are pressed flat on the ground, none of these are the proper ritual).

One silently contemplates: "The nature of the one who worships and the object worshipped is empty and quiescent; all should respond in the inconceivable interpenetration of the Way. In this place of practice of mine, like a jewel of Indra, the shadow of Śākyamuni appears within; the shadow of my own body appears therein."

[Prostrate before Śākyamuni Buddha, facing him directly and touching his feet, taking refuge and paying homage. For the prostrations to other Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, simply change "Śākyamuni Buddha" to the respective name [of the deity]. As for bowing, if one does not direct the mind [toward the object], it is merely a laborious practice of asceticism.
The *Fayuan* states: "Though one performs prostrations, if the mind wanders elsewhere, it is like the up-and-down motion of a millstone—empty and yielding nothing."
Upon completing the chanting in the hall, return to your bowl position. When entering the hall, you must remove your hat.

Enter from the southern side and perform a bow toward the Sacred Monk (Shengseng); do not enter from the center or the northern side, for this is out of respect for the Abbot. (If rising from the hall after completing a repentance ceremony, those of lesser rank go first;

they divide between the upper and lower halls. Those in the upper hall enter with the right foot first; those in the lower hall enter with the left foot first. With palms joined, return to your position, first facing your bowl position.

To inquire after one’s neighbor in the row, turn to the left and inquire after those seated on the opposite bed. (Those seated to the left, right, or opposite need only respond with palms joined when inquired after;

if one arrives later than those already seated in the upper, middle, or lower seats, one must likewise join the palms. As the ancients said: "If one does not show respect to those in the upper, middle, or lower seats, there is no difference between this and a gathering of Brahmins. When entering the room, place the hat inside and ascend the bed.
With the right hand, gather the sleeve of the left side and tuck it under the armpit to secure it; then, with the left hand, gather the sleeve of the right side.
Having tucked in the sleeves, press both hands down upon the bed and push both feet under it with the shoes.

First withdraw the left foot, then the right, and lift the body upward to sit near the edge of the mat in the *paryaṅka* (full lotus) posture. Spread the *kāṣāya* over the knees; do not expose the inner garment, nor let the robe hang over the edge of the bed.
Recite the verse for ascending the bed: "Ascending this bed of unimpeded liberation, The pure light of equal wisdom. If one is observing the fast (*upavāsa*),...
When the hour-circuit fire-board sounds and the wooden fish (mokugyo) rings in the hall, those who may not yet enter the hall must have an attendant take their alms bowl and sit outside.
Once the wooden fish has finished ringing and the long board (chōban) is heard sounding, they set down their bowls, raise their bodies, and stand upright with composure.

Then, turning to the left, they join their palms and recite the verse: "Holding this vessel, I vow that all sentient beings shall become accomplished vessels of the Dharma and receive the offerings of devas and humans. [With the left hand...]
With the left hand he takes the *patra* and with the right hand he unties the carrying strap; then, lifting the bowl with his left hand, he turns his body and places the bowl upon his forehead.
Squatting upright, he sets the bowl down on the clean board to the left, taking care not to strike anyone with his waist or back.

He remains there without leaning his body or sitting down, waiting for the drum to be struck and the *yingzhong* bell to toll in the Sangha Hall; then the assembly, seeing the dust raised by the bowl, joins their palms in reverence to welcome the Holy Monk (*āryasaṃgha*).

Entering the Hall (According to the ancient rules, one descends from the platform to welcome the Holy Monk; some say this refers to welcoming the Abbot. The Holy Monk is Piṇḍola, who, having received the Buddha’s entrustment, remains in the world to receive offerings; thus a shrine is established for him within the monastery.

The *Fayuan* states that the Holy Monk in the hall is often said to be Ājñātakauṇḍinya, but this is incorrect, as the sutras and vinaya do not permit the establishment of a shrine for him, nor do they prescribe making offerings to him).

Having finished joining the palms, move the alms bowl to rest before you. Joining the palms, silently contemplate: "The Buddha was born in Kapilavastu, attained enlightenment in Magadha, preached the Dharma in Vārāṇasī, and entered parinirvāṇa in Kuśinagara. Upon hearing the sound of the mallet:
The Head Monastic raises the verse for unfolding the bowl (when unfolding the bowl, one should wish that all sentient beings have tranquil body and mind, free from all coarseness and violence).

When the assembly has concluded, he may recite the verse: "The Tathāgata’s vessel of measure; now I am able to unfold it. May I, together with all sentient beings, realize the emptiness and stillness of the three wheels. Then, he unties the cloth bundle and unfolds the clean towel to cover his knees.
He folds the corners of the bundle into a triangle so that they do not hang down. Next, he unfolds the bowl-cloth, takes the bowl with his left hand palm-up, and places it [on the cloth].
On the single [seat], take up the *kañcika* (spoon) with the two thumbs, unfolding it from the small finger in sequence;
do not let it clatter or make a sound. Protect the fourth and fifth fingers as "touching fingers" and do not use them.

Then, fold the bowl-cloth (*pātra-śodhana*) to make it smaller, hold it close to the body, and place the bag for the spoon and chopsticks (*śalākā-kośa*) across it beneath the bowl-cloth. When exiting, the spoon comes out first; when entering, the spoon goes in first.

At the handle of the *kaṭhina* cloth, the clean end is placed facing upward on the shoulder; the bowl-brush is secured within the seam of the third bowl, protruding about half an inch, used for holding raw rice.
Once the bowls have been unfolded, the person on duty strikes the wooden mallet once and says: "Today is the [number]th day of the bright fortnight;

at dawn, each of you shall record the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*). The assembly silently contemplates [these points]. (The six recollections are twofold: the first is as seen below; the second is: mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, mindfulness of the Sangha Jewel, mindfulness of the precepts, mindfulness of generosity, and mindfulness of the devas—these are the three types of action.)
After dedicating all the roots of goodness thus cultivated to sentient beings and the Buddha-way, strike the mallet once more for the dedication (and so forth).

The Head Monk raises the name of the Buddha, and the assembly joins their palms in unison. They must not let their fingers be uneven; they must be held at the level of the chest, neither too high nor too low.
One must not rest the hands upon the knees, nor support the mouth with the hands. (The ancients said: "Uneven palms do not meet at the chest; the two hands are crossed and thrust into the nose.")

Dragging their sandals and lifting the curtain, they lack courtesy; with coarse, vomit-like voices and leaking breath, they boast of being heroes. When the ten recitations are finished and it is time to distribute the congee, the head monk himself chants the verse for the distribution of congee:

"Congee has ten benefits that enrich the practitioner; its karmic fruit is boundless, culminating in eternal bliss. Furthermore, another verse says: "Maintaining pure precepts, one is honored by others with respect. At the proper time, one should offer congee as alms. The ten benefits enrich the practitioner: Complexion, strength, longevity, and happiness;

Speech becomes clear and eloquent; Indigestion and wind-disorders are removed; Hunger and thirst are extinguished. This is what the Buddha called 'medicine. If one desires to attain the realms of humans and devas and enjoy long-lasting happiness, One should offer congee to the Sangha. This verse is chanted in unison by the assembly.

Regarding the two verses used when chanting for the meal during the fast, there are likewise two verses. One verse says: "The food of three virtues and six flavors is offered to the Buddhas and the Sangha; may all sentient beings of the Dharma-realm partake equally in this offering. This verse is chanted by the presiding head monk. Another verse says:

"This food, with its color, fragrance, and flavor, is offered above to the Buddhas of the ten directions, in the middle to the various worthies and sages, and below to the categories of the six realms; bestowed equally without distinction, may all who receive it be fully satisfied, enabling the donors now to attain immeasurable *pāramitās*.

This verse is recited by the entire assembly. Of these two verses, only one is used at a time. When receiving the food, one should hold the bowl with both hands, whether the quantity is large or small.

If there is little, one should stop taking with the right hand. When receiving food, silently recite this verse: "When receiving food, I vow that all sentient beings shall be fully endowed with the precepts and perfect all bodhi.
When receiving various flavors, recite: "When receiving flavors, I vow that all sentient beings shall obtain the supreme flavor of the Buddha’s ambrosia and be fully satisfied.

If you see the bowl is full, recite: "Seeing the bowl full, I vow that all sentient beings shall be fully satiated with all roots of goodness. When the distribution of gruel is nearly finished, strike the wooden mallet once, and the assembly performs [the ritual].

The Five Contemplations (as recited): 1. Consider the labor expended and the distance from which it was brought. 2. Reflect upon whether one’s own virtuous conduct is complete or deficient in being worthy of this offering. 3. Guard the mind against transgressions, making the abandonment of greed and other afflictions the primary principle.

4. Regard the food as excellent medicine intended to cure the suffering of the body. 5. Accept this food for the sake of accomplishing the work of the Path. Having completed these contemplations, strike the wooden gong once. The Head Monk raises the food and recites the verse:

"When partaking of food, may all sentient beings take the joy of dhyāna as their nourishment and be filled with the delight of the Dharma. After the assembly has finished reciting together, the upper and lower shoulders should be aligned, and one should face the opposite direction to bow before eating.

One must not shake both sides with one's hands directly in front of oneself. When generating the visualization during the meal, the verse says: "O assembly of spirits and deities, I now bestow this offering upon you;
may this food pervade the ten directions for all spirits and deities. The method of generating [the food] does not exceed seven grains; too few constitutes stinginess in eating.
One must not generate [the food] from the tips of the spoon or chopsticks. Using the right hand, take some rice and press it into the palm of the left hand.

Place the bowl-brush upon it (when receiving food, one uses the *ch'ung-sheng*; when not receiving food, it must not be used). To scoop rice with a bucket or ladle is improper. The purpose of the *ch'ung-sheng* is to distribute what one has eaten to various ghosts and spirits. There are three conditions for this distribution:

first, to give to the ghosts of the wilderness and to the Mother of Ghosts (*Kṣetrapati*) and her like; these beings originally ate flesh and preyed upon people, but after the Buddha converted them, they received the precepts against killing. He then instructed his disciples to provide food for them wherever possible;

those who cannot do so are not true disciples of the Buddha—this refers to the practice of distributing food at each of the seats in the refectory. Second, to give to the hungry ghosts; in the refectory, a small vessel is separately prepared, and once the meal is finished, the assembly performs a ritual to offer it, or each individual prepares a small vessel of food.
This refers to the practice of reciting mantras during the night. Generally, regarding the rules for eating: one must not bring the mouth to the food, nor bring the food to the mouth.
When picking up or setting down the bowl, as well as the spoon or chopsticks, they must not make a sound. One must not cough, touch the nose, or sneeze.
If one should sneeze, one must cover the nose with the sleeve of one's robe. One must not scratch the head, fearing that wind-blown dander might fall onto the neighboring seats.

One must not pick at one's teeth with the bowl; nor must one make noise while chewing rice or sipping soup. (The *Sifen jieben* states: "Receive food with a composed mind; receive rice with a level bowl; receive soup with a level bowl.

Eat both soup and rice together in their proper order. Do not pick at the center of the bowl to eat; do not cover the soup with rice in hopes of getting more; do not look into the bowls of neighboring seats to give rise to a mind of envy.

Do not take large mouthfuls of rice; do not open your mouth to wait for the food; do not speak with food in your mouth; do not throw balls of rice into your mouth; do not let food fall and scatter; do not leave food in your cheeks; do not slurp the food; do not lick the food with your tongue.")

One may shake one's hand while eating, but must not eat by grasping scattered grains with the hand. One should receive food according to one's capacity; one must not request more than what is required. The *Vinaya* states: "Eat according to the measure of your belly.

The *Ekottarika Āgama* states: "Eating too much leads to suffering and affliction; eating too little causes the decline of physical strength. One who eats in moderation is like a scale that is neither high nor low.
One must not use the head-bowl to hold wet food, nor use the head-bowl to rinse rice with leftover broth, nor pick at vegetables using the head-bowl.
When eating indoors, if there are vegetable scraps, place them behind the bowl in a secluded spot.

While eating, one must observe whether the shoulders are level; they must not be too slumped. Without having requested a second serving, do not scrub the bowl, nor lick it, nor make a noise while scrubbing.

Do not give rise to anger or distracting thoughts before the food has arrived. (As the ancients said: "Staring blankly in all directions, giving rise to sorrowful and angry thoughts; swallowing saliva and coughing frequently; slurping porridge and soup, stuffing the mouth full; opening the mat and spreading the cloth.")

When the bowls produce a clanging sound that reaches the neighboring seats, if one uses a fan, one must not fan those in the adjacent positions. If one is afraid of the wind, one should inform the *karmadāna* and sit in the outer hall.
When a practitioner moves their fan, they themselves must not use a fan. To wash the bowls, fill the head bowl with water and wash the bowls in succession;
the small bowls must not be washed inside the head bowl. As for the remaining bowls, as well as the spoons and chopsticks, they must still be kept apart to avoid contact.
One must not make a sound while rinsing water, nor spit water into the bowl. One must not first rinse the bowl with hot water, nor collect the water from the bowl before folding it.
One must not wipe sweat with the knee-cloth, nor pour leftover water onto the ground.
When folding the water-cloth, one should recite this verse: "The water for washing this bowl of mine Is like the nectar of the heavens; I offer it to the spirits and deities."

May the assembly all be fully satisfied. Oṃ ma-hū-ra-se svāhā. Having gathered the bowls, with the thumbs of both hands pressed firmly together, insert them one after another into the interior until finished.

Then strike the wooden gong; the head monk raises [the vessel] and recites the verse after the meal: "Meal having been finished, may all sentient beings accomplish all that they do, and be endowed with all Buddha-dharmas. Having finished eating, may their physical strength and vitality be full;

relying on the ten directions and the three periods of time, may the heroes turn cause into fruit without waiting for thought, and may all sentient beings attain supernatural powers. [Recite either of these two verses. When the assembly has finished eating in harmony:

It is not permitted to rise first; after the wooden mallet has been struck, the Abbot descends from his seat. The assembly hangs their alms bowls and must not step on the edge of the platform when descending.
They must not allow their *kāṣāya* robes to hang over the edge of the platform, but must stand close to the front to perform the greeting (*praṇāma*) before leaving the hall.

I, the bhikṣu [Name], on this day, the first day of the bright fortnight (or as appropriate from the first to the fifteenth day), or the first day of the dark fortnight (or as appropriate from the first to the fourteenth or fifteenth day).
I have no place where I am invited (the Sangha’s regular meal being intended for my own attendance);
I now go for alms.
On such-and-such a year, such-and-such a month, such-and-such a day, at such-and-such a time...
I have received full ordination for [number] years.
I now possess and maintain my three robes and alms bowl [specify if complete or deficient]. Regarding my extra robes, I have [already/not yet] performed the ritual of *viśuddhi* (purification).
I now rely upon the community for food. I am [name].
On account of obtaining food from a separate group, I am currently free from illness (and capable of practicing the Path), yet I require medical treatment.
(From the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*: this does not constitute an offense if one is not mindful [of the rule]).

The Great Master said: "Now, food is the external life-force of sentient beings; if it does not enter into contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), it nourishes birth and death. One must therefore practice contemplation. In contemplating it, one reflects that all the old food within this body has been nourished by ignorance and afflictions (*kleśa*) to produce birth and death.

The food currently being consumed is entirely the perception of *prajñā*. As the old food issues forth from the pores in succession, the pathways of the mind immediately open. Consuming this new food illuminates all darkness, extinguishing it and bringing about *prajñā*.

As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: 'Those who are equal regarding food are also equal regarding the Dharma. Because of this food, *prajñā* is realized; this food can nourish the *dharmakāya*. Once the *dharmakāya* is established, liberation is attained. This is the illumination of the three virtues (*triguṇa*) through this food."

It is neither new nor old; yet because there is old food, there is new food, and because there is new food, it is called "new. This is termed the provisional (*prajñapti*). Since the old cannot be sought, the new cannot be sought; ultimate emptiness and quiescence is termed the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*).

As for the one who eats, how could that which is eaten be considered "new"? Since there is no new food, how can there be an eater? Yet, without departing from old food, one sustains the body; the new food provides further benefit. Through the harmony of causes and conditions, they cannot be distinguished as preceding or succeeding;

this is termed the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*). Only the Middle is the provisional and empty; only the empty is the Middle and provisional; only the provisional is the Middle and empty. This inconceivable state is called the Middle Way. The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "It is not the presence of afflictions (*kleśa*), nor is it the departure from afflictions; it is not entering a state of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), nor is it arising from it."
To fix the mind in concentration is called the method of nourishing the Dharma.
Having finished reading and reciting in the hall or chanting in the pavilion, one may return to the meditation hall to read or go to the Dharma Hall to recite the texts.
One must not sit with robes hanging down, nor rest the head on a bent arm, nor gather together to talk and laugh, nor remain alone.
When greeting others with a bow, those who are newly studying the texts among the Four Books should begin with the *Sifen jiaoyi* (The Ritual of the Fourfold Teaching).
This is because this single work encompasses the teachings of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles as the Tathāgata appeared in the world and transformed beings over five periods;
by practicing this first, one may grasp the general outline and gradually enter the Buddha-way. If one cannot read the sūtras, this is the way.

One must not raise the voice too high; one must not spread the sutra out too long; one must not let the sutra hang down; one must not drape the sutra-belt over the body; and one must not walk while reciting. (Ciyun said:

"The essential gate for concentrating the mind when reciting the Buddha’s name or sutras is to rectify the heart and align the intention as if facing the Honored Countenance," and so forth. As detailed in the *Tianzhu Xuji*, the Great Master said: "Now, wishing to recite a sutra, one should sit cross-legged on a separate seat and contemplate that the seat upon which one sits is lofty, vast, and magnificent.

Next, one should contemplate the Eight Classes of Beings and the Fourfold Assembly surrounding one to listen to the Dharma. Furthermore, one must direct the mind to contemplate that one is acting as a Dharma Master to transmit the Buddha’s True Teaching and preach it for the sake of the Fourfold Assembly. One should imagine that the sound produced does not merely [arise from] this..."

From those in this single assembly to all those throughout the ten directions, being able to hear and receive [the teaching] is called the "contemplation of the provisional" (jia-guan). Next, one contemplates the person who can preach and the sutra they recite: what is this sutra? Is it the physical scroll, or is it the paper and ink? Is it the reciter’s mind, or is it the recitation from the mouth?

Or is the recitation produced by the combination of the tongue, palate, and other organs? Is there a self-body, or is there no self-body? Who is the reciter? One contemplates these four groups: do they truly exist, or are they born from conceptualization?

These four groups do not exist; that which can recite is "no-self. This is called the "contemplation of emptiness" (kong-guan). Although there is no sutra being recited, there are the scroll, paper, and written characters; although there is no person capable of reciting, there is a self-body that proclaims it for the sake of the assembly. Although it is not...

Internally and externally, one is not separate from the internal and external; although it is not a physical scroll, one is not separate from the scroll; although it is not body or speech, one is not separate from body and speech. From beginning to end, there is never any discrepancy or error—this is called the inconceivable. To be able to form this understanding and to be able to form this contemplation is called the "Three Contemplations.

Within a single mind, one attains these three contemplations without before or after, such that the three contemplations appear perfectly distinct. (The details are as set forth in the *Lüelù Sānguàn Jìngxīn Sòngjīng Fǎ*; for the remainder, one must consult that work).

Wandering: When wandering through the mountains, one must not wear straw sandals while walking in the halls (as the ancients said: "Baring one's shoulders is not permitted in the hall; straw sandals must not tread upon the Dharma Hall").

One must not lean against the railings before the hall, nor walk with reckless haste or agitation (as the ancients said: "In walking, one must move with measured steps, practicing the majestic deportment of Aśvajit;

in speech, one must lower the voice, following the rules of Upāli"). Wandering about idly within the halls and stupas is forbidden (as the ancients said: "If there is no business, one need not ascend the Buddha Hall; do not enter it for idle purposes").

When walking toward the stupa, do not change the water or add incense and lamps; even if one possesses blessings as vast as the sands of the Ganges, they will all be exhausted. When walking in the corridors, one must yield to those of seniority. One must not go barefoot, but must wear monastic shoes.
One must not walk while holding hands, nor sway the body or swing the arms. One must not lean on the waist, squat, or sit.

One must not engage in playful laughter or discuss the是非 (right and wrong) of worldly affairs. As the Ancient Sage said: "Having bid farewell to both parents and abandoned one's teacher, one seeks [the Way]."
"What does knowledge resemble? It has never been spoken of as the affairs of the Zen school; that one reaches white hair without success—whose fault is it?
When you wish to enter the latrine, you must go early and prepare yourself; you must not lose your decorum at the last moment. Take a clean cloth and place it in your left hand.
Do not walk upon the path while performing prostrations for others, nor should you receive prostrations from others. You should keep your hands joined in *añjali*.
Walking while keeping one's gaze on the ground, one should remove the *chujue* (upper robe) and hang it upon a bamboo rack, securing it with a hand-towel as a marker.
Holding a water vessel in the right hand, one approaches the latrine and must first tap at the door three times; only when no one is inside may one enter.
If someone is already there, one must not force entry. If the latrine is shared by many and someone is waiting outside, even if one has not yet finished, one must exit immediately.

When entering the latrine to change shoes, they must not be placed unevenly. Place the clean bucket in front; snap your fingers three times (to alert the dung-eating spirits and avoid splashing them with filth).

Sit upright and straight, not leaning to either side. If it is dark at night, use the latrine rake to draw lines back and forth within the hole to ascertain its length, width, and whether it is level or not. Do not strain yourself or make any noise.
When you have nasal mucus or saliva, you must not speak with another person through a wall; you should gaze straight ahead, neither lowering your head nor looking downward.

You must not hold counting-sticks (*śalākā*) to draw characters on the wall, nor use them excessively. When you have finished using the counting-sticks, you should place them in the stick-receptacle (*śalākā-koṣa*), not elsewhere.
With the left hand washed clean, you should protect the thumb while washing the second, third, and middle fingers six or seven times.

Wash with water (if a bhikṣu does not wash himself clean, he incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense; he shall not sit upon the monastic beds or seats, nor shall he pay homage to the Triple Gem—even if he pays homage, there will be no merit).

When using water, do not splash or soak [the area], and do not waste it excessively. Place the water-purification bucket back in its original position. With dry hands, put on the undergarment and enter the trousers.
With dry hands, open the door. Take the bucket out with the left hand; one must not grasp the door leaf or the door frame with wet hands.
When picking up ashes with the right hand, one must subsequently pick up earth; one must not take up ashes or earth with wet hands. Afterwards, wash with soap pods (sāgarambha) up to the elbow.
When entering or leaving the latrine, recite the mantra for each instance. Entering the Latrine (*for the purpose of excreting feces or urine*):

"May all sentient beings cast off greed, anger, and ignorance, and eliminate their sinful defilements. Oṃ haṇudāya svāhā. Washing Clean: "Oṃ hana-miḷitī svāhā. Purifying the Hands: "Oṃ cukkāraya svāhā. Purifying the Body.

*(Oṃ śrīye svāhā)* To remove impurities: *(Oṃ vajiro nāgaṭa svāhā)*. According to the Vinaya, even for minor urination one must wash and purify oneself. As the *Necklace Sūtra* (*Sragdharā-sūtra*) states:

"If one who has used the latrine does not recite this mantra, then even if they were to wash their body with the waters of ten Ganges Rivers up to the Vajra-limit, they could not be purified. For one who enters a hall or temple to gaze upon and pay homage [to the Buddha], there will be no benefit [if unpurified].

I urge you to receive and uphold it; recite this mantra seven times each time. Therefore, ghosts and spirits will always pay respectful homage.
