(For details on the methods, refer to the *Three Thousand Dignified Manners Sūtra* as cited in the *Separate Collection of India*). Bathing: Whenever beginning a bath...
Carrying bathing requisites in the right hand, one must, according to the Vinaya regulations, carry the five-strip robe (*pañcakaṭhina*) and go outside the door.
Gently lift the curtain so that no wind enters, enter through the lower gate, and perform a greeting (*praṇāma*). Returning to an empty space, bow to those on the left and right;

then, first hang the five-strip robe and hand-towel over the crossbar, next sit briefly, remove the socks, stand up, turn around, spread out the cloth mat (*kaṭhina*), and take up the bathing requisites.
Set aside the upper robe; without yet removing the *zhidie*, first take the lower garment and wrap it around the body with the foot-cloth.
Next, fasten the bathing skirt and fold the trousers, placing them inside a cloth bundle. Change into the bathing shirt and hang the *zhidie* together with the five-strip robe in one place.
Secure the hand-towel and wrap the inner garments in a bundle to cover the back. (The ancients said: "When the three beats of the drum sound, enter the hall.")

At that time, touch should be pure; one must distinguish between upper and lower robes. Speaking, laughing, or raising one's voice is strictly forbidden; do not allow coarse behavior to violate the dignified decorum (*vīryā*). When entering the bathhouse wearing slippers, one must not go barefoot.

Upon entering the room, one must stay in the lower section and wait for one’s turn before bathing; one must not occupy the upper section (to yield to the head monks and the elders). Do not let hot water splash onto others or yourself.
After wiping the body after bathing, one must not soak one's feet in the bucket, nor may one remain inside the room.
When relieving oneself internally, wash in a secluded place; do not prop your feet upon a bucket, nor rub your feet upon a trough.
Do not rub or wash one another's feet; you should use a cloth, grasping both ends to scrub your back, taking care not to splash water against either side.
Do not wash clothes within the hall while seated next to others; do not rinse cloths or towels over the trough, nor leave them there to dry.

In the bath tub (the ancients called it "donning the robe for bathing"): one must maintain reverence and composure. When the hot water arrives, strike the board; when sending off guests, do not respond with foot-wiping cloths. Place the foot-wiping cloths on the edge of the tub; how could both feet be placed inside the bucket?
One must not laugh or speak; one must not scoop out the water; one must not lift the bucket to pour over oneself.

One must cover the entire body and not allow it to be exposed. The foot-wiping cloths must not leave the body. Do not use excessive amounts of hot water. If there are sores, or if one is washing a site treated with moxibustion, take care accordingly.
Alternatively, if using ointment for scabies, one should enter the bath last; one must not cut in ahead of others. Upon emerging from the bath, one must not wipe the face with a public towel.
One must bow to those of higher and lower rank, sit with shoulders squared, put on the upper garment first, then don the *zhiduò* (straight robe), followed by the lower garment.
Unfasten the bathing skirt, fold the foot-cloth, and place the bathing skirt in the bathing bag to prevent it from getting wet. Bow to those on the left and right before exiting.
If there is a donor who provides a bath in the hall, one may recite sutras at will and dedicate the merit;
the "Brief Knowledge of Ten Matters Regarding Entering the Bathhouse" compiled by Ciyun follows the *Tianzhu bieji* (Clouds from India, Separate Collection), etc. (as detailed therein).
Sitting Meditation (Zuochan): All who study the Way examine the teachings to illumine the mind and investigate the mind through contemplation;

thus the Patriarchs taught by day and meditated by night, never letting a single year pass in vain. As for the posture of sitting meditation: if it is half-lotus, place the left foot upon the right thigh;
if it is full-lotus, further cross the right foot over the top and place it upon the left thigh, resting the left palm upon the right palm.
Place the left thigh firmly on the ground, keep the body upright and straight, aligning the nose with the navel so that the torso stands level and balanced.
Close the mouth to cut off external wind; let the teeth just barely touch one another and lift the tongue toward the palate. Close the eyes just enough to block out external light.
Next, regulate the breath until it is even and the mind is free from dullness and distraction; then, observe the deluded mind of this very moment, this present instant.

The Venerable Master of Siming said: "Observe that the capacity and measure of this single thought-moment of consciousness are boundless, and its essence is eternally abiding. It universally encompasses all Buddhas of the ten directions, all sentient beings, and the lands of space throughout the past, present, and future, leaving nothing outside.

It is like a single jewel in a celestial net or a single wave in the great ocean. The wave has no separate substance; it is entirely composed of water. Since the water is boundless, the waves are likewise limitless. Although a single jewel is small, its reflection appears in all the jewels; the reflections in all the jewels enter into that single jewel.

All the jewels are not many, and the single jewel is not few. The single thought-moment before us is also like this. Now, observe that all phenomena are the one mind, and the one mind is all phenomena. It is not that the one mind gives birth to all phenomena, nor that the one mind contains all phenomena."

Neither before nor after, there is nothing that is not capable; though one discusses how the nature and characteristics of all phenomena are fundamentally empty, yet within this single mind, the holy and the ordinary appear distinct. To establish is to destroy; neither existent nor non-existent, both object and contemplation are forgotten, and all oppositions are severed.
It cannot be deliberated by words nor conceived by the mind; therefore, it is provisionally designated as the "Inconceivable and Subtle Contemplation."
During the first watch of the night, having finished offering food and prostrating to the Buddha, one may practice meditation or recitation as one pleases;

one should be diligent and energetic, taking care not to be negligent. (The ancients said: "Frequently warn yourself of the passing time; do not let your sitting be wasted. Make the night into day and practice with diligence.

Upon hearing the bell for concentration, join your palms and recite this verse: "Upon hearing the sound of the bell, transgressions and karma are lightened; Wisdom increases and Bodhicitta arises. May I leave the hells and escape the fiery pit; May I attain Buddhahood to deliver all sentient beings. If you are prone to drowsiness...
Sleep becomes increasingly excessive; as the Sūtra says: "Do not let a lifetime pass in vain due to the cause of sleep.

If one's sleep is heavy, one must take brief rests to dispel it. The Vinaya regulations require that one wear the five-strip robe (*pañcakaṭika*) while lying on the right side (this is because the left shoulder is considered honorable).
One must not lie on one's back, for lying on the back is the sleep of a corpse, and lying face down is the sleep of a lecher; therefore, many evil dreams arise.

The Four Postures: Those who enter a monastic community must not transgress the rules of conduct regarding walking, standing, sitting, or reclining. New students, being inexperienced, should be guided with kind words and admonished;
one must never harbor feelings of resentment toward them. One must not walk through the corridors with the upper robe exposed. Within the refectory, one must not leave the white undergarment visible.
Before the meal, one must keep the robe over the shoulders; after the meal, one must maintain the robe properly. One must not fiddle with the prayer beads or make noise while playing.
After the *sāyāhna* (the third watch), one must not leave the three gates, nor enter the various dormitories or meditation halls without a valid reason.

It is fortunate that you should diligently exert yourselves three times during the day and three times at night. Regarding the matters to be performed throughout the twelve periods of the day, the Buddhist scriptures contain many admonitions that ought to be followed.
As for the daily verses, those already explained previously are sufficient; however, as there are some not yet listed, they are hereby reiterated.

Record. When sleeping: (If one is about to sleep, one should wish that all sentient beings may be entirely at peace and attain great sovereignty. When rising: (When first awakening from sleep, one should wish that all sentient beings may awaken to all-encompassing wisdom and pervade the ten directions.

Washing the hands: (Having finished the task and approaching the water, one should wish that all sentient beings may swiftly proceed within the supramundane Dharma. Washing the face: (Using water to wash the face, one should wish that all sentient beings may attain the gate of pure Dharma and be forever free from defilement.)

Ascending the Hall (When seeing the Buddha, one should wish that all beings obtain unobstructed eyes and see the Buddhas of the ten directions). Ascending the Pavilion (When ascending the multi-storied pavilion, one should wish that all beings ascend the tower of the True Dharma and perceive all things clearly).

Beholding the Stupa (When seeing a Buddha stupa, one should wish that all beings respect it as they do a stupa, receiving offerings from humans and devas). Prostrating before the Stupa (When prostrating at a stupa, one should wish that all beings have no one among humans or devas able to see the crown of their heads).

Bathing the Body (When bathing the body, one should wish that all beings be free from defilement in body and mind, radiant and pure within and without). Washing the Feet (When washing the feet, one should wish that all beings be endowed with spiritual power, moving everywhere without obstruction).
Pluck grass to purify the hands: (Pluck the grass, hold it in the hand, move it back toward the ripples on the water; there is no pure water here; at this pure place, *svāhā*).
Regarding the method for sitting in the hall—whether for ordinary monks, tea and soup services, or the new and full moon assemblies—one must sit upon the meditation cushions inside the bedding.

The space three inches outside and seven inches inside the edge of the bed is called the "pure bed" (*śuddha-śayana*); this is where the alms bowl is placed during mealtime and not a place for sitting.
Nowadays, people often sit conveniently on the outer edge, which greatly violates the established regulations; one must strictly guard against this.

Regarding communal labor (*fusshō*): whenever there is a task at a place where the assembly resides that must necessarily be accomplished through the collective effort of the community, the administrative office (*kusoshi*) first reports it to the Abbot.

Next, they instruct the attendants (*gyōja*) to convey the message to the Head Seat (*shuso*) and the Rector (*uinā*), who then assign it to the attendants of the Hall Office (*dōshi*). These attendants notify the assembly, and the notice for communal labor is hung up.

[Each person] shall wear a name-tag (with the time and location pasted upon it), or upon hearing the sound of the wooden fish or the drum, each shall take their *bān-bō* (arm-band) and place it upon the left upper arm, proceeding to the place of communal labor (*pǔqǐng*).
With the exception of those who are elderly or ill, all shall attend the communal labor together. The method for communal labor is twofold:

first, to plant pure karma within the field of merit; second, to ensure that labor is shared equally between superiors and subordinates. [As the Vinaya says: "When the Buddha spoke of the benefits of sweeping the ground..."

When the elder bhikṣus all abandoned their meditation and recitation to sweep the ground, the Buddha stopped them, saying, "I have already instructed those in charge of affairs; let a certain official in charge of affairs sweep. When [the official] replied that he could not sweep everywhere, the Buddha ordered the *khaṇḍika* (wooden gong) to be struck so that everyone would assemble together to perform the task. This was the beginning of the practice of *puping* (general mobilization for communal labor).
Instructions for Junior Monastics:

On the first and fifteenth days of the lunar month, after the formal lecture in the hall has concluded, the Head of Monastics (Canshou) shall direct the Attendant Monk (Xingzhe) to notify the attendants of each department.

A signboard shall be hung before the Hall of Practice to inform the assembly. When the signal bell for the evening meal tolls, the wooden board shall be struck three times before the Hall of Practice to assemble the junior monastics.

After offering prayers and praises at the Buddha Hall, proceed to the Abbot’s quarters and stand in line. The head of the assembly (the *sanchō*) enters to invite the Abbot, who emerges and takes his seat.
The *sanchō* raises his voice slowly and says, “*San*” (Greeting). The assembly joins in at a low voice, saying, “*Fusatsu*” (How have you been?).

After the formal salutations and listening to the Abbot’s instructions on the Dharma, the *sanchō* says, “*Chinju*” (Take care). The assembly joins in at a low voice, bows, and withdraws. If the Abbot is otherwise engaged, [the procedure continues as follows].

The *he-shi* (censor) strikes the gong and cries out, "I respectfully follow the Compassionate Decree of the Abbot; I shall attend the assembly. The assembly replies, "We do not know [your health]. He then strikes again and cries, "The session is dismissed. The assembly replies, "Take care. They all perform a mutual inquiry (*monshin*) and withdraw.
Next, they proceed to the office of the *dōkō*, the *shuso*, and the *kusoshi* for formal attendance (attendance and exemption from attendance follow the same ritual as before).

[Regarding] the method for instructing novice practitioners: one should explain the causes and conditions of leaving the household life, or explain the rules and decorum, or explain the general meaning of the sutras.

Regarding the monthly schedule, it should be known that on the first day of the year in the first month, various temples perform prayers for the new year, either conducting the *Kōmyō-kan* (Luminous Repentance) for seven days and nights, three days and nights,

or simply making offerings to the deities for three days according to the specific regulations of each temple; furthermore, the rites for the new year and the Lantern Festival are performed before the assembly hall and the administrative quarters.

The *weina* (ritual director) of the Sūtra Recitation Hall offers incense and performs the dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) before the lamp; the *zhike* (guest master) offers incense and performs the dedication before the lamp.
On the fifth day, it is the anniversary of the passing of the Venerable Fazhi. However, at Yiqing Temple in Siming, they follow the ritual text of Dharma Master Gaosheng;
as for the ancestral memorial of the Tiantai Patriarch, offerings are prepared accordingly. Now, all quarters should also commemorate the merit of his revival of the teachings and contemplation.
One should cultivate reverence; if one wishes to follow a simplified practice, it must still accord with the prohibitions observed by successive abbots of the mountain gate.
In the second month, the abbot, the head lecturer, and the head seat shall, at this time of spring's opening, deliver lectures and instructions to the assembly.
On the fifth day of the first month is the anniversary of the passing of the Venerable Jingxi; on the fifteenth day is the Buddha’s Parinirvāṇa.
On the Qingming Festival in the third month, one sweeps and sprinkles the ancestral pagodas, offers food, performs rites, and recites scriptures.
Prohibition on gathering tea leaves and bamboo shoots; the preservation of trees and mountain forests.
On the first day of the fourth month, the Hall Office issues the draft notice.

On the eighth day, for the Buddha’s Descent from Heaven, the Kitchen Office shall solemnly prepare the bathing ceremony in the Lumbinī Garden and arrange offerings while chanting sutras. From the fourteenth day, incantations shall be recited.
On the second day, the ritual scattering of water and sand for the *an-gu* (summer retreat) is performed; on the third day thereafter, the tea-offering ceremony is conducted.
On the twentieth day, the lecture and repentance service are inaugurated, with the Abbot opening the discourse. On the final day of the month (*huì-rì*), the precepts are recited.
In the fifth month, the Green Sprout Assembly (Qingmiao Hui) is established for three days; on the first day, the liturgical list for recitation is issued in advance.

The Abbot opens the lectures and requests the head officers (Tou-shou) to open the lectures as well. The administrative office (Kusi) inspects all locations to repair leaks and dredge the ditches and canals.
On the fifteenth day, the precepts are recited.
In the sixth month, during the height of the summer heat, the formal lectures may be suspended or not, depending on the practice of the abbot.
Those who follow the ancient way do not shrink from cold or heat; having entered the summer retreat for the ninety days, they must strive to attain realization.

The abbot and the head seat (shouzuo) should exhort the junior monks so that they do not become indolent, following the ancient custom of practicing through reading and the method of the "locked examination" (suoshi). On the fourteenth day, the precepts are recited.
On the first day of the seventh month, the essential period for the *Lanpen* (Ullambana) Assembly begins. For half a month, one performs the Minor Amitābha Repentance at dawn;

after the morning gruel, one performs the Major Amitābha Repentance; after the midday meal, one recites the *Lanpen Sūtra*; and until evening, one recites the *Amitābha Sūtra* while maintaining mindfulness.
In advance, one leads the assembly in preparing *hu* (offering) food with their resources. On the full moon day, the assembly is concluded and dispersed. [The retreat] concludes on the sixteenth day.
Regulation:

On the seventh day of the eighth month is the anniversary of the Venerable Zhan’an. Because this month involves brothers entering and leaving for visits, preparing for the cold, and paying respects to their parents, the study of the scrolls must not be neglected;
however, one may personally attend to lighting the lamps and should likewise exert oneself in these matters.
In the ninth month, the autumn lectures are inaugurated, during which one may expound upon the *Shuowen* (Explanations of Characters).
On the first day of the tenth month, the hearth is opened.

In the eleventh month, at the winter solstice, one either performs the *Guangming Chan* (Repentance of Radiant Light) or observes the winter vegetarian feast for the deities, according to the specific regulations of the monastery.
The Abbot invites the assembly for the winter refreshments prior to the winter solstice. On the twenty-fourth day is the anniversary of the Great Master Tiantai’s passing.
On the first day of the twelfth lunar month, the Winter Solstice Buddha Assembly (Làfó Huì) is inaugurated, with a duration of one month.
On the eighth day of the first month, the Buddha’s Enlightenment Day, the administrative office prepares red fermented rice for offerings.

At the end of the year, they compile and present various registers and accounts to calculate the funds and grain; they sweep and sprinkle the halls and pavilions, practice the rituals for the New Year repentance, and prepare gifts for the New Year celebrations.
They distribute the year-end provisions and invite the assembly for soup and fruit.
Chapter Eight: The Gate of Admonition and Exhortation;
Chapter Nine: The Gate of True Refuge.
When our Buddha entered parinirvāṇa, all his disciples rushed to the funeral rites at the Twin Śāla Trees; when the cremation was completed, his remains were divided into eight portions.
It is beneficial to construct a stupa to enshrine the objects of our reverent devotion, and there is no aspect of this that should not be performed with the utmost care.
Although the passing of a monk does not equal the magnificent renown of our Buddha, how could the rites for sending off the dead and mourning the deceased be abandoned?
As for the Buddhist rites of mourning, they need not necessarily follow secular customs; rather, let us follow the teachings of the Great Master Tiantai.
I exhort Master Yuan of Donglin to follow the proper decorum: disciples should neither wear mourning attire nor weep; if one can transfer this grief toward the Way, success will surely be attained.

This accords with the clear instructions of the Brahmajāla Sūtra: on the day a *upādhyāya* or *ācārya* passes away, as well as at the third week and the seventh week, one ought to lecture upon the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinaya.
These are the words of the Buddha. It is sufficient simply to withdraw from worldly affairs.

To diligently practice the merit of maintaining the incense and lamps and observing the fasts and precepts brings benefit both to the unseen realm and the visible world; how could this possibly contradict filial piety?

There may be those who do not understand this, who merely spy upon the accumulation of robes and bowls to plot their own personal gain, even resorting to anger, strife, and violent combat, clawing and pushing with all their might.
Such behavior is something even animals would not do, yet such people regard themselves as superior.
Those who find my teaching abominable—whom else could they be but these fellows?

When the Abbot passes away, the Venerable of the Abbot’s Quarters shall manifest his illness; perceiving that the time has come, he should request the two orders and the retired elders to inspect and seal the robes and bowl.
The traveler's belongings are to be kept for the purpose of bathing and dressing the deceased, and these shall likewise be sealed and kept in the abbot’s quarters.
A trustworthy servant shall be dispatched to guard them while they await appraisal and auction. Should any items be designated for distribution, this must be done with impartiality;

do not allow favoritism or resentment to lead to disputes later on. Furthermore, as a final instruction, junior disciples must not wear hempen mourning garments or wail loudly (this applies when a master or close relative among the śrāmaṇeras passes away).

Since pain arises from one's own mind, how could one not weep? However, one must not let out loud cries or utter words of "Heaven! or speak of transgressions and sins. When the Buddha passed into parinirvāṇa, his disciples all wept; those who had not yet abandoned desire rolled upon the ground. The *Wubai wen* (Five Hundred Questions) states:
"When the teacher passes away, one must not raise one's voice to wail loudly; one should merely shed small tears."
In cases where resources are meager, one may simply follow the frugal practice of inviting the Head Seat (Śrāmaṇera) to preside over the funeral; all other Buddhist rites are waived.

One should merely recite verses on impermanence and conduct the funeral procession for the deceased monk in accordance with the standard protocol, ensuring that the monastery’s permanent assets are not wasted.

If the abbot has performed meritorious service for the mountain gate and the monastic community, and out of remembrance of his lingering affection, his robes and bowl are somewhat abundant, then the funeral rites should be performed according to the formal ritual. If there are any remaining items...
The letter shall be dispatched immediately.
The form of a testamentary letter (yíshū zhī shì).
Upon entering the shrine and initially manifesting the passing away, the attendant immediately orders the guest master (kètóu xíngzhě) to notify the two orders and all the monastic quarters.

The elders of the two orders then proceed in succession to the abbot’s quarters to offer condolences. Once these rites are completed, the head seat (shǒuzuò), together with the elders of the two orders, deliberates upon the draft of the memorial for the funeral arrangements.
(See the following form) Notify the various monasteries and send letters inviting those who shall preside over the funeral rites.

These should be eminent virtuous monks from neighboring monasteries, long-established elders, senior dharma-kinsmen, or at least the head seat (*śrāmaṇera*) of the temple itself. If there is a final testament, it must be followed.
The junior disciples, attendants, and personal followers should personally bathe [the deceased], dress him in robes, wash his hair, and assist in arranging him within the coffin.
A shrine is established in the dormitory hall, and the final verse (*yige*) is posted on the left side of the shrine. A table and mats are set out for offerings.

The bell before the Sangha Hall is struck, and the Head Seat (*shouzuo*) and the assembly arrive at the dormitory hall to offer condolences. The junior monks recite sutras, and the Rector (*weina*) delivers a verse for the dedication of merit, saying:

"The dharmas produced by causes and conditions, I declare to be empty; They are also called provisional names, and also called the meaning of the Middle Way. I look up to your true compassion and pray you will graciously grant your clear inspection. This is for the occasion of the Head Monk’s passing and his enshrinement in the coffin. [We] recite [this verse]."

"By the merit accumulated through reciting the True Vehicle, the titles of the Holy Ones, and their respective assemblies, we respectfully offer this for the sake of Jue-tan, that his spiritual rank may be further exalted throughout the ten directions... (and so forth). That night, the chanting and dedication of merit are the same as before;

however, change the two characters "ru kan" (entering the shrine) to "ting kan" (staying at the shrine). At the shrine, offerings of gruel and rice are presented twice, and tea and soup are presented three times.
The assembly chants together, and the dedication by the *vinaya-dhara* is likewise the same.
The format for the funeral announcement requests the presiding mourner.

Generally, the presiding mourner must be one who is aged, renowned, and possessed of virtuous character; it is appropriate that the Head Seat (Shouzuo) respectfully invites such a person. However, in recent times, those holding official monastic positions have come to assume this role.
The guests invite the presiding mourner to strike the great bell to assemble the congregation. They welcome them to the front of the shrine;

once the incense has been lit, they enter the curtain to offer condolences. The junior disciple says: "It is an unfortunate event for the Dharma Gate that the Abbot has returned to the Truth. We pray that you will restrain your grief to complete the great task. The junior disciple performs a prostration with unopened sitting cloth (*chuli*), and the presiding mourner continues to console the two orders of the assembly, saying:

"It is an unfortunate event for the Dharma Gate that the Hall Head Abbot has suddenly withdrawn his transformative authority. We venture to hope that the Great Assembly will exert its strength to attend to the affairs following the abbot’s passing."

The Head Seat replies: "We still rely upon the Venerable Master’s power to provide this guidance. The assembly bows in greeting and disperses. The two orders of officials and the senior elders escort the presiding mourner back to the guest seat, where he burns incense and performs prostrations.
The presiding mourner occupies his position as host. The Head Seat takes a seat to one side; once settled, the Head Seat rises to burn incense, returns to his place, and serves tea.
When the tea offering is complete, the junior disciples line up before him, burn incense, and perform three full prostrations with their robes spread out.
After the Abbot’s attendants and the head of the practitioners have successively offered incense and performed prostrations, the Abbot’s servants complete their bows.

Tea is then served, and the two orders of officials are escorted out by the administrative office (*kusi*). The two orders of officials provide companionship as they proceed in succession to visit the various quarters for refreshments.

The funeral office staff and the presiding mourner shall inspect the quarters and return to the two orders (*liǔ xù*). The senior monks and junior disciples shall follow them to the guest seat (*kè wèi*) to present the inventory of robes and bowls (*yī bō bù*), posthumous writings, and other items.

Tea will be served, and it shall be discussed who from each group—the funeral office staff, the two orders, and the seniors—shall be invited to serve as the funeral directors. Each group shall appoint one representative.
The Treasurer shall put an end to idle gossip; he must further request the Secretary to compose the sacrificial text and issue the correspondence.

The incumbent Chief Guest Attendant shall receive outside guests. The Director of the Funeral Office, along with the assistant treasury officer, the guest master, the tea master, and their respective attendants, shall manage the affairs.
Furthermore, a roster of all personnel and servants belonging to the Funeral Office must be prepared and posted for public view. The presiding mourner must consult with the Head Seat.

The robes and alms bowls left behind by the deceased shall be approximately divided into three portions: one portion shall be used for funeral garments and the *dakṣiṇā* (monetary offerings) for the chanting of sutras at various mountains;

one portion shall be used for the preparation of vegetarian feasts (*zhai*); and one portion shall be distributed among the assembly for the purpose of reading sutras, performing Buddhist rites, and for the accounts and registers.
The incumbent *karmadāna* must be invited to deliberate together with the presiding mourners, who must maintain impartiality and integrity.
One must not act out of private interest by bringing along monastics; these individuals are not permitted to interfere in or perform manual labor.

Furthermore, it shall be deliberated upon how all Buddhist rites (the order of which is shown below) are to be requested, as well as how mourning garments are to be distributed. If there is no cloth or silk available, the value shall be converted into money and distributed.

Regarding mourning attire for filial piety (the *Śākyamuni* tradition’s funeral dress, including the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and various Vinayas, contains no regulations for this; the recent practice of wearing white headbands and hemp shrouds is deeply inappropriate). If one follows worldly customs, the dress should conform to the regulations for the living:

Attendants and junior disciples wear hempen cloth (*mábù duì*). The two orders of the monastic community wear ramie cloth (*zhǔbù duì*). The presiding mourner and senior dharma relatives wear raw silk (*shēngjuàn duì*).
The elders who manage affairs, the local people, and the dharma-relations from various mountains wear raw silk waist-cloths; the donors wear raw silk head-towels and waist-cloths;

the attendants of the abbot wear hempen trousers; the servants and work-leaders of the abbot’s quarters wear hempen head-towels and shirts; and the various servants and tenant farmers wear hempen head-towels.
The Buddha-activities are as follows: locking the shrine, hanging the portrait in the Dharma Hall, facing the spirit, maintaining mindfulness, raising the shrine,
hanging the portrait at the front of the mountain gate pavilion, offering tea and soup, holding the torch, and collecting the bones.

Entering the Stupa, Entering the Patriarchs’ Hall, Whole-Body Interment in the Stupa, Scattering Earth, Relocating the Coffin, Hanging the Portrait, and Reciting the Final Verses (After the coffin has been entered, either after three days, one day, or immediately, the coffin is moved and placed in the Dharma Hall). After being in the coffin for three days, the coffin is closed;
the Dharma Hall is prepared by placing the coffin in the western section and screening it from the front with a curtain of hempen cloth.
Incense, candles, and white flowers are arranged, with a silk curtain set up around the center. A spirit tablet is hung upon the Dharma seat, and the sacrificial offerings are laid out in rows.
Eight clusters of *sāla* flowers are fashioned from white paper and placed upon the seat to represent the appearance of the twin *sāla* groves.

In the eastern section, curtains and canopies are hung, and a bed, seat, and clothing rack are set up to place the deceased’s personal belongings thereon, following the ritual of serving them as if they were still alive.

At the two daily intervals before the spirit altar, offer tea, soup, rice, and gruel while chanting sutras (details are found in Master Ying’s *Wushan Ji*). Furthermore, prepare lamps, hand-bells (*nāṇḍi*), and flower banners;

strike the bell in front of the Sangha Hall to assemble the congregation, who shall chant sutras and perform the dedication of merit before the shrine (the same as above, but with the words "at the time of moving the shrine").

Once the rites for moving the shrine to the Dharma Hall, requesting the locking of the shrine, and hanging the portrait have been completed, if there is a handwritten [inscription], [proceed accordingly].
The attendant presents the final verse to the presiding mourner and the assembly of the head seat and others;
the presiding mourner receives it personally and hands it to the head seat, who incenses it over the incense burner and passes it to the *vinaya-dhara* (chant master) to read aloud.

The ritual assistant of the funeral office then affixes it to the upper-left corner of the curtain at the center of the Dharma Hall. The junior disciples prostrate before the portraits of the deceased and return beneath the curtain to the presiding mourner.

The senior monks of the two orders and the assembly offer incense and tea as a rite of veneration before the portrait; the junior disciples follow in order to offer incense and pay respects before the portrait, after which the portrait is returned with a bow.
Once this is concluded, the sutras are recited and the merit is dedicated (as detailed in the ritual manual).

During the night, the junior disciples guard the shrine curtains, while the funeral office arranges the sequence of offerings (as seen below). A screen is posted above the lower section of the Dharma Hall; all offering texts are recorded by the secretary of the funeral office.
Regarding this, if lay patrons (*dānapati*) from various mountains arrive, whether earlier or later, they may offer incense at any time without being restricted by fixed schedules.

However, when the funeral offerings of Dharma relatives or disciples arrive at the gate, the guest master (*kṣetrajña*) shall receive them and immediately notify the director of mourning (*śokādhyakṣa*). The director of mourning shall then escort them to the mourning quarters and provide them with the appropriate mourning attire before the offerings are presented.
All funeral gifts (*pradāna*) shall be recorded in a ledger by the director of mourning for their receipt.
For the Great Night Offering, the funeral director prepares a large quantity of sacrificial food in advance. According to the aforementioned ritual, the participants return money for the offerings;

first, the two classes of officials offer incense and perform three prostrations. Once the Venerable Vinaya Master has finished reading the liturgy, he recites the Mahākaruṇā Dhāraṇī once and performs the dedication of merit.

(The foregoing merit of recitation is respectfully dedicated for the late Venerable Master Xian, who has recently passed away, to increase his rank and station throughout the ten directions, etc. Next, after each person has completed their offerings, the Great Compassion Mantra is chanted (the dedication is the same as before).
If the junior disciples and others perform the ritual of offering, they shall perform nine prostrations; thereafter, the practitioners shall perform prostrations and chant the sutra.

Those present for the memorial service include: the attendants (*jishi*), the chief administrators (*zhishi*), the head officers (*toushou*), the presiding mourner (*zhusang*), the West Hall master (*xitang*), the elders (*qijiu*), the assembly of fellow practitioners (*jianghu dazhong*), the administrative staff (*banshi*), former personal attendants (*jiushi*),

fellow countrymen, Dharma relatives (*fajian*), the successors at various monasteries and pagoda sites (*zhan yuan*), Dharma heirs (*sifa menren*), junior disciples (*xiaoshi*), and grand-disciples (*shisun*).
The abbot’s attendants, the six groups of hall attendants, the hall administrators, the abbot’s personal servants, the palanquin bearers,
the *lao-lang*, the village headmen, the fire-watchers, and the various masters of labor shall maintain constant mindfulness.

The *vina* (chant master), together with the junior disciples, shall go to the guest quarters the day before [the funeral] carrying incense to respectfully invite the presiding mourner—or, if possible, a great abbot of a mountain monastery—to preside over the vigil.
Having arranged for seats to be set out before the spirit tablet in advance, they shall perform the evening sacrifice.

Once it is concluded, they shall recite the *Mahākaruṇā-dhāraṇī* three times, perform the ritual sprinkling (*sa-jing*), and open the service by making offerings to the Buddha (as detailed in the liturgy). Upon completion, the drum shall be struck, and the presiding master shall ascend the seat to offer incense and deliver the invocation.
[The Master] sits in the lotus position. The two ranks of attendants inquire after his well-being (as per the usual protocol). The junior disciples insert incense and perform three prostrations.

First, the master presents the outline of the discourse, expresses thanks, and concludes the session. The assembly sits to recite the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* (either one or two fascicles), chanting "The True Golden Color of Amitābha Buddha" (*etc.*) and reciting the Buddha’s name one thousand times down to one hundred times, at which point they descend from their seats and lead the assembly in walking meditation.

The Dharma Masters of the various Bodhisattva paths each chant ten invocations; the presiding master returns to his seat for the dedication of merit (*pariṇāmanā*). [Recite] "We humbly pray... (and so forth).

Relying upon the assembly, perform the repentance and the making of vows (and so forth). During the second and third periods, the teachings on the visualization gates (*darśana-mukha*) of the Pure Land are presented;

each time, the sutras are recited and the Buddha is invoked for the dedication of merit, all of which is identical to the preceding. At the conclusion of the third period, present the memorial document (*śāstra*) and proceed before the shrine (*kaṅkā*), where you personally...

The self-dedication (the Dharma Master, accompanied by an attendant carrying incense, performs the offering of food, or has them offer prayers and perform the dedication). Upon the completion of the food offering, the junior monk bows in thanks;

alternatively, invitations may be extended to the various monasteries at each of the three periods of the day, or one may simply conduct this during a single period according to the abundance of robes and bowls (performing tea, soup, and refreshments at each of the three periods).

Upon the departure of the funeral procession, the following items are suspended and offered: the portrait (zhen), tea and soup offerings, and those related to the storehouse and the funeral office (sangsi).

The funeral rites are supervised by the relevant officials, including the incense stand, the portrait stand, banners and streamers, chanting music, umbrellas and chairs before the shrine, the soup stove, the lamp-bearer, the *ruyi* scepter, the fly-whisk, and the ritual implements for burning incense and the dharma robes; the junior disciples follow the shrine.
Afterward, the great bell and various ritual implements are sounded to escort the chief seat and the assembly to the front of the shrine. There, they chant the Heart Sutra;

the rector burns incense and leads the junior disciples to perform the rite of requesting the exhumation of the shrine. Once the shrine reaches the mountain gate, the rite of inviting the spirit pavilion and hanging the portrait is performed, followed by the offering of tea and soup, each accompanied by its own ritual service.
The two orders of the assembly stand in rows at the gate awaiting the departure of the shrine. When it has emerged, the rector...
Upon entering the hall for the morning inquiry, the presiding mourner leads the assembly in chanting the name of Amitābha Buddha.
Pairs of attendants emerge from the left and right to distribute willow branches and snow-white paper streamers, walking in step side-by-side; they must not crowd shoulder-to-shoulder or converse.

The head administrator (Du-si) oversees the funeral procession, while the rector (Wei-na) and guest master (Zhi-ke) follow the prescribed rites. As for the funeral offerings (sang-chin), the junior disciple acting as the chief mourner carries the incense burner and leads the coffin.

When the cremation bier reaches the Nirvāṇa Platform, the Abbot of the Monastery offers incense and tea. Once this is completed, the Rector steps forward to burn incense and leads the junior disciples in bowing and requesting the performance of the *Bǐngjǔ* (Holding the Ruler) ritual service.
The Rector then recites the liturgy. (On this day, for the newly deceased Head Monk, since the fuel of his karmic mechanism has already been exhausted, he now responds to the fire.)

Since the True Body has vanished like clouds, it is eternally quiescent, neither departing nor arriving. When cremated by the fire of its own nature (*dharmatā-agni*), it manifests both birth and extinction. We now rely upon the Great Assembly to assist the enlightened spirit.

*Namo Amitābha Buddha of the Western World of Ultimate Bliss, the Greatly Compassionate and Greatly Merciful One.* (Recite the sacred name above to reverently praise the manner of his manifestation; he appeared in this world to act as the eyes for devas and humans, leading the net of the teachings and expanding the pivotal path of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. Now that his transformative activity has ceased and he has returned to the Truth, we hope he will turn his light back to reflect within.

As the three libations of tea are poured and the single incense burner is lit, we escort him on his journey through the clouds. *Homage to the Holy Assembly!* (The Head Seat recites the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*; the Rector performs the Dedication of Merit.)

(As before, with the only difference being the sequence of the cremation: Next, the local people lift up the scripture and the entire assembly must chant it together. When this is finished, the Head Seat leads the assembly back to the monastery for the meal.
Meanwhile, the junior monks, local people, and Dharma relatives guard the remains and collect the bones. After the meal, the Sangha Hall bell is struck to assemble the community;

they then prepare ceremonial processions to welcome the bones back to the dormitory hall, where they are enshrined, a portrait is hung, offerings are presented, and the scripture is chanted during the two periods of the day.
Serve congee and rice three times a day, and serve tea and soup daily;

the assembly shall chant sutras until the sacred remains are enshrined in the stupa (on the day of the enshrinement, the assembly shall chant according to custom for either three or five days; on other days, the junior disciples and dharma relatives shall chant).

The entire body is placed within the stupa niche at the site of the stupa. Once the Abbot has finished offering incense and tea, the Rector burns incense and leads the junior disciples to pay homage and request the ritual for entering the stupa.
The sequence for reciting the sutras is identical to that of the *Nirvāṇa* platform; however, the dedication of merit (*pariṇāmanā*) is stated as follows:

(The Stage of Entering the Coffin) The attendant covers the opening with a cloth, and then requests the ritual of scattering soil. The officiant of the funeral service welcomes the True Presence back to the Hall for offerings.

The presiding mourner burns incense and pays respects to the True Presence. Next, the assembly of monks from various mountains, the two orders of officials, and the junior disciples pay their respects to the True Presence.

After the junior disciples have inserted incense and performed three prostrations with fully spread sitting cloths (*dazhan*) to express their gratitude to the presiding mourner, the two orders of officials address the presiding mourner with the following words of thanks: [The Assembly of the Mountain Gate]...

When the late Abbot Xinxian passed away, [I] was deeply indebted for your leadership in managing the subsequent affairs. The presiding mourner replied: "I am humbly grateful for your support, which has prevented any neglect or failure. The presiding mourner, together with the entire mourning staff, tours the quarters to express their gratitude.

Subsequently, the junior disciples tour the quarters to pay their respects. Each day, tea and soup are offered before the True Body (the portrait of the deceased), and the assembly gathers to chant sutras.
This continues until the arrival of the spirit tablet to be enshrined in the Patriarchs’ Hall, at which point it ceases; or alternatively, one may wait for the new [abbot].

When the abbot arrives at the Hall of Patriarchs (Jōdō) for a ritual service, or when the sacred remains are to be enshrined in the stupa, preparations for the ceremonial procession must be made the night before.
On the actual day, the bell is struck to assemble the congregation; once the Head Monk has finished offering incense, he requests [the abbot to enter].
The ritual for raising the skeletal remains and transporting them to the stupa, the ritual for requesting entry into the stupa, the chanting of sutras and dedication of merit,

and the instructions for enshrining the entire body within the stupa are all identical. The welcoming of the true remains back to the hall for offerings and the rites of thanksgiving for the presiding mourners and others are likewise the same.
When the time for the distribution of robes arrives, seating for the assembly is arranged in the Sangha Hall or the upper and lower sections of the Dharma Hall.

A long table is placed across the center facing inward, upon which are set brushes, inkstones, and a large *qing* (gong). The Sangha bell is struck to assemble the community, and the Head Seat (*shouzuo*) and the Master [of the ceremony] take their places.

The mourners separate, and the assembly of the two orders take their seats in succession. The *vinaya-dhara* (Vina), the guest prefect (*karmadana*), and the attendants sit facing inward toward the presiding mourner’s seat. The *vinaya-dhara* recites:

"To leave behind clothing as a token of faith is the regulation established by our successive patriarchs to overcome stinginess through the Dharma; it follows the exemplary model left by the former masters. Now, this auction is held to manifest impermanence.

With these reflections, [we pay homage to] the Pure Dharmakaya Vairocana Buddha... When the assembly has finished reciting, the cage is opened and the robes and bowls are brought out according to their assigned numbers.

The *weina* strikes the chime once at the head of the assembly and says: "The method for chanting the names of those who have received robes follows established custom; you should take care regarding the new and old, the long and the short.

Once the sound of the chime has ceased, no regrets shall be permitted. This is respectfully announced. If there are many Dharma robes, they may be distributed by drawing lots (*jiu*) based on one's connections, or by adding extra portions and leaving instructions for the order of presentation.
The *weina* draws the lots and chants the names. The Director of Funerals (*sangsi*) and the others must act with a public spirit; the presiding *weina* determines the final order.

The price is struck by the sounding of the *qing* gong; the ritual assistant (*xingzhe*) gazes at those before and behind him, while the *he-ding* (the one who calls out names) announces the names, the *zhike* (guest reception officer) writes them down on the register, and the *shizhe* (attendant) issues the corresponding tickets.
Once the distribution of robes (*chang-yi*) is complete, the total amount of cash is fixed, and the presiding mourner (*zhusang*) signs the register, hands over the cash, and receives the robes.

He must not yield to private interests by reducing the price. The presiding mourner takes primary responsibility for these matters; nowadays, it is common to use lot-drawing (*jiu-nian*), which greatly reduces clamor and disorder.
Regarding the management of funeral affairs, the administrators should assemble the elders of both orders well in advance to inventory the robes and bowls.

With the exception of those items designated for bequests, they shall appraise the value of the new and old items, as well as their length and quality. This is intended to avoid the confusion that often arises during the formal chanting of the distribution of robes at the last moment.
The method is as follows: small slips of paper are inscribed with characters from the *Qianziwen* (Thousand Character Classic) in sequential order; each slip bears two characters at its ends.
Within the written document, apply the seal and official mark; according to the number of people, coordinate with the director of mourning to fix a count of one thousand and seal it.

When the appointed time arrives, present it for inspection. The two heads of the order (the *shouzuo*) shall open the seal, and the guest prefect (*zhiké*) shall distribute the portions. The attendant (*shizhe*) shall cut off half of each portion.
Once the hall administrators (*tangsi*) and their attendants have finished placing them on trays, they shall set the trays beside the head of the order and arrange water basins.

Once the Venerable Vinaya Master has finished drawing lots for the robes and announcing their prices, the Head Seat (Śrāmaṇera) shall at that time call for a junior attendant to shake the contents evenly from the tray.
Taking a half-lot with his hand, he hands it to the Head Seat, who opens it to clearly read the inscription and announces the number to the hall steward’s attendant.
The attendant then calls out the number, and those among the assembly whose own half-lot bears the same number shall respond.

If one does not wish to have this number called out for the distribution of robes and goods, one should not respond to the three calls. The head seat (shouzuo) should not throw half of the tally-sticks (*biǎo*) into the water basin;

rather, he should have them picked up again by half and call out the numbers once more. Those who respond shall have the hall attendant (*tangsi xingzhe*) go to collect the half-tallies and bring them to the head seat.
There, he shall report them to the *karmadāna* (*weina*), saying: "The item [numbered] so-and-so has been called out and assigned to [so-and-so]."

The person strikes the chime once; the Guest Master ascends the platform, the Attendant raises the marker, and the Hall Monitor’s attendant hands it to the one who has received the clothing and requisites.
These items are then returned to the shrine as before. When the chanting is completed in sequence, the Rector strikes the chime once and performs the dedication, saying:

"By the merit of the above chanting for the distribution of robes, we dedicate it to the late Abbot, may his rank be further exalted... [ten directions, etc. After the assembly disperses, each person shall take their portion according to its appraised value.

If one has designated a robe for taking but does not take it after three days, it shall be sold for its value. The ancient method for announcing the distribution of robes and the ledgers for recording income and expenditure are shown below;
the deceased monk’s belongings are listed in their entirety. [End of] the posthumous letter.

When the funeral rites are completed, the presiding mourner requests attendants to serve as special envoys; these are dispatched along various routes to deliver the deceased’s letters to monasteries, Dharma relatives, patrons, and officials.
When visiting a senior master (zunsu), one must select capable individuals to serve as special envoys.

Upon arriving at the monastery, they first go to the Guest Office (Kesi) for an audience. The Guest Master (Zhike) then escorts them to meet with the Attendants’ Office (Shisi), where preparations have been made in advance.
The attendant, carrying the books and objects in a tray and cloth, goes to the Abbot’s quarters to announce the arrival.

The Abbot should immediately receive him and instruct that the two classes of officers be invited to receive the testamentary letter. The special messenger steps forward, bows in greeting, and says, "Please, Venerable Master, sit cross-legged.

If the Abbot offers a formal inquiry, the messenger must provide an answer, insert incense, and perform full prostrations with opened sitting cloths (*kṣepa*). If the Abbot waives this, the messenger performs a touching bow as usual. They then enter their seats and burn incense.
Having finished offering incense and tea, he rises before the incense burner to express thanks for the tea and inserts another large stick of incense.

He performs the prostrations and announces: "The Abbot of [Place] passed away on the [day] of the [month]. His final letter and personal effects have been entrusted to me to deliver. He then presents the letter and the items. The Abbot says: "The Dharma-gate is in decline; I cannot bear the grief.

After the two classes of officials have completed their formal greetings, they advance to inquire after his well-being. The Chief Seat (Śrāmaṇera) takes his seat apart from the others. The special messenger stands facing the Abbot and withdraws.

After the guest has finished his tea and risen, the Abbot says: "It is a misfortune for the Dharma that the Venerable Master of [Place] has passed away; I am overcome with grief. The attendant prepares scissors and the items for copying the letter;
the server passes the letter to the Abbot, who receives it and warms it over the incense burner before handing it to the server to deliver to the Rector (Karmadāna).
The attendant hands the scissors to the messenger, who opens the seal and reads the letter. Once finished, the server bows to the special messenger, who then ascends to the Abbot's quarters.
The attendant seated opposite burns incense and offers hot water, escorting the special messenger back to his quarters. First, the former abbot inquires after his well-being;

next, the two orders of officials and the attendants inquire after him. The guest prefect leads a tour of the quarters, beginning with the administrative office (*kusi*), followed by the quarters of the senior officers (*dushou*) and the various quarters of the venerable elders (*qijiu*).
The attendants announce and request a special tea service (*tang*). When the tea service concludes, the medicinal meal (*yaoshi*) is served until evening.

When the letter of the Great Dharma Master Tangguo arrives, the two *gwanbang* (attendants) of the next rank and the head *wina* (steward) of the two ranks shall request the *shuji* (secretary) to compose the memorial service text.

The abbot’s memorial text may be composed by the *zhuchi* (abbot) himself; all those with dharma connections from the various regions and those who have served in administrative duties must offer sacrifices.
The *shizhe* (attendant) shall oversee each detail. Early the following morning, the abbot shall invite [the assembly] for soup and summon them.
After the congee has been finished, the procedure for requesting tea is as follows: A spirit table is set up in the lower section of the Dharma Hall, and offerings are arranged upon it.

The attendant covers [the table], and the hall-attendant reports to the various quarters. The "Ascending the Hall" plaque is hung; below the seat, a small table and cloth are prepared to hold the written items.

To the left of the front of the seat, the position of the Abbot is arranged. The drum is struck to assemble the assembly. The Abbot emerges and stands before his position at the foot of the Dharma seat. When the drum stops, he proceeds to the incense table, where the ritual master takes charge.

The guest leads the special envoy and the abbot forward to perform prostrations and insert incense. For the first unfolding [of the scroll], he says: "I have ventured to hold this bequeathed calligraphy and reverently read it;

your compassionate grace fills me with the utmost trepidation. For the second unfolding, he says: "At this time of year, we respectfully wish that the Abbot, the Head of the Hall, may enjoy much blessing in his daily life. He then performs three prostrations with touching of the head to the ground and presents the bequeathed letter.

The abbot receives the letter, fumigates it over the incense burner, and hands it to the envoy to pass to the *vinaya-dhara* (Rector), who reads it aloud. The special envoy then performs a formal inquiry.

Upon returning to the Guest Reception Hall, the Abbot stands waiting. [The Abbot] ascends the seat [and speaks as follows]. After descending from the seat, he proceeds before the altar of the deceased, lights incense, offers hot water, presents the sacrificial offerings, and serves tea while performing prostrations.
The Special Envoy returns to his seat and bows. The Rector (Vina) steps out of the assembly and bows to the Abbot;

the Attendant (Shizhe) carries the incense casket, and the two orders of monks step forward to burn incense. Once the burning of incense by the two orders is complete, the Abbot and the two orders perform the formal unfolding of their sitting cloths (*zhanyan*).
The Venerable Vinaya Master bows and proclaims the memorial text. The Abbot bows again; the Special Envoy returns the bow.

The Great Compassion Mantra is recited and the merit is dedicated: "The merit from the above recitation of the sutra is respectfully offered for the sake of the Dharma Master of [Name] Place, to augment his spiritual rank... (and so forth regarding the ten directions). The two classes of officials, the elders, those attending affairs on the rivers and lakes, and fellow countrymen all present offerings;

the Special Envoy returns their bows (hereafter, in the case of ritual kin, junior disciples, or those attending affairs, no return bow is made). The mantra is recited and the merit is dedicated (as before). The offering concludes.

Recite the *Amitābha Sūtra*, chant the sacred name, and dedicate the merit (with the verse beginning "All phenomena born of causes and conditions... etc., followed by: "I humbly hope that Your True Compassion will look down and clearly witness this;

the merit from the above recitation of the True Vehicle and the chanting of the sacred name is respectfully offered for the sake of the Abbot of [Place Name] to further enhance his rank... and so forth). Upon completion, dispatch a special envoy to the altar of the spirit to perform two prostrations with the body fully extended and three prostrations with the head touching the ground to express gratitude.

If the Abbot declines these, a simple prostration (*chuli*) shall suffice. Next, the envoy shall visit the various quarters (*liaos*) to offer thanks, after which the Monastery Gate (*shansan*) shall provide hospitality for the special envoy.

Please request the two orders of officials to accompany you; if you were previously the abbot of this mountain, enter the Patriarchs’ Hall together with them. Once the recitation of the sutra is finished, proceed to welcome the name tablet to the Patriarchs’ Hall.
The abbot offers incense and installs the tablet according to the ritual instructions. Upon its installation, the special messenger bows in thanks to the abbot.
If there are no letters or personal effects left behind, the disciple shall personally perform the entry into the Patriarchs’ Hall for the current abbot.
Upon first arriving at the temple, one is met by the attendant, who leads the visitor to see the Abbot. One offers incense, performs prostrations, takes a seat, burns incense, and drinks tea.

Rising, one submits one’s purpose; once this is concluded, one is escorted to the assigned quarters. Next, one visits the Head Officers, the Treasury Office (*kusō*), the Senior Monks (*kōgu*), and other locations for introductions.

On the appointed day, offerings are prepared and alms (*shōchin*) are distributed. At the Dharma Hall, a memorial service is held and sutras are chanted. Finally, the name tablet is entered into the Patriarchs’ Hall (*sodō*), where the Abbot presides.

There is a formal liturgy for this ceremony, identical to the preceding one. If a letter from the deceased Dharma Master arrives at the Abbot’s quarters, the two orders of monks shall open the letter first.
They will offer condolences to the Abbot, after which a seat for the memorial offering is established in the center of the Dharma Hall.

Incense is offered before the seat, accompanied by a formal liturgical address; one must not wail excessively, but may shed small tears. Three prostrations are made while offering hot soup, followed by three prostrations while offering food and monetary offerings (*dakṣiṇā*), and again three prostrations while offering tea. Furthermore—
After three prostrations and the completion of reading the memorial text, chant the Mahākaruṇā-dhāraṇī and perform the dedication of merit (*pariṇāmanā*). (As detailed in the ritual manual.

Both the two orders of officials, the elders, fellow practitioners from various regions, local laypeople, Dharma relatives, and junior disciples who have assisted in the funeral arrangements all receive the memorial offerings. The Abbot sits to the left of the spirit table.

(If there are abbots of other mountains or senior *Xi-táng* disciples who are of the same generation as the deceased master, they respond with a bow when the memorial is offered; those of lower rank do not respond. Once the memorial service is concluded, recite the *Mí* [Mantra].

Dedication of Merit (as before). The Head Seat leads the assembly in consoling the Abbot, saying: "It is a misfortune for the Dharma-gate that our Reverend Master has entered Nirvana; we disciples have lost our reliance and cannot overcome our profound grief.
We only hope that you may endure this with patience and continue to exert yourself in this Way."

The monastery shall provide for the funeral master, the mourning officials, and the attendants with offerings and alms, ensuring that all matters, from the highest to the lowest, are conducted according to ritual. They shall sit in the abbot’s quarters; furthermore, the two classes of senior monks are invited to serve as honored companions.
The Head Seat (Śrāmaṇera) shall take the position of presiding master, while the Chief Administrator (Karmadāna) performs the rites, identical to those performed during a special tea ceremony.
The bell is struck to assemble the community to escort the chief mourner;
the deceased monk’s robes and bowl are then inventoried.

Whenever a monk’s illness becomes terminal, those who have shared the same hall with him shall lead his fellow villagers to reminisce about their past and recite the name of Amitābha Buddha, seeking the Buddha’s compassionate light to welcome and guide him so that right mindfulness may manifest before him.

He shall first instruct the attendant of the Hall Office to petition the Abbot and the two orders of officials to come together before the patient and transcribe the oral statement (the format for which is shown below). The attendant shall then join the *weina*...
The attendants of the Hall Office shall pack the deceased’s clothing, luggage, and inventory items, sealing each one individually.

They shall leave aside those items required for dressing the deceased—namely, the outer and inner robes (*zhidu*), incense cases, prayer beads, shoes and socks, hair-cleansing cloths, and cotton for wrapping the bones—as well as other necessary articles.

These sealed belongings, along with the accompanying provisions, shall be handed over to the fellow practitioners for safekeeping. If the senior monk residing in a private quarters has many belongings, the same procedure shall apply.
The administrative office shall dispatch personnel to guard the room, securing the bedding, accounts, keys, and seals, and depositing them with the Head Seat (Śayanāsana).

If the deceased is unable to entrust these matters himself, the Abbot, Head Seat, and Rector must take charge of the proceedings. Even for those who have no personal belongings, they must be escorted with full courtesy.
If the deceased monk did not previously inform the Abbot, the two orders of officials, or the senior elders during his lifetime, [the following protocol applies].
Furthermore, as there is no formal document from one’s kin, one must not arbitrarily leave instructions regarding clothing or belongings.

Oral statement: [Name of the sick monk], residing at [Temple Name] in [Year], having been granted a *du-ge* (ordination certificate) by [Year] at [Place Name] in [Province Name] under the surname [Surname] and age [Age], has now fallen ill.

Fearing that a sudden stroke or fever may occur— (Note: The text provided appears to be a fragment of a formal monastic document, likely a *yuanwen* (petition) or *zhaohu* (summons), concerning a dying monk’s affairs.)

Whatever personal belongings I may possess are hereby entrusted to the public authorities for inventory. After my death, I hope they will provide for my transport according to the pure regulations of the monastic community.
(Date: Year Month Day; Oral Statement of the Ailing Monk [Name])

When bathing the deceased and entering them into the shrine, chant as one would for a sick monk. When the deceased closes their eyes, the meal attendants shall immediately notify the *vīnā* (rector), who shall then instruct the hall administrators and the ritual assistants to announce the preparation of hot water.
The head seat, the *vīnā*, the guest prefect, and the attendants shall then direct the personnel of the four quarters and the servants.

The belongings of the deceased monk for whom the funeral shroud has been prepared are carried back to the Hall. The Office of the Storehouse is notified, and personnel are dispatched to carry the deceased, the coffin, and the bathing boat to the Nirvāṇa Hall.
After the deceased is bathed, their hair is shaved and they are wiped dry; the bath robes and bedding are distributed according to the circumstances.

Hand towels are given to those who assisted with the bathing and the hair-shaving. The *Venerable* (Weina) takes up the censer, assists in dressing the deceased, and places them into the coffin before it.

Set out the chairs, tables, and name tablets; on the tablets, write "The newly deceased [Name]" (using the appropriate title according to rank), and prepare incense and lamps to make offerings to the assembled monks.

Recite the *Śūnyatā-parivarta* (Chapter on Emptiness) and invoke the sacred names, dedicating the merit as follows (*etc.*, simply changing the sequence for the entry into the coffin). At night, light the perpetual lamp;
the hall attendants and ritual assistants shall pre-prepare the *xueliu* (willow branches), banners, and flowers, arranging them in an orderly fashion. If it is for a West Hall Master...
A separate memorial service table is arranged for the Great Elder; his portrait is hung between the upper and lower sections, and for seven days, sutras are chanted to perform meritorious deeds.
Every evening, the *jingzi* (sutra-recitation funds) are distributed according to rank: those of the next level [receive them] for five days, and those of the following level for three days.

Daily, the *zhiling xingzhe* (attendant of the spirit altar) serves rice gruel and meals, while the *zhishi* (administrative officer) burns incense at the three periods of the day and serves tea and soup. The attendants of the Hall Office wait for the meal.
When the rice gruel is served, the bell is struck; the Head Seat leads the assembly to the front of the shrine.

Once the Abbot has finished burning incense, he recites the *Gaganagañja-parivarta* and invokes the sacred names for the dedication of merit (as in the previous procedure, it is said: "at the time of the shrine being halted").

At evening, the bell before the Sangha Hall is struck to assemble the assembly for the chanting of the *Amitābha Sūtra*, the invocation of sacred names, and the recitation of verses for dedication (and so forth). The three daily periods of worship are conducted in the same manner as at home.

When distributing alms and chanting scriptures for the human dharma-parish, the village head shall burn incense; however, on days such as the first and fifteenth of the month or the anniversary of the Emperor’s birthday, the chanting of scriptures shall be waived, and it is not permitted to process the funeral bier.
We request that these Buddhist rites be observed.
For the ceremony of holding the torch, one must request the Abbot to perform the ritual service (*buddha-śāsana-karma*).

For all other services—such as locking the coffin, raising the coffin, exhuming the bones, and entering the stupa—the rituals are concluded by reporting to the Head Seat (*shouzuo*) for consultation; then, according to seniority, the head officers (*tou-shou*) are requested in rotation to perform them (the Hall Office maintains a record book of these services for reference and to ensure the rotation is pure).
If the deceased was a West Hall monk, a private room resident, or a senior elder whose robes and bowls were somewhat abundant, then additional offerings shall be added.

For the tea service and other ritual affairs, the *xiantang* (western hall attendant), the *shouzuo* (head seat), and the *weina* (ritual director)—who are renowned masters from this mountain or elsewhere—shall be invited to the abbot’s quarters (*fangzhang*) to offer incense and inquire after his well-being. They shall announce: "On such-and-such a day, [Name] passed away; we request that Master [Qing] preside over the cremation and carry the torch.

Having inquired after his well-being, they shall withdraw, taking a servant with them to carry incense and invite the head officers (*toushou*) to perform the same rites. If the deceased has a *yixiao* (dharma-brother disciple), he shall also be included.
Go to the Abbot’s quarters and other locations to pay respects and extend the invitation.

The *guyi* (clothing-assessment) *vina* shall instruct the hall-office acolytes to invite the abbot, the two orders of officials, and the attendants (*shizhe*) to the hall office for the clothing assessment.
Present the contents of the robe-casket to the assembly; open the seal and take out the garments, arranging them on the floor within the mats. Pick up each item one by one and present it;

the *vinaya-dhara* (chant leader) shall estimate its value, while the *śrāmaṇera* (head monk), the *karmadāna* (administrative head), the *karmika* (guest master), and the *upasthāyaka* (attendant) shall determine a median price.

Record the items on the roster according to their sequence, noting the prices beneath each entry. Write small labels according to these numbers and affix them to the garments. Return them to the casket, keeping the order intact.
One should write out detailed labels according to the specific value of each item to prepare for use during the chanting of the distribution of robes.

No one, including the Abbot, the two orders of officials, or those in the various quarters, is permitted to take communal property as private shares. If the deceased’s robes and bowls are particularly abundant, they should be appraised at a low estimate to benefit the community, thereby dedicating the merit for the deceased's peace in the afterlife.

That night, if one does not perform the ritual services for the deceased, then after the assembly has finished chanting the sutras and dispersed, one should arrange chairs and stools before the shrine. Thereupon,
the attendants of the Hall Office (táng-sì xíng-zhě) shall invite the two classes of clergy, as well as senior elders, local laypeople, or dharma relatives.
Whether inviting two classes of monks for one night or up to three nights, the ceremony should be conducted according to one's means, whether resources are abundant or meager.

Once the assembly has gathered, the Head Seat (Śayanāsanadhipati) recites the Mahākaruṇā-dhāraṇī; the wine is purified, and he offers a formal announcement before the spirit, reciting the general preface to the Triple Gem of the Two Lands.
When the assembly is seated, the Head Seat recites various sūtras, concluding with the Amitābha Sūtra while maintaining mindfulness of the Buddha.
Recite the name of each Bodhisattva ten times; then address the Buddha once more to proclaim the *śukra-pratikramaṇa* (vegetarian confession) and make vows (as detailed).
Distribute hot soup and fruit offerings as alms (*dakṣiṇā*), the quantity of which is not restricted.

On the evening of the day before the funeral procession, after the afternoon session, the hall attendant (tángsī xíngzhě) informs the Abbot, the two orders of officials, and the various quarters, and hangs a notice to announce the event to the assembly in advance.
He instructs the storehouse office (kūsī) to prepare the sacrificial food. At nightfall, the bell in front of the Sangha Hall is struck to assemble the community; first, the Abbot takes his place.
The ritual attendant presents the offerings; next, the two classes of officials offer incense while the *karmadāna* reads the memorial text.

Next, the elders, fellow practitioners, local residents, and Dharma relatives each present their own offerings (either by preparing their own sacrificial food or by contributing money and reporting back). When this is finished, the *Mahākaruṇā-dhāraṇī* is recited once for the dedication of merit, saying:

"The merit from the above recitation of sutras is respectfully offered for the sake of the newly deceased [Name], to adorn the ground of his retribution," and so forth, including the verse on the ten directions. Then, the *Amitābha-sūtra* is recited as part of the *xièniàn* (focused mindfulness) practice.

The name of the Buddha is recited one thousand times; the names of the Bodhisattvas are each recited ten times for the dedication of merit (followed by the chanting of verses, etc.). We respectfully pray that the awakened spirits will look down and clearly perceive this.

Here, at the site where the body of the newly deceased [Name] has been placed in the shrine, we have taken the remaining robes and assets and charged the present assembly to chant scriptures and recite the sacred names. May the resulting merit be dedicated to the awakened spirit to adorn their place of retribution. Furthermore, we ask the assembly to labor on behalf of the awakened spirit to perform repentance (followed by the vows, etc.).

○ If there are no robes or alms bowls, omit those items; regarding the remaining robes and assets, simply state: "The assembly above has chanted the scriptures. If it concerns a person of great virtue and renown from a major monastery:
For the elders residing in the *xitang* (West Hall) or private quarters who have rendered service to the mountain gate (*shānmén*), the procedure shall be carried out as described above.

For those of secondary rank, the former abbot shall first present the food offerings, though no memorial text (*jìwén*) need be composed; alternatively, the current administrative officers may present the food while the abbot merely arrives to burn incense.

If local laypeople or Dharma relatives offer sacrifices, the ritual is completed as before, followed by the recitation of sutras, the dedication of merit (*huíxiàng*), and so forth, all according to the previous protocol. Or...

If the offerings of robes and alms bowls are somewhat abundant, one should request the abbot to preach the Dharma before the spirit tablet while reciting the Buddha’s name with urgency (or the Chief Lecturer of Qingdu, or the Head Seat;
if the deceased passed away during one of the three daily services as previously indicated, the abbot shall join in the recitation).

Regarding the funeral rites for the deceased: the storehouse (kūsi) shall, in advance, order the master craftsmen to prepare firewood for cremation; they shall dispatch servant laborers and arrange for the ritual music of *nāgapataha* and *ghaṇṭā*, as well as banners, flowers, incense, and candles.
All items for the bier and the funeral procession must be fully prepared. The attendants of the hall office (*tōsō*) shall notify [the relevant parties] one night prior.
The Abbot and the two orders hang the memorial tablet for the deceased. After the morning gruel is finished, the hall bell is struck to assemble the assembly at the front of the shrine.

The Heart Sutra is recited, and the Rector comes forward to burn incense and request the ritual for raising the shrine. The person invited to perform the service steps out of the ranks to burn incense, then withdraws to perform a bow of inquiry.
Next, he bows before the Abbot, turns around, and then performs a general bow of inquiry together with the entire assembly.
From the edge of the western corridor, proceed to the right side of the niche and strike it three times (and so forth). When finished, the drums and cymbals are sounded;
the niche is carried out to the head of the mountain gate, where the true likeness (the portrait) is hung and tea and soup are offered. The *weina* then requests the ritual proceedings.
The *shouzuo* leads the assembly, standing in two rows facing the niche as it is about to depart. The *weina* faces inward toward the assembly, bows from the center, and addresses them.
The presiding seat raises the name of the Buddha, and the assembly recites it together two times each. The procession proceeds in order behind the coffin; each person holds a willow branch.
The attendants line up outside the gate, bowing their heads with palms joined, waiting for the monks to pass by. Once the monks have passed, they follow behind to escort the procession.
The attendants march in pairs facing one another, while the *vinaya-dhara* follows the coffin and the monastery head (*du-si*) oversees the funeral.
