When the funeral procession arrives at the Nirvana Platform, the administrative officers (*karmadāna*) burn incense and offer tea. Next, the Abbot offers incense and returns to his place.

The Rector (*vinaya-dhara*) comes forward to burn incense and requests the Abbot to perform the ritual of lighting the torches. The Abbot burns incense and, together with the assembly, performs a mutual greeting.

When the Dharma discourse is concluded, the *vinaya-dhara* (ritual master) faces the shrine and recites: "On this day, [Name], who has recently entered parinirvāṇa, has exhausted the illusory existence of the floating life and penetrated the true emptiness of the fire of nature.

Having relinquished the body composed of the five aggregates, he returns to the treasury of nirvāṇa through the three wisdoms. We rely upon the venerable assembly to assist his awakened spirit. Namo Amitābha Buddha of the Western World of Ultimate Bliss, Greatly Compassionate and Greatly Merciful!

(The assembly recites ten times together. Having finished the above ten recitations of praise to assist his rebirth in the Pure Land, we pray: May his three wisdoms be perfectly luminous and his true reality never obscured. Within the grove of the seven treasures, may he constantly hear the sounds of celestial music; entering the pool of wisdom, may he sit loftily upon a golden lotus seat.

(Tea is poured for three libations, incense is burned in a single burner, and we respectfully bid farewell as you return to the West; prostrations to the assembly of Noble Ones. The Head Seat recites the Śūraṅgama Dhāraṇī, and the Guest Prefect performs the dedication, saying:

"We reverently pray that the Buddha’s compassion will look down and clearly witness this occasion. As we chant secret chapters and extol the holy names during the cremation of the newly deceased [Name], may the merit thereby generated adorn the realm of retribution for the enlightened spirit. To the ten directions... (and so forth).

Local residents, Dharma relatives, old acquaintances, and those chanting sutras to assist the funeral procession are escorted by the Rector (Karmadāna), who supervises their movements back and forth, while the hall attendants see them off.
The companions and those who have transformed the deceased shall offer a meal until the end of the *zhāi* (fasting) period, after which they collect the remains—either on that very day or later.
They may place them in a stūpa or welcome them back to the Nirvāṇa Hall for offerings and the recitation of sūtras for three days.

(Generally, a deceased monk must not don the *kāṣāya* during the cremation; the Vinaya clarifies that the three robes are only permitted to be transmitted [to another]. However, if one passes away while seated and the robe’s seams remain intact, such that it can be used to enshrine the body in a stūpa, it may still be worn over the true body. If [the body] is taken from the cremation...

Regarding the ritual for cremation, one must not wear the deceased’s robes oneself, as this constitutes the transgression of violating the Vinaya by taking clothing intended for burning. Alternatively, it is said that for a deceased monk who has no robes, one should follow the method for "the Monk Miao Donating Robes" recorded in the *Mingxiang ji*.

After the monk Miao of Longhua Temple in Jiangling passed away during the Southern Song dynasty, he returned to his room one night and spoke spiritually to his disciples, saying: "Sengsong lacks a *kāṣāya*; you must quickly have one made for him. Invite monks to offer a meal and donate robes to them; I shall be able to obtain them.

Sengsong followed these instructions, and once the meal had been offered to the monks and the robes donated, the bhikṣu Daomeng immediately saw Miao’s body wearing the robe, entering the hall and sitting in the proper monastic order to listen to the sutras. When the service concluded, he was no longer seen. From now on, when dealing with a deceased monk...

When chanting the *kāṣāya* (the robe), one should employ the method of drawing lots (*jū-nien*) among the Saṃgha to distribute it; it must not be draped over a stupa and cremated. This is explained in detail in the ninth fascicle of the *Fozu Tongji*.

After the chanting for the distribution of robes and the cremation, the attendant of the Rear Hall (hou-tang-si) informs the Abbot and the two orders of officers. Once the midday meal is finished, the robe-distribution is chanted before the Sangha Hall;
a signboard for the robe-distribution is hung to notify the assembly. When the meal hall is cleared, the Abbot and the Head of the Sangha Hall prepare the outer Sangha Hall.

The seating positions for the two orders are arranged as follows: upon entering the hall, benches and desks are placed crosswise facing inward; writing brushes, inkstones, and other necessary implements are set upon the desks;
mats are spread upon the floor, and once all preparations are complete, the Hall Attendant (Tangsi) and the Ritual Assistant (Xingzhe) inform the Abbot.

The attendants of the two orders then ring the bell to assemble the community. The Rector (Weina), the Guest Master (Zhike), and the attendants enter the hall together and take their seats in rows facing inward.
The Hall Attendant, the Ritual Assistant, and the Head of Offerings perform one round of announcing the meal:

they first bow to the Abbot and the two orders of officers, then turn to bow to the Rector, the Guest Master, and the Attendants. Having completed these bows, they carry the clothing chests before the Abbot and the two orders of officers;
they present the seals at the head seat’s station, request the key, and upon presenting it, open the chests to take out the garments according to their assigned numbers.
The *ānanda* stands up at the head of the rows, facing inward, and strikes the wooden sounding-block once, saying:

"Floating clouds disperse and the scenery does not remain; as the remaining candle wick is spent, its light is extinguished. Today’s auction of the robe is performed to manifest impermanence. We rely upon the Great Assembly to offer this for the sake of the deceased, [Name], so that their enlightened spirit may be assisted in rebirth in the Pure Land.

For this purpose, we contemplate the pure Dharma-body, Vairocana Buddha... [and so forth with the ten titles]. When the ten titles are finished, he strikes the chime once and says: "As for the method of auctioning the robe, it follows established regulations. The senior monks, both new and old, shall themselves..."

"You should chant in harmony with the sound of the *qing* bell; once it has ceased, you are not permitted to retract or regret [your actions]. This is respectfully announced. (Ring the *qing* bell once more.

Holding the ordination certificate (*duodie*), tear it across the name of the deceased monk, saying: "The ordination certificate of the deceased monk, bearing his original name—one scroll, torn in the presence of the assembly. (Ring the *qing* bell once. Hand it to an attendant to present to the Abbot and the two orders.
The attendants of the Hall Office shall take the items according to the order of the names and present them one by one, passing them along.)

The *vinaya-dhara* (Venerable Leader) raises [the item] and says, "[Name of the person], [name of the object], estimated at such-and-so much. If it is estimated at five *guan*, he begins by calling out "five hundred" (*wubai*).
A junior attendant of the Hall Office (*tangsi*) joins in the chant, and those in the assembly respond in kind, bidding up the price in succession until they reach five *guan*.

When the *vinaya-dhara* signals, he strikes the chime once and says, "[Struck for] five *guan*. This procedure is the same for all other items. Alternatively, if there are those who respond with the same voice and bid the same price, [they may share the purchase].

The chant master calls out to stop the chanting (breaking both). Once again, the *qing* is struck to signal the commencement of the distribution for the Hall Attendants (*tangsi*). The attendant-in-charge (*xingzhe*) asks the name of the designated person;

the Guest Master (*zhike*) writes the name on the list, and the Assistant (*shizhe*) issues a label according to the name and hands it to the offering-head attendant (*gongtou xingzhe*), who passes it to the one who has received the chant.
The items previously chanted over are placed into a basket. When each item has been chanted through, the *qing* is struck once.

The subsequent dedication states: "The merit from the preceding chanting of the *kāṣāya* and recitations is dedicated for the sake of [the deceased] so-and-so who has entered parinirvāṇa, to adorn the ground of retribution in the ten directions... (and so forth).

Lately, in order to quell clamor and disorder, the method of drawing lots (*jūnen*) is frequently employed (as described above). Any clothing or items not claimed within three days shall be sold at their appraised value.

(*Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*): Question: How should the robes and alms bowls of a deceased bhikṣu be divided? Answer: Since he previously also once divided the wealth and goods of others, when he has now passed away, others likewise divide his possessions.

Furthermore, the *Vinaya* states that because divisions were not equitable, the Buddha permitted the assembly to gather and sell the items to share the proceeds. The *Zenghui ji* states: "The Buddha’s original intent in instituting the division of robes was to cause those who remain to see the deceased’s belongings being distributed among the Saṃgha, so that they might reflect:

'Since he already knows this, I too shall act thus. By means of this antidote, their greedy seeking is to be stilled. Yet nowadays, failing to examine this, people instead clamor and laugh for pleasure during the auctioning, competing over high and low prices. This is a profound error. O Benevolent One!
[Those who are] thus [concerned] should observe these prohibitions).

Once the chanting for the distribution of robes within the stupa is completed, one should immediately prepare the wooden notice-board; on the third day, place the board before the Sangha Hall and instruct the assembly.

Notification: Should there be any irregularities or instances of deception, they shall be reported with due courtesy for the superior and inferior parties to verify and rectify them; if no factual basis exists, one must not cause unnecessary disturbance. Those who violate this shall be expelled or penalized.

As for those serving as abbot or administrators, they must be public-spirited, upright, impartial, and lead by example to win the trust of the assembly. Once the register has been posted, the attendant of the Hall Office shall notify the assembly in advance, hang the "Ash Tablet" (灰牌), and strike the bell to assemble the community.
They shall then perform the ritual for "Raising the Bones" (請起骨) and escort them to the stupa for enshrinement.

The ritual for entering the stupa is completed; the administrative officer seals and returns the response, and the *Śūraṅgama-mantra* is chanted for the dedication of merit (as before, with the sequence changed to "entering the stupa").
The local people chant the sutras for the dedication of merit in the same manner.

The "Board Ledger" (hankōshiki) shall be prepared in the form of a large board ledger for a value of one thousand or two thousand *kan*. If there are fields, lands, gold, or grain, they shall be returned to the permanent residence.

The funds from the chanting of the *yīqián* (clothing money) shall be used to produce the board ledger according to the prescribed format; furthermore, the funds for the distribution to the monastic community and the funds for Buddhist services shall be [accounted for] as follows:

If the proceeds from the *choufen* (distribution) amount to three thousand or five thousand *kuan* or more, it shall be deliberated upon that they be returned to the permanent endowment (*changzhu*) to establish a hall for offerings;

the remainder must not be used arbitrarily. The rules for distribution are as follows: if the amount reaches one hundred *kuan*, ten *kuan* shall be set aside for the *weina* (chanting master), who shall then divide his portion into three parts with the *tangsi* (hall administrator) and the *xingzhe* (attendant). If the amount does not reach one hundred *kuan*, no distribution shall be made. As for the scripture...
If the funds for the community of monks amount to one hundred *bai*, then the funds for Buddhist services (*foshi*) shall be one *guan*; for the Abbot’s quarters, it shall be double that.

Furthermore, for each *guan* of Buddhist service funds, an additional five *bai* shall be added. For the mid-level board accounts, four hundred or five hundred *guan* shall be allocated as a commission to be distributed among the assembly; the Buddhist services shall be reduced accordingly, following the same principle as before.

For a small palanquin costing two hundred *kuan*, one hundred *kuan*, or even ten *kuan*, excluding expenses for the carrying poles, the inner coffin, and miscellaneous items, all contributions for this meritorious act shall be managed by the Abbot and the Head Seat, with the administrative office (Kusi) making the necessary preparations. May the assembly take pity on this;
one must certainly observe the rites and protocols in seeing off the deceased. Who among men does not die?
Third-grade felt tent: Large felt tent, medium felt tent, small felt tent. For the torch-bearer:
twenty taels, ten taels (the same applies below for those establishing karmic connections).
For the offering of tea and the offering of broth: twenty taels, ten taels.
Locking the niche and opening the niche: twenty taels total; ten taels each.
Raising the remains and enshrining them in the stupa: twenty taels total; ten taels each.
The *vinaya-dhara*’s ritual for cremation: ten taels; five taels.
Supplement for the *bǐngjù* (torch-bearing) ritual: 10 taels. Supplement for the seven-person ritual: 35 taels.
The *zhīkè* (guest prefect) and *shìzhě* (attendant) handling the accounts: 20 taels and 10 taels.
The Head Seat (Shouzuo) oversees the funeral: five taels, two taels, [and one tael];
the Abbot’s Assistant (Dusi) oversees the funeral: five taels, three taels, [and one tael];
for the inventory of clothing and refreshments: ten taels, six taels, and two taels in total.
Lamp oil before the shrine: one *liang*, five *qian*, three *liang*;
for the permanent endowment (*changzhu*) memorial offerings: three *liang*, two *liang*, one *liang*;
for bathing water: five *qian*, two *qian*, one *qian*.
Bathing the Deceased: 2 liang, 1 liang, 5 qian; Shaving the Hair: 1 liang, 5 qian, 5 qian;
Moving the Coffin and Carrying the Deceased: 2 liang 5 qian, 1 liang, 5 qian.
Nail-hanging for the sacrificial feast: five *qián*, three *qián*, one *qián*.
Paper, brush, banners, flowers, *xuěliǔ* (willow branches): ten *liǎng*, five *liǎng*, two *liǎng* five *qián*.
Direct offerings of porridge and rice for the spirit: one *liǎng*, five *qián*, three *qián*.
The storehouse official and the guest master report the preparation of offerings: five *qián*, three *qián*, one *qián*.
The inventory officer issues the bowls and plates for the offering: five *qián*, three *qián*, one *qián*.
The storehouse keeper issues the materials for the preparation of the offerings: five *qián*, three *qián*, one *qián*.
Supervisor of the Kitchen (Preparer of Food): 5 mace, 3 mace, 1 mace.
Storehouse Official, Tea Head, and Senior Tea Head: 5 mace, 2 mace, 1 mace.
Venerable Abbot’s Attendant for Calling and Carrying the Incense Case: 5 mace, 2 mace, 1 mace.
The Ku-si (Treasury Office) posts the tea [announcement] and holds the incense box: five *qián*, two *qián*, one *qián*.
The Tie-tang-si (Hall Office) sounds the corridor board: one *liǎng*, five *qián*, three *qián*.
The *cān-tóu* (head of the assembly) dispatches the attendants (*xíng-zhě*): five *qián*, two *qián*, one *qián*.
Laborers assigned for supervision: five *qián*, two *qián*, one *qián*.
Head officials and the tea masters of the two quarters: one *liǎng*, five *qián*, two *qián*.
Bier-bearers: fifteen *liǎng*, seven *liǎng* five *qián*, three *liǎng*.
Gongs and Cymbals: two taels five qian; one tael; five qian. Drummers and Musicians: three taels; one tael five qian; one tael.
Two persons carrying the incense table: one tael; five qian; three qian.
For the six attendants who light the lamps and hold the hall: three taels, two taels, one tael and five mace, and nine mace.
For the distribution of snow-white willow branches and firewood: five mace, three mace, and one mace.
For the abbot’s personal servants escorting the funeral procession: three taels, one tael and five mace, and five mace.
Transformation of the deceased: one *liang*, five *qian*, three *qian*.
Supervising the work and passing the torches: five *liang*, three *qian*, one *qian*.
Carrying the bone casket: one *liang*, five *qian*, two *qian*.
The Assistant of the Hall presents the clothing: five *qian*, three *qian*, one *qian*.
The Ritual Attendant passes around the clothing tickets for chanting: five *qian*, three *qian*, one *qian*.
The Food-Server calls out the names and draws lots: five *qian*, three *qian*, one *qian*.
Master of the Chime (for chanting the distribution of robes): 3 mace; 2 mace;
4 attendants and servants to carry robe-caskets: 1 mace; 5 cash; 2 cash;
person and servant to carry stools and tables: 1 mace; 5 cash; 2 cash.
Farewell offering for the *ren* (water-bearer): fifty *liang*.
Distribution of sutra-funds for the assembly of monks: six hundred *liang*, two hundred *liang*, [and] one hundred *liang*.
For the abbot and the two orders to prepare carriages and refreshments: five *liang*, three *liang*, and one *liang*.
The above details are as previously set forth and shall serve as a permanent regulation; it is not permitted to use flowery rhetoric or clever sophistry to subvert them.

If it is proposed that a hall be established for offerings, it must be subject to public deliberation by the assembly; only when the assembly declares it acceptable may the proceedings be carried out. Although this follows the *vinaya* appropriate to the local region, it should be taken as a general standard.
Whenever a formal regulation is established, it must be inscribed upon wooden tablets to demonstrate that it is not to be altered.
Chapter Nine: The Chapter on Receipts and Disbursements; Chapter Ten:
The Chapter on the Vessel of the Dharma.

In the monastic groves, the ritual vessels and the rites of propriety depend upon this. Whether in purification and reverence, in dress, food, sleeping, rising, advancing or retreating, or in prostration;
whether in chanting, recitation, or exposition—within every aspect of daily decorum, one must invariably take this as the standard and rely upon it for self-restraint.

It is from these that rules and regulations emerge, and within them that the laws of the Dharma reside; they must not be abandoned for even a single day. Furthermore, when they move upward to inspire the worthy...
The Sage’s [teachings] below awaken the ignorant and deluded, bringing an end to suffering that is without limit, and manifesting clear faith for future generations;
even the music of Shaojun cannot compare to it, so how could the vulgar and cacophonous music of Yinwa ever suffice? Furthermore, what more need be said?
The large bell and sounding mirror were established for the sake of humans and devas; they are struck at dawn and dusk to alert those who are deluded and awaken those in darkness.

When drawing the mallet, it should be done slowly, and the sound should be raised to be long-lasting. There are three rounds in total, each consisting of thirty-six strikes, making one hundred and eight strikes in all.

An ancient worthy’s verse says: "The seven [strikes] at the beginning and eight at the end, with twenty intermediate strikes sounding sparsely; adding three final strikes at the conclusion—these together constitute one day. The one who rings the bell recites this verse of contemplation:

"May the sound of this bell transcend the Dharma-realm, Reaching all the way to the dark depths of the Iron Ring Mountains. May those who hear it purify their sensory dust and realize perfect penetration, And may all sentient beings attain true enlightenment.

While reciting this, they should chant the sacred name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva and strike the bell in accordance with each invocation; the benefit is exceedingly great. Those who hear the sound of the bell should likewise recite this verse.

**Epithets** (The *Saṃyukta-avadāna-gāthā* states: "Upon hearing the bell, one who was angry in the present life will, due to the meagerness of their karmic fruit, receive the body of a snake as retribution in the future. Wherever that snake lies and hears the sound of the bell, it must rise and join its palms with a virtuous mind;
thus all sages and saints rejoice.

Whenever encountering auspicious festivals, virtuous months, or the recitation of scriptures—whether the Emperor ascends or descends the throne, or on occasions such as the Tathāgata’s descent from Tuṣita, his attainment of enlightenment, his parinirvāṇa, or the opening of a Dharma assembly—one should observe these rites.

During the time for the *Poṣadha* ceremony, the commencement of the retreat (*kṣetra-bandhana*), and its conclusion (*kṣetra-mokṣaṇa*), when meeting the hall attendants at the fixed hour, there shall be eighteen strikes each.

This applies to the reception of officials and the departure of the Abbot or Venerable Elders, with no limit on the number of strikes; the administrative office (*kūsi*) shall take charge of this. As for the bell of the Sangha Hall (*saṃgha-śālā-ghaṇṭā*), it is struck whenever the assembly is to be convened.

For the two meals of rice gruel and vegetarian food, the drum should be struck seven times. There shall be three strikes to signal the departure from the hall. At the commencement of the retreat, [the same procedure applies].

During the three days following the lifting of the retreat restrictions (*jie zhi*), tea and soup are served seven times each day. When the Abbot (*zhuchi*) begins his lecture, he strikes the gong three times;

when the Head Monks (*tou shou*) begin their lectures, they strike it four times. During periods of study and recitation, the signal bell is struck eighteen times. At the time of the *poṣadha* ceremony, the signal is struck three times upon leaving the hall;
this is the responsibility of the Hall Master (*tang si*).
When the temple bell is struck at dawn for the morning hall session, it is followed by the long board;

if the session is held after the morning gruel or midday meal, or when chanting sutras or performing repentance rites, it is struck in coordination with the Sangha Hall bell. This is the responsibility of the Hall Master.

The *Ekottarika Āgama* states: "When the bell is struck, may the sufferings of all evil realms be brought to a halt; by hearing the sound of the bell, one shall be freed from the heavy sins of birth and death accumulated over five hundred billion kalpas.

The *Dharmaguptaka Vinaya-piṭaka* (or *Dharma-kośa Sūtra*) relates that King Kapphiṇa, due to his habit of killing, was reborn as a thousand-headed fish. A wheel of swords revolved around his body, which grew back immediately after being sliced. An Arhat serving as the *karmadāna* (steward) struck the bell at the appointed time; upon hearing the sound, the wheel of swords halted in mid-air.

The Arhat sent word to have the bell struck continuously for seven days, after which the suffering ceased. Furthermore, the *Records of Jinling* (*Jinling Zhi*) notes that there was a man who died suddenly and entered the underworld. There he saw those bound with wooden stocks and fetters, who told him: "I am the former ruler of Southern Tang."

Because Song Qiqiu’s fabrication regarding the execution of the surrendered man from Hezhou led to this [calamity], go back and report it to the Successor. Whenever bells ring at temples or monasteries, you should extend [this grace] so that I may endure my suffering; whenever I hear a bell, I shall find temporary respite. It would be even better if you could have a bell cast for me.

When the people returned and reported this fully, the Later Ruler subsequently had a great bell cast at Qingliang Temple, inscribed with: "Dedicated to the late Emperor Xiaogao, to deliver him from the perils of the underworld."
At dawn, after the great bell has ceased its long tolling of three rounds, the palace bell takes up the sound; during the midday meal, it is struck for three long rounds.
Following the wooden fish at both the noon and evening meals, it is struck three times with rapid succession, which is called "layered striking."
The long board is used for sounding the warning against fire and for signaling the watches; it is struck according to the sequence of the watches.

When the *vinaya-dhara* (Venerable Leader) conducts the roll call, it is sounded three times long. For opening the period of silence (*kai-jō*), opening the lecture (*kai-kō*), and assembling the assembly, the small board is struck once long.
To announce the bath, the various halls, including the Sangha Hall, each sound it three times.
When the Abbot returns from outside, the small board is struck three times; meanwhile, the two orders and the senior elders are requested to attend for the offering of hot water,
followed by a continuous tolling of one round on the wooden fish.

For the two periods of *zhāi* (fasting) and *zhōu* (congee), two long strikes of the bell are sounded for the general assembly; for the general mobilization (*pǔqǐng*) of the monastics, one long strike is sounded, and for the general mobilization of the practitioners (*xíngzhě*), two long strikes are sounded.

The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: There was a monk who disobeyed his teacher and slandered the Dharma, falling into the body of a fish. Upon its back was a tree that, when tossed by wind and waves, caused it to bleed in bitter pain. Its former teacher, while crossing the sea, saw the fish and rebuked it, saying: "You did not follow my instructions, which led you to fall as a fish."

The Master wished to repay his debt to the fish that had saved him from its former enmity. He asked, "What is your name? The fish replied, "I am called [Name]. The Master ordered it to repent and further prepared offerings for the Water and Land rites to deliver its spirit. Later, he dreamed of the fish, which said, "I have already cast off my fish body;

you may take me to the Sheshi Temple to personally honor the Triple Gem. The Master subsequently saw the fish-tree; he carved the shape of the fish and hung it there, causing great astonishment among the multitude.
The wooden mallet is struck during the two periods of rice gruel and porridge within the Sangha Hall for practices such as opening the alms bowls and reciting the Buddha’s name;

it is also struck when the Dharma Hall opens for a lecture, both occasions being presided over by the duty-holder of the day. During the *poṣadha* ceremony, it is struck by the one who holds the announcement staff.

The wooden mallet (*chui*) is struck within the Sangha Hall when the administrative official (*zhishi*) announces his retirement; it is likewise sounded in the Dharma Hall when the Abbot enters the monastery and is about to preach the Dharma.

The heads of the various monasteries strike it, which is called "striking the mallet for the announcement" (*baizhui*). (One day, when the World-Honored One ascended the seat and the assembly had gathered, Mañjuśrī struck the mallet for the announcement, saying:
"Observe closely the Dharma of the Dharma-King; the Dharma of the Dharma-King is thus. Thereupon, the World-Honored One descended from the seat.)

The stone chime (*qing*) is struck by the attendant of the main hall (*zhiduanzhe*) during the morning and evening incense offerings performed by the abbot and the administrative officers; it is struck by the hall office acolyte (*tangsi xingzhe*) when the assembly performs recitations;
and it is struck by the ritual master (*weina*) during the chanting for the distribution of robes. The small stone chime (*xiaoyin qing*) is handled by the hall office.
This [bell] is always kept by one’s person; it is struck when encountering a multitude for the purpose of chanting, and it serves as the signal for the commencement and conclusion of activities.

It is struck when inviting an *ācārya* during the tonsure ceremony for novice monks, and it is struck by the duty-holder (*ṛtvij*) during the period of the summer retreat (*varṣā*) while practicing recitation.

*Ganying ji* states: "In front of Ānanda’s room there was a *qing* (gong) with a capacity of five *dou*. Its four sides were inlaid with gold, inscribed with the characters 'Disciples of the Buddhas of the Past. On its nose was fashioned the form of nine dragons from *zima* gold, and atop their backs stood images of celestial beings holding mallets.

When struck, its sound vibrated throughout the great trichiliocosm, and within that sound were also expounded the various teachings and admonitions for disciples. This gong was created by the Brahmā Heaven, and after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the Sāgara Dragon King took it back into the ocean. *Zenghui ji* states:

"Before one's life has ended, one should strike the gong continuously so that the dying person may hear its sound, arouse wholesome thoughts, and attain rebirth in a favorable realm. When the Great Master was nearing death, he said to the *weina* (chant master): "At the time of my passing, I wish to hear the sound of the bell."

One should augment one’s right mindfulness with the chime, making it long and enduring so that the sound does not cease until the breath is exhausted; for this reason, it is now called the "striking of the bell of impermanence," which refers to the impermanence chime (mucalinda-ghaṇṭā).

The *nāṭaka* (small hand-bell) and *ghaṇṭā* (large bell): they are struck by the *vina* (chant leader) when bowing to the abbot and the two orders of officers as they emerge from their seats to offer incense; during the *zhuzan* (praise and invocation) in the *zangdian* (scripture hall);

when the ritual practitioner (*xingzhe*) turns the wheel; when the attendant (*shizhe*) leads the assembly in circumambulation for the funeral rites; when shaving the head; and when receiving a new abbot.

It was sounded upon entering the hospital (the *Tongdian* states: "The bronze cymbals (*tóngpó*) are several inches in diameter, with a raised center like a bubble; they are strung together with leather thongs and struck against one another to harmonize the music.
In the kingdoms of the Southern Barbarians, the large ones are several feet in diameter. As for the *náo*, it is so called because its sound is *náo-náo* [ringing])."

Regarding the method for beating the Dharma-drum: whenever the Abbot presides over a lecture or ascends the hall, as well as when the Head Monks (shoushou) conduct a lecture, the drum is struck three times (each "time" consisting of three strikes and nine rolls).

First, lightly tap the drum-sill three times; then, with a heavy hand, strike slowly and gradually. Two people look at one another to ensure that the tension is relaxed and the weight of the strokes is balanced and harmonious. The resulting sound is smooth and resonant, rising and falling in a continuous, deep, and thundering roll.

The sound is like the roar of spring thunder awakening hibernating creatures, or like the surging of the ocean tide. For the first round, the sound is drawn out and struck with long intervals; after a brief pause, it transitions to the second round, where the sounds are connected with slightly longer intervals and do not cease until the transition to the third round.

One waits for the Abbot to ascend the seat, striking once at each step as he approaches. Once he has turned on the seat, strike three times in succession with both mallets. For general sermons (*pūsē*) and *xièniàn* (commemorative recitations), one round is played. The tea drum is struck once with a long roll, presided over by the attendant official (*shìsī*).
For the two meals of rice gruel and vegetarian food, the drum is struck with three rounds each, consisting of a preceding and a succeeding set.

(For the first three *abhiñjās*: nine strikes, followed by ten strikes for each *abhiñjā*, concluding with three strikes; for the final three *abhiñjās*: nine strikes until the second strike, at which point there is a half-strike of the *yingzhong* bell; for the three intermediate *abhiñjās*, there is one *yingzhong* bell at the conclusion of each, concluding with three strikes;
the bell likewise rings three times in response. The *pǔqǐng* drum is struck once for a long duration. The watch-drum (*gēng-gǔ*) is struck three times levelly at dawn and dusk;
the remainder are struck according to the sequence of the watches, and the *kūsī* (monastery administration office) is responsible for this. The bath-drum is struck four times in succession.
He awaits the assembly and strikes [the drum] (for details, see the section on "Ruzhi yu" [Entering the Bath]). The master of the bath takes charge.

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "Śakra possesses three drums; when preaching the Dharma in the Sudharmā Hall, he strikes the third drum. The *Guangming jing* [Sutra of Radiance] says: "Striking the drum to admonish and advance, solemnly leading the assembly forward, is like the Buddha preaching the Dharma—advancing toward profound practice."
The aforementioned ritual implements (dharmayaṣṭi) should each have their standard dimensions so as not to deviate from the proper measure.

When a new abbot enters his residence, the ritual implements of all the mountain monasteries sound together. Regarding the name of these ritual implements, the Sanskrit term is generally called *ghanṭī* (pronounced *jienti*);

according to the *Śabdavidyā-śāstra*, it is translated as "gong" (*qìng*) and also as "bell" (*zhōng*). The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "Whatever makes a sound—whether of earthenware, wood, copper, or iron [is considered a ritual implement]."
All are called *gandi*. If Kāśyapa struck the copper *gandi* during the council, this was a bell.

If Ānanda ascended the lecture hall and struck the *gandi*, this was the "Dharma-Drum of the Tathāgata. Therefore, monastic communities imitate this regulation in its use, so as to proclaim commands and awaken those who are ignorant and deluded.
As for the Great Samādhi, it is eternally responsive; as for the Great Function, it is ever-active.
Constantly quiescent, one penetrates that sound is non-sound; though unheard, it is heard, as the sense organs and their objects are extinguished and purified, spontaneously and eternally so.
This is the inconceivable hearing of sound that transcends all attendants.
The Tenth Gate: The Dharma Vessel.

In the seventh month of autumn during the second year of the Hongwu era, Śramaṇa Shaozong—formerly the Right Supervisor of the Monastic Registry (Senglu Si Youshan Shi) and former abbot of Cigan Jangsi—solicited donations to reissue this work.
Left: Shi Dayou, Former Abbot of Beichan Jiangsi Temple and Chief Administrator of the Buddhist World, exhorted patrons to contribute toward the carving;
Shi Puhua, Abbot of Tianxi Jiangsi Temple and Proponent of the Teachings, exhorted patrons to contribute toward the carving;
and Shi Rulan, Abbot of Shang Tianzhu Jiangsi Temple, provided the necessary support for the project.
Following the *Jiaoyuan Qinggui*, the monk Yirú of the Ming dynasty, while serving as an envoy to our country, brought this book to Zhong’ān on Mount Lúshān.

From that time on, it was passed down, yet it remained largely unknown to the public. While I was once in Wǔchéng, I happened to obtain a copy and read it through, though I had previously thought it to be mere empty rhetoric.
If one were to imitate the regulations of the Zen monasteries by eating a late meal at night, it would violate the precepts of the Buddha-King;

how could such a practice suffice to rectify our followers? Nevertheless, if one adopts what is worth adopting and discards what is worth discarding, the circulation of this book will not fail to provide some small benefit.
Recently, someone wishing to have this work carved into printing blocks came to seek a preface; therefore, I have recorded these humble thoughts for them.
Appended at the end: On a day in the ninth month of the first year of the Jōkyō era, written respectfully by the śramaṇa Kōken of Nankei.
